questions.stem: Freshly quarried building stone is SEASONED before use principally to:
options: Allow the QUARRY SAP (natural moisture) to dry out, after which the stone becomes harder and more durable
Increase the stone's water absorption
Reduce the stone's specific gravity
Change the stone's colour to match existing work
questions.solution:
**To allow the QUARRY SAP — the natural moisture held in the stone's pores — to dry out**, after which the stone becomes harder, stronger and more durable.

**Why it matters:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Freshly quarried stone contains QUARRY SAP** | **Moisture, often carrying dissolved mineral salts** ← |
| **In that state the stone is comparatively SOFT** | **Which is an advantage — it is EASIER TO DRESS and cut** ← |
| **On drying, the dissolved salts crystallise in the pores** | **Cementing the grains and HARDENING the stone** ← |
| **Seasoning period** | **6 to 12 months in the open, protected from rain** ← |
| **Consequence of using unseasoned stone** | **It hardens IN the wall, and the accompanying shrinkage and salt crystallisation cause cracking and surface decay** ← |

> **The second and third rows together explain the traditional practice: the stone is DRESSED while soft and green, and then SEASONED before being built in — taking advantage of both states.**

> **Dressing a fully seasoned stone is far more laborious, and building an unseasoned one leads to trouble later, so the sequence is quarry → dress → season → build.**

**The QUALITIES of a good building stone:**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **CRUSHING STRENGTH** | **Above 100 MPa for heavy structural work; 60-100 MPa is acceptable for ordinary masonry** ← |
| **WATER ABSORPTION** | **Below 0.6 per cent by weight after 24 hours — a low value indicates low porosity and good durability** ← |
| **Specific gravity** | **Above 2.7 for a heavy structure; a higher value indicates a denser, more compact stone** ← |
| **HARDNESS** | **Dorry's hardness coefficient above 14 for road stone; above 17 is good** ← |
| **TOUGHNESS index** | **Above 13; above 19 is tough** |
| **DURABILITY and weather resistance** | Resistance to freeze-thaw, salts and atmospheric attack |
| **APPEARANCE and texture** | **Fine-grained, uniform, free of clay holes, cavities and bands** ← |
| **WORKABILITY** | It must be economical to dress |
| **FIRE RESISTANCE** | **Poor in stones containing much QUARTZ, which cracks on heating; better in limestone until it calcines** ← |
| **Freedom from defects** | Cracks, veins, cavities, soft patches |

> **THE WATER ABSORPTION FIGURE IS THE MOST USEFUL SINGLE INDICATOR, and the reason connects to everything else: absorption measures POROSITY, and porosity governs strength, frost resistance, salt attack and staining together.**

> **A porous stone admits water, and water carries the salts and the frost that destroy it — so a single cheap test predicts durability better than any other.**

**The classification of stones, since the properties follow from the origin:**

| Basis | Classes |
|---|---|
| **GEOLOGICAL** | **IGNEOUS (granite, basalt, trap), SEDIMENTARY (sandstone, limestone, shale), METAMORPHIC (marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss)** ← |
| **PHYSICAL** | **STRATIFIED (sandstone, slate — split easily along planes), UNSTRATIFIED (granite, trap), foliated (gneiss)** ← |
| **CHEMICAL** | **SILICEOUS (granite, quartzite — hard, durable), ARGILLACEOUS (slate, laterite — clayey), CALCAREOUS (limestone, marble — attacked by acid)** ← |

| Stone | Typical use |
|---|---|
| **GRANITE** | **Heavy engineering work, bridge piers, kerbs, facing — very strong and durable** ← |
| **BASALT / TRAP** | **Road metal, aggregate, rubble masonry — very tough** ← |
| **SANDSTONE** | **General building, carving; quality depends on the CEMENTING material (siliceous best, argillaceous worst)** ← |
| **LIMESTONE** | **Building, and the raw material for CEMENT and LIME** ← |
| **MARBLE** | Flooring, cladding, decorative work |
| **SLATE** | **Roofing — it splits into thin, impervious sheets** ← |
| **QUARTZITE** | Aggregate; poor for fine dressing |
| **GNEISS** | Common in Nepal; rough masonry and road work |

> **The CALCAREOUS group's vulnerability deserves a note: limestone and marble are attacked by acid, so they weather badly in a polluted urban atmosphere where rain carries sulphur dioxide.**

> **The visible result is the loss of carved detail on old limestone buildings in industrial cities — a purely chemical attack that no amount of structural quality prevents, and a reason to choose siliceous stone for exposed carved work in a polluted setting.**

**And the STRATIFICATION rule for laying stone, which is a practical detail with a real consequence:**

> **A stratified stone must be laid with its BEDDING PLANES PERPENDICULAR to the direction of the load — that is, horizontal in a wall, exactly as it lay in the quarry.**

| Laid correctly (natural bed horizontal) | Laid on edge or on face |
|---|---|
| **The load compresses the layers together** ← | **The load tends to SPLIT the layers apart** ← |
| **Full strength available** | **Greatly reduced strength; the stone flakes and delaminates in weathering** ← |

> **The exceptions are deliberate and few: stones in an ARCH are laid with their beds radial (perpendicular to the thrust line, which is the same principle), and a CORNICE or projecting course is laid on edge so that the weather runs across the beds rather than into them.**

> **Otherwise, laying a stratified stone against its natural bed is a straightforward error that shows itself within a few years as the face delaminates and falls away in sheets.**

examTip.trick: **Quarry sap dries out and its dissolved salts crystallise in the pores, HARDENING the stone.** Season 6-12 months. Sequence: quarry → DRESS while soft → season → build.
examTip.trap: **Water absorption below 0.6 % is the most useful single indicator** — it measures POROSITY, which governs strength, frost resistance, salt attack and staining all together.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lay a STRATIFIED stone with its natural bed HORIZONTAL** — perpendicular to the load, so the layers are compressed rather than split. Exceptions: arch stones (beds radial) and cornices (on edge, so weather runs across the beds).

questions.stem: Steel reinforcement embedded in sound concrete does not normally corrode because:
options: Concrete is completely impermeable to water and air
The steel is coated with grease before placing
The concrete's HIGH ALKALINITY (pH about 13) forms a PASSIVE oxide film on the steel surface
The concrete's temperature is too low for corrosion
questions.solution:
**The concrete's HIGH ALKALINITY — a pore-solution pH of about 12.5 to 13.5 — forms a PASSIVE oxide film on the steel that protects it.**

**How the protection works and how it is lost:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement hydration leaves calcium hydroxide in the pores** | **Giving a pH of about 13** ← |
| **At that pH a thin, dense, adherent OXIDE FILM forms on the steel** | **The PASSIVE layer — it stops further corrosion** ← |
| **The steel remains passive indefinitely while the pH stays high** | **This is CHEMICAL protection, not physical exclusion** ← |

> **Option (a) is the common misconception: concrete is NOT impermeable — it is a porous material, and both water and air reach the steel readily.**

> **The protection is chemical, and that is why COVER alone is not sufficient and why the concrete's QUALITY matters as much as its thickness.**

**The two mechanisms that destroy passivity:**

| Mechanism | Process |
|---|---|
| **CARBONATION** | **Atmospheric CO₂ diffuses in and reacts with the calcium hydroxide, converting it to calcium carbonate and dropping the pH BELOW 9 — at which the passive film is no longer stable** ← |
| **CHLORIDE attack** | **Chloride ions penetrate and break down the passive film LOCALLY, even at high pH — producing intense PITTING corrosion** ← |

| Feature | CARBONATION | CHLORIDE |
|---|---|---|
| **Corrosion pattern** | **GENERAL, over a broad area** ← | **LOCALISED PITTING — deep, and it can sever a bar** ← |
| **Advance** | **A front moving inward, roughly as √time** ← | **Diffusion, also roughly as √time** |
| **Source** | **Atmospheric CO₂ — worst in urban air at moderate humidity** ← | **Sea spray, de-icing salt, contaminated aggregate or mixing water, some admixtures** ← |
| **Warning** | Cracking and spalling once it starts | **Little — a pitted bar may be severely reduced while the surface looks sound** ← |

> **THE CHLORIDE CASE IS THE MORE DANGEROUS FOR THE REASON IN THE LAST ROW: general corrosion announces itself by cracking the cover, whereas pitting can reduce a bar's section drastically with almost no external sign.**

> **A prestressing tendon is especially vulnerable, because it is highly stressed and a small loss of section is proportionally serious — and because stress-corrosion cracking can occur.**

**Why corrosion CRACKS the concrete — the mechanism that makes it structural:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Rust (iron oxides) occupies 2 to 6 TIMES the volume of the steel consumed** ← | **The critical fact** |
| **That expansion generates bursting pressure within the concrete** | ← |
| **The cover CRACKS along the line of the bar, then DELAMINATES and SPALLS** ← | ← |
| **The steel is then directly exposed and corrodes far faster** | **A self-accelerating process** ← |
| **Loss of bar section AND loss of bond** | **Both reduce the member's capacity** ← |

> **So the damage is not merely the metal lost — it is the destruction of the cover, and hence of the bond and of the protection for whatever steel remains.**

> **THAT SELF-ACCELERATION IS WHY EARLY INTERVENTION MATTERS SO MUCH: rust staining and fine cracking along a bar line are the last cheap moment to act, and once spalling has begun the repair is a major operation.**

**The defences, in order of importance:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Adequate COVER** | **The first defence — and it must be ACHIEVED on site, with proper spacers, not merely specified** ← |
| **LOW WATER-CEMENT RATIO** | **The most important quality measure — it governs PERMEABILITY, which governs how fast CO₂ and chlorides penetrate** ← |
| **Full COMPACTION and proper CURING** | **A honeycombed or poorly cured cover is no cover at all** ← |
| **LIMIT the chloride content of the mix** | **From aggregate, water and admixtures** ← |
| **Supplementary cementitious materials (fly ash, slag, silica fume)** | **Refine the pore structure and greatly reduce chloride diffusion** ← |
| **Corrosion inhibitors, coatings, membranes** | Secondary measures |
| **Epoxy-coated, galvanised or stainless steel bars** | **For severe exposure; expensive, and epoxy coating is vulnerable to damage during handling** ← |
| **CATHODIC protection** | For remedial work on major structures |

> **THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE ANSWER IN PRACTICE, and they cost almost nothing: cover, a low water-cement ratio, and proper compaction and curing.**

> **The exotic measures in the lower rows are for genuinely severe exposure, and they are frequently specified as a substitute for getting the basics right — which does not work, since an epoxy-coated bar in porous, poorly compacted concrete with 15 mm of cover will still corrode where the coating is damaged.**

> **And the CURING point deserves emphasis because it is the most neglected: the outer 20 to 30 mm — precisely the cover zone — is the part most affected by early drying, and it is the part on which the whole protection depends.**

> **Concrete that is well designed and well placed but poorly cured has its protective layer compromised exactly where it matters, and no inspection of the finished surface will reveal it.**

examTip.trick: **Protection is CHEMICAL, not physical** — pH ~13 maintains a passive oxide film. Option (a) is the common misconception: concrete is porous, and water and air do reach the steel.
examTip.trap: **CARBONATION gives GENERAL corrosion that cracks the cover and warns you; CHLORIDES give localised PITTING that can sever a bar with almost no external sign.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Rust occupies 2-6 times the steel's volume**, so it bursts the cover, spalls it, and then accelerates. The defences that matter are COVER, LOW w/c and proper CURING — the cover zone is exactly what poor curing ruins.

questions.stem: The SOUNDNESS of cement is tested by the Le Chatelier apparatus to detect unsoundness caused by an excess of:
options: FREE LIME
Tricalcium silicate
Gypsum only
Alkalis
questions.solution:
**FREE LIME (uncombined CaO).**

**What "soundness" means, and why it is tested:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Definition** | **A cement is SOUND if it does NOT undergo appreciable volume change AFTER SETTING** ← |
| **The danger** | **Expansion occurring AFTER the concrete has hardened, when it can no longer accommodate it** ← |
| **Consequence** | **Cracking, disintegration and loss of strength — appearing MONTHS or YEARS later** ← |

> **THE TIMING IS THE WHOLE POINT: expansion BEFORE setting is harmless, because the plastic concrete simply accommodates it.**

> **Expansion AFTER setting is destructive, because the hardened concrete is rigid and the expansion must crack it.**

> **And because the reaction is slow, an unsound cement gives no sign at all during construction — the concrete tests perfectly at 28 days and disintegrates later, by which time the whole structure has been built with it.**

**The causes of unsoundness and their tests:**

| Cause | Test | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **FREE LIME (CaO)** | **LE CHATELIER apparatus** ← | **10 mm expansion (14 mm for rapid hardening)** ← |
| **MAGNESIA (MgO), as periclase** | **AUTOCLAVE test — the accelerated conditions are needed to reveal it** ← | **0.8 per cent expansion** ← |
| **Excess GYPSUM (SO₃)** | **Also detected by the autoclave; controlled by limiting SO₃ in the chemical analysis** ← | SO₃ limited to about 2.5-3 % |

> **Option (c) names gypsum alone, which is a real cause of unsoundness but not the one the Le Chatelier apparatus is designed for — which makes it the best-made distractor.**

> **The essential division: LE CHATELIER detects FREE LIME; the AUTOCLAVE detects MAGNESIA (and confirms lime).**

> **Magnesia needs the autoclave's high temperature and pressure because periclase hydrates so slowly that at ordinary temperatures the expansion would take years to appear — far too long for an acceptance test.**

**Why free lime is present at all:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **INSUFFICIENT BURNING of the raw mix in the kiln** | **Lime that has not combined with the silica and alumina** ← |
| **Excess LIME in the raw mix proportions** | Beyond what can combine |
| **Inadequate GRINDING and mixing of the raw materials** | Local excesses |
| **Rapid cooling of the clinker** | Locks in uncombined lime |

> **The free lime is HARD-BURNT, which is what makes it dangerous: ordinary quicklime slakes at once, whereas lime that has been through the kiln at 1,450 °C hydrates only slowly.**

> **So it sits inert through mixing, setting and early hardening, and then hydrates over months — expanding as it does so, inside a rigid material.**

**The Le Chatelier test itself:**

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Apparatus** | **A small split brass cylinder with two long INDICATOR ARMS attached either side of the split** ← |
| **Filling** | **Cement paste at standard consistency; covered and immersed in water at 27 °C for 24 hours** ← |
| **First reading** | **The distance between the indicator tips** ← |
| **Then** | **Boiled for 3 hours, cooled, and measured again** ← |
| **Result** | **The INCREASE in the distance is the expansion — the split cylinder AMPLIFIES a small volume change into a large, measurable movement of the arm tips** ← |
| **Limit** | **10 mm** |

> **The BOILING is the accelerating step: it makes the slow hydration of free lime occur in three hours instead of months, which is what turns a long-term risk into a same-day test.**

> **And the split-cylinder-with-arms arrangement is a neat piece of instrument design — a lever that converts an expansion of a fraction of a millimetre into several millimetres of arm movement, readable with an ordinary rule.**

**The other standard tests on cement, as a set:**

| Test | Measures | Requirement (OPC 33) |
|---|---|---|
| **FINENESS** | **Specific surface, by Blaine air permeability or dry sieving** | **Minimum 225 m²/kg; sieve residue max 10 %** ← |
| **STANDARD CONSISTENCY** | **The water needed for the Vicat plunger to penetrate to 5-7 mm from the bottom** ← | **Typically 26-33 per cent** |
| **SETTING TIME** | **Vicat needle** | **INITIAL not less than 30 min; FINAL not more than 600 min** ← |
| **SOUNDNESS** | **Le Chatelier and autoclave** ← | **10 mm; 0.8 per cent** |
| **COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH** | **70.6 mm cubes of 1:3 cement-sand mortar** ← | **16, 22 and 33 MPa at 3, 7 and 28 days** ← |
| **Heat of hydration** | Calorimetry | For low-heat cement |
| **Chemical composition** | **Lime saturation factor, alumina-iron ratio, insoluble residue, MgO, SO₃, loss on ignition** | ← |

> **The SETTING TIME limits in the third row have a clear practical basis and are worth understanding rather than memorising:**

> **The INITIAL set must not be too EARLY — at least 30 minutes — so there is time to mix, transport, place and compact the concrete before it begins to stiffen.**

> **The FINAL set must not be too LATE — within 10 hours — so that formwork can be struck and the work can proceed at a reasonable rate.**

> **Both limits are therefore construction requirements rather than material properties, which is why they are expressed as one-sided limits rather than as a target value.**

examTip.trick: **LE CHATELIER detects FREE LIME (limit 10 mm); the AUTOCLAVE detects MAGNESIA (limit 0.8 %).** Option (c), gypsum, is a real cause of unsoundness but not what Le Chatelier is for.
examTip.trap: **Unsoundness is expansion AFTER setting** — before setting it is harmless. And because free lime is HARD-BURNT it hydrates over months, so the concrete tests perfectly at 28 days and disintegrates later.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOILING for 3 hours is the accelerator** — it compresses months of slow hydration into a same-day test, and the split cylinder's arms amplify a fractional millimetre into a readable one. Setting times (30 min / 600 min) are CONSTRUCTION limits, not material properties.

questions.stem: In the FIELD SILT TEST on sand, a sample is placed in a measuring jar with water, shaken and allowed to settle. The silt content is judged from:
options: The time taken for the water to become clear
The total volume of the sample after settling
The thickness of the SILT LAYER that settles ON TOP of the sand, as a percentage of the sand's depth
The colour of the water above the sand
questions.solution:
**The thickness of the SILT LAYER that settles ON TOP of the sand, expressed as a percentage of the depth of the sand beneath it.**

**The test:**

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Fill a 200 ml measuring jar to the 100 ml mark with the sand to be tested** ← |
| **2** | **Add water to the 150 ml mark; a little salt may be added to hasten settlement** ← |
| **3** | **SHAKE vigorously and stand on a level surface** ← |
| **4** | **Allow to settle for about 3 HOURS** ← |
| **5** | **The SILT settles as a distinct layer ON TOP of the sand, because its particles are FINER and settle more slowly** ← |
| **6** | **Silt content = (thickness of silt layer / thickness of sand layer) × 100 per cent** ← |
| **Field limit** | **Commonly 8 per cent by volume; above that the sand should be washed** ← |

> **THE PHYSICS OF THE SEPARATION IS THE POINT OF STEP 5: settling velocity varies as the SQUARE of the particle diameter, so the coarse sand drops within seconds and the fine silt takes hours.**

> **The silt therefore arrives last and forms a clearly visible band on top of the sand — the same principle as the settling basin and the sedimentation tank, applied in a jam jar.**

**Why silt in sand matters:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Silt and clay coat the aggregate particles** | **PREVENTING the cement paste from bonding to them** ← |
| **Greatly increased SURFACE AREA** | **So MORE WATER is needed for the same workability — which raises the w/c ratio and lowers strength** ← |
| **Increased SHRINKAGE** | Clay in particular |
| **Reduced strength and durability** | Following from both effects above |
| **CLAY is worse than silt** | **It swells and shrinks with moisture, and its coating is more tenacious** ← |

> **THE BOND-PREVENTION MECHANISM IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST DAMAGING: concrete's strength depends on the paste gripping the aggregate, and a film of clay between them is a debonding layer at every interface.**

> **So a small percentage of clay by weight does damage out of all proportion to its quantity, because it is distributed as a coating over the entire aggregate surface.**

**The specification limits, since the field test is only an indicator:**

| Material | Maximum silt, clay and fine dust (IS 383) |
|---|---|
| **UNCRUSHED (natural) fine aggregate** | **3 per cent by weight** ← |
| **CRUSHED fine aggregate** | **15 per cent by weight — the "fines" here are rock dust, not clay** ← |
| **Uncrushed coarse aggregate** | **3 per cent** |
| **Crushed coarse aggregate** | 3 per cent |

> **The CRUSHED aggregate's much higher allowance in the second row is not an inconsistency: the fines in crushed sand are angular rock powder of the same mineral as the parent rock, which is inert and can even improve the grading.**

> **The fines in natural sand are silt and CLAY washed in from the catchment, which are harmful for the reasons above.**

> **So the limit is about the NATURE of the fines rather than their quantity — and the field jar test, which measures volume rather than composition, cannot make that distinction, which is why it is a screening test and the laboratory test governs.**

**The other FIELD tests every site engineer should be able to run:**

| Test | Method | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| **SILT content** | **Jar sedimentation, 3 hours** ← | Cleanliness of sand |
| **BULKING of sand** | **Measure damp sand's volume, then saturate it and measure the drop** ← | **The volume correction for volume batching — 20-30 per cent** ← |
| **ORGANIC impurities** | **Sodium hydroxide solution; a dark brown colour indicates organic matter** ← | Organic contamination |
| **Cement — FIELD checks** | **Colour (uniform greenish grey), no lumps, cool to the hand, floats briefly on water, feels smooth when rubbed** ← | Freshness and storage condition |
| **Bricks — field checks** | **Uniform colour and shape, metallic RING when struck, no scratch with a fingernail, no breakage when dropped from 1 m** ← | Quality of burning |
| **SLUMP** | Cone and rod | Workability, batch to batch |

> **The CEMENT FIELD CHECKS in the fourth row are worth carrying because they detect the commonest site defect — cement that has absorbed moisture in storage.**

> **A cool feel and the absence of lumps indicate cement that has not begun to hydrate; warmth or hard lumps mean it has, and its strength is already partly lost.**

> **Soft lumps that crumble between the fingers are acceptable; hard lumps are not, and the bag should be rejected rather than broken up and used — a distinction that is routinely ignored on site and that directly costs strength.**

examTip.trick: **Sand to 100 ml, water to 150 ml, shake, settle 3 hours** — the FINER silt settles LAST and forms a visible band ON TOP. Silt % = silt thickness ÷ sand thickness. Field limit about 8 % by volume.
examTip.trap: **Silt coats the aggregate and PREVENTS BOND** — so a small percentage does damage out of proportion to its quantity, being spread over the whole aggregate surface.
examTip.mnemonic: **IS 383: 3 % for UNCRUSHED sand but 15 % for CRUSHED** — because crushed "fines" are inert rock dust, not clay. The jar test measures volume, not composition, so it screens; the lab test governs.

questions.stem: In multi-coat plastering, each successive coat should be:
options: Richer and thicker than the coat beneath it
WEAKER (leaner) and THINNER than the coat beneath it
Of exactly the same mix and thickness as the coat beneath
Applied only after the previous coat has fully dried out
questions.solution:
**WEAKER (leaner in cement) and THINNER than the coat beneath it.**

**Why the strength must DECREASE outward:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Each coat SHRINKS as it dries** | **And shrinkage is restrained by the coat beneath** ← |
| **A STRONGER coat over a weaker one** | **Its shrinkage stress exceeds the bond and the weaker backing's strength — so it CRACKS the backing or DETACHES** ← |
| **A WEAKER coat over a stronger one** | **The strong backing restrains it, and the weak coat relieves the stress in many FINE cracks rather than a few wide ones** ← |
| **The weaker coat is also more permeable** | **So moisture can escape outward rather than being trapped behind a dense skin** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE IS THE SAME ONE MET IN MASONRY MORTAR: THE OUTER, SACRIFICIAL LAYER SHOULD BE THE WEAKER, so that any distress occurs where it is cheap to repair rather than in the substrate.**

> **A hard cement-rich finishing coat over a lean undercoat is one of the commonest causes of plaster failure — it crazes, then delaminates in sheets, taking the undercoat with it.**

> **And option (d) is wrong for a related reason: each coat must be applied while the previous one has set but is still slightly GREEN and damp, so that a good bond forms. A fully dried undercoat sucks the water out of the new coat and prevents proper hydration at the interface.**

**The coats and their thicknesses:**

| Work | Coats | Thickness |
|---|---|---|
| **INTERNAL plaster, ordinary** | **ONE or TWO coats** | **12 mm total (or 12 + 3)** ← |
| **EXTERNAL plaster** | **TWO or THREE coats** | **Typically 12 mm rendering + 6-9 mm floating + 2-3 mm setting = 20 mm** ← |
| **Ceiling plaster** | One coat | **6 mm — thin, since it must not fall** ← |
| **On concrete surfaces** | One coat | 6 to 10 mm, after hacking |

| Coat | Name | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **FIRST** | **RENDERING coat** | **Levels the surface irregularities and provides the key; the RICHEST and THICKEST** ← |
| **SECOND** | **FLOATING coat** | **Brings the surface to a true plane** ← |
| **THIRD** | **SETTING (finishing) coat** | **The final smooth or textured surface; the LEANEST and THINNEST** ← |

> **The undercoat is SCRATCHED or combed before it sets, to give a mechanical KEY for the next coat — a detail as important as the mix, and one that is frequently omitted.**

**The mixes and the preparation:**

| Situation | Mix (cement : sand) |
|---|---|
| **External, exposed** | **1:4 to 1:5** ← |
| **Internal walls** | **1:5 to 1:6** ← |
| **Ceilings** | **1:3 to 1:4 — richer, because adhesion against gravity is critical** ← |
| **On a smooth concrete surface** | Richer, plus hacking or a bonding agent |

> **The CEILING's richer mix in the third row is the exception that proves the rule: it is the one place where adhesion matters more than shrinkage, because the plaster must hold its own weight against gravity.**

**The preparation, which decides whether the plaster stays on:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **RAKE the masonry joints to about 10-15 mm depth** | **To provide a mechanical key** ← |
| **HACK a smooth concrete surface, or apply a bonding agent** | **A smooth surface offers no key at all** ← |
| **CLEAN off dust, loose mortar, grease and efflorescence** | ← |
| **WET the surface thoroughly before plastering** | **A dry masonry surface sucks the water out of the plaster, so it never hydrates properly at the interface — the commonest cause of hollow plaster** ← |
| **CURE the plaster for 7 to 10 days** | **Plaster is thin, has a large exposed surface, and dries out far faster than concrete** ← |

> **THE WETTING AND THE CURING ARE THE TWO STEPS MOST OFTEN SKIMPED, AND THEY CAUSE MOST PLASTER DEFECTS:**

> **Plaster applied to dry brickwork is drawn dry before it hydrates, producing a weak, dusty, hollow-sounding layer that separates in due course.**

> **And uncured plaster crazes with drying shrinkage over its whole surface — the fine map cracking seen on so much new work, which then admits water and dirt.**

> **Both are avoided at the cost of some water and a few days' attention, and neither can be remedied afterwards.**

**And POINTING, which is the alternative treatment for exposed masonry:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **Finishing the MORTAR JOINTS only, leaving the units exposed** ← |
| **Used where** | **The masonry itself is of good appearance — face brickwork, ashlar stone** ← |
| **Joints are raked out** | **To 20 mm and refilled with a richer mortar** ← |

| Type of pointing | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLUSH** | **Level with the face — the most DURABLE, since it leaves no ledge to hold water** ← |
| **Struck / weathered** | **Sloped outward to shed water — good weather resistance** ← |
| **Keyed (grooved)** | **A concave groove; decorative and reasonably durable** |
| **V-pointing** | A V groove |
| **Raised / tuck** | **Decorative; projects from the face and is the LEAST durable** ← |

> **The ranking by durability follows a single rule: any profile that leaves a horizontal LEDGE holds water, and water held against the joint is what destroys it — so flush and weathered profiles outlast the decorative ones by a wide margin.**

examTip.trick: **Each coat WEAKER and THINNER than the one beneath** — a strong coat over a weak one cracks or detaches, because its shrinkage exceeds what the backing can restrain.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is wrong: apply the next coat while the previous is set but still GREEN.** A fully dried undercoat sucks the water out and prevents hydration at the interface.
examTip.mnemonic: **WET the wall before plastering and CURE for 7-10 days** — the two most-skimped steps, causing hollow plaster and map crazing respectively. And in POINTING, any profile leaving a horizontal LEDGE holds water: flush and weathered last longest.

questions.stem: For a comfortable stair, the relation between the RISE (R) and the TREAD (T), both in millimetres, is commonly taken as:
questions.solution:
**2R + T = 550 to 650 mm.**

**The three empirical rules, which are used together as a check:**

| Rule | Range | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **2R + T** | **550 to 650 mm** ← | **The average PACE of a person on the level is about 600 mm, and climbing takes twice the effort per unit of rise** ← |
| **R × T** | **40,000 to 45,000 mm²** ← | An empirical product |
| **R + T** | **400 to 450 mm** ← | A simple sum check |

> **THE FIRST RULE HAS THE CLEAREST PHYSICAL BASIS, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising: a person's normal stride on the flat is about 600 mm, and lifting the body vertically costs roughly twice as much effort as moving it horizontally.**

> **So the "effective" distance covered by one step is the tread plus TWICE the rise, and comfort requires that quantity to match the natural pace of about 600 mm.**

> **That is why the coefficient is 2 and why the target is 600 — both follow from human locomotion rather than from convention.**

**Checking a typical stair against all three:**

| Stair | 2R + T | R × T | R + T | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **R = 150, T = 300** | **600 ✓** | **45,000 ✓** | **450 ✓** | **Ideal — a generous public stair** ← |
| **R = 175, T = 250** | **600 ✓** | **43,750 ✓** | **425 ✓** | **Comfortable — a typical residential stair** ← |
| **R = 200, T = 200** | **600 ✓** | **40,000 ✓** | **400 ✓** | **Steep but within all three rules — a ladder-like service stair** ← |
| **R = 250, T = 200** | **700 ✗** | 50,000 ✗ | 450 ✓ | **Too steep — fails two of the three** ← |

> **The third row is instructive: a stair can satisfy all three rules and still be uncomfortably steep, so the rules are NECESSARY rather than sufficient, and the code's separate limits on rise and tread also apply.**

**The dimensional requirements:**

| Element | Residential | Public buildings |
|---|---|---|
| **RISE** | **150 to 190 mm** ← | **150 mm maximum** ← |
| **TREAD (going)** | **250 mm minimum** ← | **250 to 300 mm** |
| **WIDTH of flight** | **Minimum 900 mm (750 mm for an internal stair in a small dwelling)** ← | **1,500 mm and above; 2,000 mm for assembly buildings** ← |
| **HEADROOM** | **Minimum 2,100 to 2,300 mm, measured vertically from the nosing line** ← | Same |
| **Steps per FLIGHT** | **Maximum 12 to 15; minimum 3** ← | Same |
| **LANDING length** | **Not less than the flight's width** ← | Same |
| **Handrail height** | **850 to 900 mm above the nosing line** | Same, plus a second lower rail where children use it |

> **THE MAXIMUM OF 12 TO 15 STEPS PER FLIGHT IS A SAFETY PROVISION, not merely a comfort one: a longer flight is tiring, and a fall down a long flight is far more injurious than a fall down a short one.**

> **The landing breaks the fall and provides a rest, and requiring it to be at least as long as the flight is wide ensures a person can stop and turn on it.**

> **The MINIMUM of 3 steps has a different rationale: a flight of one or two steps is easily overlooked and is a common tripping hazard, particularly where the lighting is poor or the floor finish continues across it.**

**UNIFORMITY, which is the requirement that overrides all the others:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **ALL risers in a flight must be EQUAL, and all treads equal** ← | **Without exception** |
| **Why** | **A person climbing a stair does so with their EYES ELSEWHERE, having unconsciously learned the rhythm from the first two or three steps** ← |
| **A single odd riser** | **Breaks that rhythm and causes a stumble or a fall** ← |
| **The worst case** | **An odd step at the TOP or BOTTOM, where it is least expected** ← |

> **THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SINGLE FACT ABOUT STAIR DESIGN AND IT IS ROUTINELY VIOLATED IN PRACTICE — usually because a floor finish was added or changed after construction, altering the top or bottom riser by 15 or 20 mm.**

> **A variation of even 10 mm in one riser is enough to cause falls, and stair falls are a leading cause of injury in buildings.**

> **So the setting out must allow for the FINISHED floor levels at both ends, not the structural ones — and where a finish is changed later, the stair must be adjusted with it.**

> **That is a small detail with a large consequence, and it is the kind of thing that is decided correctly on the drawing or not at all.**

**And the terminology, for completeness:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Rise / riser** | **The vertical height of one step; the board closing it** |
| **Tread / going** | **The horizontal depth of the step; the going excludes the nosing overlap** ← |
| **NOSING** | **The projecting front edge of the tread — it adds to the effective tread without adding to the going** ← |
| **Flight** | An unbroken series of steps |
| **Landing** | A level platform between flights |
| **Stringer (string)** | The inclined member supporting the steps |
| **Newel post, baluster, handrail, balustrade** | The guarding assembly |
| **Soffit, waist** | **The underside of the stair slab, and its thickness measured perpendicular** ← |
| **Winder** | **A tapered step turning a corner — permitted but less safe, since the tread narrows toward the inside** ← |

examTip.trick: **2R + T = 550 to 650 mm** — because the natural pace is ~600 mm and climbing costs roughly twice the effort per unit of rise. Check also R × T = 40,000-45,000 and R + T = 400-450.
examTip.trap: **The rules are necessary, not sufficient** — R = 200, T = 200 satisfies all three and is still ladder-like. The code's separate rise and tread limits apply as well.
examTip.mnemonic: **ALL risers in a flight must be EQUAL** — people climb with their eyes elsewhere, having learned the rhythm from the first steps. A 10 mm odd riser causes falls, and it usually comes from a floor FINISH added after setting out.

questions.stem: A rectangular section is 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep. Its moment of inertia about an axis along its BASE (parallel to the width) is:
options: 200 × 10⁶ mm⁴
questions.solution:
**266.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴.**

**By the parallel axis theorem:**

| Step | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Centroidal moment of inertia** | **bd³/12 = 100 × 200³/12 = 100 × 8,000,000/12** | **66.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **Area** | **100 × 200** | **20,000 mm²** |
| **Distance centroid to base** | **200/2** | **100 mm** ← |
| **A h² term** | **20,000 × 100²= 20,000 × 10,000** | **200 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **I about the BASE** | **66.67 + 200** | **266.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |

> **Check by the direct formula: I about the base of a rectangle = bd³/3 = 100 × 8,000,000/3 = 266.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴ ✓**

> **That the two agree is not a coincidence — bd³/3 IS bd³/12 + (bd)(d/2)², and the direct formula is simply the parallel axis theorem already applied.**

**Each distractor is a named wrong step:**

| Option | The error |
|---|---|
| **66.67 × 10⁶** | **The CENTROIDAL value — the A h² term omitted entirely** ← |
| **200 × 10⁶** | **The A h² term ALONE — the centroidal term omitted** ← |
| **16.67 × 10⁶** | **db³/12 = 200 × 100³/12 — the moment of inertia about the VERTICAL centroidal axis, with b and d interchanged** ← |

> **The last of these is the most instructive error: interchanging b and d gives an answer sixteen times too small, because the CUBED dimension is the one that matters.**

> **The rule that prevents it: IN bd³/12, THE CUBED DIMENSION IS ALWAYS THE ONE PERPENDICULAR TO THE AXIS — the depth measured across the axis, not along it.**

**The PARALLEL AXIS THEOREM and its properties:**

> **I_axis = I_centroidal + A h²**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **The A h² term is ALWAYS POSITIVE** | **So the moment of inertia is a MINIMUM about the CENTROIDAL axis** ← |
| **It works only FROM the centroidal axis** | **To go between two non-centroidal axes, pass THROUGH the centroid** ← |
| **The two axes must be PARALLEL** | Hence the name |
| **For a thin element far from the axis, A h² DOMINATES** | **Often by a factor of hundreds** ← |

> **The FIRST ROW is worth carrying as a check: any moment of inertia about a non-centroidal axis must be GREATER than the centroidal value, so an answer smaller than 66.67 × 10⁶ here would be impossible.**

> **That single check eliminates the 16.67 × 10⁶ option immediately, without any recollection of which dimension is cubed.**

**The standard results, as a working set:**

| Section | About the CENTROIDAL axis | About the BASE |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × d** | **bd³/12** ← | **bd³/3** ← |
| **TRIANGLE, base b, height h** | **bh³/36** ← | **bh³/12** ← |
| **CIRCLE, diameter D** | **πD⁴/64** | — |
| **Semicircle, radius r** | 0.11 r⁴ | **πr⁴/8 about the diameter** ← |
| **Hollow rectangle** | **(BD³ − bd³)/12** ← | — |
| **Hollow circle** | **π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64** ← | — |

> **The TRIANGLE's pair is worth noting because the ratio differs from the rectangle's: bh³/36 to bh³/12 is a factor of 3, whereas the rectangle's bd³/12 to bd³/3 is a factor of 4.**

> **The difference arises because the triangle's centroid is at h/3 from its base rather than at d/2, so the A h² term is (bh/2)(h/3)² = bh³/18 rather than bd³/4.**

> **Checking: bh³/36 + bh³/18 = bh³/36 + 2bh³/36 = 3bh³/36 = bh³/12 ✓**

**And the POLAR moment of inertia, since it follows immediately:**

> **J = I_xx + I_yy — the PERPENDICULAR AXIS THEOREM, valid for a PLANE LAMINA only.**

| Section | J |
|---|---|
| **Circle** | **πD⁴/32 — exactly twice I_xx, by symmetry** ← |
| **Rectangle b × d** | **bd(b² + d²)/12** |
| **Hollow circle** | **π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32** |

> **The circle's result follows in one line: I_xx = I_yy = πD⁴/64 by symmetry, so J = 2 × πD⁴/64 = πD⁴/32 — and J is what governs the TORSION of a circular shaft, exactly as I governs bending.**

> **The restriction to a plane lamina in the perpendicular axis theorem is a real one and is often forgotten: the theorem does not apply to a three-dimensional body, and using it on one gives a wrong answer with no warning.**

examTip.trick: **I_base = bd³/12 + (bd)(d/2)² = 66.67 + 200 = 266.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴**, which equals bd³/3 — the direct formula is the parallel axis theorem already applied.
examTip.trap: **In bd³/12 the CUBED dimension is the one PERPENDICULAR to the axis.** Interchanging b and d here gives 16.67 × 10⁶ — sixteen times too small.
examTip.mnemonic: **A h² is always POSITIVE, so the centroidal value is a MINIMUM** — any answer below 66.67 × 10⁶ is impossible here, which kills two distractors without any formula. Triangle: bh³/36 centroidal, bh³/12 about the base.

questions.stem: A hollow rectangular (box) section has outside dimensions 200 mm wide × 300 mm deep and inside dimensions 150 mm × 250 mm. Its moment of inertia about the centroidal axis parallel to the 200 mm side is:
questions.solution:
**254.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴.**

**The computation:**

> **I = (BD³ − bd³)/12, valid because the two rectangles share the SAME centroid.**

| Term | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Outer, BD³** | **200 × 300³ = 200 × 27,000,000** | **5,400 × 10⁶** ← |
| **Inner, bd³** | **150 × 250³ = 150 × 15,625,000** | **2,343.75 × 10⁶** ← |
| **Difference** | **5,400 − 2,343.75** | **3,056.25 × 10⁶** |
| **Divide by 12** | **3,056.25/12** | **254.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |

**Each distractor is a named wrong step:**

| Option | The error |
|---|---|
| **450.0 × 10⁶** | **The SOLID outer section only: 200 × 300³/12 — the hole ignored** ← |
| **195.3 × 10⁶** | **The inner rectangle only: 150 × 250³/12** ← |
| **645.3 × 10⁶** | **The two ADDED instead of subtracted: 450.0 + 195.3** ← |

> **The 645.3 distractor is worth noting because it is physically impossible: a hollow section cannot have a GREATER moment of inertia than the solid section that contains it.**

> **That check disposes of it instantly, and it is the kind of sense test worth applying before any arithmetic is examined.**

**The essential condition on the subtraction method:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The hole and the outer section must share the SAME CENTROID** ← | **Only then may their moments of inertia simply be subtracted** |
| **If the hole is OFF-CENTRE** | **The composite centroid must be found FIRST, and BOTH parts transferred to it by the parallel axis theorem** ← |

> **So the neat (BD³ − bd³)/12 form is a special case, and applying it to an eccentric hole gives a wrong answer with no warning — which is the trap in any composite-section problem.**

> **The general procedure for a composite section is always the same, and it is worth stating as a sequence:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Divide the section into simple shapes, with HOLES treated as NEGATIVE areas** ← |
| **2** | **Find the composite CENTROID: ȳ = Σ(A_i y_i)/ΣA_i, with negative areas carrying negative signs** ← |
| **3** | **For each part, compute its OWN centroidal I** |
| **4** | **Transfer each to the composite centroid: I_i + A_i h_i²** ← |
| **5** | **SUM them, subtracting the negative areas' contributions** ← |

**Why HOLLOW sections are so efficient — the point of the exercise:**

> **Compare the box section above with a SOLID section of the SAME AREA.**

| Section | Area | I | Radius of gyration |
|---|---|---|---|
| **The BOX: 200×300 outer less 150×250 inner** | **60,000 − 37,500 = 22,500 mm²** | **254.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← | **√(254.7×10⁶/22,500) = 106 mm** ← |
| **A SOLID square of the same area** | **22,500 mm² → 150 × 150** | **150⁴/12 = 42.2 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← | **√(42.2×10⁶/22,500) = 43 mm** ← |

> **THE BOX HAS SIX TIMES THE MOMENT OF INERTIA OF A SOLID SECTION OF THE SAME AREA — that is, of the same weight and the same material cost.**

> **The reason is the one met in the parallel axis theorem: the A h² term dominates, so material placed FAR from the neutral axis contributes enormously and material near it contributes almost nothing.**

> **A hollow section removes precisely the material that was doing least, and keeps what was doing most.**

> **That single principle explains the shape of nearly every efficient structural member — the I-section, the box girder, the tubular strut, the hollow-core slab, the bicycle frame — and it explains why nature builds bones, bamboo and plant stems hollow.**

**And the LIMITS of the principle, since it cannot be pushed indefinitely:**

| Limit | Note |
|---|---|
| **LOCAL BUCKLING** | **A very thin wall buckles locally before the section can yield — which is what the section CLASSIFICATION in IS 800 controls** ← |
| **Shear capacity** | **A thin web carries less shear** |
| **Connection difficulty** | **A closed section cannot be bolted from inside** ← |
| **Corrosion of the inner surface** | **Inaccessible for inspection or painting — so it must be SEALED** ← |
| **Handling and fabrication** | Thin material is easily damaged |

> **THE LOCAL BUCKLING LIMIT IS THE GOVERNING ONE and it sets a practical bound on how thin the walls may be made: beyond a certain width-to-thickness ratio, adding to the section's overall size while thinning its walls stops improving the capacity and starts reducing it.**

> **So the efficient section is not the thinnest possible one but the thinnest that remains COMPACT — which is precisely the judgement that section classification exists to make, and the reason it is the first step in any steel design.**

examTip.trick: **I = (BD³ − bd³)/12 = (5,400 − 2,343.75)×10⁶/12 = 254.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴.** The 645.3 distractor is physically impossible — a hollow section cannot exceed the solid one containing it.
examTip.trap: **The simple subtraction works ONLY if the hole is CONCENTRIC.** An off-centre hole requires finding the composite centroid first and transferring both parts to it.
examTip.mnemonic: **The box has SIX TIMES the I of a solid section of the same AREA** — because A h² dominates, so removing material near the neutral axis costs almost nothing. The limit is LOCAL BUCKLING, which is what section classification controls.

questions.stem: In compass surveying, LOCAL ATTRACTION at a station is detected by checking whether:
options: The sum of the interior angles equals (n − 2) × 180°
The FORE BEARING and BACK BEARING of a line differ by exactly 180°
The chain length has been correctly standardised
The magnetic declination has been applied
questions.solution:
**By checking whether the FORE BEARING and the BACK BEARING of a line differ by exactly 180°.**

**The test and what it tells you:**

| Observation | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| **FB and BB differ by EXACTLY 180°** | **BOTH stations are FREE of local attraction** ← |
| **The difference is NOT 180°** | **AT LEAST ONE of the two stations is affected — the test does not by itself say which** ← |

> **The test works because the magnetic meridian is the same at both ends of a line if neither end is disturbed — so the two bearings must be exactly reciprocal.**

> **Any departure means the needle was deflected at one end or the other, and the amount of the departure is the total disturbance at the two stations combined.**

**What causes local attraction:**

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **Iron and steel objects near the instrument** | **Railings, pipes, rails, reinforcement, vehicles, a steel tape or arrows laid nearby** ← |
| **The surveyor's own equipment and possessions** | **Steel-toed boots, keys, a mobile telephone, spectacle frames, a chain held too close** ← |
| **Electric current — overhead lines, cables, transformers** | ← |
| **Magnetic rocks and ore bodies in the ground** | **Which cannot be avoided by moving a few metres** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMONEST CAUSE AND THE EASIEST TO OVERLOOK: the surveyor is often the source of the disturbance they are measuring.**

> **The practical discipline is to keep all iron and steel — including the chain, arrows and any personal items — several metres from the compass while observing, and never to rest the compass on a steel surface.**

**How the observations are CORRECTED, which is the part that requires care:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute FB − BB for every line and identify which differ from 180°** ← |
| **2** | **Find a line whose FB and BB differ by EXACTLY 180° — both its stations are UNAFFECTED** ← |
| **3** | **Starting from those known-good stations, work OUTWARD around the traverse, correcting each station in turn** ← |
| **4** | **At an affected station, the CORRECTION is the same for every bearing observed there — the needle is deflected by one amount, whatever it is pointed at** ← |

> **STEP 4 IS THE KEY INSIGHT AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THE CORRECTION POSSIBLE: local attraction deflects the NEEDLE, and the needle establishes the reference direction for every bearing taken at that station.**

> **So all the bearings from an affected station are wrong by the SAME amount and in the SAME direction — which means one correction fixes them all, and the traverse can be worked through systematically.**

> **If instead every bearing at a station were wrong by a different amount, no correction would be possible and the observations would simply be lost.**

> **And if NO line has a difference of exactly 180°, then every station is affected. The usual recourse is to take the line whose difference is CLOSEST to 180° and correct from it, or better, to observe the traverse again with a theodolite, which is unaffected by magnetism.**

**BEARINGS and their conversion, since the test depends on them:**

| System | Note |
|---|---|
| **WHOLE CIRCLE BEARING (WCB)** | **Measured CLOCKWISE from magnetic north, 0° to 360°** ← |
| **QUADRANTAL / REDUCED BEARING (QB)** | **Measured from NORTH or SOUTH, east or west, 0° to 90° — e.g. N 45° E, S 30° W** ← |

| WCB range | Quadrant | Rule for the reduced bearing |
|---|---|---|
| **0° to 90°** | **NE** | **RB = WCB, as N…E** ← |
| **90° to 180°** | **SE** | **RB = 180° − WCB, as S…E** ← |
| **180° to 270°** | **SW** | **RB = WCB − 180°, as S…W** ← |
| **270° to 360°** | **NW** | **RB = 360° − WCB, as N…W** ← |

> **And the back bearing rule: BB = FB + 180° if FB is less than 180°; BB = FB − 180° if FB is greater than 180°.**

**The other angular corrections, to distinguish them:**

| Correction | For | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **LOCAL ATTRACTION** | **A disturbance of the NEEDLE at a particular station** ← | This question |
| **MAGNETIC DECLINATION** | **The angle between MAGNETIC and TRUE north** ← (option d) | **Converts magnetic bearings to true bearings; a regional, not local, quantity** ← |
| **Angular MISCLOSURE** | **The traverse's angles not summing correctly** ← (option a) | Distributed among the angles |

> **Option (d) names DECLINATION, which is a real and different correction: it varies slowly across a region and over time, and it is applied to every bearing in the survey equally.**

> **Local attraction, by contrast, varies from station to station and even from one setup to another a few metres away — which is precisely why it must be detected station by station rather than assumed.**

> **The two are sometimes confused because both convert one bearing to another, and the distinction is worth holding: DECLINATION is where NORTH is; LOCAL ATTRACTION is where the NEEDLE wrongly says it is.**

examTip.trick: **FB and BB must differ by EXACTLY 180°.** If they do, both stations are clean; if not, at least one is affected — and the test alone does not say which.
examTip.trap: **All bearings taken AT an affected station are wrong by the SAME amount** — the needle is deflected once, whatever it points at. That is what makes a single correction per station possible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Start from a line whose FB−BB is exactly 180° and work OUTWARD.** And keep the distinction: DECLINATION is where north actually is (regional); LOCAL ATTRACTION is where the needle wrongly says it is (station by station).

questions.stem: In a construction contract, the principal purpose of the SPECIFICATIONS is to:
options: Fix the total price of the contract
Show the dimensions and positions of the works
List the quantities of each item of work
Define the QUALITY of materials and WORKMANSHIP, and the manner of execution, which the drawings cannot convey
questions.solution:
**To define the QUALITY of materials and WORKMANSHIP, and the manner of execution** — matters the drawings cannot convey.

**The division of labour between the contract documents:**

| Document | What it defines |
|---|---|
| **DRAWINGS** | **The GEOMETRY — dimensions, positions, shapes, levels** ← (option b) |
| **SPECIFICATIONS** | **The QUALITY — what materials, to what standard, worked in what manner** ← |
| **BILL OF QUANTITIES** | **The QUANTITY of each item, and the rates** ← (option c) |
| **CONDITIONS OF CONTRACT** | **The RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS of the parties — payment, time, variations, disputes** ← |
| **The AGREEMENT** | Binds them all together |

> **Every option therefore names a real contract document's function, and the question tests which document does which — a distinction that matters, because an item put in the wrong document may not be enforceable in the way intended.**

> **A drawing can show a wall 230 mm thick; only the specification can say whether its bricks must be first class, what mortar is required, how the joints are to be raked, and how long it is to be cured.**

**The purposes of a specification, in full:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Define the QUALITY and standard of every material and operation** | **The primary purpose** ← |
| **It forms part of the CONTRACT and is legally binding** ← | **So an unclear specification is an unenforceable one** |
| **It is the basis of the RATE ANALYSIS** | **A contractor cannot price work without knowing its quality** ← |
| **It is the basis of INSPECTION and ACCEPTANCE** | **The inspector's authority derives from it** ← |
| **It guides the contractor's method and planning** | ← |
| **It resolves disputes about what was required** | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN WHY A VAGUE SPECIFICATION IS SO EXPENSIVE:**

> **A contractor pricing work with an unclear specification must either assume the highest standard (raising the price) or the lowest (creating a dispute at inspection).**

> **Both outcomes cost the employer money, and both are caused by the same failure of drafting.**

> **A clear specification is therefore not merely a quality document but a COMMERCIAL one — it lets every tenderer price the same thing, which is the whole basis of competitive bidding.**

**The types of specification:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **GENERAL (brief) specification** | **A short description of the class of work for each item — used for estimating and for a general idea of quality** ← |
| **DETAILED specification** | **A full description of the materials, proportions, methods, tests and workmanship for each item — the contract document** ← |
| **PRESCRIPTIVE (method) specification** | **States exactly WHAT to use and HOW to do it — the employer takes the design risk** ← |
| **PERFORMANCE specification** | **States the RESULT to be achieved and leaves the method to the contractor — the contractor takes the risk** ← |
| **Standard specification** | **A published document (a departmental or national standard) incorporated by reference** ← |
| **Particular / special specification** | Project-specific amendments to the standard |

> **THE PRESCRIPTIVE-AGAINST-PERFORMANCE CHOICE IS THE SUBSTANTIVE ONE, and it allocates risk:**

| | PRESCRIPTIVE | PERFORMANCE |
|---|---|---|
| **The employer says** | **"Use M25 concrete, 1:1:2, cured 14 days"** | **"Achieve 25 MPa characteristic strength and a 50-year design life"** ← |
| **If the result is unsatisfactory despite compliance** | **The EMPLOYER bears it — the contractor did as instructed** ← | **The CONTRACTOR bears it — the result was not achieved** ← |
| **Scope for the contractor's innovation** | **NONE** | **Full — and this is where economies come from** ← |
| **Ease of inspection** | **EASY — check the method** ← | **Harder — the result may not be measurable until later** ← |

> **The last row is the practical difficulty with performance specifications and the reason prescriptive ones persist: a durability requirement of "50 years" cannot be tested at handover, so the specification must fall back on prescriptive proxies — cover, water-cement ratio, cement content — which are measurable now.**

> **Most real specifications are therefore a MIXTURE, performance-based where the result can be measured and prescriptive where it cannot.**

**And the ORDER OF PRECEDENCE, which is where the documents meet:**

> **The documents will occasionally CONTRADICT one another — a drawing showing one thing and the specification another — and the contract must say which prevails.**

| Typical order (highest first) | Note |
|---|---|
| **The Agreement** | ← |
| **Conditions of Contract (special, then general)** | ← |
| **SPECIFICATIONS** | **Usually above the drawings** ← |
| **DRAWINGS** | ← |
| **Bill of Quantities** | ← |
| **Other documents** | Correspondence, minutes |

> **The order varies between forms of contract, and the important point is that IT MUST BE STATED — a contract with no precedence clause leaves a genuine contradiction to be resolved by argument or by a tribunal.**

> **The better practice, of course, is to have no contradictions: the specification and the drawings should be checked against each other before tender, and a discrepancy found at that stage costs an hour, while the same discrepancy found on site costs a variation, a delay and often a claim.**

examTip.trick: **DRAWINGS give the geometry; SPECIFICATIONS give the quality; the BOQ gives the quantity; the CONDITIONS give the rights and obligations.** Every option names a real document's function.
examTip.trap: **A vague specification is a COMMERCIAL failure, not just a quality one** — tenderers either price the highest standard (dear) or the lowest (a dispute at inspection), and competitive bidding requires everyone to price the same thing.
examTip.mnemonic: **PRESCRIPTIVE puts the design risk on the EMPLOYER; PERFORMANCE puts it on the CONTRACTOR.** Real specifications mix the two — performance where the result is measurable, prescriptive where it is not (durability becomes cover and w/c).

questions.stem: The COEFFICIENT OF CURVATURE of a soil is defined as:
options: D₆₀ / D₁₀
D₃₀² / (D₁₀ × D₆₀)
D₁₀ / D₆₀
D₃₀ / D₁₀
questions.solution:
**C_c = D₃₀² / (D₁₀ × D₆₀).**

**The two grading coefficients:**

| Coefficient | Expression | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| **UNIFORMITY coefficient, C_u** | **D₆₀ / D₁₀** ← (option a) | **The RANGE of particle sizes — how spread out the grading is** ← |
| **COEFFICIENT OF CURVATURE, C_c** | **D₃₀² / (D₁₀ D₆₀)** ← | **The SHAPE of the grading curve — whether the intermediate sizes are present** ← |

> **Option (a) is the UNIFORMITY coefficient, which makes it the designed distractor — both are read from the same grading curve and are constantly interchanged.**

> **The D notation: D₁₀ is the particle size below which 10 per cent of the sample lies by weight, read off the grading curve at the 10 per cent ordinate. D₁₀ is also called the EFFECTIVE SIZE.**

**The criteria for a WELL-GRADED soil:**

| Soil | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Well-graded GRAVEL (GW)** | **C_u > 4 AND C_c between 1 and 3** ← |
| **Well-graded SAND (SW)** | **C_u > 6 AND C_c between 1 and 3** ← |
| **Failing either condition** | **POORLY graded — GP or SP** ← |

> **BOTH conditions must be satisfied, and that is why two coefficients are needed rather than one.**

> **C_u alone can be misleading: a GAP-GRADED soil — containing plenty of coarse and plenty of fine material but nothing in between — has a LARGE C_u and is very poorly graded indeed.**

> **C_c detects exactly that gap. A gap-graded soil's D₃₀ falls in the missing range, so C_c comes out well outside the 1 to 3 band and the soil is correctly rejected.**

> **So C_u asks "is the range wide?" and C_c asks "is the range FILLED?" — and a good grading needs both.**

**Why well grading matters:**

| Property | WELL-graded | POORLY graded (uniform) |
|---|---|---|
| **PACKING** | **Small particles fill the voids between larger ones** ← | Large voids remain |
| **Density achievable** | **HIGH** ← | Lower |
| **Void ratio and porosity** | **LOW** | High |
| **Shear strength** | **HIGHER — better interlock** ← | Lower |
| **Permeability** | **LOWER — the voids are blocked** ← | Higher |
| **Compressibility** | Lower | Higher |
| **Suits** | **Embankments, sub-bases, concrete aggregate, compacted fill** ← | **DRAINAGE layers and filters, where permeability is wanted** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE QUALIFICATION THAT MATTERS: well grading is not universally desirable.**

> **A drainage blanket or a filter layer needs to pass water freely, so a UNIFORM (poorly graded) material is deliberately specified there — which is why single-sized gravel is used behind retaining walls and in chimney drains.**

> **So "poorly graded" is a description of the grading curve, not a judgement of the material's fitness — and specifying a well-graded material for a drain would be an error.**

**A worked example:**

> **A sand has D₁₀ = 0.15 mm, D₃₀ = 0.45 mm and D₆₀ = 1.20 mm.**

| Quantity | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **C_u** | **1.20/0.15** | **8.0 — exceeds 6 ✓** ← |
| **C_c** | **0.45²/(0.15 × 1.20) = 0.2025/0.18** | **1.125 — within 1 to 3 ✓** ← |
| **Classification** | Both satisfied | **WELL-GRADED SAND (SW)** ← |

> **And a gap-graded comparison: if the same soil had D₃₀ = 0.18 mm (the intermediate sizes largely missing), then C_c = 0.0324/0.18 = 0.18 — far below 1, so despite C_u of 8.0 the soil is POORLY graded, and correctly identified as such.**

**How the grading curve is obtained:**

| Fraction | Method |
|---|---|
| **Coarser than 75 µm** | **SIEVE ANALYSIS — a nest of standard sieves, shaken** ← |
| **FINER than 75 µm** | **SEDIMENTATION — the HYDROMETER or pipette method, based on Stokes' law** ← |
| **A soil containing both** | **A COMBINED analysis: wet sieving to separate at 75 µm, then each fraction by its own method** ← |

> **The 75 µm sieve is the practical limit of sieving — below that the openings become impossible to manufacture accurately and the particles bind together electrostatically and by surface moisture rather than passing freely.**

> **So the two methods measure quite different things and are joined at that boundary: sieving measures the SMALLEST DIMENSION that will pass a square opening, while sedimentation measures an EQUIVALENT SETTLING DIAMETER.**

> **For a flaky clay particle those two are not the same at all, which is worth remembering when a combined curve shows a discontinuity at 75 µm — the step is often an artefact of the change in method rather than a real feature of the soil.**

examTip.trick: **C_c = D₃₀²/(D₁₀ D₆₀); C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀** (option a). Well graded needs BOTH: C_u > 4 (gravel) or > 6 (sand), AND C_c between 1 and 3.
examTip.trap: **C_u alone cannot detect GAP GRADING** — a gap-graded soil has a large C_u and is very poorly graded. C_c catches it, because D₃₀ falls in the missing range. C_u asks "is the range wide?"; C_c asks "is it FILLED?"
examTip.mnemonic: **"Poorly graded" is not a verdict on fitness** — a uniform single-sized gravel is exactly what a FILTER or drainage layer needs. Specifying a well-graded material for a drain would be the error.

questions.stem: The HYDROMETER method of particle size analysis is based on:
options: The percentage of the sample retained on each of a nest of sieves
The plasticity of the fine fraction
The electrical conductivity of the soil suspension
STOKES' LAW — the settling velocity of a particle in a fluid varies as the SQUARE of its diameter
questions.solution:
**STOKES' LAW** — the terminal settling velocity of a spherical particle in a fluid varies as the SQUARE of its diameter.

> **v = (γ_s − γ_w) D² / (18 μ)**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **v** | Terminal settling velocity |
| **γ_s, γ_w** | Unit weights of the solid and the fluid |
| **D** | **The particle's diameter — appearing SQUARED** ← |
| **μ** | The fluid's dynamic viscosity |

**How the method exploits it:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **The soil is dispersed in water in a 1,000 ml cylinder** | **With a DEFLOCCULATING agent (sodium hexametaphosphate) so the clay particles separate** ← |
| **All particle sizes start uniformly distributed** | ← |
| **LARGER particles settle FASTER** (as D²) | **So at any given time, all particles larger than a certain size have fallen below the measuring depth** ← |
| **The HYDROMETER measures the SUSPENSION'S DENSITY at a known depth** | **Which gives the WEIGHT of solids still in suspension there** ← |
| **Stokes' law converts the TIME and DEPTH into the corresponding DIAMETER** | ← |
| **Readings over minutes to hours build the whole fine grading curve** | **The finest particles take many hours** ← |

> **So a reading at time t and depth H tells you what proportion of the sample is FINER than the diameter that would have settled exactly H in time t — which is precisely one point on the grading curve.**

> **The DEFLOCCULATING AGENT in the first row is essential and is not a refinement: clay particles carry surface charges and naturally FLOCCULATE into clusters, which would settle as large particles and make the soil appear far coarser than it is.**

> **Omitting the dispersant is the commonest error in the test, and it produces a plausible-looking curve that is entirely wrong.**

**The assumptions Stokes' law makes, and where they fail:**

| Assumption | Reality for soil |
|---|---|
| **The particles are SPHERICAL** | **Clay particles are PLATY — flat flakes** ← |
| **They settle independently, without interference** | **True only in a dilute suspension** ← |
| **The flow around them is LAMINAR** | **Fails for particles larger than about 0.2 mm, which settle too fast** ← |
| **The particles are large relative to the fluid's molecules** | **Fails below about 0.2 µm, where Brownian motion dominates** ← |

> **THE PLATY-PARTICLE PROBLEM IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL ONE, and it is why the result is called an EQUIVALENT DIAMETER rather than a diameter:**

> **A flat clay flake settles far more slowly than a sphere of the same mass, so it is reported as being smaller than it is in its largest dimension.**

> **The figure obtained is therefore "the diameter of the SPHERE that would settle at the same rate" — a defined, reproducible and useful quantity that is not a physical measurement of the particle.**

> **The third and fourth rows set the method's working range: roughly 0.2 mm down to 0.2 µm, which is exactly the range sieving cannot reach and is why the two methods complement one another.**

**The PARTICLE SIZE classification, which the curve is read against:**

| Fraction | Size range (IS classification) |
|---|---|
| **BOULDER** | **Above 300 mm** |
| **COBBLE** | **80 to 300 mm** |
| **GRAVEL** | **4.75 to 80 mm** ← |
| **SAND — coarse / medium / fine** | **2.0-4.75 / 0.425-2.0 / 0.075-0.425 mm** ← |
| **SILT** | **0.002 to 0.075 mm** ← |
| **CLAY** | **Below 0.002 mm (2 µm)** ← |

> **The 75 µm boundary between sand and silt is the same boundary at which the test method changes, which is not a coincidence — it is the practical limit of sieving, and the classification was drawn to match it.**

> **And the 2 µm boundary defining CLAY is a SIZE definition, which must be distinguished from CLAY MINERALS: a rock flour ground to below 2 µm is "clay-sized" and has none of clay's plasticity, while the ACTIVITY index (PI divided by the percentage finer than 2 µm) exists precisely to separate the two.**

**And the corrections the hydrometer reading requires:**

| Correction | Reason |
|---|---|
| **MENISCUS correction** | **The hydrometer is read at the TOP of the meniscus in an opaque suspension, but calibrated at the bottom** ← |
| **TEMPERATURE correction** | **Viscosity changes markedly with temperature, and it appears in Stokes' law** ← |
| **DISPERSING AGENT correction** | **The added chemical raises the suspension's density** ← |

> **The TEMPERATURE correction is the most significant of the three, because water's viscosity falls by about 2 per cent per degree — so a 5 °C error changes the computed diameter appreciably.**

> **That is why the test is run in a constant-temperature bath where accuracy matters, and why the temperature is recorded at every reading where it is not.**

examTip.trick: **Stokes' law: v = (γ_s − γ_w)D²/(18μ)** — settling velocity varies as the SQUARE of the diameter, so a reading at a known time and depth gives the proportion finer than one particular size.
examTip.trap: **The DEFLOCCULATING agent is essential** — clay particles naturally flocculate and would settle as large clusters, making the soil appear far coarser. Omitting it gives a plausible curve that is entirely wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **Clay particles are PLATY, not spherical, so the result is an EQUIVALENT settling diameter, not a measurement.** The method works from ~0.2 mm to ~0.2 µm — exactly the range sieving cannot reach below 75 µm.

questions.stem: The coefficient of permeability of a CLAY is typically of the order of:
options: Less than 10⁻⁹ m/s
10⁻³ m/s
10⁻¹ m/s
10⁻⁵ m/s
questions.solution:
**Less than 10⁻⁹ m/s.**

**Typical values across the soil types:**

| Soil | Coefficient of permeability, k (m/s) | Drainage character |
|---|---|---|
| **Clean GRAVEL** | **10⁻² to 1** ← | **Very good** |
| **Clean SAND, sand-gravel mixtures** | **10⁻⁵ to 10⁻²** ← (option d is in this band) | **Good** |
| **Fine sand, SILTY sand** | **10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁵** | Fair |
| **SILT, clayey silt** | **10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶** ← | **Poor** |
| **CLAY** | **Below 10⁻⁹** ← | **PRACTICALLY IMPERVIOUS** |

> **The range spans about TEN ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE from gravel to clay — a factor of ten thousand million — which is a far wider variation than any other soil property shows.**

> **No other engineering material property varies so much between members of the same family, and that is what makes permeability the dominant variable in every seepage, drainage and consolidation problem.**

> **Options (b), (c) and (d) all fall in the sand-to-gravel range, so the question turns on knowing where clay sits — several orders of magnitude below them.**

**Why clay is so nearly impervious:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The pores are extremely FINE** | **Flow through a capillary varies as the FOURTH POWER of its radius, so tiny pores throttle the flow enormously** ← |
| **The water nearest the particle surfaces is ADSORBED and nearly immobile** | **The ADSORBED (double layer) water is held electrically and does not flow** ← |
| **The flow path is extremely TORTUOUS** | ← |
| **The particles are PLATY and align, blocking the path** | ← |

> **The SECOND ROW is the distinctive one and is peculiar to clays: a substantial part of the pore water is chemically bound to the particle surfaces and takes no part in flow at all, so the EFFECTIVE porosity is far smaller than the total porosity.**

> **That is why a clay with 50 per cent porosity can be less permeable than a sand with 35 per cent — the quantity of voids matters far less than their SIZE and their connectivity.**

**The consequences of that ten-order range:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Clay is used as an IMPERVIOUS CORE in earth dams and as a landfill liner** ← | **Its low k is the design property** |
| **Clay CONSOLIDATES very slowly** | **Water must escape for the soil to compress, and it cannot escape quickly** ← |
| **Sand consolidates almost instantly** | **So settlement in sand is complete by the end of construction** ← |
| **Excavations in sand require DEWATERING; in clay they often do not** | ← |
| **Undrained conditions apply to clay under rapid loading; drained to sand always** ← | **The basis of the UU / CU / CD distinction** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CONNECTS PERMEABILITY TO EVERYTHING ELSE IN SOIL MECHANICS, and it deserves stating plainly: the choice between a total-stress and an effective-stress analysis is decided by whether the soil can drain in the time available.**

> **A sand drains as fast as it is loaded, so it is ALWAYS drained. A clay drains over years, so it is UNDRAINED during construction and drained only in the long term.**

> **Every distinction between short-term and long-term stability, between φ_u = 0 and c′-φ′ analysis, and between immediate and consolidation settlement, follows from those ten orders of magnitude.**

**How permeability is measured:**

| Method | Suits | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **CONSTANT HEAD permeameter** | **COARSE soils, k above about 10⁻⁴ m/s** ← | **A measurable quantity flows in reasonable time** |
| **FALLING HEAD permeameter** | **FINE soils, k below about 10⁻⁴ m/s** ← | **The flow is too small to measure directly, so the FALL of the head in a standpipe is measured instead** ← |
| **From the CONSOLIDATION test** | **Very fine soils — k = c_v m_v γ_w** ← | Indirect, for clays |
| **FIELD pumping test** | **Large-scale in-situ value** ← | **The most reliable, since it samples a large volume including its fissures and layering** ← |
| **Allen Hazen's formula** | **k ≈ C D₁₀² for clean sands, with D₁₀ in cm and k in cm/s** ← | A rough estimate |

> **THE FIELD PUMPING TEST'S ADVANTAGE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS SUBSTANTIAL AND IS OFTEN DECISIVE:**

> **A laboratory specimen is a hundred millimetres of intact soil. A real deposit contains sand lenses, fissures, root holes and layering, and the seepage travels through those rather than through the soil matrix.**

> **So the field value of a stratified deposit can be a hundred times the laboratory value, and always exceeds it — which means a dewatering scheme designed on laboratory permeability will be badly undersized.**

> **And the ANISOTROPY that produces it is systematic: a layered deposit is far more permeable HORIZONTALLY (along the layers) than VERTICALLY (across them), commonly by a factor of 10 to 100, since the vertical flow is throttled by the least permeable layer while the horizontal flow follows the most permeable one.**

examTip.trick: **Gravel 10⁻²-1, sand 10⁻⁵-10⁻², silt 10⁻⁸-10⁻⁶, CLAY below 10⁻⁹ m/s.** Ten orders of magnitude — a wider range than any other soil property shows.
examTip.trap: **Porosity does not govern permeability — pore SIZE does.** Clay at 50 % porosity is less permeable than sand at 35 %, because flow through a capillary varies as the FOURTH power of its radius and much of clay's water is adsorbed and immobile.
examTip.mnemonic: **FIELD permeability exceeds LABORATORY permeability, often a hundredfold** — fissures, lenses and layering carry the flow. And a layered deposit is 10-100× more permeable HORIZONTALLY than vertically.

questions.stem: In a correctly drawn FLOW NET, the flow lines and the equipotential lines:
options: Are parallel to one another everywhere
Intersect at 45 degrees
Intersect at RIGHT ANGLES, forming approximate curvilinear SQUARES
Intersect at angles that vary across the net
questions.solution:
**They intersect at RIGHT ANGLES, forming approximate curvilinear SQUARES.**

**The properties of a flow net:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Flow lines and equipotentials intersect ORTHOGONALLY** ← | **Because water flows in the direction of the steepest head gradient, which is perpendicular to the lines of equal head** ← |
| **The figures formed are curvilinear SQUARES** | **Their average length equals their average width** ← |
| **The DISCHARGE between any two adjacent flow lines is the SAME** ← | **Each "flow channel" carries an equal share** ← |
| **The HEAD DROP between any two adjacent equipotentials is the SAME** ← | **Δh = H / N_d** ← |
| **A boundary that is impervious is a FLOW LINE** | **Water cannot cross it** ← |
| **A boundary of constant head (the reservoir bed, the tailwater bed) is an EQUIPOTENTIAL** ← | ← |
| **The net is UNIQUE for a given geometry** | Independent of the permeability and the head |

> **THE ORTHOGONALITY IN THE FIRST ROW IS NOT A DRAWING CONVENTION BUT A PHYSICAL NECESSITY: flow follows the steepest gradient of head, and the steepest gradient from any point is always perpendicular to the contour of equal head through it.**

> **It is the same relationship as between contour lines and the direction of steepest slope on a topographic map — water running down a hillside crosses the contours at right angles, and seepage crosses equipotentials at right angles for exactly the same reason.**

**The discharge computation, which is what the net is drawn for:**

> **q = k H (N_f / N_d)** per unit length of structure

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **k** | Coefficient of permeability |
| **H** | **The TOTAL head lost across the structure** ← |
| **N_f** | **The number of FLOW CHANNELS (spaces BETWEEN flow lines, not the lines themselves)** ← |
| **N_d** | **The number of EQUIPOTENTIAL DROPS (spaces between equipotentials)** ← |

> **THE COUNTING OF SPACES RATHER THAN LINES IS THE COMMONEST ERROR: a net with 5 flow lines has 4 flow channels, and one with 11 equipotentials has 10 drops.**

> **A useful check: N_f/N_d for a typical sheet-pile problem is usually between 0.2 and 0.5. A ratio above 1 almost always means the lines have been counted instead of the spaces.**

**What the net yields beyond the discharge:**

| Quantity | How it is obtained |
|---|---|
| **Discharge** | **q = k H N_f/N_d** ← |
| **PORE PRESSURE at any point** | **Count the drops from the upstream boundary: h = H − (n_d × H/N_d), then u = γ_w × (that head plus the elevation head)** ← |
| **UPLIFT pressure on a structure's base** | **Read the pore pressures along the base and integrate** ← |
| **EXIT GRADIENT** | **i_e = Δh / l, with l the length of the LAST field at the downstream exit** ← |
| **Seepage FORCE** | **j = i γ_w per unit volume** |

> **THE EXIT GRADIENT IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SAFETY OUTPUT, and the net shows it directly: the field at the downstream exit is the SMALLEST square in the net, so the same head drop occurs over the shortest distance — and the gradient is therefore greatest there.**

> **That is a visual demonstration of why PIPING begins at the downstream exit, and it is why a deep downstream cut-off is so effective: lengthening the last flow path enlarges that final field and reduces the exit gradient directly.**

**How a flow net is drawn, since it is a graphical solution:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Draw the boundaries to scale, and identify which are flow lines and which are equipotentials** ← |
| **2** | **Sketch three or four flow lines, evenly spaced, following the boundary shapes** ← |
| **3** | **Draw equipotentials perpendicular to them, aiming for squares** ← |
| **4** | **CHECK: can a circle be inscribed in each figure, touching all four sides?** ← |
| **5** | **ADJUST and repeat — it is an iterative sketching process** ← |
| **6** | **The last row of fields may be part-squares; count them as a fraction** ← |

> **The INSCRIBED CIRCLE TEST in step 4 is the practical check for a curvilinear square, and it works where simply looking at the shape does not — the figures are curved, so "square" cannot be judged by eye.**

> **A flow net is a graphical solution to the LAPLACE EQUATION, which governs steady two-dimensional flow through an isotropic homogeneous medium — and the reason the sketching method works at all is that Laplace's equation has a unique solution for given boundary conditions.**
