> **So any net satisfying the boundary conditions and the square rule IS the solution, however it was arrived at — which is why a careful sketch is as valid as a numerical computation, and why the technique survived long after computers could solve the equation directly.**

> **For an ANISOTROPIC soil the net cannot be drawn directly, because the flow is no longer perpendicular to the equipotentials. The section is first TRANSFORMED by scaling the horizontal dimension by √(k_v/k_h), the net is drawn on the transformed section in the ordinary way, and the discharge is computed with an equivalent permeability of √(k_h k_v).**

examTip.trick: **Orthogonal intersections forming curvilinear SQUARES** — because flow follows the steepest head gradient, which is always perpendicular to lines of equal head. The same relation as contours and downhill flow on a map.
examTip.trap: **q = kH(N_f/N_d) counts SPACES, not lines** — 5 flow lines give 4 channels. A ratio above 1 almost always means lines were counted.
examTip.mnemonic: **The smallest field is at the downstream EXIT, so the exit gradient is greatest there** — which is why piping starts there and why a deep DOWNSTREAM cut-off works. Check squares by the INSCRIBED CIRCLE test.

questions.stem: In the stability analysis of a slope, a BASE FAILURE is one in which the slip surface:
options: Passes through the TOE of the slope
Passes BELOW the toe, through the soil beneath the slope's base
Intersects the slope FACE above the toe
Follows the ground surface without entering the soil
questions.solution:
**One in which the slip surface passes BELOW the toe**, through the soil beneath the base of the slope.

**The three modes of rotational slip:**

| Mode | Where the surface passes | When it occurs |
|---|---|---|
| **TOE failure** | **Through the TOE of the slope** ← (option a) | **The COMMONEST — for STEEP slopes, and for soils with an appreciable friction angle** ← |
| **SLOPE (face) failure** | **Intersects the FACE ABOVE the toe** ← (option c) | **Where a HARD STRATUM lies at shallow depth, or the upper part of the slope is markedly weaker** ← |
| **BASE failure** | **BELOW the toe, through the underlying soil** ← | **For FLAT slopes in SOFT CLAY (φ ≈ 0), with a firm stratum well below** ← |

> **Options (a) and (c) name the other two modes, so the option set requires all three to be distinguished.**

**What decides which mode occurs:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Slope ANGLE** | **STEEP slopes fail through the toe; FLAT slopes tend to base failure** ← |
| **The soil's FRICTION ANGLE** | **A frictional soil (φ > 0) fails through the toe; a purely cohesive soil (φ ≈ 0) can fail below it** ← |
| **DEPTH to a firm stratum** | **The DEPTH FACTOR D_f = (depth to firm stratum)/(height of slope) — a large D_f permits base failure** ← |
| **A weak layer within the soil** | **Forces a NON-CIRCULAR surface through it** ← |

> **THE DEPTH FACTOR IS THE CONTROLLING PARAMETER FOR THE φ = 0 CASE, and the rule is neat:**

| Depth factor D_f | Mode |
|---|---|
| **Small (a firm stratum close below)** | **The slip surface is CONFINED — toe or slope failure** ← |
| **Large (deep soft clay)** | **BASE failure, with the circle extending well below and beyond the toe** ← |
| **For a slope angle above about 53°** | **TOE failure occurs whatever the depth factor** ← |

> **The 53° threshold is a genuinely useful figure: above it the slope is steep enough that the critical circle always passes through the toe, so the depth to the firm stratum ceases to matter.**

**TAYLOR'S STABILITY NUMBER, which is how these cases are solved:**

> **S_n = c_m / (F γ H), or in the common form c_m = S_n γ H**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S_n** | **Taylor's stability number, read from his charts against the slope angle and φ** ← |
| **c_m** | The cohesion mobilised |
| **γ, H** | Unit weight and slope height |

> **The CRITICAL HEIGHT of a slope follows directly: H_c = c/(S_n γ), the height at which the factor of safety is exactly 1.**

> **And for a purely cohesive soil (φ = 0) with a vertical cut, the classical result is H_c = 4c/γ — a vertical face in clay will stand to that height and no further.**

> **That is the calculation behind the trench-collapse warning met earlier: a clay of c_u = 25 kPa and γ = 18 kN/m³ gives H_c = 100/18 = 5.5 m, and with a factor of safety of 1.5 the safe unsupported depth is well under 4 m — and that assumes the clay's undrained strength persists, which drying, wetting and vibration all reduce.**

**The methods of slope stability analysis:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **TAYLOR'S stability charts** | **Quick, for simple homogeneous slopes; no pore pressure** ← |
| **SWEDISH CIRCLE / φ = 0 method** | **For undrained clay; a single moment equation about the circle's centre** ← |
| **METHOD OF SLICES — FELLENIUS (ordinary)** | **Simple; ignores the inter-slice forces, so it is CONSERVATIVE, sometimes by 10-20 per cent** ← |
| **BISHOP'S simplified method** | **Includes the inter-slice NORMAL forces; more accurate; requires ITERATION** ← |
| **Janbu, Morgenstern-Price, Spencer** | **For NON-CIRCULAR surfaces and rigorous force equilibrium** ← |
| **Infinite slope analysis** | **For a long slope with a shallow slip parallel to the surface — the usual HILLSIDE case** ← |

> **THE INFINITE SLOPE CASE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE MOST RELEVANT TO NEPAL, and it is worth noting why: a Himalayan hillside failure is typically a shallow translational slide of a metre or two of weathered soil over rock, extending for a great distance along the slope.**

> **That is not a rotational circle at all, and analysing it as one gives the wrong answer. The infinite slope analysis is the correct model, and for a cohesionless soil with seepage parallel to the surface it gives the memorable result:**

> **F = (γ′/γ_sat) × (tan φ / tan β) — roughly HALF the dry-slope value, since γ′/γ_sat ≈ 0.5.**

> **So a slope that is stable when dry has its factor of safety approximately HALVED when fully saturated with seepage — which is precisely why Nepali hillsides fail during the monsoon and stand for the rest of the year, and why drainage is the single most effective slope stabilisation measure available.**

examTip.trick: **TOE failure through the toe (steep slopes, φ > 0); SLOPE failure above the toe (hard stratum shallow); BASE failure below the toe (flat slopes, soft clay, deep firm stratum).** Options (a) and (c) are the other two modes.
examTip.trap: **Above a slope angle of about 53°, TOE failure occurs whatever the depth factor** — the depth to the firm stratum stops mattering.
examTip.mnemonic: **For a Nepali hillside use the INFINITE SLOPE model, not a circle** — the failure is a shallow translational slide. And F ≈ (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β) means saturation roughly HALVES the factor of safety, which is why drainage is the best stabilisation there is.

questions.stem: In slope stability analysis, the FACTOR OF SAFETY with respect to SHEAR STRENGTH is defined as the ratio of:
options: The height of the slope to its critical height
The resisting moment to the overturning moment about the toe
The cohesion available to the cohesion mobilised, only
The AVAILABLE shear strength to the shear stress MOBILISED along the slip surface
questions.solution:
**The AVAILABLE shear strength to the shear stress MOBILISED along the slip surface.**

> **F = τ_f / τ_m = (c′ + σ′ tan φ′) / (c_m + σ′ tan φ_m)**

**The several definitions of the factor of safety, which are NOT interchangeable:**

| Definition | Expression | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **With respect to SHEAR STRENGTH, F_s** | **τ_f / τ_m** ← | **The fundamental definition — BOTH c and φ are reduced by the same factor** ← |
| **With respect to COHESION, F_c** | **c / c_m** ← (option c) | **Only the cohesion is factored; φ is taken as fully mobilised** ← |
| **With respect to FRICTION, F_φ** | **tan φ / tan φ_m** | Only the friction is factored |
| **With respect to HEIGHT, F_H** | **H_c / H** ← (option a) | **The critical height divided by the actual height** ← |
| **MOMENT ratio (for a circular slip)** | **Resisting moment / disturbing moment** ← (option b) | **Equivalent to F_s for a circle, since the radius is common to both** ← |

> **Every option therefore names a real and used definition, which is what makes this question one of discrimination rather than recall.**

> **The condition F_c = F_φ = F_s is what defines the factor of safety with respect to STRENGTH, and it is the one intended whenever "the factor of safety" is quoted without qualification.**

**Why the distinctions matter — they give DIFFERENT numbers:**

> **For a c-φ soil, the several factors are generally unequal, and quoting the wrong one overstates the safety.**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **F_c is always the LARGEST** | **Because factoring cohesion alone requires a larger reduction to reach equilibrium** ← |
| **F_s lies between F_c and F_φ** | ← |
| **F_H can be very much larger than F_s** | **Because strength does not vary linearly with height — a slope at half its critical height is far more than twice as safe** ← |

> **THE F_H POINT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST MISLEADING IN PRACTICE: a slope at 60 per cent of its critical height might have F_H = 1.67 and F_s = 1.2, and only the second is the meaningful measure.**

> **Quoting a factor of safety without saying which definition was used is therefore not a pedantic omission but a substantive one.**

**The values required in practice:**

| Situation | Minimum F |
|---|---|
| **Permanent slopes, long-term (drained) conditions** | **1.3 to 1.5** ← |
| **End-of-construction (undrained) conditions** | **1.25 to 1.3** ← |
| **Temporary works and short-term excavations** | **1.2 to 1.3** |
| **Under EARTHQUAKE loading (pseudo-static)** | **1.0 to 1.15 — deliberately low** ← |
| **Where failure would endanger life or major property** | **1.5 and above** ← |

> **THE SEISMIC VALUE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS DELIBERATELY CLOSE TO UNITY, and the reasoning is worth stating because it looks alarming:**

> **The pseudo-static analysis applies the design earthquake acceleration as a permanent horizontal force, which is severe and unrealistic — a real earthquake applies it for a fraction of a second at a time, reversing repeatedly.**

> **A slope may exceed F = 1 momentarily and simply displace a few millimetres rather than failing, since the driving force reverses before a failure can develop.**

> **So a pseudo-static F just above 1 does not mean the slope is on the point of collapse; it means it may deform slightly during the earthquake — which is what NEWMARK'S SLIDING BLOCK analysis quantifies, computing the accumulated displacement rather than a pass-or-fail factor.**

**And what actually reduces the factor of safety in service, which is where slopes are lost:**

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **RAINFALL and rising pore pressure** | **The dominant cause — it reduces effective stress and hence strength** ← |
| **LOADING at the crest** | **A building, a spoil heap, a road embankment placed on the head of a slope** ← |
| **EXCAVATION at the toe** | **Removing the material that was buttressing the slope — the commonest engineering-induced cause** ← |
| **Vegetation removal** | Loss of root reinforcement and of transpiration |
| **Vibration** | Earthquake, blasting, traffic |
| **Progressive weathering and softening** | **Long-term strength loss in stiff clays** ← |
| **Erosion of the toe by a river** | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER DESCRIBE THE COMMONEST WAY ENGINEERING WORK CAUSES A LANDSLIDE, and both are avoidable: LOAD AT THE CREST and CUT AT THE TOE are the two worst things that can be done to a slope, and a hill road frequently does both at once.**

> **Cutting into the hillside removes the toe support of the slope above, and casting the spoil over the edge loads the crest of the slope below — so a single carelessly built road can destabilise the hillside on both sides of it.**

> **That is the mechanism behind the strong statistical association between road construction and landslide frequency in Nepal, and it is why spoil disposal and cut-slope design are not environmental afterthoughts but the core of hill road engineering.**

examTip.trick: **F_s = available shear strength ÷ mobilised shear stress, with BOTH c and φ reduced by the same factor.** Every option is a real definition — F_c, F_H and the moment ratio are all used.
examTip.trap: **F_H can be far larger than F_s** — a slope at 60 % of its critical height may show F_H = 1.67 and F_s = 1.2. Quoting a factor without naming the definition is a substantive omission.
examTip.mnemonic: **LOAD AT THE CREST and CUT AT THE TOE are the two worst things you can do to a slope — and a hill road does both at once.** That is why spoil disposal and cut-slope design are the core of hill road engineering, not an afterthought.

questions.stem: For a soil sampler to obtain a good UNDISTURBED sample, its AREA RATIO should not exceed about:
options: 10 per cent
25 per cent
50 per cent
100 per cent
questions.solution:
**10 per cent.**

**The area ratio and what it measures:**

> **A_r = (D_o² − D_i²) / D_i² × 100 per cent**

> **where D_o is the sampler's OUTSIDE diameter and D_i its INSIDE diameter at the cutting edge.**

| What it represents | Note |
|---|---|
| **The volume of soil DISPLACED by the sampler's wall, as a proportion of the sample's volume** ← | **A thick wall pushes soil aside, and that soil has to go somewhere** ← |
| **A LOW area ratio means a THIN wall** | **Less displacement, less disturbance** ← |
| **A HIGH area ratio means the sample is severely remoulded** | ← |

> **The displaced soil is forced sideways and downward, compressing and shearing the material the sampler is about to enter — so the sample is disturbed BEFORE it is even collected.**

**Typical values:**

| Sampler | Area ratio | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **THIN-WALLED (Shelby) tube** | **About 10 per cent** ← | **UNDISTURBED sampling of soft to firm clays** ← |
| **Piston sampler** | **10 per cent or less** | **The best undisturbed samples in soft clay** ← |
| **SPLIT-SPOON sampler (SPT)** | **Over 100 per cent** ← | **DISTURBED samples only — its purpose is the blow count, not the sample** ← |
| **Thick-walled open drive sampler** | 20 to 30 per cent | Disturbed to semi-disturbed |

> **THE SPLIT-SPOON'S FIGURE MAKES THE POINT VIVIDLY: its wall displaces more soil than the sample it collects, so the material recovered is thoroughly remoulded.**

> **That is not a defect — the SPT exists to measure PENETRATION RESISTANCE, and its sample is a bonus used for identification and classification only. Using an SPT sample for a strength or consolidation test is the error.**

**The other design requirements for an undisturbed sampler:**

| Parameter | Requirement | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **AREA ratio** | **≤ 10 per cent** ← | Minimise displacement |
| **INSIDE CLEARANCE ratio** | **0.5 to 3 per cent: (D_s − D_i)/D_i, with D_s the inside diameter of the tube above the cutting edge** ← | **Allows the sample to expand slightly and reduces FRICTION as it moves up the tube** ← |
| **OUTSIDE CLEARANCE ratio** | **0 to 2 per cent** | **Reduces friction on the OUTSIDE during withdrawal** ← |
| **RECOVERY ratio** | **Length of sample recovered ÷ depth of penetration; should be close to 1** ← | **Below 1 means the sample compressed; ABOVE 1 means it swelled or the tube collected material from a collapse** ← |
| **Cutting edge taper angle** | **10 to 15 degrees; a sharper edge cuts rather than displaces** ← | ← |

> **THE INSIDE CLEARANCE IS THE MOST SUBTLE OF THESE AND IT SOLVES A REAL PROBLEM: without it, the sample would rub against the full length of the tube as it is driven, and the friction would compress and shear it progressively.**

> **A slight enlargement above the cutting edge means the sample touches the tube only at the edge itself, and slides freely thereafter.**

> **Too MUCH clearance, however, lets the sample expand and lose its structure — hence the narrow 0.5 to 3 per cent band, which is a genuine optimum rather than a tolerance.**

**The sources of disturbance, of which the sampler is only one:**

| Stage | Disturbance |
|---|---|
| **BORING** | **Stress relief at the bottom of the hole; the base heaves as the overburden is removed** ← |
| **Sampling** | **Displacement by the wall; friction; shearing at the edge** ← |
| **WITHDRAWAL** | **Suction at the base; the sample may slip out** ← |
| **TRANSPORT** | **Vibration, shock, temperature change** ← |
| **STORAGE** | **Moisture loss; the ends must be SEALED WITH WAX immediately** ← |
| **EXTRUSION in the laboratory** | **Must be pushed out in the SAME DIRECTION it entered, or it is sheared** ← |
| **Trimming and mounting** | Final handling |

> **THE EXTRUSION DIRECTION IN THE SIXTH ROW IS A DETAIL WORTH KNOWING, because it is easy to get wrong and it destroys the sample: pushing the sample back out through the cutting edge forces it through the constriction a second time.**

> **And the STRESS RELIEF in the first row is the disturbance that cannot be eliminated at all: removing the overburden allows the soil to swell, and a sample can never be returned to its in-situ stress state exactly.**

> **That inescapable disturbance is one of the main arguments for IN-SITU testing — the vane shear, the pressuremeter, the cone penetrometer and the plate load test all measure the soil where it lies, avoiding sampling entirely.**

> **For SOFT SENSITIVE clays, where sampling disturbance can destroy most of the strength, in-situ testing is not merely preferable but necessary — a laboratory result on such a sample measures the handling rather than the soil.**

examTip.trick: **A_r = (D_o² − D_i²)/D_i² × 100 ≤ 10 %** for an undisturbed sample. A thin-walled Shelby tube achieves about 10 %; the SPT split spoon exceeds 100 %.
examTip.trap: **The SPT sample is DISTURBED by design** — the tool exists to measure the blow count, and its sample is for identification only. Using it for strength or consolidation testing is the error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Inside clearance 0.5-3 % lets the sample slide free of the tube after the cutting edge** — too little and friction shears it, too much and it swells. And extrude the sample the SAME WAY it entered, or it passes the constriction twice.

questions.stem: A COUNTERFORT retaining wall differs from a cantilever retaining wall in that the counterforts are:
options: Placed on the front (exposed) face and act in compression
Provided only at the two ends of the wall
Placed on the BACKFILL side, tying the stem to the heel slab, and act in TENSION
Horizontal beams spanning between the toe and the heel
questions.solution:
**Placed on the BACKFILL side, tying the stem to the heel slab, and acting in TENSION.**

**Counterfort against buttress — the pair that must be distinguished:**

| | COUNTERFORT | BUTTRESS |
|---|---|---|
| **Position** | **On the BACKFILL (earth) side — hidden in the fill** ← | **On the FRONT (exposed) side** ← (option a) |
| **Action** | **TENSION — it hangs the stem back to the heel** ← | **COMPRESSION — it props the stem** ← |
| **Structural efficiency** | **Less efficient — concrete is weak in tension, so the counterfort needs reinforcement** ← | **MORE efficient — concrete is strong in compression** ← |
| **Appearance and usable space** | **BETTER — nothing projects on the visible face** ← | **Worse — the buttresses occupy space in front** ← |
| **Which is normally used** | **COUNTERFORT, despite being structurally inferior** ← | Rare |

> **THE CHOICE BETWEEN THEM IS DECIDED BY SPACE AND APPEARANCE RATHER THAN BY STRUCTURAL LOGIC, which is worth noticing: the buttress is the better structure and the counterfort is the one that gets built.**

> **A buttress projecting into the space in front of a wall is usually unacceptable — it obstructs a road, a walkway or a building line — while a counterfort disappears into the backfill and costs nothing in usable space.**

> **So the reinforcement needed to make concrete work in tension is accepted as the price of keeping the front face clear.**

**The types of retaining wall and their height ranges:**

| Type | Resists overturning by | Economical height |
|---|---|---|
| **GRAVITY wall (mass concrete, masonry)** | **Its own WEIGHT alone; designed for NO TENSION anywhere** ← | **Up to about 3 m** ← |
| **SEMI-GRAVITY** | Weight, with nominal reinforcement | 3 to 4 m |
| **CANTILEVER (T or L shaped)** | **The WEIGHT OF BACKFILL on the heel slab, plus the wall's own weight; the stem cantilevers from the base** ← | **Up to about 6 to 7 m** ← |
| **COUNTERFORT** | **As the cantilever, with counterforts reducing the stem's span** ← | **Above 6 to 7 m** ← |
| **Buttressed** | As counterfort, props in front | Above 6 to 7 m |
| **Crib, gabion, reinforced earth** | **Flexible systems; reinforced earth is economical to great heights** ← | Various |

> **THE CANTILEVER WALL'S MECHANISM IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE KEY IDEA AND IS OFTEN MISSED: it does not resist by its own weight, which is small.**

> **It resists by the WEIGHT OF THE SOIL SITTING ON ITS HEEL SLAB — the backfill is made to hold itself back.**

> **That is why the heel slab extends well into the fill, and it is why a cantilever wall is so much more economical than a gravity wall: the stabilising mass is soil that was going to be there anyway, and costs nothing.**

**Why the COUNTERFORT is needed above 6 or 7 metres:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Earth pressure increases LINEARLY with depth** | **So the stem's bending moment grows as the CUBE of the height** ← |
| **At 7 m the stem base becomes very thick** | **Uneconomical, and difficult to construct** ← |
| **A counterfort converts the stem from a CANTILEVER into a CONTINUOUS SLAB spanning horizontally between the counterforts** ← | **Reducing its moments dramatically** ← |
| **Typical counterfort spacing** | **One third to one half of the wall height** ← |

> **The H³ dependence in the first row is what makes tall cantilever walls uneconomic: doubling the height multiplies the stem moment by EIGHT, so the thickness required grows very quickly.**

> **Interrupting that cantilever with counterforts at intervals changes the span direction entirely, and the stem then behaves as a slab spanning a few metres horizontally rather than a cantilever standing several metres vertically.**

**The stability checks, which apply to every type:**

| Check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Against OVERTURNING about the toe** | **Factor of safety ≥ 1.5 (2.0 where the surcharge is uncertain)** ← |
| **Against SLIDING on the base** | **≥ 1.5; often the CRITICAL check, and a SHEAR KEY is added if it fails** ← |
| **BEARING pressure at the base** | **Maximum within the safe bearing capacity; and NO TENSION, so the resultant within the MIDDLE THIRD** ← |
| **Against deep-seated slip** | **A slope stability analysis of the whole mass — often overlooked** ← |
| **Structural design of stem, toe, heel and counterforts** | To the computed pressures |

> **SLIDING IS FREQUENTLY THE GOVERNING CHECK, and the SHEAR KEY is the standard remedy: a downstand beneath the base that mobilises passive resistance in the soil in front of it.**

> **And the DEEP-SEATED SLIP in the fourth row is the check most often omitted and the one that produces the most spectacular failures: the wall itself may be perfectly satisfactory while the entire hillside, wall and all, slides on a surface passing well below the base.**

> **A retaining wall built on a marginally stable slope adds weight to it, and can be the load that initiates the slide — so the wall must be checked as part of the slope, not merely as a structure standing on it.**

> **That check belongs to slope stability rather than to retaining wall design, which is precisely why it falls between the two and gets missed.**

examTip.trick: **COUNTERFORT: backfill side, TENSION. BUTTRESS: front face, COMPRESSION.** Option (a) is the buttress — structurally the better of the two, and the one rarely built because it occupies space in front.
examTip.trap: **A cantilever wall resists by the WEIGHT OF BACKFILL ON ITS HEEL, not by its own weight** — which is why the heel extends into the fill and why it is far cheaper than a gravity wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stem moment grows as H³, so cantilever walls become uneconomic above 6-7 m** — counterforts turn the stem into a slab spanning horizontally. And check the DEEP-SEATED SLIP: the wall can be perfect while the whole hillside moves.

questions.stem: In a WELL (caisson) foundation for a bridge pier, the STEINING is the:
options: Wedge-shaped cutting edge at the bottom of the well
THICK CYLINDRICAL WALL of the well, which provides the weight to sink it and transfers the load
Concrete plug placed at the bottom after sinking
Slab cast over the top of the well to support the pier
questions.solution:
**The THICK CYLINDRICAL WALL of the well** — which provides the weight to sink it and transfers the pier's load to the founding stratum.

**The components of a well foundation:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **CUTTING EDGE** | **A wedge-shaped steel-shod edge at the bottom that CUTS into the soil as the well sinks** ← (option a) |
| **WELL CURB** | **The tapered reinforced concrete transition between the cutting edge and the steining** ← |
| **STEINING** | **The thick wall — provides SINKING WEIGHT, resists the soil pressure, and carries the load** ← |
| **BOTTOM PLUG** | **Concrete placed at the base after sinking, transmitting the load to the founding stratum** ← (option c) |
| **SAND FILLING** | **Fills the dredge hole; adds weight and stability, and reduces the steining's bending** ← |
| **TOP PLUG** | Concrete over the sand filling |
| **WELL CAP** | **The slab over the top, on which the pier stands** ← (option d) |

> **Every distractor names a real component of the same structure, so the question requires the parts to be known individually.**

**The steining's three functions, which is why it is so thick:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provides the WEIGHT to sink the well** ← | **The well sinks under its own weight as the soil is dredged from within — so it must be heavy enough to overcome the skin friction** ← |
| **Resists the EXTERNAL earth and water pressure** | Acting as a ring in compression |
| **Transfers the superstructure's load to the base** | ← |

> **THE SINKING FUNCTION IS WHAT DICTATES THE THICKNESS, and it explains a feature that otherwise looks wasteful: the steining is far thicker than strength alone requires.**

> **The well sinks only if its weight exceeds the SKIN FRICTION on its outside surface, and that friction grows as the well goes deeper — so the deeper the well must sink, the heavier the steining must be.**

> **Typical thickness is 0.4 to 0.8 times the well's outside diameter for deep wells, which is a very substantial wall.**

> **Where the well refuses to sink despite its weight, the remedies are to add KENTLEDGE (temporary weight on top), to dewater the inside (reducing the buoyancy), to apply a BENTONITE slurry to the outside (reducing the friction), or to use water jetting.**

**Why a well foundation is used at all:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **It can be sunk to GREAT DEPTH through soft alluvium to a firm stratum** ← | **Which is the usual condition of a large Indian or Nepali river** |
| **It resists SCOUR** | **Founded well below the maximum scour depth, computed from Lacey** ← |
| **It carries very large VERTICAL and HORIZONTAL loads and moments** | **From the superstructure, from water current, from impact and from earthquake** ← |
| **It provides a large, rigid, monolithic foundation** | ← |
| **It can be sunk through water without a cofferdam** | ← |

> **THE SCOUR REQUIREMENT IS USUALLY WHAT DETERMINES THE DEPTH, and it connects directly to the river training discussed earlier: the well must be founded a prescribed distance BELOW the deepest scour the river can produce.**

> **Lacey's normal scour depth R = 0.473(Q/f)^(1/3) is multiplied by a factor for the location (up to 2.0 at a pier nose), and the well's grip length below that is then specified.**

> **A bridge pier undermined by scour is among the commonest causes of bridge failure worldwide, and the well foundation exists largely to prevent it.**

**The DIFFICULTIES of well sinking, which make it a specialised operation:**

| Difficulty | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **TILT and SHIFT — the well leans or moves off position** ← | **Eccentric dredging, kentledge on the high side, water jetting on the high side, pulling with hooks; strict limits are specified (tilt 1 in 60, shift 150 mm)** ← |
| **The well refuses to sink** | Kentledge, dewatering, bentonite, jetting |
| **SUDDEN sinking, when a soft layer is met** | **Dangerous; can crack the steining and cause a large tilt** ← |
| **Obstructions — boulders, old timber, rock ledges** | Divers, blasting, chiselling |
| **Sand blowing into the well under a head difference** | Maintain water inside |

> **TILT AND SHIFT ARE THE CHARACTERISTIC PROBLEM OF WELL SINKING, and correcting them is a real art: the well is many metres across and hundreds of tonnes in weight, and once it begins to lean it tends to continue.**

> **The correction is applied continuously as the sinking proceeds — dredging preferentially on the high side so that the well drops there faster — and it demands constant monitoring, because a tilt allowed to develop is far harder to correct than one caught early.**

> **An excessive final tilt is not merely untidy: it displaces the pier from its designed position, introduces eccentric loading, and may require the well cap to be built eccentrically to bring the pier back onto its line.**

**And the SHAPES of well, since each suits a condition:**

| Shape | Note |
|---|---|
| **CIRCULAR** | **The commonest — a simple shape, uniform strength in all directions, easy to sink, and least liable to tilt** ← |
| **DOUBLE-D** | **Two circles joined; suits a long pier without an excessively large single well** ← |
| **Twin circular** | Two separate wells under one cap |
| **RECTANGULAR / square** | **Suits a long pier, and is more difficult to sink; corners attract stress** ← |
| **Dumb-bell, twin hexagonal, twin octagonal** | For very large piers |

> **The CIRCULAR well's dominance follows from the sinking process rather than from the structure: a circular well presents uniform friction all round, so it sinks evenly and resists tilting, while a rectangular one meets uneven resistance and tilts readily.**

> **That is a good illustration of a recurring theme in foundation engineering — the CONSTRUCTION method frequently governs the design more than the structural requirements do.**

examTip.trick: **Cutting edge → curb → STEINING (the thick wall) → bottom plug → sand filling → top plug → well cap.** Every distractor names another real component.
examTip.trap: **The steining's thickness is set by the SINKING requirement, not by strength** — it must outweigh the skin friction, which grows with depth. Typically 0.4-0.8 × the diameter.
examTip.mnemonic: **TILT and SHIFT are the characteristic problem** (limits 1 in 60 and 150 mm) — corrected by dredging preferentially on the high side, continuously. And CIRCULAR wells dominate because they sink evenly, not because they are structurally better.

questions.stem: A clay layer 4 m thick, drained on BOTH faces, reaches 50 per cent consolidation in 1 year. If the same layer were drained on ONE face only, the time to reach 50 per cent consolidation would be:
options: 6 months
2 years
1 year
4 years
questions.solution:
**4 years.**

**The reasoning:**

> **T_v = c_v t / d², where d is the length of the DRAINAGE PATH.**

| Drainage | Drainage path d | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **DOUBLE drainage (both faces)** | **H/2 = 4/2 = 2 m** ← | **Water escapes to the nearer face, so the longest journey is half the layer** ← |
| **SINGLE drainage (one face)** | **H = 4 m** ← | **Water from the far side must travel the FULL thickness** ← |

> **For the same degree of consolidation, T_v is the same, so c_v t/d² is the same, and therefore t ∝ d².**

> **Doubling the drainage path from 2 m to 4 m therefore multiplies the time by 2² = 4.**

> **t = 1 year × 4 = 4 YEARS** ←

| Distractor | The error |
|---|---|
| **2 years** | **Time taken as proportional to d rather than to d²** ← |
| **6 months** | The relation inverted |
| **1 year** | Drainage conditions assumed not to matter |

> **THE SQUARE LAW IS THE WHOLE POINT AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL RELATION IN CONSOLIDATION: TIME VARIES AS THE SQUARE OF THE DRAINAGE PATH.**

> **A 2 m thick clay layer consolidates in a quarter of the time of a 4 m layer, not half — and a 20 m layer takes a hundred times as long as a 2 m one.**

> **That is why thick clay deposits take decades to consolidate and why the drainage conditions must be established before any settlement rate is computed.**

**Identifying the drainage conditions, which is where the error is usually made:**

| Condition | Drainage path |
|---|---|
| **Clay between two SAND layers** | **DOUBLE — d = H/2** ← |
| **Clay over IMPERVIOUS rock, with sand above** | **SINGLE — d = H** ← |
| **Clay over rock with an impervious surface above** | **No drainage — it does not consolidate at all** |
| **Clay with a thin SAND SEAM within it** | **The seam acts as a drainage face, so d is measured to the NEAREST drainage boundary** ← |

> **THE SAND SEAM CASE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE THAT OVERTURNS PREDICTIONS IN PRACTICE: a thin, easily overlooked sand lens within a clay layer halves or quarters the drainage path and can reduce a predicted consolidation time by an order of magnitude.**

> **Settlements have repeatedly occurred far FASTER than predicted for exactly this reason — and since faster settlement is generally welcome, the error is discovered without much harm.**

> **The reverse error is the damaging one: assuming double drainage where an impervious stratum in fact seals one face, and finding that a settlement expected to finish in five years is still continuing at twenty.**

**The other terms in the consolidation calculation:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **T_v — TIME FACTOR** | **Dimensionless; depends only on the DEGREE of consolidation** ← |
| **T_v at 50 per cent** | **0.197** ← |
| **T_v at 90 per cent** | **0.848** ← |
| **c_v — coefficient of consolidation** | **m²/year; from the oedometer test, by the square-root-of-time or log-time fitting method** ← |
| **U — degree of consolidation** | The proportion of the ultimate settlement achieved |

> **The pair of T_v values gives a useful shortcut: since T_v at 90 per cent is 4.3 times that at 50 per cent, the time to reach 90 per cent is 4.3 times the time to reach 50 per cent.**

> **So the clay in this question, taking 4 years to reach 50 per cent under single drainage, would take about 17 years to reach 90 per cent — which puts the practical difficulty of consolidation settlement in perspective.**

**And the engineering responses to slow consolidation:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **PRELOADING (surcharging)** | **Load the site with fill BEFORE construction, let it consolidate, then remove the fill and build** ← |
| **VERTICAL (sand or band) DRAINS** | **Install closely spaced vertical drains, so the water escapes HORIZONTALLY over a short distance instead of vertically over a long one** ← |
| **Surcharge PLUS drains** | **The standard combination for soft ground** ← |
| **Vacuum consolidation** | Applies suction instead of a surcharge |
| **Stone columns, soil replacement, piling** | Avoid the problem rather than solve it |

> **THE VERTICAL DRAIN IS THE MOST ELEGANT OF THESE, AND ITS EFFECTIVENESS FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM THE SQUARE LAW THIS QUESTION DEMONSTRATES:**

> **A 10 m clay layer with double drainage has a drainage path of 5 m. Install band drains at 1.5 m spacing, and the water need only travel about 0.75 m horizontally to reach one.**

> **The path is reduced by a factor of nearly 7, so the time falls by a factor of nearly 50 — turning a twenty-year consolidation into a few months.**

> **And the horizontal permeability of a layered clay is typically several times the vertical, which improves the result further.**

> **That is why preloading with vertical drains is the standard treatment for soft alluvial ground beneath embankments and reclamations, and why it makes construction possible on deposits that would otherwise be unusable.**

examTip.trick: **T_v = c_v t/d², so for the same U, t ∝ d².** Double drainage d = H/2 = 2 m; single drainage d = H = 4 m. Doubling the path QUADRUPLES the time: 1 year → 4 years.
examTip.trap: **A thin SAND SEAM within a clay layer acts as a drainage face** and can cut the predicted time by an order of magnitude. The damaging error is the reverse — assuming double drainage where one face is sealed.
examTip.mnemonic: **T_v = 0.197 at 50 %, 0.848 at 90 % — so t₉₀ ≈ 4.3 t₅₀.** And VERTICAL DRAINS exploit the square law: cutting the path from 5 m to 0.75 m cuts the time nearly fiftyfold, turning twenty years into months.

questions.stem: The SPECIFIC WEIGHT of a fluid is:
options: Its weight per unit VOLUME, equal to ρg
Its mass per unit volume
The ratio of its density to the density of water
The volume occupied by unit mass
questions.solution:
**Its WEIGHT per unit VOLUME, γ = ρg.**

**The four related properties, which the option set draws on:**

| Property | Symbol | Definition | SI unit | For water at 4 °C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DENSITY (mass density)** | **ρ** | **MASS per unit volume** ← (option b) | **kg/m³** | **1,000 kg/m³** |
| **SPECIFIC WEIGHT (weight density)** | **γ** | **WEIGHT per unit volume = ρg** ← | **N/m³** | **9,810 N/m³ (9.81 kN/m³)** ← |
| **SPECIFIC VOLUME** | **v** | **VOLUME per unit mass = 1/ρ** ← (option d) | **m³/kg** | **0.001 m³/kg** |
| **SPECIFIC GRAVITY (relative density)** | **S** | **The ratio of the fluid's density to WATER's** ← (option c) | **DIMENSIONLESS** ← | **1.0** |

> **Every distractor is one of the other three, so the question is purely one of definition — and the four are constantly interchanged.**

**The distinction that matters most in practice:**

> **DENSITY is a property of the SUBSTANCE. SPECIFIC WEIGHT depends on the LOCAL GRAVITY as well.**

| Location | ρ for water | g | γ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sea level** | **1,000 kg/m³** | **9.81 m/s²** | **9,810 N/m³** |
| **On the Moon** | **1,000 kg/m³ — UNCHANGED** ← | **1.62 m/s²** | **1,620 N/m³ — a sixth** ← |

> **So density travels and specific weight does not — which is why fundamental relations are usually written in terms of ρ, and why hydrostatic pressure (p = γh = ρgh) can be written either way.**

> **And SPECIFIC GRAVITY is dimensionless, so it is the same number in every system of units — which is why material data tables quote it in preference to density.**

**Typical values worth carrying:**

| Fluid or material | Specific gravity |
|---|---|
| **Water (the reference)** | **1.00** |
| **Sea water** | **1.025** ← |
| **MERCURY** | **13.6** ← |
| **Petrol / kerosene** | **0.7 to 0.8** ← |
| **Engine oil** | 0.88 to 0.94 |
| **Concrete** | 2.4 (plain) to 2.5 (reinforced) |
| **Soil solids** | **2.65 to 2.70** ← |
| **Steel** | 7.85 |
| **Air at 20 °C** | **0.0012 — about 1/800 of water** ← |

> **MERCURY's 13.6 is the figure to have by heart, because it converts every manometer reading: 1 mm of mercury equals 13.6 mm of water, and a standard atmosphere of 760 mm Hg is 760 × 13.6 = 10,336 mm ≈ 10.33 m of water.**

> **That single multiplication reproduces the atmospheric-pressure figure met in the absolute-pressure discussion without any need to memorise it separately.**

**And the AIR row, which is easy to dismiss and matters in two places:**

> **Air's density is about 1/800 of water's, which is why buoyancy in air is normally neglected — but it is not always negligible.**

| Where air's density matters | Note |
|---|---|
| **WIND LOADING on structures** | **p = ½ρV², and ρ = 1.2 kg/m³ — the whole of wind engineering rests on it** ← |
| **Weighing a large light object precisely** | Air buoyancy correction |
| **Hot air balloons and chimney draught** | **Density difference from temperature** ← |
| **DENSITY ALTITUDE for aircraft and turbines** | **The runway-length correction met earlier** ← |

> **The WIND LOADING row is the one a civil engineer uses constantly, and it is worth noticing that the same ½ρV² that gives a negligible pressure for slow air gives a substantial one at speed: at 40 m/s (144 km/h), ½ × 1.2 × 40² = 960 N/m², approaching a kilonewton per square metre.**

> **That is comparable with a floor's imposed load, applied horizontally to the whole face of a building — which is why wind governs the lateral design of tall and light structures.**

examTip.trick: **γ = ρg, weight per unit VOLUME, in N/m³.** The distractors are density (b), specific gravity (c) and specific volume (d) — all four are constantly interchanged.
examTip.trap: **Density is a property of the SUBSTANCE; specific weight depends on LOCAL GRAVITY too.** Water's density is the same on the Moon; its specific weight is a sixth.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mercury's SG of 13.6 converts every manometer reading** — and 760 mm Hg × 13.6 = 10.33 m of water, which reproduces atmospheric pressure without memorising it. Air is 1/800 of water, yet ½ρV² at 40 m/s is nearly 1 kN/m².

questions.stem: The NO-SLIP CONDITION in fluid mechanics states that:
options: A fluid cannot sustain a shear stress at rest
The fluid in contact with a solid boundary has the SAME VELOCITY as the boundary, so the relative velocity there is ZERO
The pressure is the same in all directions at a point
A fluid always flows from high pressure to low pressure
questions.solution:
**The fluid in contact with a solid boundary has the SAME VELOCITY as that boundary** — the relative velocity at the surface is zero.

**What follows from it:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A VELOCITY GRADIENT must exist near the wall** | **The velocity goes from zero at the surface to the free-stream value away from it** ← |
| **A SHEAR STRESS therefore acts at the wall** | **τ = μ(du/dy), and du/dy is greatest at the wall** ← |
| **The BOUNDARY LAYER exists** | **The thin region in which that gradient is confined** ← |
| **VISCOUS DRAG on every surface** | **Skin friction — the resistance a pipe or a ship's hull offers** ← |
| **Pipe friction and head loss** | **All of it originates here** ← |

> **THE NO-SLIP CONDITION IS THE ORIGIN OF EVERY VISCOUS EFFECT IN ENGINEERING FLUID MECHANICS, and it is worth appreciating that it is an EXPERIMENTAL observation rather than a derived result.**

> **There is no first-principles proof of it; it is what is observed for ordinary fluids on ordinary surfaces, and the whole of boundary layer theory is built on it.**

> **Option (a) states the definition of a FLUID (a substance that deforms continuously under any shear stress), option (c) is PASCAL'S LAW, and option (d) is a loose statement about flow direction — all real statements, none of them this one.**

**The BOUNDARY LAYER, which the condition creates:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Definition** | **The thin layer near a surface in which the velocity rises from zero to about 99 per cent of the free-stream value** ← |
| **Outside it** | **The flow behaves as if INVISCID — which is why Bernoulli's frictionless assumption works so well away from surfaces** ← |
| **It THICKENS along the surface** | As more fluid is retarded |
| **It begins LAMINAR and becomes TURBULENT** | **Transition at a Reynolds number of about 5 × 10⁵ on a flat plate** ← |
| **A turbulent boundary layer is THICKER and has MORE drag** | **But it resists SEPARATION better** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS PRANDTL'S GREAT INSIGHT OF 1904 AND IT RECONCILED TWO CENTURIES OF DISAGREEMENT: mathematicians had solved inviscid flow elegantly and predicted zero drag, while engineers measured substantial drag.**

> **Prandtl's resolution was that viscosity matters ONLY in a thin layer near the surface, and can be ignored everywhere else — so the elegant inviscid solution is right for the bulk of the flow, and the drag comes entirely from the thin layer the mathematicians had neglected.**

> **That division is why an engineer can use Bernoulli's equation freely in the middle of a pipe and must add a friction term for the wall.**

**SEPARATION, which is the boundary layer's most consequential behaviour:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **In an ADVERSE pressure gradient (pressure rising downstream)** | **The slow fluid near the wall is decelerated further** ← |
| **It comes to rest and then REVERSES** | ← |
| **The boundary layer SEPARATES from the surface** | **Leaving a wide turbulent WAKE** ← |
| **The result** | **A large increase in drag (FORM drag), loss of lift, and violent unsteady forces** ← |

> **A TURBULENT boundary layer separates LATER than a laminar one, because turbulent mixing continuously feeds high-momentum fluid toward the wall.**

> **That is why a golf ball has DIMPLES: they trip the boundary layer into turbulence, which delays separation, narrows the wake and REDUCES the total drag — a case where deliberately increasing skin friction reduces the overall resistance by a much larger amount.**

**And where separation matters in civil engineering:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A SUDDEN ENLARGEMENT in a pipe** | **The jet separates and the eddy loss is (V₁−V₂)²/2g** ← |
| **Flow past a BRIDGE PIER** | **Separation forms vortices that scour the bed and shed alternately** ← |
| **VORTEX SHEDDING from a chimney, cable or tall building** | **Alternate shedding produces an oscillating CROSS-WIND force** ← |
| **A sharp-edged pipe entry** | **Separation at the lip forms the vena contracta — hence K = 0.5, against 0.05 for a bell-mouth** ← |
| **Draft tube and diffuser design** | **The 4-8° cone angle exists precisely to avoid separation** ← |

> **THE VORTEX SHEDDING ROW CARRIES A REAL STRUCTURAL DANGER: if the shedding frequency approaches a structure's natural frequency, RESONANCE follows.**

> **The Strouhal relation f = St·V/D (St ≈ 0.2 for a cylinder) gives that frequency, and it rises with wind speed — so there is generally a CRITICAL WIND SPEED at which a slender chimney, mast or cable will resonate.**

> **The remedies are to change the natural frequency, to add damping, or to spoil the shedding with helical strakes — which is why tall steel chimneys so often carry a spiral fin near the top.**

> **And the same phenomenon in water is what causes bridge pier scour and the oscillation of suspension bridge decks, which is where this thread of fluid mechanics reaches the civil engineer most directly.**

examTip.trick: **Zero RELATIVE velocity at a solid surface** — which forces a velocity gradient, hence wall shear, hence the boundary layer and all viscous drag. Option (a) defines a FLUID; option (c) is Pascal's law.
examTip.trap: **It is an EXPERIMENTAL observation, not a derived result** — and Prandtl's insight was that viscosity matters only inside the thin boundary layer, which is why Bernoulli works everywhere else.
examTip.mnemonic: **A TURBULENT boundary layer separates LATER** — hence golf-ball dimples, where more skin friction gives less total drag. And vortex shedding at f = 0.2V/D resonates slender chimneys, which is why they carry helical strakes.

questions.stem: A rectangular pontoon 6 m long and 4 m wide floats in water at a draft of 1.2 m. Its centre of gravity is 1.5 m above the base. The METACENTRIC HEIGHT is:
questions.solution:
**0.21 m.**

**The computation:**

> **GM = BM − BG = I/V − BG**

| Step | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **I — second moment of the WATERLINE area about the longitudinal axis** | **LB³/12 = 6 × 4³/12 = 6 × 64/12** | **32.0 m⁴** ← |
| **V — volume of water DISPLACED** | **6 × 4 × 1.2** | **28.8 m³** ← |
| **BM = I/V** | **32.0/28.8** | **1.111 m** ← |
| **B — centre of buoyancy above the base** | **draft/2 = 1.2/2** | **0.60 m** ← |
| **BG** | **1.50 − 0.60** | **0.90 m** ← |
| **GM = BM − BG** | **1.111 − 0.900** | **0.21 m** ← |

> **GM is POSITIVE, so the pontoon is in STABLE equilibrium.**

| Distractor | The error |
|---|---|
| **1.11 m** | **BM alone — BG not subtracted** ← |
| **0.90 m** | **BG alone** ← |
| **2.01 m** | **BM + BG — added instead of subtracted** ← |

> **The B in the fourth row is at HALF the draft only because the section is rectangular: the centre of buoyancy is the centroid of the DISPLACED VOLUME, which for a rectangular pontoon is at half the immersed depth.**

> **For a ship-shaped hull it must be computed from the actual submerged form.**

**The stability criterion:**

| Condition | State |
|---|---|
| **M ABOVE G — GM POSITIVE** | **STABLE — a tilt produces a RIGHTING couple that restores it** ← |
| **M coincides with G — GM = 0** | **NEUTRAL** |
| **M BELOW G — GM NEGATIVE** | **UNSTABLE — a tilt produces an OVERTURNING couple and the body capsizes** ← |

> **THE MECHANISM IS WORTH PICTURING: when a floating body tilts, the shape of the immersed volume changes, so the centre of BUOYANCY shifts sideways — toward the submerged side — while the centre of GRAVITY stays put.**

> **The two forces (weight down through G, buoyancy up through the new B) then form a COUPLE.**

> **If the shifted buoyancy line crosses the centre line ABOVE G, the couple pushes the body back upright. If it crosses BELOW G, the couple tips it further.**

> **The crossing point is the METACENTRE, M — and its height above G is therefore the whole measure of stability.**

**The righting moment, which is what GM buys:**

> **Righting moment = W × GM × sin θ**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A LARGE GM gives a large righting moment** | **Very stable — but a SHORT, VIOLENT roll period, which is uncomfortable and can damage cargo** ← |
| **A SMALL positive GM** | **A slow, easy roll — comfortable, but little margin** ← |
| **Time period of roll T = 2π√(k²/(g·GM))** | **With k the radius of gyration — so T falls as GM rises** ← |

> **THE TRADE IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS A REAL DESIGN DECISION in naval architecture: passengers and cargo want a gentle roll, and safety wants a large GM, and the two are opposed.**

> **Typical values: 0.3 to 1.0 m for a passenger ship, 1 to 2 m for a cargo ship, and much larger for a wide shallow pontoon like the one in this question, where B³ in the numerator makes BM large.**

**Why WIDTH dominates stability — the practical lesson:**

> **BM = I/V, and for a rectangular waterplane I = LB³/12 — so BM varies as the CUBE of the BEAM.**

| Beam | BM, relative |
|---|---|
| **B** | **1** |
| **1.2 B** | **1.73** ← |
| **1.5 B** | **3.38** ← |
| **2 B** | **8.0** ← |

> **So a 20 per cent increase in width nearly DOUBLES the metacentric height, while increasing the length does nothing at all for transverse stability (L appears linearly in both I and V, and cancels).**

> **That is why a raft, a pontoon or a catamaran is made WIDE rather than long, why a narrow canoe is so easily capsized, and why loading cargo high (raising G) is far more dangerous on a narrow vessel than on a broad one.**

> **It is also why the cross-section, not the length, is what a stability calculation turns on — and why a barge that is perfectly stable empty can become unstable when loaded, since raising G reduces GM directly while BM is unchanged.**

examTip.trick: **GM = I/V − BG.** Here I = 6×4³/12 = 32, V = 6×4×1.2 = 28.8, BM = 1.111; B is at half the draft (0.6), so BG = 0.9 and **GM = 0.21 m**.
examTip.trap: **The distractors are BM alone (1.11), BG alone (0.90) and BM + BG (2.01)** — the subtraction is the step to get right. Positive GM means stable.
examTip.mnemonic: **BM varies as the CUBE of the BEAM** (I = LB³/12), so 20 % more width nearly DOUBLES GM, while extra length does nothing — L cancels between I and V. Hence rafts are WIDE, and loading cargo high is worst on a narrow hull.

questions.stem: A rectangular plate 2 m wide and 3 m long is submerged in water, inclined at 30° to the horizontal, with its upper edge 1 m below the free surface. The total hydrostatic force on the plate is about:
questions.solution:
**About 103.0 kN.**

**The computation:**

> **F = ρ g h̄ A, where h̄ is the VERTICAL depth of the plate's CENTROID.**

| Step | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Depth of the UPPER edge** | Given | **1.00 m** |
| **Vertical drop over the plate's 3 m length** | **3 × sin 30° = 3 × 0.5** | **1.50 m** ← |
| **Depth of the LOWER edge** | **1.00 + 1.50** | **2.50 m** ← |
| **Depth of the CENTROID, h̄** | **(1.00 + 2.50)/2** | **1.75 m** ← |
| **Area** | **2 × 3** | **6.0 m²** |
| **Force** | **9,810 × 1.75 × 6.0** | **103,005 N ≈ 103.0 kN** ← |

**Each distractor is a named wrong step:**

| Option | The error |
|---|---|
| **58.9 kN** | **Depth taken as the UPPER edge, 1.0 m** ← |
| **147.2 kN** | **Depth taken as the LOWER edge, 2.5 m** ← |
| **88.3 kN** | **The 3 m taken as a VERTICAL drop rather than a slope length: h̄ = 1 + 1.5/2... using 1.5** ← |

> **The commonest real error is the last one: forgetting the sin 30°, and treating the plate's 3 m dimension as if it were vertical.**

> **THE INCLINATION ENTERS THE FORCE ONLY THROUGH THE CENTROID'S DEPTH — and that is the essential point about F = ρg h̄ A.**

> **The formula is the SAME for a vertical plate, an inclined plate and a horizontal plate. What changes is h̄, and nothing else.**

> **So there is no separate "inclined plate formula" to remember: find the vertical depth of the centroid, and the rest is identical.**

**The CENTRE OF PRESSURE, which is where the inclination does appear explicitly:**

> **h_p = h̄ + (I_G sin²θ) / (A h̄)**

| Term | Note |
|---|---|
| **I_G** | **The second moment of the plate's area about its own centroidal axis** |
| **sin²θ** | **The inclination enters HERE, squared** ← |
| **h_p is ALWAYS below h̄** | **The added term is always positive** ← |

> **For this plate: I_G = bd³/12 = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴, so**

> **h_p = 1.75 + (4.5 × 0.5²)/(6 × 1.75) = 1.75 + 1.125/10.5 = 1.75 + 0.107 = 1.857 m**

> **The centre of pressure is therefore about 107 mm below the centroid — a small but real offset that determines the moment the plate's supports must resist.**

| Limiting case | Result |
|---|---|
| **θ = 90° (VERTICAL plate)** | **sin²θ = 1, so the offset is greatest** ← |
| **θ = 0° (HORIZONTAL plate)** | **sin²θ = 0, so h_p = h̄ — the pressure is UNIFORM over a horizontal plate** ← |
| **Deeply submerged** | **A h̄ is large, so the offset → 0 and h_p approaches h̄** ← |

> **The HORIZONTAL case makes physical sense at once: every point of a horizontal plate is at the same depth, so the pressure is uniform and its resultant acts at the centroid.**

> **And the DEEP case is worth carrying as a check: the deeper a surface, the more nearly uniform the pressure across it, so the centre of pressure converges on the centroid.**

**A worked check by the pressure-diagram method, since it is a useful alternative:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Pressure at the upper edge** | **9,810 × 1.0 = 9.81 kPa** |
| **Pressure at the lower edge** | **9,810 × 2.5 = 24.53 kPa** |
| **Mean pressure** | **(9.81 + 24.53)/2 = 17.17 kPa** ← |
| **Force = mean pressure × area** | **17.17 × 6.0 = 103.0 kN ✓** ← |

> **The two methods agree, and the second is often quicker for a rectangle: the pressure varies LINEARLY with depth, so its average over a plane surface of uniform width is simply the mean of the end values.**

> **The mean-pressure shortcut works only where the surface's WIDTH is constant, though. For a triangular or circular plate the area is not distributed evenly with depth, and h̄ must be the true centroid — which is why ρg h̄ A is the general form and the pressure diagram is the special case.**

examTip.trick: **F = ρg h̄ A with h̄ the VERTICAL centroid depth.** Here the 3 m is along the SLOPE, so the vertical drop is 3 sin30° = 1.5 m, h̄ = (1 + 2.5)/2 = 1.75, and F = 103 kN.
examTip.trap: **Forgetting sin θ and treating the slope length as vertical** gives 88.3 kN. And the distractors at 58.9 and 147.2 use the upper and lower edge depths instead of the centroid.
examTip.mnemonic: **There is no separate inclined-plate formula — only h̄ changes.** The inclination appears explicitly in the CENTRE OF PRESSURE: h_p = h̄ + I_G sin²θ/(A h̄), which is zero for a horizontal plate and vanishes with depth.

questions.stem: A PATHLINE differs from a STREAMLINE in that a pathline is:
options: A line everywhere tangent to the velocity vector at one instant
The actual TRAJECTORY traced by ONE fluid particle over a period of TIME
The locus of all particles that have passed through one fixed point
A line of constant pressure in the flow
questions.solution:
**The actual TRAJECTORY traced by ONE fluid particle over a period of TIME.**

**The three flow lines, which are constantly confused:**

| Line | Definition | Fixed in |
|---|---|---|
| **STREAMLINE** | **A line everywhere TANGENT to the velocity vector at ONE INSTANT** ← (option a) | **TIME — a snapshot of the whole field** ← |
| **PATHLINE** | **The path traced by ONE PARTICLE over TIME** ← | **The PARTICLE — follow it and see where it goes** ← |
| **STREAKLINE** | **The locus of all particles that have PASSED THROUGH one fixed point** ← (option c) | **The POINT — like a dye trace or a smoke plume** ← |

> **The everyday analogies make the distinction stick:**

| Line | Physical analogy |
|---|---|
| **STREAMLINE** | **A photograph of many short arrows, one at each point, all at the same instant** ← |
| **PATHLINE** | **A long-exposure photograph of ONE glowing particle** ← |
| **STREAKLINE** | **The smoke plume from a chimney, or dye injected steadily at one point** ← |

> **IN STEADY FLOW ALL THREE COINCIDE, which is why the distinction seems pedantic in most textbook problems — the velocity field does not change, so a particle simply follows the streamline it is on, and every particle released from a point follows the same route.**

> **In UNSTEADY flow they are entirely different lines, and that is when the distinction earns its keep: the streamline pattern itself is changing, so a particle wanders across streamlines as it goes.**

> **A chimney plume on a gusty day is the clearest demonstration — the visible smoke (a streakline) is a wavy ribbon, while no individual smoke particle ever followed that shape.**

**The properties of a STREAMLINE, since it is the one used in analysis:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **There can be NO FLOW ACROSS a streamline** | **The velocity is tangent to it by definition** ← |
| **Streamlines CANNOT CROSS one another** | **A crossing point would need two velocities at once — except at a STAGNATION point, where the velocity is zero** ← |
| **A STREAM TUBE is a bundle of streamlines** | **It behaves like a pipe with impermeable walls, which is what makes the continuity equation work** ← |
| **Closely spaced streamlines mean HIGH velocity** | **The same discharge through a narrower tube** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY THE CONCEPT MATTERS AT ALL: because nothing crosses a streamline, a stream tube can be treated exactly as a solid-walled pipe.**

> **Continuity (A₁V₁ = A₂V₂) and Bernoulli's equation along a streamline both depend on that — and it is the device that lets a continuous flow field be analysed one tube at a time.**

> **And the fourth row is the reading rule for any flow net or streamline plot: where the lines crowd together, the flow is fast, and by Bernoulli the pressure there is low.**

**The other terms in flow description, for completeness:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **STEADY flow** | **Conditions at a POINT do not change with TIME: ∂V/∂t = 0** ← |
| **UNIFORM flow** | **Conditions do not change with POSITION at an instant: ∂V/∂s = 0** ← |
| **Laminar** | Orderly layers; low Reynolds number |
| **Turbulent** | Chaotic mixing; high Reynolds number |
| **ROTATIONAL** | **Fluid elements SPIN about their own axes; vorticity is non-zero** ← |
| **IRROTATIONAL** | **No spin; the condition for a velocity potential to exist** ← |
| **Compressible / incompressible** | Whether the density changes |

> **THE STEADY-AGAINST-UNIFORM DISTINCTION IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS ANOTHER STANDARD CONFUSION, and the two are independent — a flow can be either, both or neither:**

| Example | Steady? | Uniform? |
|---|---|---|
| **Constant discharge through a pipe of CONSTANT diameter** | **YES** | **YES** ← |
| **Constant discharge through a TAPERING pipe** | **YES** | **NO — the velocity changes along it** ← |
| **Increasing discharge through a constant pipe** | **NO** | **YES** ← |
| **Increasing discharge through a tapering pipe** | **NO** | **NO** |

> **STEADY is about TIME; UNIFORM is about SPACE — and holding that one line straight resolves the whole family of terms.**

> **It also names the four classes of open channel flow met earlier: steady uniform (normal depth), steady non-uniform (gradually or rapidly varied), and their unsteady counterparts (a flood wave, a surge).**

examTip.trick: **STREAMLINE fixes TIME (a snapshot); PATHLINE fixes the PARTICLE (a long exposure); STREAKLINE fixes the POINT (a smoke plume).** Options (a) and (c) are the other two.
examTip.trap: **All three COINCIDE in steady flow** — which is why the distinction seems pedantic until the flow is unsteady, when a chimney plume is a wavy ribbon no single particle ever traced.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nothing crosses a streamline, so a STREAM TUBE is effectively a solid pipe** — which is what makes continuity and Bernoulli work. And STEADY is about TIME while UNIFORM is about SPACE; a taper is steady but not uniform.

questions.stem: The force exerted by a flowing fluid on a pipe BEND is calculated using:
options: Bernoulli's equation alone
The continuity equation alone
Only the static pressure acting on the projected area
The IMPULSE-MOMENTUM equation, combining the change of momentum with the pressure forces at the two ends
questions.solution:
**The IMPULSE-MOMENTUM equation**, combining the change of MOMENTUM through the bend with the PRESSURE forces at the two ends.

**The governing relations:**

> **F_x = ρQ(V₁ₓ − V₂ₓ) + p₁A₁ₓ − p₂A₂ₓ**

> **F_y = ρQ(V₁ᵧ − V₂ᵧ) + p₁A₁ᵧ − p₂A₂ᵧ**

> **Resultant F = √(F_x² + F_y²), at an angle tan⁻¹(F_y/F_x)**

| Contribution | Note |
|---|---|
| **MOMENTUM change, ρQ ΔV** | **The fluid's DIRECTION changes, so its momentum changes even at constant speed** ← |
| **PRESSURE forces, pA at each end** | **Usually the LARGER contribution in a water pipeline** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW CONTAINS THE POINT MOST OFTEN MISSED: momentum is a VECTOR, so turning the flow changes it even when the speed is unaltered.**

> **A 90° bend at constant diameter has the same velocity magnitude at inlet and outlet, and the momentum change is nevertheless √2 times ρQV — because the direction has rotated by a right angle.**

**Why the other options fail:**

| Option | Why it is insufficient |
|---|---|
| **Bernoulli alone** | **An ENERGY equation — it gives pressures and velocities but no FORCES** ← |
| **Continuity alone** | **Gives velocities from areas; no forces at all** ← |
| **Static pressure on the projected area** | **Ignores the momentum change entirely — it would be right only for a stationary fluid** ← |

> **All three are used IN the calculation — continuity gives the velocities, Bernoulli gives the pressures — but only the MOMENTUM equation yields a force.**

> **THAT DIVISION OF LABOUR IS THE GENERAL RULE IN FLUID MECHANICS: continuity for the velocities, energy for the pressures, MOMENTUM for the forces.**

**A worked example, since the magnitudes surprise people:**

> **Water flows at 2 m/s through a 300 mm pipe with a 90° bend, at a gauge pressure of 300 kPa.**

| Quantity | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Area** | **π × 0.3²/4** | **0.0707 m²** |
| **Discharge** | **0.0707 × 2** | **0.1414 m³/s** |
| **ρQV (momentum term, each direction)** | **1000 × 0.1414 × 2** | **283 N** ← |
| **pA (pressure term, each direction)** | **300,000 × 0.0707** | **21,206 N** ← |
| **F_x** | **283 + 21,206** | **21,489 N** |
| **F_y** | **283 + 21,206** | **21,489 N** |
| **RESULTANT** | **√2 × 21,489** | **30,390 N ≈ 30.4 kN** ← |

> **THE PRESSURE TERM IS SEVENTY-FIVE TIMES THE MOMENTUM TERM in this example — which is the practical lesson for water pipelines.**

> **At ordinary water velocities the momentum contribution is almost negligible and the thrust is essentially pA. That is why thrust block design is usually done on pressure alone, and why the resultant of about 30 kN — three tonnes — must be resisted by a substantial concrete block.**

> **The momentum term dominates only at very high velocity or very low pressure, as in a free jet striking a plate.**

**Where these forces must be resisted — THRUST BLOCKS:**

| Location | Why a thrust develops |
|---|---|
| **BENDS** | **The change of direction; the thrust acts OUTWARD along the bisector** ← |
| **TEES and branches** | The branch flow's momentum and pressure |
| **REDUCERS** | **The unbalanced pressure on the change of area** ← |
| **DEAD ENDS and valves** | **The full pA against the closed end — the largest thrust of all** ← |
| **Steep gradients** | The downhill component of the pipe's weight |

> **The thrust block must resist the force by BEARING against undisturbed soil, so it is cast against the trench wall rather than into backfill — and its size follows from the soil's safe bearing capacity, which is why a large thrust in soft ground needs a very large block or a tied joint instead.**

> **The DEAD END row deserves the emphasis: a closed valve at the end of a 300 mm main at 300 kPa carries 21 kN — over two tonnes — trying to push the pipe out of the ground, permanently and whenever the main is charged.**

**And the OTHER applications of the momentum equation, since the bend is only one:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Force on a pipe bend, reducer or nozzle** | ← this question |
| **HYDRAULIC JUMP** | **Its conjugate depths, because the energy loss is unknown but the momentum is conserved** ← |
| **Force of a JET on a flat or curved plate** | **Fixed or moving — the basis of turbine theory** ← |
| **Propulsion of a jet or rocket** | — |
| **SUDDEN ENLARGEMENT loss** | **Derived by combining momentum with energy** ← |
| **Force on a sluice gate** | ← |

> **The unifying feature of every entry is the one that decided this question: MOMENTUM IS USED WHERE THE LOSSES ARE UNKNOWN BUT THE FORCES ARE WANTED — it needs no knowledge of what happens inside the control volume, only conditions at its boundaries.**

examTip.trick: **F = ρQΔV + pA at each end, combined as vectors.** Momentum is a VECTOR, so a 90° bend changes it even at constant speed. Continuity gives velocities, Bernoulli gives pressures, MOMENTUM gives forces.
examTip.trap: **At ordinary water velocities the pA term dwarfs the ρQV term** — 21 kN against 283 N in the worked example. Thrust blocks are therefore designed essentially on pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Thrust at bends, tees, reducers and DEAD ENDS** — the closed end carries the full pA, over two tonnes on a 300 mm main at 300 kPa. Cast the block against UNDISTURBED soil, not backfill.

questions.stem: For the transmission of power through a pipeline, the power delivered is a MAXIMUM when the friction head loss equals:
options: One THIRD of the total head at inlet
One half of the total head
Two thirds of the total head
The whole of the total head
questions.solution:
**One THIRD of the total head at inlet: h_f = H/3.**

**The derivation, which is a short piece of calculus worth following:**

> **Power delivered at the far end: P = ρg Q (H − h_f)**

> **For a pipe, h_f = kQ² (from Darcy-Weisbach at a fixed diameter), so Q = √(h_f/k) and:**

> **P = ρg √(h_f/k) (H − h_f) = (ρg/√k)(H h_f^½ − h_f^{3/2})**

> **Differentiate with respect to h_f and set to zero:**

> **dP/dh_f = (ρg/√k)(½ H h_f^{−½} − (3/2) h_f^{½}) = 0**

> **½ H = (3/2) h_f, therefore h_f = H/3** ←

**The efficiency at that condition:**

> **η = (H − h_f)/H = (H − H/3)/H = 2/3 = 66.7 per cent**

| Quantity at maximum power | Value |
|---|---|
| **Friction head lost** | **H/3 — one third** ← |
| **Head available at the far end** | **2H/3 — two thirds** ← |
| **Transmission EFFICIENCY** | **66.7 per cent** ← |

> **Option (c), two thirds, is the head DELIVERED rather than the head LOST — a real quantity in the same calculation, offered for the other, which is what makes it the designed distractor.**

**Why the maximum exists at all — the physical reasoning:**

| If the discharge is | Then |
|---|---|
| **VERY SMALL** | **Friction is negligible, so nearly the full head H reaches the far end — but there is almost no FLOW, so the POWER (ρgQ × head) is small** ← |
| **VERY LARGE** | **A great deal of flow, but friction consumes nearly all the head, so the head delivered approaches zero — and again the power is small** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE** | **A compromise gives the maximum product of flow and head** ← |

> **So the maximum arises because POWER IS A PRODUCT OF TWO QUANTITIES THAT MOVE IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, and the optimum divides the head in the ratio 1:2 between friction and delivery.**

> **That is the same structure as the economic diameter problem, the crashing optimum and the balancing depth — a product or a sum of two opposed effects, with a stationary point between them.**

**THE CRITICAL QUALIFICATION, which is where this result is misapplied:**

> **MAXIMUM POWER IS NOT MAXIMUM EFFICIENCY. At the maximum-power condition, a THIRD of the energy is being thrown away as friction.**

| Objective | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Maximum POWER from a given pipe** | **h_f = H/3, efficiency 66.7 per cent** ← |
| **Maximum EFFICIENCY** | **h_f → 0, which means Q → 0 and no useful power at all** ← |
| **What is actually wanted in practice** | **The ECONOMIC optimum — usually far closer to the efficient end** ← |

> **The h_f = H/3 result answers the question "what is the most power this EXISTING pipe can deliver?" — which is the right question when the pipe is already built and cannot be changed.**

> **It is emphatically NOT the right basis for DESIGNING a new pipeline. A design losing a third of its head to friction for the whole of its life would be grossly uneconomic, and the economic diameter calculation typically settles on a friction loss of 3 to 10 per cent instead.**

> **So the two results belong to different questions, and confusing them produces a badly oversized pump and an undersized pipe.**

**Where the result is genuinely used:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Assessing an EXISTING pipeline's maximum output** | **A hydropower penstock already in place** ← |
| **HYDRAULIC power transmission by pipe** | **Historically used to drive machinery and cranes in docks and cities** ← |
| **Nozzle sizing for a PELTON turbine on a given penstock** | **The nozzle throttles the flow, and the power peaks at exactly this condition** ← |
| **Fire hose and monitor design** | Where the pipe is fixed and the jet power is wanted |

> **THE PELTON APPLICATION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE MOST RELEVANT HERE, and it is a satisfying closure: for a penstock already built, the jet diameter that extracts the most power from it is the one making the penstock's friction loss one third of the gross head.**

> **In practice the penstock is designed generously enough that its friction is far below H/3 at the design flow — so the plant operates well on the efficient side of the maximum, delivering somewhat less than the theoretical peak power but wasting far less water in friction.**

> **Which is precisely the distinction between the two questions above, resolved in favour of economics rather than of peak output.**

examTip.trick: **h_f = H/3, giving an efficiency of 2/3 = 66.7 %.** From P = ρgQ(H − h_f) with h_f = kQ²: differentiate and ½H = 1.5 h_f. Option (c) is the head DELIVERED, not lost.
examTip.trap: **Maximum POWER is not maximum EFFICIENCY** — at this condition a THIRD of the energy is wasted in friction. It answers "what can this EXISTING pipe deliver?", never "what pipe should I build?"
examTip.mnemonic: **Power is a product of two opposed quantities — flow and delivered head — so it has a maximum between them.** Same structure as economic diameter, crashing and balancing depth. Design instead for 3-10 % friction loss.

questions.stem: For the MOST ECONOMICAL (best hydraulic) RECTANGULAR open channel section, the relation between the bed width b and the depth of flow y is:
options: b = y
b = 4y
b = 2y
b = y/2
questions.solution:
**b = 2y** — the bed width is twice the depth of flow.

**The derivation:**

> **For a rectangular channel: A = by and P = b + 2y.**

> **The most economical section carries the maximum discharge for a given area, which by Manning means the MINIMUM WETTED PERIMETER (since Q ∝ A R^(2/3) = A(A/P)^(2/3), so Q is greatest when P is least).**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Express P in terms of A and y** | **b = A/y, so P = A/y + 2y** ← |
| **Differentiate with A held constant** | **dP/dy = −A/y² + 2 = 0** ← |
| **Therefore** | **A = 2y², and since A = by, by = 2y², so b = 2y** ← |

> **And the hydraulic radius follows: R = A/P = 2y²/(2y + 2y) = 2y²/4y = y/2.**

| Result for the most economical RECTANGLE | Value |
|---|---|
| **Bed width** | **b = 2y** ← |
| **HYDRAULIC RADIUS** | **R = y/2 — HALF the depth** ← |
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4y** |
| **Area** | **A = 2y²** |

**The corresponding results for the other sections, since they follow the same rule:**

| Section | Condition for the most economical section | Hydraulic radius |
|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE** | **b = 2y** ← | **R = y/2** ← |
| **TRAPEZOID** | **The sloping side length equals HALF the top width; and a SEMICIRCLE centred at the water surface is tangent to all three sides** ← | **R = y/2** ← |
| **Trapezoid, best side slope** | **60° to the horizontal — that is, a HALF HEXAGON** ← | R = y/2 |
| **TRIANGLE** | **Side slopes at 45°, so the vertex angle is 90°** ← | **R = y/(2√2)** |
| **CIRCLE, maximum DISCHARGE** | **Depth = 0.95 D** ← | — |
| **Circle, maximum VELOCITY** | **Depth = 0.81 D** ← | — |

> **THE RECURRING R = y/2 IN THE FIRST THREE ROWS IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS TOPIC: for the best hydraulic rectangle, trapezoid and half-hexagon alike, the hydraulic radius is exactly half the depth.**

> **It is not a coincidence. In every case the most economical section is the one in which a SEMICIRCLE centred on the water surface can be inscribed to touch every wetted side — and for such a section R = y/2 follows geometrically.**

> **The underlying reason is that the SEMICIRCLE itself is the most efficient open channel section of all, having the least perimeter for a given area. Every other shape's optimum is simply the closest that shape can come to a semicircle.**

> **A rectangle approximates it as a half-square, a trapezoid as a half-hexagon, and the more sides available the closer the approach — which is why the trapezoid outperforms the rectangle and the semicircle beats both.**

**Why the semicircle is nevertheless rarely built:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Difficult and expensive to EXCAVATE and to form** | **In earth it cannot be cut accurately; in concrete it needs curved formwork** ← |
| **UNSTABLE in earth** | **The sides would slump to the soil's angle of repose** ← |
| **Awkward to MAINTAIN and to de-silt** | **No flat invert for machinery** ← |
| **The TRAPEZOID is the practical compromise** | **Its side slopes are set by SOIL STABILITY, not by hydraulics** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL RESOLUTION AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: in an earth canal the side slope is fixed by the soil's stability — 1:1 in stiff clay, 1.5:1 or 2:1 in ordinary soil, 2:1 to 3:1 in sand — and NOT by the 60° hydraulic optimum.**

> **So the "most economical section" is computed with the side slope already fixed by geotechnics, and only the width-to-depth ratio is optimised.**

> **A canal cut to the hydraulically ideal 60° in sandy soil would simply collapse, and the hydraulic gain is small compared with the certainty of that failure.**

**And the qualification on "most economical", which is worth making:**

| The hydraulic optimum minimises | It does NOT account for |
|---|---|
| **The WETTED PERIMETER, hence the lining area and the friction** ← | **The EXCAVATION volume, which may be cheaper in a wider, shallower section** ← |
| — | **The DEPTH of cut, which rises steeply in cost** ← |
| — | **Land width acquired** |
| — | **The freeboard, berms and bank volumes** |
| — | **Balancing cut against fill** |

> **A deep narrow section has the least perimeter and the most excavation depth, and deep excavation is disproportionately expensive — so the true economic section is usually WIDER and SHALLOWER than the hydraulic optimum.**

> **The hydraulic result is therefore a starting point and a useful check, not the answer: it tells you the best section for LINING cost and friction, and the full cost comparison must add the earthwork.**

> **That is the same pattern as the balancing depth discussed under canal sections — hydraulics proposes, earthwork economics disposes.**

examTip.trick: **b = 2y, and R = y/2.** From P = A/y + 2y, differentiate at constant A: dP/dy = −A/y² + 2 = 0, giving A = 2y².
examTip.trap: **R = y/2 for the best rectangle, trapezoid AND half-hexagon alike** — because in each case a SEMICIRCLE centred on the water surface touches every wetted side. The semicircle is the true optimum; every shape's best is its nearest approach to it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Side slopes are fixed by SOIL STABILITY, not by the 60° hydraulic optimum** — 1:1 clay, 1.5-2:1 ordinary, 2-3:1 sand. And the hydraulic optimum ignores EXCAVATION DEPTH, so the true economic section is wider and shallower.

questions.stem: In gradually varied flow, an M1 water surface profile occurs when:
options: The bed slope is steep and the depth is below critical
The bed is horizontal and the depth is above normal
The bed slope is adverse
The bed slope is MILD and the actual depth is ABOVE the normal depth — the backwater curve upstream of a dam or weir
questions.solution:
**The bed slope is MILD and the actual depth is ABOVE the normal depth** — the familiar BACKWATER CURVE upstream of a dam, weir or bridge constriction.

**How gradually varied flow profiles are named:**

> **The LETTER gives the bed slope, and the NUMBER gives the zone in which the actual depth lies.**

| Letter | Bed slope | Relation of normal depth y_n to critical depth y_c |
|---|---|---|
| **M — MILD** | **y_n > y_c** ← | **Normal flow is SUBCRITICAL** |
| **S — STEEP** | **y_n < y_c** ← | **Normal flow is SUPERCRITICAL** |
| **C — CRITICAL** | **y_n = y_c** | — |
| **H — HORIZONTAL** | **Bed slope zero; y_n is infinite** ← | — |
| **A — ADVERSE** | **The bed rises downstream; y_n does not exist** ← (option c) | — |

| Zone | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Zone 1** | **The actual depth is ABOVE BOTH y_n and y_c** ← |
| **Zone 2** | **BETWEEN y_n and y_c** ← |
| **Zone 3** | **BELOW BOTH** ← |

> **So M1 means MILD slope, zone 1 — depth above both the normal and the critical depth.**

**The commonly met profiles:**

| Profile | Where it occurs | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| **M1** | **Upstream of a DAM, WEIR or constriction on a mild slope** ← | **BACKWATER — depth increases downstream, asymptotic to horizontal at the obstruction and to y_n far upstream** ← |
| **M2** | **Upstream of a FREE OVERFALL, or where a mild slope meets a steeper one** ← | **DRAWDOWN — depth decreases toward the fall** ← |
