| **M3** | **Downstream of a SLUICE GATE on a mild slope** ← | **Depth increases until a HYDRAULIC JUMP returns it to normal** ← |
| **S1** | Upstream of an obstruction on a steep slope | Backwater |
| **S2** | **Where a mild slope steepens** | Drawdown |
| **S3** | **Below a sluice gate on a steep slope** | — |
| **H2, H3** | Horizontal channels | — |
| **A2, A3** | Adverse slopes | — |

> **THE M1 CURVE IS THE MOST IMPORTANT IN PRACTICE, and its consequences reach well beyond hydraulics:**

| Consequence of the M1 backwater | Note |
|---|---|
| **The raised water level extends KILOMETRES upstream on a flat river** | **This is the AFFLUX met in weir and barrage design** ← |
| **Land is submerged that was not before** | **Requiring marginal bunds and land acquisition** ← |
| **Sedimentation increases in the backwater reach** | **The velocity falls, so the sediment drops** ← |
| **Bridge and culvert afflux is computed from it** | ← |
| **The reservoir's true extent is set by the backwater, not by the dam's level alone** ← | **A point routinely underestimated in submergence estimates** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT AFFECTS RESETTLEMENT PLANNING DIRECTLY: the area submerged by a reservoir is not simply the land below the full supply level.**

> **During a flood, the M1 backwater raises the water surface above that level for a long distance upstream — so land well above the nominal reservoir level floods, and a submergence estimate drawn from a contour map alone is an underestimate.**

**The RULES that let a profile be sketched without computation:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Zone 1 and Zone 3 profiles have depth INCREASING downstream** | **Zone 2 profiles have depth DECREASING** ← |
| **A profile approaches y_n ASYMPTOTICALLY** | **It never quite reaches normal depth** ← |
| **A profile approaches y_c VERTICALLY (at right angles)** | **Which is why gradually varied flow theory FAILS at the critical depth — the assumptions break down** ← |
| **SUBCRITICAL profiles are computed UPSTREAM from a downstream control** | ← |
| **SUPERCRITICAL profiles are computed DOWNSTREAM from an upstream control** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A REAL LIMITATION, not a curiosity: gradually varied flow theory assumes the depth changes SLOWLY, and near the critical depth it changes very rapidly.**

> **So a computation carried into the critical region produces nonsense, and the transition through critical must be handled separately — as a hydraulic jump (analysed by MOMENTUM) or as a free overfall.**

> **And the last two rows repeat the control principle met under specific energy, which is the single most useful idea for actually performing these computations: START AT THE CONTROL AND WORK AWAY FROM IT, in the direction the disturbances can travel.**

> **A backwater computation for a dam therefore begins at the dam — where the depth is known — and steps upstream, which is why the standard-step method proceeds in that direction and why beginning at the wrong end produces a plausible but entirely wrong profile.**

examTip.trick: **LETTER = bed slope (M mild, S steep, C critical, H horizontal, A adverse); NUMBER = zone (1 above both y_n and y_c, 2 between, 3 below).** M1 is the backwater above a dam on a mild slope.
examTip.trap: **A profile meets y_c VERTICALLY, and gradually varied flow theory FAILS there** — the slow-change assumption breaks down. Transitions through critical need the momentum equation (a jump) instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **The M1 backwater sets a reservoir's true submerged area, not the full supply level** — land above the nominal level floods during a flood, so contour-map estimates understate resettlement. Compute subcritical profiles UPSTREAM from the control.

questions.stem: The THIESSEN POLYGON method of computing the mean areal rainfall over a catchment:
options: Takes the simple arithmetic average of all the gauge readings
Weights each gauge by the AREA of the polygon nearer to it than to any other gauge
Draws contours of equal rainfall and averages between them
Uses only the gauge nearest the catchment's centroid
questions.solution:
**It weights each gauge by the AREA of the polygon closer to that gauge than to any other** — the gauge's area of influence.

**The three methods compared:**

| Method | How it works | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETIC MEAN** | **A simple average of all gauges** ← (option a) | **FLAT terrain, UNIFORMLY distributed gauges, uniform rainfall — the crudest** ← |
| **THIESSEN POLYGON** | **Each gauge weighted by its polygon's area: P̄ = Σ(Pᵢ Aᵢ)/ΣAᵢ** ← | **Non-uniform gauge SPACING; the usual working method** ← |
| **ISOHYETAL** | **Draw ISOHYETS (contours of equal rainfall); average between adjacent pairs, weighted by the area between them** ← (option c) | **MOUNTAINOUS terrain — the most ACCURATE and the most laborious** ← |

> **Options (a) and (c) are the other two standard methods, so the question requires the three to be distinguished.**

**How the Thiessen polygons are constructed:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Plot the gauges and JOIN each to its neighbours with straight lines, forming triangles** ← |
| **2** | **Draw the PERPENDICULAR BISECTOR of every connecting line** ← |
| **3** | **The bisectors enclose a polygon around each gauge — every point inside it is NEARER that gauge than any other** ← |
| **4** | **Measure each polygon's area within the catchment boundary** ← |
| **5** | **P̄ = Σ(Pᵢ Aᵢ) / ΣAᵢ** ← |

> **A gauge OUTSIDE the catchment can still contribute, if its polygon overlaps the boundary — which is a real advantage, since a nearby external gauge often represents part of the catchment better than a distant internal one.**

> **The arithmetic mean cannot use such a gauge at all, and that is one of the ways Thiessen improves on it.**

**A worked example:**

| Gauge | Rainfall (mm) | Polygon area (km²) | P × A |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **80** | **12** | **960** |
| **B** | **120** | **28** | **3,360** ← |
| **C** | **60** | **10** | **600** |
| **TOTAL** | — | **50** | **4,920** |

| Method | Result |
|---|---|
| **THIESSEN** | **4,920/50 = 98.4 mm** ← |
| **Arithmetic mean, for comparison** | **(80 + 120 + 60)/3 = 86.7 mm** ← |

> **The difference of nearly 12 mm — about 13 per cent — arises entirely because gauge B, with the HIGHEST rainfall, also commands the LARGEST area, and the arithmetic mean gives it no more weight than the others.**

> **On a catchment of 50 km² that 12 mm is 600,000 m³ of water, so the choice of method has a real effect on any runoff or flood estimate drawn from it.**

**The strengths and weaknesses of Thiessen:**

| Advantage | Limitation |
|---|---|
| **Accounts for non-uniform gauge spacing** | **Assumes rainfall varies LINEARLY between gauges and is uniform within each polygon** ← |
| **Objective and reproducible — no judgement required** ← | **Takes NO ACCOUNT OF TOPOGRAPHY, which is its serious defect** ← |
| **The polygons need be drawn only ONCE for a fixed network** ← | **The whole network must be REDRAWN if a gauge is added or lost** ← |
| **Can use gauges outside the catchment** | — |

> **THE TOPOGRAPHY DEFECT IN THE SECOND ROW IS DECISIVE IN NEPAL, and it deserves stating plainly: Thiessen's polygons are drawn from GEOMETRY alone, and take no notice of a ridge between two gauges.**

> **In the Himalaya, OROGRAPHIC effects mean rainfall can differ by a factor of two or three across a single ridge — the windward slope receiving vastly more than the leeward one, over a horizontal distance of a few kilometres.**

> **A Thiessen polygon straddling that ridge will assign a windward gauge's reading to leeward ground, or the reverse, with no mechanism to detect the error.**

> **The ISOHYETAL method handles it, because the person drawing the isohyets can bend them around the topography using knowledge the gauge readings alone do not contain — which is exactly why it is more accurate and why it requires judgement.**

> **For Nepali catchments the isohyetal method, or a modern gridded product informed by elevation, is therefore the appropriate choice, and Thiessen is a reasonable approximation only for the flat Terai.**

**And the RAIN GAUGE NETWORK itself, since every method depends on it:**

| Terrain | Recommended gauge density (WMO/IS guidance) |
|---|---|
| **Flat plains** | **One gauge per 520 km²** ← |
| **Elevated / hilly regions** | **One per 260 to 390 km²** ← |
| **Mountainous with rapid variation** | **One per 130 km²** ← |
| **Arid and polar** | One per 1,500 to 10,000 km² |
| **Minimum for a small catchment** | **At least 3 gauges, and ideally 10 per cent of the network as recording gauges** ← |

> **The density RISES with terrain variability for the reason just discussed — the more the rainfall varies over short distances, the more gauges are needed to capture it.**

> **And the OPTIMUM number for a required accuracy is given by N = (C_v/ε)², with C_v the coefficient of variation of the existing gauges' readings and ε the permissible percentage error — a genuinely useful relation, since it turns "we need more gauges" into a defensible number.**

examTip.trick: **Perpendicular bisectors between gauges enclose each gauge's area of influence; P̄ = Σ(PᵢAᵢ)/ΣAᵢ.** Options (a) and (c) are the arithmetic-mean and isohyetal methods.
examTip.trap: **Thiessen takes NO account of TOPOGRAPHY** — a polygon can straddle a ridge and assign windward rainfall to leeward ground. In the Himalaya, where orographic effects double or triple rainfall across a ridge, the ISOHYETAL method is needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **A gauge OUTSIDE the catchment can still contribute if its polygon overlaps** — something the arithmetic mean cannot do. And the optimum gauge count for a given accuracy is N = (C_v/ε)².

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a point load of 20 kN at 2 m and a point load of 30 kN at 5 m from the left support A. The bending moment at the section 5 m from A is:
questions.solution:
**71.25 kN·m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction at A — moments about B** | **R_A × 8 = 20 × (8 − 2) + 30 × (8 − 5) = 120 + 90 = 210** | **R_A = 26.25 kN** ← |
| **Reaction at B** | **50 − 26.25** | **R_B = 23.75 kN** |
| **BM at 5 m from A** | **R_A × 5 − 20 × (5 − 2) = 26.25 × 5 − 20 × 3 = 131.25 − 60** | **71.25 kN·m** ← |

> **Check from the RIGHT-hand side: BM = R_B × 3 = 23.75 × 3 = 71.25 kN·m ✓**

> **That check is worth making every time, and it is free: the moment at a section may be computed from EITHER side, and the two must agree. A disagreement means an arithmetic slip in the reactions.**

**Each distractor is a named wrong step:**

| Option | The error |
|---|---|
| **131.25 kN·m** | **R_A × 5 alone — the 20 kN load's moment about the section omitted** ← |
| **52.5 kN·m** | **R_A × 2 — the bending moment at the OTHER load point (2 m), a real value at the wrong section** ← |
| **118.75 kN·m** | **R_B × 5 — the right-hand reaction used with the left-hand distance** ← |

> **The 131.25 error is the commonest: taking moments of the reaction while forgetting the loads that lie BETWEEN the support and the section.**

> **The safeguard is the rule itself: the bending moment at a section is the algebraic sum of the moments of ALL forces on one side of it — every reaction and every load, not the reaction alone.**

**Locating the MAXIMUM bending moment, which is what the calculation is usually for:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **The maximum BM occurs where the SHEAR FORCE is ZERO or changes sign** ← | **Because V = dM/dx** |
| **For point loads, that is always AT a load point** | **The shear is constant between loads and jumps at each one** ← |
| **So compute the BM at every load point and take the largest** | ← |

> **Applying that here: the shear is +26.25 kN from A to the first load, +6.25 kN between the loads, and −23.75 kN beyond the second — so it changes sign AT the 30 kN load.**

> **The maximum bending moment is therefore the 71.25 kN·m just computed, and no other section need be checked.**

**The standard results for comparison, so the answer can be sense-checked:**

| Loading on a simply supported span L | Maximum BM |
|---|---|
| **Central point load W** | **WL/4** ← |
| **UDL of w per metre** | **wL²/8** ← |
| **Point load W at distance a from one end** | **Wab/L** ← |
| **Two equal loads W at the third points** | **WL/3** |

> **A quick sanity check on this problem: the 30 kN load alone at 5 m would give Wab/L = 30 × 5 × 3/8 = 56.25 kN·m, and the 20 kN load alone would give 20 × 2 × 6/8 = 30 kN·m at ITS own position.**

> **The computed 71.25 kN·m lies sensibly between the larger of these and their sum, which is what superposition would lead one to expect — so the answer passes inspection before any recalculation.**

> **SUPERPOSITION is in fact the neatest route to the whole problem, and it is worth noting: because the beam is linear and elastic, the bending moment at any section is simply the SUM of the moments each load would produce there acting alone.**

> **At the 5 m section, the 30 kN load contributes Wab/L = 56.25 kN·m, and the 20 kN load contributes R_A' × 5 − 20 × 3 where R_A' = 20 × 6/8 = 15, giving 75 − 60 = 15 kN·m.**

> **The total is 56.25 + 15 = 71.25 kN·m ✓ — the same answer by an entirely independent route, which is as good a verification as recomputing.**

examTip.trick: **R_A = 26.25 kN, then BM = 26.25×5 − 20×3 = 71.25 kN·m.** Check from the other side: R_B × 3 = 23.75 × 3 = 71.25 ✓ — always free, and it catches reaction errors.
examTip.trap: **131.25 is R_A × 5 with the 20 kN load's moment forgotten** — the commonest slip. The BM is the sum of the moments of ALL forces on one side, not the reaction alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum BM is where the SHEAR changes sign — for point loads, always AT a load point.** And SUPERPOSITION gives an independent check: 56.25 (from the 30 kN, as Wab/L) + 15 (from the 20 kN) = 71.25.

questions.stem: At the section where a CONCENTRATED LOAD acts on a beam, the shear force diagram shows:
options: A gradual change over the load's width
No change at all
A SUDDEN JUMP equal to the magnitude of the load, and the bending moment diagram shows a KINK
A jump in the bending moment
questions.solution:
**A SUDDEN JUMP in the shear force, equal to the magnitude of the load — and a KINK (an abrupt change of slope) in the bending moment diagram.**

**Why each behaves as it does:**

| Diagram | Behaviour at a point load | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **SHEAR FORCE** | **A vertical JUMP equal to the load** ← | **The load is a finite force applied over zero length, so the shear either side differs by exactly that force** ← |
| **BENDING MOMENT** | **CONTINUOUS, but with a sudden change of SLOPE — a kink** ← | **Since V = dM/dx and V jumps, the SLOPE of M jumps — but M itself does not** ← |

> **THE RELATION V = dM/dx EXPLAINS BOTH ROWS AT ONCE, and it is the reliable way to reason about any discontinuity:**

> **A jump in V is a jump in the SLOPE of M, which is a kink. A jump in M itself would require an INFINITE shear, which a finite load cannot produce.**

> **Option (d) inverts this — the bending moment does NOT jump at a point load.**

**What DOES make the bending moment jump:**

| Applied action | Shear force diagram | Bending moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **Concentrated LOAD** | **JUMP equal to the load** ← | **Kink (slope change)** ← |
| **Concentrated MOMENT (couple)** | **NO change** ← | **JUMP equal to the couple** ← |
| **UDL** | Sloping line | Parabola |
| **Support reaction** | **Jump equal to the reaction** | Kink |

> **THE COUPLE ROW IS THE COMPLEMENT OF THIS QUESTION AND IS WORTH HOLDING ALONGSIDE IT: a concentrated MOMENT leaves the shear untouched and makes the BENDING MOMENT jump.**

> **The two are perfect opposites — a force jumps V and kinks M; a couple leaves V alone and jumps M — and knowing the pair makes any diagram with mixed loading straightforward to sketch.**

> **A couple arises in practice from an eccentric bracket connection, a column moment transferred into a beam, or a cantilever framing into the side of a beam.**

**The complete set of rules for sketching diagrams by inspection:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Start at one end and work across, accumulating** | ← |
| **SFD: start at zero, jump UP at an upward reaction, DOWN at a downward load** ← | **The diagram must return to zero at the far end — a check** ← |
| **Between loads with no UDL, the shear is CONSTANT** | Horizontal line |
| **Under a UDL, the shear falls LINEARLY at the rate w per metre** | ← |
| **BMD: the change in M between two sections equals the AREA of the SFD between them** ← | **The fastest route to any moment** ← |
| **BMD is ZERO at a simple support and at a free end** ← | **Unless a couple is applied there** |
| **BMD is maximum where the SFD crosses zero** | ← |
| **A kink in the BMD points TOWARD the load** | A shape check |

> **THE TWO CHECKS IN THE SECOND AND SIXTH ROWS SHOULD BE APPLIED TO EVERY DIAGRAM DRAWN, and between them they catch nearly every arithmetic error:**

> **The SFD must close to zero at the far end, because the beam is in vertical equilibrium — if it does not, the reactions are wrong.**

> **And the BMD must be zero at each simple support, because a pin or a roller cannot transmit a moment — if it is not, the accumulated areas are wrong.**

**And the practical significance of the SHEAR JUMP, which is not merely a diagram feature:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The shear is DIFFERENT on the two sides of a load** | **So a design check must use the LARGER of the two** ← |
| **At a support, the critical shear is taken at a distance d from the face, not at the centre line** ← | **IS 456 permits this, since the load close to the support transfers directly by compression** ← |
| **A heavy point load near a support produces a very high local shear** | **Often the governing check** ← |
| **The load must be transmitted into the beam by BEARING or by a hanger** ← | **A load hung from the SOFFIT needs suspension reinforcement to carry it up into the compression zone** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A DETAILING REQUIREMENT THAT IS EASY TO OVERLOOK AND HAS CAUSED FAILURES: where a secondary beam frames into the SIDE of a main beam, its reaction is applied near the main beam's SOFFIT rather than on its top.**

> **That load must be carried UP to the compression zone before it can be resisted, and plain flexural reinforcement will not do it — the load simply tears the bottom of the beam away.**

> **The remedy is SUSPENSION (hanger) reinforcement: closed stirrups concentrated at the junction, designed to carry the full reaction upward, in addition to the ordinary shear steel.**

> **It is a small quantity of steel and its omission is a genuine structural defect, invisible in any analysis that treats the load as simply "a point load on the beam".**

examTip.trick: **V jumps by the load; M kinks but stays continuous** — because V = dM/dx, so a jump in V is a jump in M's SLOPE. A jump in M would need infinite shear.
examTip.trap: **A concentrated COUPLE is the exact opposite: no change in V, a JUMP in M.** Hold the pair together and any mixed-loading diagram becomes straightforward.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two free checks: the SFD must close to ZERO at the far end, and the BMD must be ZERO at every simple support.** And a beam framing into the SIDE of another needs SUSPENSION stirrups — the load must be carried up to the compression zone.

questions.stem: In a thin cylindrical shell of internal diameter d and thickness t under an internal pressure p, the CIRCUMFERENTIAL (hoop) stress is:
options: pd/(2t)
pd/(4t)
pd/t
pd/(8t)
questions.solution:
**pd/(2t).**

**The two stresses in a thin cylinder:**

| Stress | Expression | Acts |
|---|---|---|
| **CIRCUMFERENTIAL (hoop)** | **σ_h = pd/(2t)** ← | **Around the circumference, tending to split the cylinder ALONG its length** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL (axial)** | **σ_l = pd/(4t)** ← (option b) | **Along the axis, tending to pull the ends apart** ← |
| **The ratio** | **σ_h = 2 σ_l — the hoop stress is TWICE the longitudinal** ← | ← |

**The derivations, which are two different free bodies:**

| Stress | Cut | Force balance |
|---|---|---|
| **HOOP** | **A LONGITUDINAL cut, giving a half-cylinder of length L** | **Pressure force p × (d × L) resisted by 2 × (σ_h × t × L), so σ_h = pd/(2t)** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL** | **A TRANSVERSE cut, giving an end cap** | **Pressure force p × (πd²/4) resisted by σ_l × (πd × t), so σ_l = pd/(4t)** ← |

> **The factor-of-two difference arises entirely from the GEOMETRY of the two cuts: the hoop cut exposes an area proportional to the DIAMETER, while the longitudinal cut exposes one proportional to the CIRCUMFERENCE — and πd is greater than d by a factor of π, while the resisting areas differ correspondingly.**

> **THE CONSEQUENCE IS THE PRACTICAL POINT: A PRESSURISED CYLINDER FAILS BY SPLITTING ALONG ITS LENGTH, not around its circumference — because the hoop stress is twice as large.**

| Observation | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **A burst pipe splits LENGTHWISE** ← | **The hoop stress governs** |
| **A sausage splits lengthwise when cooked** | **The same mechanics** ← |
| **A boiler's LONGITUDINAL riveted joint must be stronger than its circumferential joint** ← | **It resists the larger stress** ← |
| **Spiral-welded pipe puts its weld at an angle** | **So the weld sees less than the full hoop stress** ← |

> **The BOILER JOINT row is the classical engineering application: the longitudinal seam carries twice the stress of the circumferential seam, so it is given a higher joint efficiency — double-riveted or double-welded where the circumferential seam is single.**

**The conditions for "THIN":**

| Criterion | Note |
|---|---|
| **d/t greater than about 20** (some texts use 15) | **Then the stress may be taken as UNIFORM through the thickness** ← |
| **Below that, the shell is THICK** | **The stress varies markedly through the wall and LAME'S equations are needed** ← |

> **In a thick cylinder the hoop stress is greatest at the INNER surface and least at the outer — so simply thickening a thick cylinder gives diminishing returns, because the added material is at the low-stress outside.**

> **That is why very high pressure vessels are made by COMPOUNDING (shrinking one cylinder onto another to pre-compress the inner one) or by autofrettage, rather than by making the wall ever thicker.**

**The strains and the volumetric change, which follow from the two stresses:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Circumferential strain** | **ε_h = (pd/2tE)(1 − ν/2)** ← |
| **Longitudinal strain** | **ε_l = (pd/2tE)(1/2 − ν)** ← |
| **VOLUMETRIC strain** | **δV/V = (pd/2tE)(5/2 − 2ν)** ← |

> **The longitudinal strain expression contains a result worth noticing: for ν = 0.5 it becomes ZERO, and for ν greater than 0.5 it would be NEGATIVE — the cylinder would get SHORTER as it was pressurised.**

> **Since ν cannot exceed 0.5, a pressurised cylinder always lengthens or stays the same, never shortens — which is a small consistency check between two apparently unrelated parts of the syllabus.**

**And the SPHERICAL shell, for comparison:**

| Vessel | Stress |
|---|---|
| **Cylinder — hoop** | **pd/(2t)** |
| **Cylinder — longitudinal** | **pd/(4t)** |
| **SPHERE — the same in every direction** | **pd/(4t)** ← |

> **A SPHERE'S STRESS IS HALF A CYLINDER'S MAXIMUM, for the same diameter, pressure and thickness — so a sphere needs only half the wall thickness and is the most material-efficient pressure vessel there is.**

> **It is also the most expensive to fabricate, since every plate must be curved in two directions and every weld is a compound curve.**

> **Hence the familiar compromise: spherical vessels where the pressure is high and the quantity of material dominates (LPG storage spheres), and cylindrical vessels with dished ends where fabrication cost dominates — which covers most pipes, boilers and tanks.**

examTip.trick: **Hoop pd/(2t), longitudinal pd/(4t) — hoop is TWICE longitudinal.** Option (b) is the longitudinal stress. The factor of two comes from the geometry of the two cuts.
examTip.trap: **A pressurised cylinder splits LENGTHWISE**, because the hoop stress governs — which is why a boiler's longitudinal seam must be stronger than its circumferential one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Thin means d/t > about 20**; below that use Lame's equations, where the stress peaks at the INNER face so thickening gives diminishing returns. A SPHERE carries pd/(4t) in every direction — half a cylinder's maximum, hence the most efficient vessel.

questions.stem: A uniform bar of length L, cross-sectional area A and total weight W hangs vertically from its upper end. Its extension under its OWN WEIGHT is:
options: WL/(AE)
2WL/(AE)
WL/(2AE)
WL/(4AE)
questions.solution:
**WL/(2AE)** — exactly HALF the extension the same load W would cause if hung at the free end.

**The derivation:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **The force varies along the bar** | **At a distance x from the BOTTOM, only the weight BELOW that section is carried: P(x) = Wx/L** ← |
| **Extension of an element dx** | **dδ = P(x) dx/(AE) = (Wx/L) dx/(AE)** ← |
| **Integrate from 0 to L** | **δ = (W/(LAE)) ∫₀^L x dx = (W/(LAE))(L²/2)** ← |
| **Result** | **δ = WL/(2AE)** ← |

> **The physical interpretation is neat and worth carrying: the self-weight acts as though the ENTIRE weight W were concentrated at the bar's CENTROID — that is, at MID-HEIGHT — so it stretches only the upper half of the bar's length.**

> **Hence exactly half the extension of a load hung at the bottom, which stretches the whole length.**

| Loading | Extension |
|---|---|
| **Load W applied at the FREE END** | **WL/(AE)** ← (option a) |
| **SELF-WEIGHT W distributed uniformly** | **WL/(2AE) — HALF** ← |

**In terms of the material's own properties:**

> **Since W = ρgAL (with ρ the density), substituting gives:**

> **δ = ρgAL × L/(2AE) = ρgL²/(2E)**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The AREA cancels entirely** | **A thicker bar weighs proportionally more, so its self-weight extension is UNCHANGED** ← |
| **The extension varies as the SQUARE of the length** | **Doubling the length QUADRUPLES the self-weight extension** ← |
| **The stress at the top is ρgL, also independent of area** | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IMPORTANT RESULT: MAKING A HANGING BAR THICKER DOES NOT REDUCE ITS SELF-WEIGHT STRESS OR EXTENSION AT ALL.**

> **The added area carries exactly the added weight, so nothing is gained. The only remedies are a shorter bar, a lighter material, or a higher modulus.**

**Where that matters, since it is a genuine engineering limit:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A long HOISTING ROPE in a deep mine shaft** | **Below a certain depth the rope cannot even carry itself, whatever its diameter** ← |
| **A deep BORED PILE's reinforcement cage during lifting** | ← |
| **Long suspender cables and drilling strings** | ← |
| **A hanging concrete pile during handling** | **Which is why lifting points are specified at particular positions** ← |

> **THE MINE ROPE CASE IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE CLASSIC ILLUSTRATION OF THE LIMIT: the maximum length of a uniform bar or rope that can hang under its own weight is L_max = σ_allow/(ρg), and it depends ONLY on the material's strength-to-weight ratio.**

> **For steel with σ_allow = 150 MPa and ρg = 78.5 kN/m³: L_max = 150,000/78.5 = 1,910 m.**

> **So a uniform steel rope cannot exceed about 1.9 km even carrying nothing else — which is precisely why deep mine hoisting uses TAPERED ropes, thicker at the top where the accumulated weight is greatest and thinner below.**

> **A tapered member of uniform stress is the logical answer, and it is the same reasoning that produces the tapered chimney, the tapered tower and the tapered cable stay.**

**And the related standard extension results, as a working set:**

| Case | Extension |
|---|---|
| **Uniform bar, load P at the end** | **PL/(AE)** ← |
| **Uniform bar, SELF-WEIGHT W** | **WL/(2AE)** ← |
| **Bar of varying section, load P** | **∫ P dx/(A(x)E) — integrate, or sum PLᵢ/(AᵢE) for a stepped bar** ← |
| **TAPERED circular bar, diameters d₁ to d₂, load P** | **4PL/(π E d₁ d₂)** ← |
| **Tapered rectangular bar, widths b₁ to b₂, thickness t** | **PL ln(b₁/b₂)/(Et(b₁ − b₂))** |

> **The TAPERED CIRCULAR result in the fourth row is worth noting for its elegance: the extension depends on the PRODUCT of the two end diameters, so it is exactly what a uniform bar of diameter √(d₁d₂) — the GEOMETRIC MEAN — would give.**

> **That is a satisfying result and a useful check: a taper from 40 mm to 90 mm behaves in extension exactly like a uniform bar of √(40 × 90) = 60 mm, not like one of the arithmetic mean 65 mm.**

examTip.trick: **WL/(2AE) — exactly HALF the end-loaded case (option a)**, because the self-weight acts as though concentrated at MID-HEIGHT and so stretches only half the length.
examTip.trap: **Written as ρgL²/(2E), the AREA CANCELS** — making a hanging bar thicker changes neither its self-weight stress nor its extension. The added area carries exactly the added weight.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum hanging length L_max = σ_allow/(ρg) — about 1.9 km for steel, whatever the diameter.** Hence TAPERED mine ropes. And a tapered circular bar extends like a uniform one of the GEOMETRIC mean diameter, √(d₁d₂).

questions.stem: In a FLITCHED BEAM — a timber beam strengthened by steel plates bolted to its sides — the analysis assumes that:
options: Both materials undergo the SAME CURVATURE, so the strain at any depth is the same in both and the stresses are in the ratio of their moduli
Each material carries half the bending moment
Only the steel plates carry the bending moment
The two materials act independently, each with its own curvature
questions.solution:
**Both materials undergo the SAME CURVATURE**, so the strain at any given depth is identical in both and the stresses there are in the ratio of their elastic moduli.

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The plates are BOLTED to the timber, so they deflect together** | **COMPATIBILITY — the same curvature, and hence the same strain at the same depth** ← |
| **At depth y: ε_steel = ε_timber** | ← |
| **By Hooke's law: σ_s/E_s = σ_t/E_t** | **So σ_s/σ_t = E_s/E_t = m, the MODULAR RATIO** ← |
| **The moments carried are in the ratio of their EI values** ← | **EQUILIBRIUM: M_total = M_steel + M_timber** ← |

> **THIS IS THE SAME LOGIC AS THE COMPOSITE BAR IN AXIAL LOADING, transferred to bending: compatibility fixes the strains, Hooke's law converts them to stresses, and equilibrium shares the load.**

> **In axial loading the load divides in the ratio of AE; in bending it divides in the ratio of EI. Stiffness attracts load in both cases.**

> **Option (d) is the opposite assumption and would describe two SEPARATE beams merely stacked together, which is a quite different and far weaker arrangement.**

**The EQUIVALENT SECTION method, which is how the calculation is actually done:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Choose one material as the reference — usually the TIMBER** ← |
| **2** | **Replace the steel by an EQUIVALENT WIDTH of timber: multiply the steel's width by the modular ratio m = E_s/E_t** ← |
| **3** | **Analyse the resulting single-material section in the ordinary way: I, then σ = My/I** ← |
| **4** | **Convert back: the actual stress in the steel is m × the stress computed at that depth in the equivalent timber** ← |

> **The WIDTH is multiplied and the DEPTH is not — and the reason is important: multiplying the depth would move the material to a different distance from the neutral axis, changing the strain there and destroying the compatibility the method rests on.**

> **Widening keeps every fibre at its original depth, so the strains are unaltered and only the stiffness is scaled — which is exactly what is wanted.**

**A worked example, since the numbers show why flitching is done:**

> **A timber beam 100 mm wide × 200 mm deep (E_t = 10 GPa), with two steel plates each 10 mm × 200 mm bolted to its sides (E_s = 200 GPa). Modular ratio m = 20.**

| Component | Actual width | Equivalent timber width | I about the centroid |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Timber** | **100 mm** | **100 mm** | **100 × 200³/12 = 66.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴** |
| **Two steel plates** | **2 × 10 = 20 mm** | **20 × 20 = 400 mm** ← | **400 × 200³/12 = 266.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **TOTAL equivalent** | — | **500 mm** | **333.4 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |

| Comparison | Value |
|---|---|
| **Timber alone** | **66.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴** |
| **Flitched beam (equivalent)** | **333.4 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **Improvement** | **FIVE TIMES the stiffness, for 20 mm of steel** ← |

> **The two thin plates occupy a sixth of the timber's area and contribute FOUR FIFTHS of the section's stiffness — because steel is twenty times stiffer, and the equivalent-width transformation makes that visible directly.**

**Why a flitched beam is used at all:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Greatly increased strength and stiffness for a modest depth** | **Where headroom forbids a deeper timber** ← |
| **Uses timber's low cost and steel's strength together** | ← |
| **The timber holds the thin steel plates against BUCKLING** ← | **A genuine structural benefit — a 10 mm plate alone would buckle laterally** ← |
| **Repair and STRENGTHENING of existing timber floors** | **The commonest modern use, in conservation work** ← |
| **Lighter than an equivalent steel beam; easier to fix joists to** | ← |

> **THE BUCKLING POINT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISSED and it is genuinely mutual: the steel strengthens the timber in bending, and the timber restrains the steel against lateral-torsional buckling.**

> **Neither material could be used so efficiently alone, which is what makes the combination more than the sum of its parts.**

> **The design must ensure the BOLTS can transfer the horizontal shear between the two materials — because if they slip, the compatibility assumption fails and the components revert to acting independently, with a fraction of the combined stiffness.**

> **That is the same requirement as the shear connectors in a composite steel-and-concrete beam, and the same failure mode: without adequate connection, two bonded 100 mm layers behave as two separate 100 mm layers rather than as one 200 mm section.**

examTip.trick: **Same CURVATURE → same strain at a given depth → σ_s/σ_t = E_s/E_t = m.** Moments divide in the ratio of EI, exactly as axial load divides in the ratio of AE.
examTip.trap: **In the equivalent section, multiply the WIDTH by m, never the depth** — changing the depth would move material to a different distance from the neutral axis and destroy the compatibility the method rests on.
examTip.mnemonic: **The benefit is mutual: steel strengthens the timber in bending, and the timber restrains the thin plates against BUCKLING.** And the bolts must transfer the horizontal shear — if they slip, the two revert to acting independently.

questions.stem: A BEAM OF UNIFORM STRENGTH is one in which:
options: The cross-section is the same throughout its length
The material is the same throughout
The SECTION is varied along the span so that the maximum bending stress is the SAME at every section
The deflection is the same at every point
questions.solution:
**One in which the SECTION is varied along the span so that the maximum bending stress reaches the SAME value at every section.**

**The idea:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **In a beam of CONSTANT section, the bending moment varies along the span** | **So the stress varies too — reaching the allowable value at ONE section only** ← |
| **Everywhere else the material is UNDERSTRESSED** ← | **Which is wasted material** |
| **A beam of uniform strength varies its section IN PROPORTION to the moment** | **So every section is working at the allowable stress** ← |
| **The result** | **The MINIMUM material for the given loading** ← |

> **Option (a) describes a PRISMATIC beam, which is the very thing a beam of uniform strength is not — and it is the natural misreading of the phrase, since "uniform" is doing quite different work in the two expressions.**

> **"Uniform strength" means uniform STRESS, achieved by a VARYING section.**

**How the section is varied:**

> **The requirement is σ = M/Z = constant, so Z must vary in direct proportion to M.**

| Method | Consequence for a simply supported beam with a central load |
|---|---|
| **Keep the DEPTH constant, vary the WIDTH** | **Z = bd²/6, so b ∝ M — the beam becomes a DIAMOND (two triangles) in plan** ← |
| **Keep the WIDTH constant, vary the DEPTH** | **Z = bd²/6, so d ∝ √M — the profile is PARABOLIC in elevation** ← |
| **Vary BOTH** | Intermediate |

> **The two rows produce quite different shapes from the same requirement, and the reason is the SQUARE on the depth: width enters Z linearly, so it must follow M directly, while depth enters as d² and need only follow √M.**

> **That is why varying the depth is the more effective route — a modest change of depth achieves what a large change of width would.**

**Where beams of uniform strength appear in practice:**

| Example | Note |
|---|---|
| **LEAF SPRINGS in vehicles** | **The classic case: a diamond plate cut into strips and stacked, which is exactly the constant-depth varying-width solution** ← |
| **HAUNCHED beams in reinforced concrete frames** | **Deepened at the supports, where the hogging moment is greatest** ← |
| **Cantilever brackets and canopies** | **Tapering to a thin free end where the moment is zero** ← |
| **Plate girders with CURTAILED flange plates** | **Extra plates only where the moment demands them** ← |
| **Bridge girders of varying depth** | **Deep over the piers, shallow at midspan** ← |
| **Aircraft wings, wind turbine blades, tapered poles** | ← |

> **THE LEAF SPRING IS THE MOST ELEGANT OF THESE and is worth picturing: the theoretical shape is a single flat plate, diamond-shaped in plan, of constant thickness.**

> **Cut that diamond into parallel strips and stack them, and you have the familiar leaf spring — mechanically identical, but compact and manufacturable.**

> **The stacking is not a compromise on the theory; it is a rearrangement of exactly the right amount of material into a practical form.**

**Why beams of uniform strength are NOT used everywhere, since they save material:**

| Objection | Note |
|---|---|
| **FABRICATION cost** | **A varying section costs far more to make than a prismatic one, in steel, timber or concrete** ← |
| **Formwork** | **A haunched concrete beam needs purpose-made formwork that cannot be reused as easily** ← |
| **The saving is modest** | **Typically 15-30 per cent of the material, against a much larger increase in labour** ← |
| **The theoretical shape often fails on SHEAR** | **The section tapering to zero at a support is precisely where the SHEAR is greatest** ← |
| **Deflection may govern instead of stress** | **A uniform-strength beam is not a uniform-stiffness beam** ← |

> **THE SHEAR OBJECTION IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL LIMITATION, and it shows the theory's boundary: at a simple support the bending moment is zero, so the uniform-strength rule calls for zero section — and yet the SHEAR there is at its maximum.**

> **A beam tapering to nothing at its support would fail instantly in shear.**

> **So every real beam of uniform strength is truncated at a minimum section governed by shear, bearing and practicality — the theoretical profile applies over the middle region only.**

> **That is a good general lesson about optimisation: an objective function optimised in isolation produces a shape that violates a constraint the objective never mentioned, and the useful answer is always the optimum SUBJECT TO the other requirements.**

> **The material saving in the third row explains why the technique survives where fabrication is cheap relative to material — long-span bridges, aircraft, wind turbine blades — and is abandoned where it is not, which is most ordinary building work.**

examTip.trick: **"Uniform strength" means uniform STRESS, from a VARYING section** — Z varied in proportion to M. Option (a) describes a PRISMATIC beam, the natural misreading.
examTip.trap: **Constant depth → width ∝ M (a diamond in plan); constant width → depth ∝ √M (a parabola)** — because depth enters Z as d². Varying the depth is the more effective route.
examTip.mnemonic: **The theoretical profile tapers to ZERO at a simple support — exactly where SHEAR is greatest**, so every real one is truncated. An objective optimised alone violates the constraints it never mentioned.

questions.stem: The METHOD OF SECTIONS is preferred to the method of joints for analysing a truss when:
options: Every member force in the truss is required
The force in only a FEW SPECIFIC members, possibly in the middle of the truss, is required
The truss is statically indeterminate
The truss carries no external loads
questions.solution:
**When the force in only a FEW SPECIFIC members is required**, particularly members in the middle of the truss.

**The two methods compared:**

| | METHOD OF JOINTS | METHOD OF SECTIONS |
|---|---|---|
| **What is isolated** | **ONE JOINT at a time** ← | **A whole PORTION of the truss, cut by an imaginary section** ← |
| **Equations available** | **TWO per joint (ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0) — no moment equation, since all forces pass through the joint** ← | **THREE (ΣF_x, ΣF_y, ΣM = 0) — a moment equation is available because the forces are spread out** ← |
| **Unknowns solvable at once** | **TWO** ← | **THREE** ← |
| **Best for** | **ALL member forces** ← (option a) | **A FEW specific members** ← |
| **To reach a middle member** | **Must work joint by joint from a support — laborious and error-accumulating** ← | **Cut straight through it and solve in ONE step** ← |

> **THE DECISIVE ADVANTAGE IS IN THE LAST ROW: the method of sections reaches any member DIRECTLY.**

> **To find the force in a member at mid-span by the method of joints, one must solve every joint from the support inward — perhaps eight or ten joints — and any arithmetic error along the way propagates to the answer.**

> **The method of sections cuts through that member and solves for it in a single equation, independent of everything else.**

**The rules for applying it:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cut through NOT MORE THAN THREE members with unknown forces** | **Only three equations are available** ← |
| **The cut must SEPARATE the truss into two distinct parts** | ← |
| **Take moments about the point where TWO of the three unknowns INTERSECT** ← | **That eliminates both at once and gives the third directly** ← |
| **Either portion may be used — choose the SIMPLER one** ← | **Usually the side with fewer loads** ← |
| **Assume all unknown forces are TENSILE** | **A negative answer then means compression, with no sign confusion** ← |

> **THE MOMENT-CENTRE CHOICE IN THE THIRD ROW IS WHAT MAKES THE METHOD POWERFUL, and it deserves stating as a technique rather than a rule:**

> **If a section cuts a top chord, a diagonal and a bottom chord, then taking moments about the joint where the DIAGONAL and the BOTTOM chord meet eliminates both, leaving the TOP chord force alone in the equation.**

> **One equation, one unknown — no simultaneous solution at all.**

> **Choosing a different moment centre isolates a different member, so all three can be found by three independent single-unknown equations rather than by solving three simultaneously.**

> **And where two of the cut members are PARALLEL, they cannot intersect at a finite point — so the diagonal is found instead by resolving VERTICALLY (ΣF_y = 0), since the parallel chords contribute nothing vertical.**

**ZERO-FORCE MEMBERS, which should always be identified first:**

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| **TWO non-collinear members at an UNLOADED joint** | **BOTH carry zero force** ← |
| **THREE members at an unloaded joint, two of them COLLINEAR** | **The THIRD (the odd one out) carries zero** ← |
| **Two members at a joint with a load ALONG one of them** | The other is zero |

> **Identifying these before starting can remove a third of the members from the analysis, and they are not useless despite carrying no load: they hold the compression members against BUCKLING, they carry load under DIFFERENT load cases, and they maintain the truss's geometry.**

> **So a zero-force member must never be deleted from the structure on the strength of one load case.**

**And the assumptions the whole analysis rests on, which are worth being honest about:**

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| **Members are joined by FRICTIONLESS PINS** | **Real joints are BOLTED or WELDED and are partly rigid** ← |
| **Loads are applied only at the JOINTS** | **A purlin between panel points bends the member** ← |
| **Members are STRAIGHT and their centroidal axes MEET at a point** | **An eccentric connection introduces a moment** ← |
| **Self-weight is neglected or lumped at the joints** | ← |

> **Because of the first assumption every member carries only AXIAL force, which is what makes truss analysis so simple — and real trusses develop small bending moments at their joints as a result of the rigidity that assumption ignores.**

> **These are called SECONDARY STRESSES, and they are generally accepted as small (5 to 10 per cent) and ignored — provided the third assumption holds.**

> **Where the centroidal axes do NOT meet at a point, the eccentricity produces a moment that is NOT small, and that is a detailing error rather than an acceptable idealisation.**

> **Hence the rule on every truss drawing: THE SETTING-OUT LINES OF ALL MEMBERS AT A JOINT MUST INTERSECT AT A SINGLE POINT — and where they cannot, the resulting moment must be designed for explicitly.**

examTip.trick: **Sections gives THREE equations (including moments) and reaches a mid-truss member in ONE step; joints gives TWO and must work inward from a support.** Option (a) is when joints is better.
examTip.trap: **Cut no more than THREE unknown members, and take moments about where TWO of them INTERSECT** — that leaves one unknown in one equation, so no simultaneous solution is needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Find ZERO-FORCE members first** — but never delete them: they brace compression members and carry load in other cases. And all member axes at a joint must meet at ONE point, or the eccentric moment is a real defect, not a secondary stress.

questions.stem: In the CONJUGATE BEAM method, the deflection of the real beam at a section is obtained as:
options: The shear force in the conjugate beam at that section
The reaction of the conjugate beam at that section
The slope of the conjugate beam at that section
The BENDING MOMENT in the conjugate beam at that section
questions.solution:
**The BENDING MOMENT in the conjugate beam at that section.**

**The two correspondences, which are the whole method:**

| In the REAL beam | Equals, in the CONJUGATE beam |
|---|---|
| **SLOPE θ** | **The SHEAR FORCE** ← (option a) |
| **DEFLECTION y** | **The BENDING MOMENT** ← |

> **The conjugate beam is a fictitious beam of the same span, loaded with the real beam's M/EI diagram as though it were a distributed load.**

**Why it works — the parallel between two pairs of equations:**

| Real beam | Conjugate beam |
|---|---|
| **d²y/dx² = M/EI** | **d²M/dx² = −w** ← |
| **Integrating once gives the SLOPE** | **Integrating the load once gives the SHEAR** ← |
| **Integrating twice gives the DEFLECTION** | **Integrating twice gives the BENDING MOMENT** ← |

> **THE TWO DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS HAVE IDENTICAL FORM, so loading a fictitious beam with M/EI and computing its shear and moment performs exactly the same two integrations — but as ordinary statics, which is far easier than calculus.**

> **That is the entire insight: a DEFLECTION problem is converted into a STATICS problem, and the familiar machinery of reactions, shear and moment does the integration.**

**The SUPPORT CONVERSIONS, which are the method's one subtlety:**

> **The conjugate beam's supports must be chosen so that its shear and moment reproduce the real beam's slope and deflection — so the supports CHANGE.**

| Real support | Real slope / deflection | Conjugate support |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple support (end)** | **Slope free, deflection zero** | **SIMPLE support** — shear free, moment zero ← |
| **FIXED end** | **Slope ZERO, deflection ZERO** | **FREE end** — no shear, no moment ← |
| **FREE end (cantilever tip)** | **Slope free, deflection free** | **FIXED end** — shear and moment both exist ← |
| **Interior support (continuous beam)** | **Deflection zero, slope continuous** | **Internal HINGE** ← |
| **Internal hinge** | **Deflection continuous, slope discontinuous** | **Interior SUPPORT** ← |

> **THE FIXED AND FREE ENDS SWAP, which is the rule most often forgotten and the source of most errors in the method.**

> **The logic is straightforward once seen: a fixed end has NO slope and NO deflection, so its conjugate must have NO shear and NO moment — and that is a FREE end.**

> **A free end has both slope and deflection, so its conjugate must carry both shear and moment — and that is a FIXED end.**

**A worked example — the standard cantilever:**

> **A cantilever of length L with a point load W at the free end. Find the tip deflection.**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Real BMD** | **Triangular: 0 at the tip, −WL at the fixed end** |
| **Conjugate LOAD** | **The M/EI diagram: a triangle of peak WL/EI at what was the fixed end** ← |
| **Conjugate beam** | **FIXED at what was the free end; FREE at what was the fixed end** ← |
| **Total conjugate load** | **½ × L × WL/EI = WL²/(2EI)** |
| **Its centroid from the conjugate's FIXED end (the real tip)** | **2L/3** ← |
| **Bending moment at the conjugate's fixed end** | **(WL²/2EI) × (2L/3) = WL³/(3EI)** ← |
| **Therefore the real tip DEFLECTION** | **WL³/(3EI)** ✓ |

> **The standard result, obtained by taking one moment — no integration and no boundary conditions to impose.**

**How it compares with the alternatives:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **CONJUGATE BEAM** | **Purely mechanical — no judgement about reference tangents; handles VARIABLE EI easily; the support conversions must be got right** ← |
| **MOMENT-AREA** | **The same mathematics, but requires choosing a reference tangent — which is a judgement, and an advantage where the choice is obvious** ← |
| **Double integration** | Gives the complete deflected shape as an equation |
| **Macaulay's method** | Best for several point loads |
| **Unit load / virtual work** | Best for trusses and frames |

> **The conjugate beam and moment-area methods are mathematically IDENTICAL — both integrate the M/EI diagram twice — and they differ only in bookkeeping.**

> **Moment-area asks the user to choose a tangent and to think about deviations from it; the conjugate beam removes that choice by encoding the boundary conditions in the SUPPORTS instead.**

> **That makes the conjugate beam more mechanical and therefore less error-prone for continuous and propped beams, where choosing a good reference tangent is not obvious — and it is why the method is worth knowing even after the moment-area theorems are understood.**

> **Both share the same real advantage over double integration: a beam of VARYING EI is handled without difficulty, because the M/EI diagram is simply drawn with its ordinates divided by the local EI and then treated as an ordinary load.**

examTip.trick: **Real SLOPE = conjugate SHEAR; real DEFLECTION = conjugate BENDING MOMENT.** Load the conjugate beam with the M/EI diagram — because d²y/dx² = M/EI has the same form as d²M/dx² = −w.
examTip.trap: **FIXED and FREE ends SWAP.** A fixed end has no slope and no deflection, so its conjugate must have no shear and no moment — a FREE end. Getting this backwards is the usual error.
examTip.mnemonic: **It converts a DEFLECTION problem into a STATICS problem** — the integrations become reactions, shear and moment. Mathematically identical to moment-area, but the boundary conditions live in the SUPPORTS rather than in a chosen tangent.

questions.stem: CLAPEYRON'S THREE MOMENT EQUATION relates:
options: The moments at three points along a single simply supported span
The support moments at THREE CONSECUTIVE SUPPORTS of a continuous beam, over two adjacent spans
The three components of reaction at a fixed support
The moments carried by three members meeting at a rigid joint
questions.solution:
**The support moments at THREE CONSECUTIVE SUPPORTS of a continuous beam**, over the two adjacent spans between them.

**The equation, for two spans L₁ and L₂ with constant EI:**

> **M_A L₁ + 2 M_B (L₁ + L₂) + M_C L₂ + 6A₁x̄₁/L₁ + 6A₂x̄₂/L₂ = 0**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **M_A, M_B, M_C** | **The bending moments at the three consecutive supports** ← |
| **A₁, A₂** | **The AREAS of the free (simply supported) bending moment diagrams for each span** ← |
| **x̄₁** | **The distance of A₁'s centroid from the OUTER support A** ← |
| **x̄₂** | **The distance of A₂'s centroid from the OUTER support C** ← |

> **Note the asymmetry in the last two rows: BOTH centroid distances are measured from the OUTER supports, away from the common support B — which is the detail most often got wrong.**

> **Where the supports SETTLE, additional terms 6EIδ/L appear, which is how the settlement moments met earlier enter the analysis.**

**How it is used:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Write the equation for each pair of adjacent spans** ← |
| **2** | **A beam with n internal supports gives n equations** ← |
| **3** | **The end conditions supply the outer moments: ZERO at a simple end, or an overhang moment if there is one** ← |
| **4** | **A FIXED end is handled by adding an imaginary span of zero length, or of infinite EI** ← |
| **5** | **Solve the simultaneous equations for the support moments** ← |
| **6** | **The span moments and reactions then follow by statics** ← |

> **THE FIXED-END DEVICE IN STEP 4 IS THE METHOD'S ONE PIECE OF TRICKERY, and it works because a zero-length span imposes exactly the condition a fixed end requires — zero rotation at that support.**

**How it compares with the alternatives:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **THREE MOMENT equation** | **Best for CONTINUOUS BEAMS; gives exact simultaneous equations; becomes unwieldy beyond three or four spans** ← |
| **MOMENT DISTRIBUTION** | **Iterative rather than simultaneous; handles FRAMES and sway; scales to any size** ← |
| **SLOPE-DEFLECTION** | **Simultaneous equations in the ROTATIONS; the conceptual parent of the stiffness method** ← |
| **Matrix stiffness** | **The general method; what all software uses** ← |

> **The three moment equation is a FORCE (flexibility) method — its unknowns are the support MOMENTS, which are forces.**

> **Moment distribution and slope-deflection are DISPLACEMENT methods — their unknowns are rotations.**

> **So the choice between them follows the rule met under indeterminacy: use the method whose number of unknowns is smaller. For a continuous beam of three or four spans the support moments are few, and Clapeyron's method is efficient; for a multi-storey frame the rotations are fewer and the displacement methods win decisively.**

**Why CONTINUITY is worth the extra analysis, which is the point of the whole topic:**

| Advantage of a continuous beam over simply supported spans | Note |
|---|---|
| **SMALLER maximum moments** | **wL²/8 becomes wL²/12 at the supports and wL²/24 at mid-span for a fully fixed span** ← |
| **Smaller DEFLECTIONS** | **Roughly a fifth of the simply supported value for a fixed span** ← |
| **REDUNDANCY — alternative load paths** | ← |
| **Fewer joints and bearings to build and maintain** | **A significant cost on a bridge** ← |
| **Better appearance; a shallower deck** | ← |

| Disadvantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stresses from SUPPORT SETTLEMENT** | **6EIδ/L² — and a stiffer beam suffers MORE** ← |
| **Stresses from temperature and shrinkage** | ← |
| **More complex analysis and detailing** | Now trivial with software |
| **Reinforcement must be provided at the TOP over supports** | **Where a simply supported beam needs none — and this is a common detailing error** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS A CONSTRUCTION FAILURE MODE RATHER THAN AN ANALYTICAL ONE: a continuous beam HOGS over its supports, so the tension there is at the TOP.**

> **A slab or beam detailed as though simply supported — with all its main steel at the bottom — will crack over every support, because there is no reinforcement where the tension actually is.**

> **The cracking appears on the top surface, often under the floor finish where it is not seen, and the member sheds its continuity moment by cracking until it behaves as a series of simply supported spans — which it was not designed as either.**

> **So the analysis and the detailing must agree: if the structure is analysed as continuous, it must be REINFORCED as continuous, and the top steel over the supports is not optional.**

examTip.trick: **M_A L₁ + 2M_B(L₁+L₂) + M_C L₂ + 6A₁x̄₁/L₁ + 6A₂x̄₂/L₂ = 0** — three consecutive support moments over two adjacent spans.
examTip.trap: **Both centroid distances x̄ are measured from the OUTER supports**, away from the common support B. And a FIXED end is handled by adding an imaginary span of zero length.
examTip.mnemonic: **It is a FORCE method (unknowns = moments); moment distribution and slope-deflection are DISPLACEMENT methods (unknowns = rotations)** — choose whichever has fewer unknowns. And a continuous beam HOGS over supports: the top steel there is not optional.

questions.stem: In the SLOPE-DEFLECTION method of structural analysis, the unknowns solved for are the:
options: Bending moments at the supports
Reactions at the supports
Areas of the bending moment diagrams
JOINT ROTATIONS (and sway displacements), from which the end moments are then computed
questions.solution:
**The JOINT ROTATIONS — together with any sway displacements — from which the member end moments are then computed.**

**The slope-deflection equation:**

> **M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3Δ/L) + FEM_AB**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **θ_A, θ_B** | **The ROTATIONS of the two ends — the UNKNOWNS** ← |
| **Δ** | **The relative lateral displacement of the ends — the SWAY** ← |
| **FEM_AB** | **The FIXED END MOMENT for the loading on that span** ← |
| **2EI/L** | The member's stiffness |

> **The method is therefore a DISPLACEMENT (stiffness) method: it solves for displacements first and derives the forces from them, which is the opposite of the force methods.**

| Method type | Unknowns | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **FORCE (flexibility)** | **FORCES — redundant reactions or moments** ← | **Three moment equation, consistent deformation, Castigliano** ← |
| **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness)** | **DISPLACEMENTS — rotations and translations** ← | **SLOPE-DEFLECTION, moment distribution, matrix stiffness** ← |

> **Option (a) names the unknowns of the THREE MOMENT equation — a real method with a real set of unknowns, and precisely the opposite kind — which is what makes it the designed distractor.**

**The procedure:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Identify the unknown joint rotations and sway displacements — the degrees of kinematic indeterminacy** ← |
| **2** | **Compute the FIXED END MOMENTS for every member under its loading** ← |
| **3** | **Write the slope-deflection equation for each member end** ← |
| **4** | **Apply JOINT EQUILIBRIUM: ΣM = 0 at every rigid joint** ← |
| **5** | **For a frame that can SWAY, add a SHEAR equation for each independent sway degree of freedom** ← |
| **6** | **Solve the simultaneous equations for the rotations** |
| **7** | **Substitute back to obtain every end moment** ← |

> **STEP 5 IS THE ONE THAT DISTINGUISHES FRAMES FROM BEAMS AND IS ROUTINELY OVERLOOKED:**

> **A continuous beam has only rotational unknowns, and joint equilibrium alone is enough.**

> **A frame free to sway sideways has an ADDITIONAL unknown — the lateral displacement — and joint equilibrium provides no equation for it. The missing equation comes from horizontal equilibrium of the storey: the sum of the column shears must equal the applied horizontal force.**

> **Omitting that shear equation leaves the system underdetermined, and the analysis simply cannot be completed — which at least makes the error self-announcing.**

**Its relationship to the other methods:**

| Relationship | Note |
|---|---|
| **MOMENT DISTRIBUTION is slope-deflection solved ITERATIVELY** ← | **Hardy Cross's contribution was a method of successive approximation to the same equations, avoiding simultaneous solution** ← |
| **MATRIX STIFFNESS is slope-deflection written in matrix form and generalised** ← | **Same equations, systematised for a computer** ← |
| **So all three are the same theory** | **Differing only in how the equations are solved** ← |

> **THAT LINEAGE IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS WHY THESE METHODS ARE ALL TAUGHT: slope-deflection states the physics, moment distribution made it hand-computable before computers, and matrix stiffness made it universal after them.**

> **Understanding slope-deflection is therefore understanding what every structural analysis program is doing internally — it assembles a stiffness matrix from exactly these member relations, applies the same joint equilibrium, and solves the same simultaneous equations, merely with thousands of unknowns instead of three.**

**And why the DISPLACEMENT methods won, which is the practical conclusion:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The formulation is entirely SYSTEMATIC** | **No judgement about which redundants to release — the unknowns are simply the joint freedoms** ← |
| **It handles ANY structure by the same procedure** | **Beams, frames, trusses, grids, three-dimensional structures** ← |
| **D_k grows more slowly than D_s in large structures** | **A multi-storey frame has dozens of redundants and comparatively few joints** ← |
| **It suits matrix formulation and hence computation** | ← |
| **Support settlements and temperature effects enter naturally** | **As prescribed displacements** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DECISIVE ONE FOR AUTOMATION: a force method requires someone to CHOOSE a set of redundants, and a bad choice produces an ill-conditioned system while a good one requires insight.**

> **A displacement method requires no such choice — the unknowns are dictated by the structure's geometry — so it can be coded once and applied to anything.**

> **That is why every commercial analysis package is built on the stiffness method and none on the flexibility method, and it is a good example of a technique winning not because it is more accurate (both are exact) but because it can be MECHANISED.**

examTip.trick: **M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3Δ/L) + FEM** — the unknowns are the ROTATIONS θ and the sway Δ. Option (a) names the THREE MOMENT equation's unknowns, the opposite kind of method.
examTip.trap: **A frame free to SWAY needs an extra SHEAR equation per sway degree of freedom** — joint equilibrium alone gives no equation for the lateral displacement, and omitting it leaves the system underdetermined.
examTip.mnemonic: **Moment distribution is slope-deflection solved ITERATIVELY; matrix stiffness is it written in matrices.** All three are one theory. Displacement methods won because they need no CHOICE of redundants — so they can be mechanised.

questions.stem: As per IS 1893, the IMPORTANCE FACTOR I to be used for a hospital or an emergency-services building is:
questions.solution:
**1.5.**

**The values:**

| Building | Importance factor I |
|---|---|
| **Important service and community buildings** — **HOSPITALS, schools, fire and police stations, emergency shelters, power stations, water towers, telephone exchanges, monumental structures, and assembly buildings for more than 300 persons** | **1.5** ← |
| **ALL OTHER buildings** | **1.0** ← |

> **Option (b) is the value for ordinary buildings, which makes it the designed distractor — both are real values from the same clause.**

**Where I sits in the expression, and why it acts as it does:**

> **A_h = (Z/2) × (I/R) × (S_a/g)**

| Factor | Position | Effect of increasing it |
|---|---|---|
| **I — importance** | **NUMERATOR** ← | **INCREASES the design force** ← |
| **R — response reduction** | **DENOMINATOR** | Decreases the design force |

> **So raising I from 1.0 to 1.5 increases the design seismic force by FIFTY PER CENT — the building is deliberately made stronger than the code's ordinary requirement.**

**What the factor actually buys, which is worth being precise about:**

| It does NOT mean | It DOES mean |
|---|---|
| **That the hospital is designed for a bigger earthquake** ← | **That it is designed for a larger FORCE from the same earthquake** ← |
| **That it will be undamaged** | **That it will suffer LESS damage, and is far more likely to remain FUNCTIONAL** ← |

> **THE FUNCTIONALITY REQUIREMENT IS THE WHOLE POINT AND IT IS DIFFERENT IN KIND FROM THE ORDINARY OBJECTIVE.**

> **For a normal building the code's aim is LIFE SAFETY: the occupants must be able to get out, and the building may then be a write-off.**

> **For a hospital, that is useless. A hospital that survives the earthquake but cannot operate has failed at the moment it was most needed — because an earthquake is precisely when a hospital's services are in greatest demand.**

> **The same reasoning covers fire stations, water supply, power and communications: these are the LIFELINE facilities on which the whole emergency response depends.**

**Why 1.5 is nevertheless a crude instrument:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A stronger STRUCTURE does not guarantee a working hospital** | **The equipment, the pipes, the ceilings, the power supply and the lifts must all survive too** ← |
| **NON-STRUCTURAL damage is what actually closes hospitals** ← | **Fallen ceilings, ruptured water and medical gas lines, toppled equipment, blocked corridors** ← |
| **A factor on the base shear addresses none of that** | ← |

> **THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT IN THIS TOPIC and it is well documented: hospitals have been evacuated after earthquakes that left their structures essentially intact, because a water tank burst, the ceiling came down over the operating theatre, or the emergency generator toppled off its mounting.**

> **So modern practice supplements the importance factor with explicit requirements for NON-STRUCTURAL elements — anchoring equipment, bracing suspended ceilings and services, flexible connections at joints, and restraining tanks and generators.**

> **Those measures cost very little relative to the structure and they are what actually keeps the facility working, which is why they have moved from good practice into the codes.**

**The other factors in A_h, for completeness:**

| Factor | Represents | Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Z** | **The site's seismic HAZARD** | **0.10 (Zone II) to 0.36 (Zone V)** ← |
| **I** | **The building's IMPORTANCE** | **1.0 or 1.5** ← |
| **R** | **DUCTILITY and reserve capacity of the system** | **1.5 (unreinforced masonry) to 5.0 (ductile SMRF)** ← |
| **S_a/g** | **DYNAMIC amplification with period and SOIL** | **Up to 2.5 on the plateau** ← |

> **Working a hospital example in Zone V on a ductile frame: A_h = (0.36/2)(1.5/5.0)(2.5) = 0.18 × 0.3 × 2.5 = 0.135.**

> **Against 0.09 for an ordinary building on the same site and system — exactly the 50 per cent increase the importance factor imposes.**

> **At 13.5 per cent of the seismic weight, that is a substantial lateral design force, and it is worth noting how it compares with wind: for a low-rise heavy masonry or concrete building in Nepal, the seismic force generally governs, while for a tall light steel structure wind may govern instead — so both must be checked rather than assumed.**

examTip.trick: **1.5 for hospitals, schools, fire and police stations, power, water, communications and assembly over 300 persons; 1.0 for everything else.** I is in the NUMERATOR of A_h, so it raises the design force by 50 %.
examTip.trap: **It does not mean a bigger earthquake — it means a larger force from the SAME earthquake.** And the objective changes in kind: from LIFE SAFETY to remaining FUNCTIONAL.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hospitals are evacuated after earthquakes that left the structure intact** — fallen ceilings, burst water lines, toppled generators. A factor on base shear addresses none of that, which is why NON-STRUCTURAL anchorage now sits alongside it in the codes.

questions.stem: In IS 875 (Part 3), the design wind speed is V_z = V_b k₁ k₂ k₃. The factor k₃ accounts for:
options: The probability or risk level, based on the structure's design life
The terrain category, the height above ground and the size of the structure
TOPOGRAPHY — the local effect of a hill, ridge, escarpment or cliff
The importance of the structure in a cyclonic region
questions.solution:
**TOPOGRAPHY** — the local speed-up caused by a hill, ridge, escarpment or cliff.

**The four factors:**

| Factor | Accounts for | Typical range |
|---|---|---|
| **k₁ — RISK (probability) coefficient** | **The structure's DESIGN LIFE and the consequence of failure** ← (option a) | **0.71 to 1.08** ← |
| **k₂ — TERRAIN, HEIGHT and SIZE** | **Ground roughness, height above ground, and the structure's size class** ← (option b) | **0.67 to 1.17** ← |
| **k₃ — TOPOGRAPHY** | **Local acceleration over hills, ridges and escarpments** ← | **1.0 to 1.36** ← |
| **k₄ — IMPORTANCE in a CYCLONIC region** | **Coastal areas subject to cyclones** ← (option d) | **1.0 to 1.30** |

> **Every option names one of the four real factors, so the question tests which is which.**

> **Note that k₃ is NEVER LESS THAN 1.0 — topography can only INCREASE the wind speed, never reduce it below the open-country value. A sheltered valley is not credited with a reduction, because the shelter cannot be relied upon and the wind may come from any direction.**

**Why topography accelerates the wind:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **The air flowing over a hill is CONSTRICTED between the ground and the undisturbed flow above** ← | **The same discharge through a narrower passage means a higher velocity — continuity, exactly as in a pipe** ← |
| **The acceleration is greatest at the CREST** | **And falls away down both slopes** ← |
| **The effect appears above an upwind slope of about 3° (1 in 20)** | **Below that, k₃ = 1.0** ← |
| **Maximum k₃ = 1.36** | **For a slope of 17° (about 1 in 3) or steeper** ← |

> **A k₃ of 1.36 raises the wind PRESSURE by 1.36² = 1.85 — nearly DOUBLING it — because pressure varies as the SQUARE of the velocity.**

> **THAT SQUARING IS THE POINT MOST OFTEN MISSED: every one of these k factors multiplies the SPEED, and the design pressure follows as p_z = 0.6 V_z².**

> **So a 36 per cent increase in speed is an 85 per cent increase in load, and a designer who applies the factors to the pressure rather than to the speed will be badly wrong.**

**The design pressure and the sequence:**

| Step | Expression |
|---|---|
| **1 — Basic wind speed V_b** | **From the map — 33 to 55 m/s across India; Nepal's hills and Terai fall in a similar range** ← |
| **2 — Design wind speed** | **V_z = V_b k₁ k₂ k₃ k₄** ← |
| **3 — Design wind PRESSURE** | **p_z = 0.6 V_z² (in N/m², with V_z in m/s)** ← |
| **4 — Design wind FORCE** | **F = (C_pe − C_pi) A p_z, or C_f A p_z for a whole structure** ← |

> **The 0.6 in step 3 is ½ρ with ρ = 1.2 kg/m³ — so the expression is simply the dynamic pressure ½ρV², with the air density already substituted.**

**The PRESSURE COEFFICIENTS in step 4, which decide where the load acts:**

| Surface | Typical coefficient |
|---|---|
| **Windward wall** | **+0.7 (PRESSURE, pushing in)** ← |
| **Leeward wall** | **−0.25 to −0.5 (SUCTION)** ← |
| **Side walls** | **−0.5 to −0.7 (suction)** |
| **FLAT or low-pitch ROOF, windward slope** | **−0.8 to −1.2 — strong SUCTION, LIFTING the roof** ← |
| **Local suction at eaves, ridges and corners** | **Up to −2.0 — the highest of all** ← |
| **INTERNAL pressure, with a large opening on the windward side** | **+0.7 — adding to the roof's uplift** ← |

> **THE ROOF SUCTION IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE FACT THAT MATTERS MOST IN PRACTICE, and it is counter-intuitive: wind does not press a light roof down, it SUCKS IT UP.**

> **A low-pitched roof behaves like an aerofoil, and the suction over it commonly exceeds the roof's own weight — which is why light roofs are lost in storms while the walls beneath them stand.**

> **And the INTERNAL PRESSURE row compounds it: if a windward door or window blows in, the internal pressure becomes strongly positive and ADDS to the external suction, so the net uplift can double.**

> **That is why the failure sequence in a storm is so often: a window breaks, the internal pressure rises, and the roof departs.**

> **The design consequences are direct — light roofs need HOLDING DOWN rather than merely supporting, their fixings must be designed for uplift, and the 0.9 dead load factor met earlier applies precisely here, because the roof's weight is the only thing resisting.**

examTip.trick: **k₁ risk/design life, k₂ terrain-height-size, k₃ TOPOGRAPHY, k₄ cyclonic importance.** All four options are real factors. k₃ is never below 1.0 — topography can only speed the wind up.
examTip.trap: **The k factors multiply the SPEED, and pressure goes as V².** So k₃ = 1.36 raises the LOAD by 1.85 — applying the factors to the pressure instead is a large error. p_z = 0.6 V_z², the 0.6 being ½ρ.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wind SUCKS a low-pitched roof UP (−0.8 to −1.2, and −2.0 locally at eaves and corners)** — and if a windward window breaks, internal pressure of +0.7 ADDS to it. Hence the storm sequence: window in, roof off.

questions.stem: The minimum period for which concrete made with ordinary Portland cement should be CURED, in ordinary weather, is:
options: 7 days
3 days
24 hours
28 days
questions.solution:
**7 days** (extended to 10 to 14 days for concrete containing mineral admixtures or blended cements, and in hot or dry weather).

**What curing is for:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Retain enough MOISTURE for HYDRATION to continue** ← | **Cement cannot hydrate without water; if the concrete dries, hydration STOPS and does not restart on rewetting to the same effect** ← |
| **Control the TEMPERATURE** | Both against heat and against freezing |
| **Prevent early-age drying (PLASTIC) SHRINKAGE cracking** | ← |
| **Develop the surface's DURABILITY** | **The outer 20-30 mm — the cover zone — is what curing most affects** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE POINT THAT MAKES CURING A DURABILITY MEASURE RATHER THAN A STRENGTH ONE, and it is the argument that carries most weight:**

> **The concrete most affected by poor curing is the SURFACE layer, because that is where the water is lost — and the surface layer is precisely the COVER that protects the reinforcement.**

> **So badly cured concrete may still test adequately on cubes (which are cured in a tank) while its cover zone is porous, permeable and offers far less protection against carbonation and chlorides.**

> **The defect is therefore invisible in the test results and invisible on the finished surface, and it shortens the structure's life by decades.**

**The strength consequence, which is substantial:**

| Curing | Strength at 28 days, relative to continuous moist curing |
|---|---|
| **Continuously moist for 28 days** | **100 per cent** ← |
| **Moist for 7 days, then air** | **About 85 per cent** |
| **Moist for 3 days, then air** | **About 75 per cent** ← |
| **NO curing — air dried from the start** | **About 50 per cent** ← |

> **Losing HALF the strength through no curing at all is a bigger effect than almost any other site variable — larger than a reasonable error in the mix proportions, and entirely free to avoid.**

**The methods:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **PONDING** | **Best for slabs and flat roofs — a bund of sand or clay holding 25-50 mm of water** ← |
| **WET COVERING** | **Hessian, jute, straw or sand kept continuously damp — for walls, columns and beams** ← |
| **SPRINKLING or fogging** | **Must be CONTINUOUS; intermittent wetting and drying is WORSE THAN NONE** ← |
| **MEMBRANE curing compound** | **A sprayed film sealing the moisture in — where water is scarce, and for large areas** ← |
| **Polythene sheeting** | Cheap; must be sealed at the edges |
| **STEAM curing** | **Accelerated, for precast units — high early strength, at some cost in ultimate strength** ← |
| **Leaving the FORMWORK in place** | **Helps, but the exposed top surface still needs attention** ← |

> **THE WARNING IN THE THIRD ROW DESERVES EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE: intermittent wetting is genuinely worse than leaving the concrete alone.**

> **Each wet-and-dry cycle causes the surface to expand and contract while the interior does not, producing tensile stresses and a network of fine surface cracks.**

> **So a slab sprinkled twice a day in hot weather is worse off than one sealed with a membrane and left, and that is a common site practice worth correcting.**

**The extended periods, and why:**

| Concrete | Minimum curing |
|---|---|
| **OPC, ordinary weather** | **7 days** ← |
| **Concrete with MINERAL ADMIXTURES (fly ash, slag, silica fume)** | **10 to 14 days** ← |
| **Hot, dry or windy weather** | **Extended, plus protection from sun and wind** ← |
| **Water-retaining structures, marine works** | **14 days and more** |

> **The blended-cement row has a clear reason: the POZZOLANIC reaction is SLOW, and it requires the calcium hydroxide produced by the cement's own hydration before it can begin at all.**

> **So a fly-ash concrete gains strength later and depends on curing for longer — and cutting its curing to 7 days penalises it far more than it would an OPC mix.**

> **That is a real and common error, because fly-ash concrete is specified for its durability benefits and then cured as though it were ordinary OPC, which forfeits precisely the benefit it was chosen for.**

> **And the HOT WEATHER row compounds the same problem: evaporation rises steeply with temperature and wind, and the critical figure is an evaporation rate above about 1 kg/m² per hour, beyond which plastic shrinkage cracking is likely and windbreaks, fogging or night placing become necessary.**

examTip.trick: **7 days for OPC; 10-14 days for blended cements and mineral admixtures, and in hot weather.** No curing at all costs about HALF the 28-day strength.
examTip.trap: **Curing chiefly protects the COVER ZONE, so poor curing is invisible** — cubes are tank-cured and still pass, while the surface that protects the reinforcement is left porous.
examTip.mnemonic: **INTERMITTENT wetting is worse than none** — each wet-dry cycle cracks the surface. And fly-ash concrete needs LONGER curing because the pozzolanic reaction is slow, so curing it like OPC forfeits the durability it was chosen for.

questions.stem: BLEEDING in fresh concrete is:
options: The separation of coarse aggregate from the mortar
The loss of workability with time after mixing
The upward movement of WATER to the surface, caused by the settlement of the solid particles
The formation of surface cracks before the concrete sets
questions.solution:
**The upward movement of WATER to the surface of freshly placed concrete**, caused by the heavier solid particles settling.

**Bleeding against segregation, which the option set turns on:**

| | BLEEDING | SEGREGATION |
|---|---|---|
