| **What separates** | **WATER from the solids** ← | **COARSE AGGREGATE from the mortar** ← (option a) |
| **Direction** | **Water rises; solids settle** | **Coarse aggregate falls or is thrown out** |
| **Cause** | **Excess water; too few FINES; over-vibration** ← | **Excessive DROP height; over-vibration; a harsh or badly graded mix; too wet or too dry** ← |
| **Visible as** | **A sheen of water on the surface** ← | **Coarse aggregate concentrated at the bottom, honeycombing, sand streaks** ← |

> **Option (a) is SEGREGATION, option (b) is SLUMP LOSS and option (d) is PLASTIC SHRINKAGE cracking — three real defects of fresh concrete, offered for the fourth.**

**The consequences of bleeding:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **LAITANCE — a weak, dusty layer of cement fines on the surface** ← | **Must be REMOVED before the next lift is placed, or it becomes a plane of weakness** ← |
| **A WEAK, porous top surface** | **Poor abrasion resistance on a floor** ← |
| **Water trapped UNDER coarse aggregate and UNDER reinforcement** ← | **Leaving voids that weaken the bond, particularly beneath TOP bars** ← |
| **Increased permeability along the bleed channels** | **Vertical capillaries left by the rising water** ← |
| **PLASTIC SETTLEMENT cracking over reinforcement** | **The concrete settles and the bars do not** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ORIGIN OF THE "TOP BAR EFFECT", which is a real and quantified phenomenon: reinforcement near the TOP of a deep pour has measurably poorer bond than identical steel near the bottom.**

> **Water bleeding upward collects under the horizontal bars, and when it eventually evaporates it leaves a void along the bar's underside.**

> **Codes recognise this by requiring a LONGER development length for top bars — IS 456 and others increase it, and the effect is greatest in deep members and in wet, over-sanded mixes.**

> **So bleeding is not merely a surface nuisance; it degrades the bond in exactly the reinforcement carrying the hogging moment over supports.**

**How bleeding is controlled:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reduce the WATER content** | **The root cause; use a plasticiser to keep the workability** ← |
| **Increase the FINES** | **More cement, finer sand, or a mineral admixture — fines hold the water** ← |
| **Use AIR ENTRAINMENT** | **The bubbles physically obstruct the rising water — a very effective remedy** ← |
| **Use a finer cement, or add fly ash or silica fume** | **Silica fume nearly eliminates bleeding** ← |
| **Avoid OVER-VIBRATION** | **Which drives the water up** ← |
| **Place in shallower lifts** | Less head to bleed under |

> **THE AIR-ENTRAINMENT REMEDY IN THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH NOTING because it is a second benefit of a measure introduced for freeze-thaw resistance: the entrained bubbles block the bleed channels mechanically.**

> **And SILICA FUME in the fourth row is so effective that it introduces the opposite problem — a silica fume concrete bleeds almost not at all, so there is no bleed water to keep the surface damp, and PLASTIC SHRINKAGE cracking becomes very likely unless curing begins immediately.**

> **That is a good illustration of a general truth about concrete: correcting one defect frequently creates the conditions for another, and the mix must be considered as a whole rather than adjusted for one property at a time.**

**A little bleeding is not wholly bad, which is the qualification:**

| Benefit of modest bleeding | Note |
|---|---|
| **The bleed water keeps the surface DAMP** | **Delaying plastic shrinkage cracking until finishing and curing can begin** ← |
| **It lowers the water-cement ratio of the concrete BELOW the surface** | **Which is a small strength gain where it matters** ← |

> **The practical rule that follows is about TIMING rather than quantity: DO NOT FINISH OR TROWEL THE SURFACE WHILE BLEED WATER IS STILL PRESENT.**

> **Working that water back into the surface raises its local water-cement ratio drastically and produces a weak, dusting, easily abraded finish — which is the commonest cause of poor concrete floors.**

> **Wait for the bleed water to evaporate or remove it, and only then finish. That single piece of discipline distinguishes a durable floor from one that dusts within a year.**

examTip.trick: **Bleeding separates WATER from the solids; SEGREGATION separates coarse aggregate from the mortar.** Options (a), (b) and (d) are segregation, slump loss and plastic shrinkage — three other real defects.
examTip.trap: **Bleed water trapped under TOP bars leaves voids and degrades bond** — the "top bar effect", which codes recognise by requiring a longer development length for top reinforcement.
examTip.mnemonic: **NEVER trowel while bleed water is present** — working it back in raises the surface w/c and gives a dusting floor. And silica fume nearly eliminates bleeding, which then makes plastic shrinkage cracking very likely.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the maximum spacing of VERTICAL STIRRUPS in a beam is the least of:
options: d, 16 times the stirrup diameter, or 300 mm
d/2, or 200 mm
1.5d, or 450 mm
questions.solution:
**0.75d, or 300 mm — whichever is LESS** (with d the effective depth). For inclined stirrups at 45°, the limit is d or 300 mm.

**The spacing rules:**

| Shear reinforcement | Maximum spacing |
|---|---|
| **VERTICAL stirrups** | **The LESSER of 0.75d and 300 mm** ← |
| **INCLINED stirrups at 45°** | **The lesser of d and 300 mm** ← |
| **In a seismic (ductile) design, within 2d of the support** | **Much closer — the lesser of d/4 and 8 times the smallest longitudinal bar** ← |

> **The inclined stirrup is permitted a WIDER spacing because it crosses a 45° diagonal crack more efficiently — a vertical stirrup meets the crack at 45°, while an inclined one can be placed perpendicular to it.**

**Why a maximum spacing exists at all:**

> **The purpose is to ensure that EVERY POSSIBLE DIAGONAL CRACK IS CROSSED BY AT LEAST ONE STIRRUP.**

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Stirrups spaced at 0.75d or less** | **A 45° crack of horizontal extent d must cross at least one stirrup** ← |
| **Stirrups spaced WIDER than d** | **A diagonal crack can form BETWEEN two stirrups and cross neither — the shear reinforcement is then entirely bypassed** ← |

> **THAT IS THE WHOLE REASONING, and it explains why the limit is expressed in terms of the EFFECTIVE DEPTH rather than as an absolute dimension: the crack's horizontal extent scales with the beam's depth, so the stirrup spacing must too.**

> **The absolute 300 mm cap then applies to deep beams, where 0.75d would otherwise permit an unreasonably wide spacing.**

**MINIMUM shear reinforcement, which applies even where none is required by calculation:**

> **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Guards against a SUDDEN diagonal tension failure** | **Which is BRITTLE and gives no warning** ← |
| **Covers unforeseen loads, settlement and torsion** | ← |
| **Holds the longitudinal bars in position during casting** | ← |
| **Restrains the compression steel against BUCKLING** | ← |
| **Provides some crack control** | ← |

> **The minimum applies wherever the computed shear stress exceeds HALF the concrete's design shear strength (τ_v > 0.5 τ_c) — so in practice nearly every beam carries stirrups throughout, including regions where the shear calculation shows none is needed.**

> **That is deliberate: shear failure is brittle, and a nominal amount of steel converts a sudden collapse into a visible, gradual one.**

**The design procedure, so the spacing is placed in context:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute the nominal shear stress τ_v = V_u/(b d)** ← |
| **2** | **Find the concrete's design shear strength τ_c, from the table against the steel percentage and the grade** ← |
| **3** | **If τ_v ≤ 0.5 τ_c** | **Nominal stirrups only** ← |
| **4** | **If 0.5 τ_c < τ_v ≤ τ_c** | **MINIMUM shear reinforcement** ← |
| **5** | **If τ_c < τ_v ≤ τ_c,max** | **Design stirrups for the EXCESS shear V_us = V_u − τ_c b d** ← |
| **6** | **If τ_v > τ_c,max** | **NOT PERMITTED — the section must be enlarged or the concrete grade raised** ← |

> **STEP 6 IS AN ABSOLUTE LIMIT AND NOT A DESIGN CHOICE, and the reason is worth knowing: beyond τ_c,max the failure mode changes.**

> **The concrete in the diagonal compression struts CRUSHES before the stirrups can yield — so adding more stirrups achieves nothing at all, because they will never be stressed.**

> **That is a genuine trap: the arithmetic of "more shear, more stirrups" continues to give an answer past the point where the mechanism it assumes has ceased to exist.**

> **The only remedies are a bigger section or stronger concrete, and IS 456 sets τ_c,max at 2.8 MPa for M20 rising to 4.0 MPa for M40.**

**And the mechanism the stirrups actually work by, since it is not obvious:**

| Contribution to shear resistance | Note |
|---|---|
| **The uncracked concrete in the COMPRESSION zone** | ← |
| **AGGREGATE INTERLOCK across the crack faces** ← | **A substantial contribution, lost if the crack opens wide** ← |
| **DOWEL ACTION of the longitudinal bars** | ← |
| **The STIRRUPS crossing the crack** | ← |

> **The stirrups' most important role is arguably INDIRECT: by keeping the diagonal crack NARROW, they preserve the aggregate interlock, which carries a large share of the shear.**

> **So shear reinforcement does not simply add its own tensile capacity to the total — it protects the concrete mechanisms that were already there, which is why a modest amount of steel produces a disproportionate improvement.**

examTip.trick: **Vertical stirrups: the lesser of 0.75d and 300 mm. Inclined at 45°: the lesser of d and 300 mm.** The inclined bar gets more room because it crosses the diagonal crack more directly.
examTip.trap: **The limit exists so every 45° crack is crossed by at least one stirrup** — spacing wider than d lets a crack form between two stirrups and bypass both entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Beyond τ_c,max the concrete STRUTS crush and more stirrups achieve NOTHING** — enlarge the section instead. And stirrups work partly by keeping cracks NARROW, preserving the aggregate interlock that was already carrying the shear.

questions.stem: In a reinforced concrete beam, a bar is CURTAILED (stopped off) where it is no longer required for flexure. As per IS 456, it must be extended beyond that theoretical cut-off point by:
options: The development length in every case
10 times the bar diameter
Half the effective depth
The EFFECTIVE DEPTH d, or 12 times the bar diameter, whichever is GREATER
questions.solution:
**The EFFECTIVE DEPTH d, or 12 times the bar diameter — whichever is GREATER.**

**Why the extension is needed at all:**

> **The theoretical cut-off point is where the bending moment falls to the value the remaining bars can carry — so in a pure flexural analysis the bar could stop there.**

> **It cannot, for two reasons:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **DIAGONAL TENSION shifts the tension force TOWARD the support** ← | **A diagonal crack means the steel at a section is resisting the moment from a section further along — so more steel is needed than pure flexure suggests** ← |
| **The bar must DEVELOP its stress** | **A bar stopped at the point of full stress has no anchorage at all** ← |

> **THE FIRST REASON IS THE ONE THE d OR 12φ RULE ADDRESSES, and it is worth understanding because it is not obvious:**

> **In a beam with diagonal cracking, the tensile force in the steel at any section does NOT correspond to the moment at that section — it corresponds to the moment at a section about d further away, toward midspan.**

> **The effect is called the SHIFT RULE, and extending every bar by d beyond its theoretical cut-off is how the code accounts for it.**

**The full set of curtailment requirements:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Extend d or 12φ beyond the theoretical cut-off, whichever is greater** ← | **This question** |
| **The continuing bars must provide at least TWICE the shear required, OR** | **See the alternatives below** ← |
| **The shear at the cut-off must not exceed two thirds of the permitted value, OR** | ← |
| **Extra stirrups must be provided over a distance of 0.75d from the cut-off** ← | **The usual practical answer** |
| **At a SIMPLY SUPPORTED end: L_d ≤ 1.3 M₁/V + L₀** | **Where M₁ is the moment capacity of the bars continuing, V the shear, and L₀ the anchorage beyond the support centre** ← |
| **At least ONE THIRD of the positive steel must continue into a simple support** ← | **And one quarter into a continuous support** ← |

> **THE SECOND, THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE ALTERNATIVES — only ONE need be satisfied — and the reason they exist is that curtailing a bar creates a WEAK POINT.**

> **A curtailment introduces a stress concentration and a discontinuity precisely in the tension zone, and diagonal cracks tend to initiate there.**

> **The three alternatives are three different ways of ensuring the section can tolerate that: extra shear capacity from the remaining bars, a reduced shear demand, or extra stirrups locally.**

> **In practice the extra stirrups are usually the simplest, and many designers avoid the issue entirely by curtailing bars in the COMPRESSION zone or not at all.**

**The reason for the last row, which is a genuine safety provision:**

> **Continuing a third of the bottom steel into a simple support is not for flexure — the moment there is nominally zero.**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provides ANCHORAGE for the diagonal tension at the support** ← | **Where the shear is greatest** |
| **Guards against unexpected NEGATIVE moment or support settlement** | ← |
| **Provides a tie against PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE** ← | **Continuous bottom steel lets a damaged span hang in catenary rather than fall** ← |
| **Accommodates the shift rule at the support** | ← |

> **The PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE role in the third row is the same reasoning as the integrity reinforcement in flat slabs met earlier, and it has become an explicit code requirement for the same reason — a local failure must not propagate.**

**Why curtailment is done at all, since it introduces these complications:**

| Motive | Note |
|---|---|
| **ECONOMY of steel** | **The moment falls toward the supports, so the full area is needed only near midspan** ← |
| **Reduced CONGESTION** | **Fewer bars at the supports, where stirrups, column bars and top steel all compete for space** ← |
| **Easier concrete placement** | Follows from the above |

> **The saving is real but modest — typically 10 to 20 per cent of the flexural steel in a beam — and it must be weighed against the detailing complexity, the extra stirrups, and the risk of a bar being curtailed in the wrong place on site.**

> **For small beams the economy rarely justifies it, and running all the bars full length is both cheaper overall and less error-prone.**

> **For long-span and heavily reinforced members the saving becomes worthwhile, and it is there that the curtailment rules earn their keep — which is a reasonable general position on any detailing refinement: optimise where the quantities are large, and simplify where they are not.**

examTip.trick: **d or 12φ beyond the theoretical cut-off, whichever is GREATER** — because diagonal cracking SHIFTS the tension force toward the support by about d (the shift rule).
examTip.trap: **A curtailment is a weak point in the tension zone**, so one of three extra conditions must also be met — twice the shear capacity in the continuing bars, shear below two thirds of the permitted value, or extra stirrups over 0.75d.
examTip.mnemonic: **At least ONE THIRD of the bottom steel continues into a simple support** — not for flexure (the moment is zero) but for anchorage against diagonal tension and as a tie against PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the PITCH of lateral ties in a reinforced concrete column must not exceed the least of:
options: The least lateral dimension of the column; 16 times the smallest longitudinal bar diameter; or 300 mm
The effective depth; 12 times the bar diameter; or 250 mm
Twice the least lateral dimension; 20 bar diameters; or 450 mm
Half the least lateral dimension; 8 bar diameters; or 150 mm
questions.solution:
**The LEAST of: the column's least lateral dimension; 16 times the diameter of the smallest longitudinal bar; and 300 mm.**

**The tie requirements in full:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **PITCH (spacing)** | **The least of: the least lateral dimension; 16 × smallest longitudinal bar diameter; 300 mm** ← |
| **DIAMETER of the tie** | **The GREATER of: one quarter of the largest longitudinal bar diameter; and 6 mm** ← |
| **Arrangement** | **Every corner and alternate bar must be held by the corner of a tie** ← |
| **Unsupported bar spacing** | **No longitudinal bar may be further than 75 mm from a restrained bar** ← |

**What the ties are FOR — and it is not what most people assume:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevent BUCKLING of the longitudinal bars** ← | **THE PRIMARY PURPOSE — a slender bar in compression buckles outward and spalls the cover** ← |
| **Hold the longitudinal bars in POSITION during concreting** | ← |
| **CONFINE the concrete core** | **Increasing its strength and, far more importantly, its DUCTILITY** ← |
| **Resist SHEAR** | **A secondary role in an ordinary column; a primary one under seismic load** ← |

> **THE BUCKLING PURPOSE IN THE FIRST ROW EXPLAINS THE 16φ RULE DIRECTLY, and the reasoning is the Euler formula applied to a single bar:**

> **A longitudinal bar is a slender strut, and the ties are its lateral supports. Its unsupported length is the tie pitch, so its slenderness is (pitch/bar radius of gyration).**

> **Limiting the pitch to 16 bar diameters caps that slenderness at a value at which the bar can reach its yield stress before buckling — so the steel's full strength is available.**

> **A wider pitch would let the bar buckle first, and its capacity would be governed by Euler rather than by f_y — which would waste most of the steel's strength and produce a sudden, brittle failure as the cover spalls.**

**CONFINEMENT, which is the third purpose and the one that matters in an earthquake:**

| Effect of closely spaced ties | Note |
|---|---|
| **The core concrete is restrained against LATERAL EXPANSION** ← | **Which puts it into TRIAXIAL compression** ← |
| **Triaxially compressed concrete is much STRONGER** | Modestly so |
| **And FAR more DUCTILE** | **Ultimate strain rising from 0.0035 to 0.01-0.02 — a five-fold increase** ← |
| **The column can then sustain large deformations without losing capacity** | **Which is exactly what surviving an earthquake requires** ← |

> **THAT FIVE-FOLD INCREASE IN DUCTILITY IS WHAT THE RESPONSE REDUCTION FACTOR R IS PAYING FOR, and it connects this detailing rule directly to the seismic analysis.**

> **A design using R = 5 assumes the structure can deform inelastically without collapsing. Confinement is the physical provision that delivers it — and without close ties, the R = 5 assumption is unsupported.**

**The SEISMIC requirements of IS 13920, which tighten all of this:**

| Provision | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **SPECIAL CONFINING reinforcement over a length l₀ at each column end** | **l₀ = the greater of: the larger lateral dimension; one sixth of the clear height; or 450 mm** ← |
| **Spacing within l₀** | **The lesser of: one quarter of the minimum dimension; and 100 mm (but not less than 75 mm)** ← |
| **HOOKS bent at 135°, with an extension of 6 diameters (min 65 mm)** ← | **A 90° hook OPENS OUT when the cover spalls, and the confinement is lost exactly when it is needed** ← |
| **Ties also required through the BEAM-COLUMN JOINT** | **The joint is otherwise unconfined and is where failures concentrate** ← |

> **THE 135° HOOK REQUIREMENT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT SEISMIC DETAILING RULE, and its omission is the most common serious defect in Nepali and Indian construction.**

> **A 90° hook relies on the cover concrete to hold it closed. Under severe shaking the cover spalls off first — and the hook then straightens, the tie opens, the confinement disappears and the longitudinal bars buckle.**

> **A 135° hook is anchored into the CORE, which does not spall, so it holds the tie closed however badly the cover is damaged.**

> **The cost difference is nil — it is the same length of steel, bent differently — and the difference in performance is between a column that survives and one that fails. It is, on any reckoning, the highest-value detail in earthquake-resistant concrete construction.**

**And the LONGITUDINAL steel limits that accompany the ties:**

| Provision | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum longitudinal steel** | **0.8 per cent of the gross area** ← |
| **Maximum** | **6 per cent (4 per cent where bars are lapped, for congestion)** ← |
| **Minimum number of bars** | **4 in a rectangular column; 6 in a circular one** ← |
| **Minimum bar diameter** | **12 mm** ← |
| **Maximum spacing of longitudinal bars along the perimeter** | **300 mm** |

> **The MINIMUM of 0.8 per cent exists partly for a reason unconnected with strength: concrete CREEPS under sustained load, and as it does so it transfers load progressively onto the steel.**

> **A column with too little steel would see that steel overstressed over time — so the minimum guarantees enough area to accept the redistributed load, quite apart from any calculation of the column's capacity.**

examTip.trick: **Least of: the least lateral dimension; 16 × smallest longitudinal bar diameter; 300 mm.** Tie diameter: the greater of ¼ the largest bar and 6 mm.
examTip.trap: **The 16φ rule is Euler's formula applied to one bar** — the tie pitch is the bar's unsupported length, and 16 diameters caps its slenderness so it yields before it buckles.
examTip.mnemonic: **135° HOOKS, not 90°** — a 90° hook relies on the cover, which spalls first, and then the tie opens and the bars buckle. Same steel, different bend, and the difference between a column surviving and failing.

questions.stem: A COMBINED FOOTING supporting two columns is generally adopted when:
options: The soil has a very high bearing capacity
The two columns carry equal loads
The columns are CLOSE TOGETHER so their isolated footings would overlap, or one column stands on a PROPERTY LINE
The structure is founded on rock
questions.solution:
**When the columns are so CLOSE TOGETHER that their isolated footings would overlap, or when one column stands on a PROPERTY LINE and cannot have a footing centred beneath it.**

**The two situations, which are quite different problems with the same solution:**

| Situation | Why a combined footing |
|---|---|
| **Columns CLOSE together** | **Their separate footings would overlap or nearly touch, so a single footing is simpler and cheaper** ← |
| **A column on a PROPERTY LINE or against an existing building** | **An isolated footing cannot extend beyond the boundary, so it would be ECCENTRIC beneath the column — producing a large moment and uneven pressure** ← |
| **Very high column loads on weak soil** | Footings become large and merge |
| **Where DIFFERENTIAL settlement between two columns must be avoided** | **A common footing settles as one** ← |

> **THE PROPERTY LINE CASE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE CLASSIC ONE AND IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING, because the mechanism is not obvious:**

> **A footing under a boundary column can extend only INWARD. Its centroid therefore lies inside the column's line of action, so the load is eccentric — and an eccentric load on a footing produces a trapezoidal or triangular pressure distribution, with a high pressure at one edge and possibly uplift at the other.**

> **The footing would also tend to ROTATE, tilting the column.**

> **A combined footing solves it by extending back to include the NEXT internal column: the two loads together have a resultant, and the footing is shaped and positioned so that its CENTROID COINCIDES with that resultant — restoring a uniform pressure.**

> **THAT CENTROID-ON-RESULTANT PRINCIPLE IS THE WHOLE DESIGN IDEA, and it is what determines the footing's shape.**

**The shapes, and when each is used:**

| Shape | Used when |
|---|---|
| **RECTANGULAR** | **The two column loads are EQUAL, or nearly so — the resultant is near the middle and a symmetrical footing works** ← |
| **TRAPEZOIDAL** | **The loads are UNEQUAL and the space is restricted — the footing is made WIDER under the HEAVIER column to bring the centroid onto the resultant** ← |
| **STRAP (cantilever) footing** | **The columns are FAR APART — two separate footings joined by a rigid STRAP BEAM that transfers the moment, avoiding an expensive slab between them** ← |

> **THE STRAP FOOTING IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ECONOMICAL ANSWER FOR WIDELY SPACED COLUMNS, and its mechanism is neat: the strap beam does not bear on the soil at all.**

> **It acts purely as a lever, transferring part of the boundary column's load onto the interior footing and so counteracting the eccentricity — the two footings then each carry a concentric load.**

> **Because the strap carries no bearing pressure, it is designed for BENDING and SHEAR only, and it is usually cast clear of the ground or on a compressible layer so that it cannot pick up soil reaction and upset the assumption.**

**The design of a combined footing:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Find the RESULTANT of the two column loads and its position** ← |
| **2** | **Choose the footing's length and shape so its CENTROID coincides with that resultant** ← |
| **3** | **Size the area from the total load and the safe bearing capacity, giving a UNIFORM pressure** ← |
| **4** | **Treat the footing as an inverted BEAM loaded upward by the soil pressure and supported by the two columns** ← |
| **5** | **Draw the SFD and BMD — note the HOGGING moment BETWEEN the columns** ← |
| **6** | **Design the longitudinal steel: TOP steel between the columns, BOTTOM steel under them** ← |
| **7** | **Design transverse steel, and check one-way and punching shear** | ← |

> **STEP 6 IS THE DETAILING POINT THAT IS MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG, and it follows directly from step 4:**

> **A combined footing is an UPSIDE-DOWN CONTINUOUS BEAM — the load (soil pressure) acts UPWARD and the supports (columns) act downward.**

> **So the moment between the columns is HOGGING in the ordinary sense but produces tension on the TOP of the footing, exactly as a continuous beam does over its supports.**

> **Reinforcement placed only at the bottom, as in an isolated footing, leaves the tension face unreinforced — and the footing cracks along its top surface between the columns, where nobody can see it.**

> **That is a genuine and recurring error, and it comes from applying the isolated-footing habit to a member that behaves quite differently.**

**And the family of foundations, to place this one:**

| Foundation | When |
|---|---|
| **ISOLATED (pad) footing** | **The normal case — one column, adequate soil, adequate space** ← |
| **COMBINED footing** | **This question** ← |
| **STRIP footing** | **A load-bearing wall, or a row of closely spaced columns** ← |
| **RAFT (mat)** | **Where the footings would cover more than about 50 per cent of the plan area, or the soil is weak and variable** ← |
| **PILES** | **Where a competent stratum is deep, or uplift or lateral load must be resisted** ← |
| **Well / caisson** | **Bridge piers in rivers** |

> **The 50 PER CENT RULE in the raft row is the useful practical threshold: once individual footings would occupy half the building's footprint, it is cheaper and simpler to excavate once and pour a single raft — and the raft brings the further benefit of bridging local soft spots and evening out differential settlement.**

examTip.trick: **Columns too close for separate footings, or a column on a PROPERTY LINE where an isolated footing would be eccentric.** The design idea: shape the footing so its CENTROID sits on the RESULTANT of the two loads.
examTip.trap: **A combined footing is an UPSIDE-DOWN continuous beam** — the soil pushes up, the columns push down, so the moment between them puts the TOP in tension. Bottom-only steel, as in an isolated footing, leaves the tension face bare.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rectangular for equal loads, TRAPEZOIDAL for unequal (wider under the heavier), STRAP for widely spaced.** The strap beam carries no bearing pressure — it is purely a lever, and is cast clear of the ground so it stays that way.

questions.stem: As per IS 800, the design tensile strength of a steel tension member is taken as the LEAST of the strengths corresponding to:
options: Gross section yielding and net section rupture only
Gross section YIELDING, net section RUPTURE, and BLOCK SHEAR
Net section rupture and buckling
Bearing and shear on the bolts
questions.solution:
**Gross section YIELDING, net section RUPTURE, and BLOCK SHEAR** — the design strength is the LEAST of the three.

**The three limit states:**

| Limit state | Design strength | Partial factor | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GROSS SECTION YIELDING** | **T_dg = A_g f_y / γ_m0** | **γ_m0 = 1.10** ← | **DUCTILE — the member yields and stretches visibly before failing** ← |
| **NET SECTION RUPTURE** | **T_dn = 0.9 A_n f_u / γ_m1** | **γ_m1 = 1.25** ← | **BRITTLE — fracture at the bolt holes** ← |
| **BLOCK SHEAR** | **T_db — a combination of shear along one plane and tension across another** ← | 1.25 | **BRITTLE — a block of material tears out** ← |

> **Option (a) omits block shear, which is a real and often governing limit state — and that omission is precisely the error the question is built around.**

**Why the two partial factors DIFFER, which is the interesting part:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **γ_m0 = 1.10 governs YIELDING, which is DUCTILE** | **The member deforms visibly and gives warning; a modest factor suffices** ← |
| **γ_m1 = 1.25 governs RUPTURE, which is BRITTLE** | **Sudden, with no warning; a larger factor is warranted** ← |
| **And the 0.9 in the rupture expression** | **A further reduction, for the stress concentration around the holes** ← |

> **THE CODE THEREFORE PENALISES BRITTLE FAILURE MODES DELIBERATELY, and the two factors together mean a member is pushed toward failing by yielding rather than by rupture — which is the same design philosophy as under-reinforcing a concrete beam.**

> **A tension member designed so that gross yielding governs will stretch and sag noticeably before it breaks. One in which net rupture governs will snap without warning.**

**BLOCK SHEAR, which is the mode most often forgotten:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **What happens** | **A BLOCK of material containing the bolt group TEARS OUT of the member** ← |
| **The failure surface** | **SHEAR along the line of bolts parallel to the force, plus TENSION across the line perpendicular to it** ← |
| **When it governs** | **Where the bolts are grouped close to an EDGE or an END, with short edge distances** ← |
| **Common in** | **Gusset plates, coped beam ends, angle connections with few bolts** ← |

> **Block shear is not a member failure but a CONNECTION failure — and it is why generous EDGE and END distances matter: they lengthen the tearing planes and raise the block shear capacity directly.**

> **IS 800 requires an end distance of at least 1.5 times the hole diameter and an edge distance of 1.5 times for a rolled edge — and increasing them beyond the minimum is a cheap way to remove block shear as the governing mode.**

**The NET AREA and the SHEAR LAG effect, which complete the picture:**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **Net area A_n** | **The gross area LESS the bolt holes, with the hole taken as the bolt diameter plus 2 mm** ← |
| **STAGGERED holes** | **Add s²/4g for each stagger, since a zigzag failure path is longer** ← |
| **SHEAR LAG** | **Where only PART of the section is connected — as a single angle bolted through one leg — the stress does not distribute evenly** ← |
| **The result** | **An effective net area LESS than the geometric net area** ← |

> **THE SHEAR LAG CASE IN THE THIRD ROW IS EXTREMELY COMMON IN PRACTICE: a single angle in a truss is almost always connected through one leg only.**

> **The load enters through that leg, and the outstanding leg is engaged only gradually along the connection's length — so near the joint the outstanding leg carries very little, and the connected leg is overstressed.**

> **IS 800 handles it with a reduction factor β that depends on the connection's length and the section's geometry, and the effect is substantial — an angle connected through one leg may be reduced to 60 to 80 per cent of its geometric net capacity.**

> **The remedies are a LONGER connection (which lets the stress even out), connecting BOTH legs, or adding a LUG ANGLE to bring the outstanding leg into the connection.**

**And a note on why a tension member is such a satisfying thing to design:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **A tension member CANNOT BUCKLE** | **So its full material strength is available, unlike a strut** ← |
| **Its capacity is independent of LENGTH** | **A 3 m tie and a 30 m tie of the same section carry the same load** ← |
| **Slenderness is limited only for HANDLING, sag and vibration** | **Hence the loose limit of 400, against 180 for a compression member** ← |

> **That is why cables and ties are so efficient, and why a structural system that carries load in TENSION — a suspension bridge, a cable roof, a tied arch — can span so much further than one relying on compression.**

> **The penalty is that tension members must be CONNECTED, and as this question shows, the connection is where the three limit states arise and where the capacity is usually lost.**

examTip.trick: **The LEAST of gross yielding (A_g f_y/1.10), net rupture (0.9 A_n f_u/1.25) and BLOCK SHEAR.** Option (a) omits block shear, which often governs.
examTip.trap: **γ_m0 = 1.10 for DUCTILE yielding, γ_m1 = 1.25 for BRITTLE rupture** — the code deliberately penalises the brittle mode, pushing the member toward failing by stretching rather than snapping.
examTip.mnemonic: **A single angle bolted through ONE leg suffers SHEAR LAG** — the outstanding leg engages only gradually, cutting capacity to 60-80 %. Cure with a longer connection, both legs, or a LUG ANGLE. And generous EDGE distances remove block shear cheaply.

questions.stem: ASHLAR masonry differs from RUBBLE masonry in that ashlar uses:
options: Stones laid without any mortar
Stones of irregular shape as they come from the quarry
Only stones smaller than 150 mm
Accurately DRESSED stones of uniform size, laid in regular courses with THIN, uniform joints
questions.solution:
**Accurately DRESSED stones of uniform size, laid in regular courses with THIN, uniform joints.**

**The two classes of stone masonry:**

| | RUBBLE masonry | ASHLAR masonry |
|---|---|---|
| **Stones** | **ROUGH, irregular, largely as quarried** ← (option b) | **Finely DRESSED to accurate rectangular shapes** ← |
| **Courses** | **Irregular or roughly coursed** | **REGULAR, of uniform height** ← |
| **Joint thickness** | **THICK — 10 to 20 mm and uneven** ← | **THIN — 3 to 6 mm and uniform** ← |
| **Strength** | **Lower — the load path is irregular** | **HIGHER — stones bear directly on one another** ← |
| **Cost** | **LOW — little dressing, unskilled labour** ← | **HIGH — extensive dressing and skilled masons** ← |
| **Mortar required** | **MORE — thick joints** | **Less** |
| **Appearance** | Rustic | **Fine; used for facing and monumental work** ← |

> **Option (b) describes RUBBLE, which makes it the designed distractor.**

> **The essential distinction is the DRESSING: the amount of labour spent shaping each stone before it is laid, which determines everything else in the table.**

**The subdivisions of each:**

| RUBBLE types | Note |
|---|---|
| **Random rubble, UNCOURSED** | **The cheapest and roughest; stones of all sizes fitted as they come** ← |
| **Random rubble, coursed** | Brought to a level course at intervals |
| **SQUARE rubble** | Stones roughly squared |
| **POLYGONAL rubble** | Stones dressed to irregular polygons fitting together |
| **Flint / dry rubble** | **Dry rubble is laid WITHOUT mortar** ← (option a) |

| ASHLAR types | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ashlar FINE (plain)** | **Every face finely dressed; the finest and most expensive** ← |
| **Ashlar ROUGH-TOOLED** | Beds and joints fine; the face rough-tooled |
| **Ashlar ROCK (quarry) FACED** | **A deliberately rough projecting face with a fine chamfered margin — a decorative effect** ← |
| **Ashlar CHAMFERED** | The margin bevelled at 45° |
| **Ashlar BLOCK-IN-COURSE** | Between ashlar and rubble in quality |

> **Option (a) names DRY RUBBLE, which is a genuine technique — used for retaining walls, terracing and boundary walls, and relying on friction and interlock rather than on mortar.**

> **Dry stone walling is entirely appropriate for a retaining wall, because it is FREE-DRAINING — no water pressure can build up behind it, which removes the commonest cause of retaining wall failure.**

**The general RULES of stone masonry, which apply to both classes:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lay every stone on its NATURAL BED** ← | **Perpendicular to the load, as discussed for stratified stone** ← |
| **BREAK JOINT — no vertical joint continuous through two courses** ← | **The same bond principle as brickwork** ← |
| **Use THROUGH (bond) STONES at intervals** ← | **Extending the full thickness of the wall, at about 1.5 to 1.8 m centres** ← |
| **Fill all joints solidly; no HOLLOW joints** | ← |
| **Use the LARGEST stones at the bottom courses** | Stability |
| **Wet the stones before laying** | So they do not absorb the mortar's water |
| **Avoid excessive small chips and spalls in the joints** | **A sign of poor stone selection and a weak wall** ← |

> **THE THROUGH STONE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE MOST OFTEN OMITTED, and its absence produces a characteristic failure:**

> **Without through stones, a thick stone wall becomes TWO INDEPENDENT SKINS with a rubble-filled core between them.**

> **Under load or lateral shaking the two skins separate and bulge outward — DELAMINATION — and the wall collapses even though neither skin was itself overloaded.**

> **That is precisely the failure mode observed repeatedly in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake in traditional stone masonry buildings, and it is why through stones (and, better, horizontal seismic bands) are the first improvement recommended for such construction.**

> **The remedy is cheap: a through stone at every 1.5 m or so in both directions, or in modern practice a bar or a band of reinforced concrete tying the two skins together.**

**And the comparison with brickwork, since the two are alternatives:**

| Aspect | STONE masonry | BRICK masonry |
|---|---|---|
| **Strength** | **Higher for good stone** | Lower |
| **Durability and weathering** | **Excellent** ← | Good |
| **Unit size and uniformity** | **Irregular — needs skilled fitting** ← | **Uniform and modular — much faster to lay** ← |
| **Speed of construction** | **SLOW** ← | Fast |
| **Wall thickness required** | **THICKER — 350 mm and above** ← | 230 mm typical |
| **Availability in Nepal** | **Excellent — stone is local nearly everywhere** ← | Requires clay and fuel |
| **Seismic performance** | **POOR unless well built with through stones and bands** ← | Poor unless reinforced |

> **The AVAILABILITY row is why stone masonry remains so widespread in rural Nepal despite the labour it requires: the material is on the site, and transporting bricks up a hillside is expensive.**

> **And the SEISMIC row is the reason it deserves attention rather than dismissal — a very large part of Nepal's building stock is stone masonry, it performed badly in 2015, and the improvements that would change that are inexpensive and well established.**

examTip.trick: **ASHLAR: finely dressed, uniform, regular courses, THIN joints (3-6 mm). RUBBLE: rough, irregular, thick uneven joints.** Option (b) is rubble; option (a) is DRY rubble, a real technique.
examTip.trap: **The distinction is the DRESSING** — the labour spent shaping each stone before laying, which then determines strength, joint thickness, cost and appearance together.
examTip.mnemonic: **THROUGH STONES every 1.5-1.8 m are the most-omitted rule** — without them a thick wall becomes two skins that DELAMINATE and bulge outward. That was a leading failure mode in 2015, and the remedy costs almost nothing.

questions.stem: MALARIA and DENGUE are classified as:
options: Water-borne diseases
Water-related INSECT VECTOR diseases
Water-washed diseases
Water-based diseases
questions.solution:
**Water-related INSECT VECTOR diseases** — the pathogen is carried by an insect that BREEDS in or near water.

**The four classes of water-related disease:**

| Class | Mechanism | Examples | Controlled by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WATER-BORNE** | **The pathogen is IN the water and is SWALLOWED** ← | **CHOLERA, typhoid, paratyphoid, bacillary and amoebic dysentery, gastroenteritis, hepatitis A and E, polio** ← | **Treating and protecting the water supply** ← |
| **WATER-WASHED (water-scarce)** | **Caused by a LACK of water for personal and domestic HYGIENE** ← | **Trachoma, scabies, conjunctivitis, skin infections, louse-borne typhus** ← | **The QUANTITY of water available, not its quality** ← |
| **WATER-BASED** | **Part of the parasite's LIFE CYCLE occurs in an AQUATIC HOST** ← | **Schistosomiasis (bilharzia), guinea worm** ← | **Avoiding contact with infested water; controlling the host snail** ← |
| **WATER-RELATED INSECT VECTOR** | **An insect that BREEDS in or near water transmits it** ← | **MALARIA, DENGUE, filariasis, Japanese encephalitis, yellow fever** ← | **Eliminating BREEDING SITES; nets and screening** ← |

> **All four options name a real class, so the question requires the mechanism to be matched to the disease.**

**Why the classification MATTERS — it dictates the intervention:**

| Class | The engineering response |
|---|---|
| **Water-borne** | **TREAT the water — filtration and disinfection** ← |
| **Water-washed** | **Supply MORE water, and provide washing facilities — treatment alone achieves nothing** ← |
| **Water-based** | **Avoid contact; manage the water body** |
| **Insect vector** | **DRAIN standing water and remove breeding sites — treating the drinking water is IRRELEVANT** ← |

> **THAT IS THE POINT OF THE WHOLE CLASSIFICATION, and it is a genuinely useful one: chlorinating a village's drinking water will do nothing whatever about its malaria, and providing a tap in every house does more for trachoma than any amount of treatment.**

> **The WATER-WASHED row is the one most often underestimated: these diseases respond to the QUANTITY of water, not its quality.**

> **A community with a small quantity of very clean water may suffer more skin and eye disease than one with abundant water of moderate quality — because people wash when water is easy to get and do not when it must be carried a kilometre.**

> **So the distance to the source and the quantity supplied are health parameters in their own right, which is why rural water supply standards specify both a per-capita quantity and a maximum walking distance (commonly 150 m, or 15 minutes).**

**THE MALARIA AND DENGUE CASE IN NEPAL, since it is the question's subject:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The vector** | **ANOPHELES mosquitoes for malaria; AEDES aegypti and albopictus for dengue** ← |
| **Breeding sites — Anopheles** | **Clean, still or slow-moving water: pools, paddy fields, irrigation channels, borrow pits** ← |
| **Breeding sites — AEDES** | **SMALL ARTIFICIAL containers of clean water: tyres, buckets, roof gutters, water storage vessels, flower pots** ← |
| **Historic distribution** | Malaria mainly in the Terai and inner Terai |
| **Recent change** | **Dengue has spread rapidly UPWARD into the hills and Kathmandu, as temperatures have risen** ← |

> **THE AEDES BREEDING SITES IN THE THIRD ROW HAVE A DIRECT AND UNCOMFORTABLE CONNECTION TO WATER SUPPLY ENGINEERING:**

> **Aedes breeds in small containers of CLEAN water — and an INTERMITTENT water supply forces every household to store water in exactly such containers.**

> **So an unreliable piped supply creates thousands of mosquito breeding sites across a city, and the dengue burden rises with the unreliability of the supply.**

> **That is one more argument for CONTINUOUS supply, alongside the contamination-through-negative-pressure argument met earlier: intermittent supply causes disease by two entirely separate mechanisms.**

> **Where storage is unavoidable, the engineering answer is to require COVERED, sealed vessels with tight lids — which is cheap, effective, and a legitimate part of a water supply project's scope rather than somebody else's problem.**

**And the BORROW PIT entry deserves a closing note, because it is created by civil engineering itself:**

> **Excavating material for an embankment leaves pits that fill with rainwater and hold it for months — ideal Anopheles habitat, sited by the engineer.**

> **The remedy is straightforward and belongs in the specification: shape borrow areas to DRAIN, connect them to a watercourse, or backfill and level them on completion.**

> **It costs very little at the time and a great deal to correct afterwards, and it is a good example of the general principle that a project's health and environmental effects are cheapest to deal with while the plant is still on site.**

examTip.trick: **Four classes: water-BORNE (swallowed — cholera, typhoid), water-WASHED (too little water for hygiene — trachoma, scabies), water-BASED (aquatic host — schistosomiasis), and INSECT VECTOR (breeds in water — malaria, dengue).** All four options are real classes.
examTip.trap: **The class dictates the intervention** — chlorinating the drinking water does nothing for malaria, and water-WASHED diseases respond to QUANTITY, not quality. Hence the maximum walking distance in rural standards.
examTip.mnemonic: **AEDES breeds in small containers of CLEAN water — so an INTERMITTENT supply, which forces household storage, creates the breeding sites.** Unreliable supply causes disease twice over: contamination at low pressure, and dengue in the storage jars.

questions.stem: An INFILTRATION GALLERY is:
options: A covered service reservoir for treated water
A settling basin at the head of a canal
An open channel carrying raw water to the treatment plant
A HORIZONTAL perforated conduit laid in a water-bearing stratum, usually beneath or beside a river bed, collecting water by SEEPAGE
questions.solution:
**A HORIZONTAL perforated conduit laid in a water-bearing stratum**, usually beneath or beside a river bed, which collects water by seepage through the surrounding ground.

**Its features:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Construction** | **Perforated pipe, porous concrete pipe, or a masonry conduit with open joints, laid in a trench and surrounded by graded GRAVEL** ← |
| **Depth** | **Typically 3 to 8 m below ground, within the water-bearing stratum** ← |
| **Slope** | **Laid at a gentle gradient to a collecting sump, from which the water is pumped** ← |
| **Water quality** | **NATURALLY FILTERED by its passage through the sand and gravel — far better than the river water above it** ← |
| **Yield** | **Moderate; typically 1.5 × 10⁴ litres per metre of gallery per day** ← |

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) name a service reservoir, a settling basin and an approach channel — all real components of a water supply system, none of them this one.**

**Why it is used — the NATURAL FILTRATION advantage:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The water passes through several metres of SAND and GRAVEL before reaching the pipe** ← | **Which is a slow sand filter operating at no cost** ← |
| **TURBIDITY is largely removed** | **Even when the river above is heavily silted in the monsoon** ← |
| **Bacterial load is greatly reduced** | **The same biological mechanisms as a slow sand filter** ← |
| **The temperature is steadier** | ← |
| **So the TREATMENT required is far less** | **Often disinfection alone** ← |

> **THE MONSOON POINT IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE DECISIVE ONE FOR NEPAL, and it is worth stating plainly:**

> **A Himalayan river in the monsoon may carry several thousand NTU of turbidity, which would overwhelm any conventional treatment plant and requires heavy coagulant dosing and frequent desludging.**

> **An infiltration gallery beneath the same river bed draws water that has been filtered by the bed itself, and its turbidity stays low all year.**

> **So the gallery converts a difficult, variable surface source into something close to a groundwater source — which is exactly the trade a small town's water supply wants, since it removes the need for a coagulation plant and the skilled operation that goes with it.**

> **This is called RIVERBANK or RIVERBED FILTRATION, and it is an increasingly favoured technique internationally for precisely these reasons.**

**The limitations, stated fairly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **CLOGGING of the surrounding gravel over time** | **Fine silt gradually blinds the filter, and the yield falls** ← |
| **Hard to clean or maintain once buried** | **Which is why the gravel pack's grading matters so much at construction** ← |
| **Yield limited by the stratum's permeability** | Not suitable in clay |
| **Vulnerable to a change in the river's course** | **A braided Himalayan river may migrate away from the gallery entirely** ← |
| **Can be damaged or exposed by SCOUR during a flood** | ← |
| **Higher construction cost than a simple intake** | ← |

> **The RIVER MIGRATION risk in the fourth row is a real Nepali hazard: a braided river in the Terai can shift its channel by hundreds of metres in a single monsoon, leaving a gallery high and dry.**

> **The response is to site the gallery where the channel is confined — at a stable reach, or where the river is constrained by rock or by training works — which is the same site-selection judgement as for a bridge or a headworks.**

**The other SOURCES of water, to place the gallery among them:**

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURFACE — river, lake, reservoir, impounded storage** | **Large yield; variable quality; needs full treatment** ← |
| **SPRING** | **Gravity-fed, naturally filtered, excellent for hill schemes — the mainstay of rural Nepali supply** ← |
| **INFILTRATION gallery / infiltration well** | **This question — the boundary between surface and ground water** ← |
| **Open (dug) WELL** | Shallow aquifer; small yield; easily contaminated |
| **TUBE WELL — shallow or deep** | **Large yield from a confined aquifer; the Terai's principal source; ARSENIC risk in places** ← |
| **Rainwater harvesting** | **Supplementary; valuable where no other source exists** ← |

> **THE SPRING ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS FOR NEPAL: the great majority of rural hill water supply schemes are gravity systems fed from a protected spring, and they need no pumping, no power and minimal treatment.**

> **The engineering is almost entirely in the SPRING PROTECTION — a sealed intake chamber built into the hillside, excluding surface water and animals — and in the conveyance.**

> **A spring source that is properly protected at its eye, and a supply that is chlorinated and continuous, will deliver safe water indefinitely at almost no operating cost, which is why the model has been so widely and successfully replicated.**

> **And its principal vulnerability is not engineering but hydrological: spring yields are falling in many parts of the mid-hills, attributed to changing rainfall patterns and to land-use change reducing recharge — which brings the discussion back to the catchment treatment measures met under watershed management.**

examTip.trick: **A horizontal perforated conduit in a water-bearing stratum, collecting by SEEPAGE** — typically 3-8 m deep beneath a river bed, in a graded gravel surround.
examTip.trap: **Its value is NATURAL FILTRATION** — the water passes through metres of sand and gravel, so turbidity stays low even when the river above carries thousands of NTU in the monsoon. Treatment reduces to disinfection alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **A braided Himalayan river can migrate away from the gallery in one monsoon** — so site it at a confined, stable reach, the same judgement as for a bridge. And for hill Nepal, the protected SPRING remains the mainstay.

questions.stem: A RESERVOIR INTAKE tower is provided with several inlet PORTS at different levels principally so that:
options: Water can be drawn from the level at which the QUALITY is best at that season
The tower is structurally lighter
The reservoir can be emptied more quickly
Fish can pass through the tower
questions.solution:
**So that water can be drawn from whichever LEVEL has the best QUALITY at that season.**

**Why the quality varies with depth — the mechanism:**

> **A deep reservoir STRATIFIES: it separates into layers of different temperature and density that do not readily mix.**

| Layer | Character |
|---|---|
| **EPILIMNION — the warm upper layer** | **Mixed by wind; well oxygenated; but carries ALGAE, which cause taste, odour and filter clogging** ← |
| **THERMOCLINE (metalimnion)** | **A zone of rapid temperature change that acts as a BARRIER to mixing** ← |
| **HYPOLIMNION — the cold lower layer** | **No algae and low turbidity; but often ANAEROBIC, with dissolved IRON, MANGANESE, hydrogen sulphide and taste problems** ← |

> **SO NEITHER THE TOP NOR THE BOTTOM IS RELIABLY THE BEST, and which is better changes through the year — which is exactly why multiple ports are provided.**

| Season or condition | Preferred draw-off |
|---|---|
| **Summer, with an ALGAL BLOOM at the surface** | **A LOWER port, below the bloom** ← |
| **When the hypolimnion has gone ANAEROBIC (iron, manganese, H₂S)** | **A HIGHER port, above the anoxic zone** ← |
| **During a flood, with a turbid inflow layer** | **A port above or below the turbid layer** ← |
| **When the reservoir is drawn down** | **Whichever ports remain submerged** ← |

> **Options (b), (c) and (d) each name a real consideration for an intake tower — its structural weight, the need for a low-level outlet, and fish passage — but none is the reason for the multiple ports.**

**The seasonal OVERTURN, which is worth knowing because it produces sudden quality problems:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Summer** | **Strong stratification; the layers do not mix** ← |
| **Autumn cooling** | **The surface cools, becomes DENSER, and sinks** ← |
| **OVERTURN** | **The whole reservoir MIXES from top to bottom, in a matter of days** ← |
| **The consequence at the intake** | **The anaerobic bottom water, with its iron, manganese, sulphide and taste, is suddenly distributed THROUGHOUT the reservoir** ← |

> **A treatment plant drawing from a stratified reservoir can therefore meet a sudden and severe deterioration in raw water quality within a day or two, with no change in the weather that an operator would notice.**

> **Anticipating the overturn — and having the aeration and oxidation capacity to deal with it — is a real operational requirement, and it is one of the reasons raw water quality is monitored at several depths rather than only at the intake.**

**The types of intake, to place this one:**

| Intake | Note |
|---|---|
| **RESERVOIR intake (tower)** | **Multiple ports; often incorporated into the dam or standing free with a bridge** ← |
| **RIVER intake** | **On the bank or in the channel; must cope with floods, scour, floating debris and varying stage** ← |
| **Canal intake** | **A simple chamber in the canal bank, with a screen and a pipe** ← |
| **Lake intake** | **Usually a SUBMERGED intake on the bed, safe from ice, waves and navigation** ← |
| **Spring intake** | A sealed collection chamber at the spring's eye |

> **The essential requirements common to all of them are worth listing, since they recur:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sited where the water QUALITY is best** | **Upstream of any discharge, and on the OUTER bank of a bend for a river** ← |
| **Safe from FLOODS, SCOUR and debris** | **Founded below the scour depth, and accessible in flood** ← |
| **Adequate SUBMERGENCE** | **To prevent a vortex drawing air, and to stay below the lowest water level** ← |
| **SCREENED against trash, fish and ice** | ← |
| **A BELL-MOUTHED entry, and a low entry velocity** | **0.15 to 0.3 m/s, so that fish can escape and silt is not drawn in** ← |
| **Accessible for maintenance at all seasons** | ← |

> **THE ENTRY VELOCITY IN THE FIFTH ROW IS MUCH LOWER THAN AT A HYDROPOWER INTAKE, and the reason is instructive: a water supply intake is drawing a small flow and can afford a large opening, so it takes the opportunity to exclude sediment and to avoid impinging fish.**

> **A hydropower intake, drawing many cubic metres per second, cannot make its opening large enough for such a velocity and must deal with sediment downstream in a settling basin instead.**

> **The same structure, serving two purposes, therefore ends up with entry velocities differing by a factor of five — which is a reminder that a design rule quoted without its context can be quite wrong when transplanted.**

examTip.trick: **Reservoirs STRATIFY: the warm EPILIMNION carries algae; the cold HYPOLIMNION is often anaerobic with iron, manganese and H₂S.** Neither is reliably best, and which is better changes with the season — hence multiple ports.
examTip.trap: **The autumn OVERTURN mixes the whole reservoir in days**, distributing the anaerobic bottom water throughout — so raw water quality can deteriorate sharply with no visible change in conditions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Entry velocity 0.15-0.3 m/s at a water supply intake, against 0.6-1.0 at a hydropower trashrack** — the small flow can afford a big opening, so it excludes silt and spares fish. A rule quoted without its context transplants badly.

questions.stem: Compared with chlorination, the principal DISADVANTAGE of ULTRAVIOLET disinfection for a piped water supply is that UV:
options: Cannot destroy bacteria
Produces trihalomethanes
Leaves NO RESIDUAL, so the water is unprotected against recontamination in the distribution system
Changes the taste of the water
questions.solution:
**It leaves NO RESIDUAL**, so the water has no continuing protection against recontamination in the distribution system.

**UV against chlorine:**

| Aspect | ULTRAVIOLET | CHLORINE |
|---|---|---|
| **RESIDUAL protection** | **NONE — it acts only at the lamp** ← | **YES — the whole reason it dominates** ← |
| **By-products** | **NONE** ← | **TRIHALOMETHANES and other DBPs** ← (option b, which is chlorine's problem) |
| **Effect on TASTE and odour** | **NONE** ← (option d) | **Detectable above about 0.3 mg/L** |
| **Against BACTERIA and VIRUSES** | **Very effective** ← (so option (a) is false) | Very effective |
| **Against CRYPTOSPORIDIUM and GIARDIA** | **EXCELLENT — and these are highly CHLORINE-RESISTANT** ← | **POOR — a major weakness** ← |
| **Contact time needed** | **Seconds** | **30 minutes** |
| **Requires** | **Clear water and a reliable POWER supply** ← | Dosing equipment and chemical supply |
| **Affected by TURBIDITY** | **Severely — particles SHADE the organisms from the light** ← | Also impaired, but less so |

> **Options (a), (b) and (d) are each false of UV — and (b) and (d) are in fact CHLORINE's disadvantages, which is what makes them well-made distractors.**

**Why the residual matters so much, which is the whole answer:**

> **Disinfection at the works deals with the organisms present AT THAT MOMENT. The RESIDUAL deals with everything that happens afterwards.**

| Threat during distribution | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ingress through leaking joints at LOW PRESSURE** | **The dominant hazard in an INTERMITTENT supply** ← |
| **Cross-connections and back-siphonage** | ← |
| **Biofilm regrowth on pipe walls** | ← |
| **Contamination in service reservoirs and household tanks** | ← |

> **A UV plant delivering perfectly sterile water into a leaking, intermittently pressurised network offers no protection at all beyond the plant's outlet — and in such a network, that is where most contamination occurs.**

> **THE RESIDUAL IS ALSO A MONITORING TOOL, which is its second and underrated value: measuring free chlorine takes seconds in the field, whereas a bacteriological test takes a day or two in a laboratory.**

> **So an absent residual is an immediate warning that something is wrong, detected on the spot. UV offers no such indicator — a failed lamp produces water that looks and tests exactly like treated water until a bacteriological sample comes back.**

**Where UV IS the right choice:**

| Situation | Why |
|---|---|
| **POINT-OF-USE treatment in a household** | **No distribution system to protect — the water is used immediately** ← |
| **Where CRYPTOSPORIDIUM is the concern** | **Chlorine barely touches it; UV is highly effective** ← |
| **Where THM formation must be avoided** | **Waters high in natural organic matter** ← |
| **WASTEWATER effluent disinfection before discharge** | **No residual is wanted — indeed a chlorine residual would harm the receiving water's ecology** ← |
| **As a PRIMARY disinfectant, with a small chlorine dose added afterwards for the residual** | **The best of both — increasingly the standard for large plants** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MODERN RESOLUTION AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: UV does the killing, including of the chlorine-resistant protozoa, and a small chlorine dose afterwards provides the residual.**

> **Because the UV has already done the disinfection, the chlorine dose can be much smaller than it would otherwise need to be — so the THM formation is correspondingly reduced.**

> **The combination is therefore better than either alone on every count except cost, which is why it has become standard practice for large municipal plants in countries that can afford it.**

**And the CRYPTOSPORIDIUM point deserves expansion, because it changed disinfection practice:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A protozoan parasite forming a tough OOCYST** | **Which chlorine at practical doses does not inactivate** ← |
| **Causes severe diarrhoeal illness; dangerous to the immunocompromised** | ← |
| **The Milwaukee outbreak of 1993** | **Over 400,000 people affected — from a conventionally treated and chlorinated supply** ← |
| **The response** | **Emphasis on FILTRATION as the barrier against protozoa, and the adoption of UV and ozone** ← |

> **The lesson drawn from it is the MULTIPLE BARRIER principle met earlier, applied with more precision: different barriers stop different organisms, and chlorination alone is not a complete disinfection strategy.**

> **Filtration removes the protozoan cysts that chlorine cannot kill; chlorine kills the bacteria and viruses that filtration may pass; and the residual protects what follows.**

> **Each is necessary, and none is sufficient — which is the argument for the whole treatment train rather than for any single process in it.**

examTip.trick: **UV leaves NO RESIDUAL** — it acts only at the lamp. Options (b) and (d), THMs and taste, are CHLORINE's disadvantages, and (a) is simply false.
examTip.trap: **UV excels against CRYPTOSPORIDIUM and GIARDIA, which are highly chlorine-RESISTANT** — the Milwaukee 1993 outbreak affected 400,000 people from a properly chlorinated supply.
examTip.mnemonic: **The modern answer is BOTH: UV for the killing, a small chlorine dose after it for the residual** — and because UV has done the work, the chlorine dose and hence the THMs are much smaller. The residual is also a two-second field test.

questions.stem: In estimating the quantity of sanitary sewage from a town, the dry weather flow is normally taken as:
options: 120 to 150 per cent of the water supplied
70 to 80 per cent of the water supplied, plus an allowance for infiltration
Equal to the rainfall over the area
25 to 30 per cent of the water supplied
questions.solution:
**70 to 80 per cent of the water supplied, plus an allowance for GROUNDWATER INFILTRATION.**

**Why the sewage is LESS than the water supplied:**

| Water that does NOT reach the sewer | Note |
|---|---|
| **Garden and lawn watering** | ← |
| **Street washing and public use** | ← |
| **Industrial use consumed in the product, or evaporated** | ← |
| **Drinking, cooking and evaporation** | ← |
| **LOSSES and leakage from the distribution system** | **The largest item — water that never reaches a tap at all** ← |
| **Car washing, construction and other outdoor use** | ← |

> **The commonly quoted figure is 80 per cent, and 70 per cent is used where outdoor use is high.**

> **Options (a) and (d) are far outside the range, and option (c) describes STORM water rather than sanitary sewage.**

**INFILTRATION, which is added back — and can be very large:**

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **GROUNDWATER entering through defective joints, cracks and porous pipe** ← | **Especially where the sewer is below the water table** ← |
| **INFLOW through manhole covers, illegal roof and yard connections** ← | **Strictly a different thing, and usually far larger** ← |
| **Typical allowance** | **From a few per cent to 100 per cent of the dry weather flow, depending on the sewer's condition** ← |

> **THE INFLOW ITEM IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE THAT WRECKS TREATMENT PLANTS, and the distinction from infiltration is worth keeping:**

> **INFILTRATION is groundwater seeping in slowly and steadily — it dilutes the sewage and adds to the flow, but predictably.**

> **INFLOW is rainwater entering DIRECTLY through illegal roof connections, yard gullies and open manholes — it arrives suddenly and in enormous volume during a storm.**

> **A separate sewerage system receiving substantial inflow behaves like a combined system without having been designed as one: the treatment plant is hydraulically overwhelmed within minutes, its settled sludge is washed out, and the biological process may take days to recover.**

> **So a sewerage scheme's performance frequently depends less on its design than on whether the illegal connections are found and disconnected — which is an enforcement problem rather than an engineering one, and is correspondingly hard.**

**The PEAK FACTORS, since a sewer is sized on the peak rather than the average:**

| Flow | Value |
|---|---|
| **Average dry weather flow (DWF)** | **The base figure computed above** ← |
| **MAXIMUM (peak) flow** | **2 to 3 × DWF for a town; up to 4 for a small population** ← |
| **MINIMUM flow** | **Typically 1/3 to 1/2 of DWF, at night** ← |

> **THE MINIMUM FLOW IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE MAXIMUM, and it is the figure most often neglected:**

> **The sewer must carry the PEAK flow without surcharging, AND it must maintain the SELF-CLEANSING VELOCITY of 0.6 m/s at the MINIMUM flow.**

> **Those two requirements pull in opposite directions — a large sewer passes the peak easily and runs too slowly at night, silting up.**

> **That tension is the central difficulty of sewer design, and it is why the design is checked at both extremes and why the egg-shaped section and staged construction exist as answers to it.**

**And the STORM water estimate, which option (c) gestures at:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **RATIONAL method: Q = C i A / 3.6** | **With C the runoff coefficient, i the intensity in mm/h and A the area in hectares, giving Q in litres/second** ← |
| **Time of concentration** | **The storm duration used is the time for the whole catchment to contribute** ← |
| **Runoff coefficient C** | **0.7 to 0.95 for paved and built-up areas; 0.05 to 0.35 for parks and open ground** ← |
| **Design return period** | **2 to 10 years for the piped system; 100 years for the overland flow path** ← |

> **The contrast in magnitude is the point worth carrying: sanitary sewage from a town might be 200 litres per second, and the storm runoff from the same area in a heavy shower several THOUSAND.**

> **A COMBINED sewer must therefore be sized almost entirely for the storm flow, and the sanitary flow becomes a rounding error in its capacity — which is why combined sewers are so large, why they cannot deliver a self-cleansing velocity in dry weather, and why they overflow to the river during storms.**

> **That last consequence — the combined sewer overflow — is the strongest argument for the SEPARATE system, and it is why separate systems are now standard for new development everywhere.**

examTip.trick: **70-80 % of the water supplied, plus infiltration.** The shortfall is garden watering, industrial consumption, evaporation and — the largest item — distribution LOSSES that never reach a tap.
examTip.trap: **INFILTRATION (groundwater, slow and steady) is not INFLOW (rainwater through illegal roof connections, sudden and enormous).** Inflow turns a separate system into a combined one and overwhelms the treatment plant in minutes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design for the PEAK (2-3 × DWF) and check the MINIMUM (⅓ to ½ DWF) for self-cleansing** — the two pull opposite ways, and that tension is the whole difficulty of sewer design.

questions.stem: A TRAP in house drainage works by:
options: Filtering solids out of the waste water
Slowing the flow so that grease can be collected
Venting foul gases to the atmosphere above roof level
Retaining a WATER SEAL that prevents foul air from the drain entering the building
questions.solution:
**By retaining a WATER SEAL that prevents foul air from the drain entering the building.**

**How it works:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A U-shaped bend retains a small quantity of water permanently** ← | **The WATER SEAL** |
| **Seal depth** | **50 mm for a waste appliance; 75 mm for a soil appliance and for a gully** ← |
| **The seal blocks the passage of GAS while allowing water to pass through** ← | **Which is the whole trick** |
| **Every appliance must be trapped** | **Basin, sink, bath, WC, floor drain, gully** ← |

> **The gases excluded are not merely unpleasant: sewer gas contains HYDROGEN SULPHIDE and METHANE and can carry pathogens, so the trap is a health provision rather than an amenity.**

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) describe a filter, a GREASE TRAP and a VENT PIPE — the last two being real parts of the same drainage system, which is what makes them good distractors.**

**The types of trap:**

| Trap | Note |
|---|---|
| **P-TRAP** | **Outlet roughly HORIZONTAL — the commonest** ← |
| **S-TRAP** | **Outlet VERTICAL, downward — more prone to SELF-SIPHONAGE** ← |
| **Q-trap** | Between the two; used in upper floors |
| **BOTTLE trap** | Compact, accessible; used under basins |
| **GULLY trap** | **Outside the building, receiving waste water from sinks and baths before it enters the drain** ← |
| **FLOOR trap (nahani trap)** | **In a bathroom or kitchen floor, taking the floor washings** ← |
| **INTERCEPTING trap** | **In the last manhole, between the house drain and the public sewer — a second line of defence** ← |
| **GREASE trap** | **In a commercial kitchen, retaining fat before it reaches the drain** ← (option b) |

> **THE S-TRAP'S WEAKNESS IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE REASON IT HAS LARGELY BEEN SUPERSEDED: its vertical outlet allows the discharging water to fill the outlet pipe completely, which acts as a siphon and draws the seal out behind it.**

> **A P-trap's horizontal outlet does not fill in the same way, so the seal survives.**

**HOW A WATER SEAL IS LOST — the five mechanisms, which is the substance of the topic:**

| Mechanism | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| **SELF-SIPHONAGE** | **The appliance's OWN discharge siphons the seal out — worst with an S-trap and a small basin** ← | **A vent pipe; a P-trap; a larger waste pipe** ← |
| **INDUCED siphonage** | **Discharge from ANOTHER appliance in the same stack draws the seal out** ← | **A separate vent (anti-siphonage) pipe** ← |
| **BACK PRESSURE** | **A surge in the stack pushes air BACKWARD through the seal, blowing it out — worst at the BOTTOM of a tall stack** ← | **Vent; and a large-radius bend at the stack's foot** ← |
| **EVAPORATION** | **An appliance not used for weeks simply dries out** ← | **Run the tap; or a trap-seal protection device** ← |
| **CAPILLARY ACTION** | **A rag or a length of hair hanging over the trap's bend wicks the water out** ← | Cleaning |
| **Momentum / wavering** | Gusts of wind across the vent | Correct venting |

> **THE FIRST THREE ARE ALL PRESSURE EFFECTS, AND ALL THREE ARE CURED BY THE SAME MEASURE — VENTILATION — which is why the vent pipe is as essential to a drainage system as the traps themselves.**

> **A drainage stack with no vent is a closed system: water falling down it pushes air ahead of it and draws air behind it, and the only places that air can come from or go to are the traps.**

> **So the trap seals are alternately sucked out and blown out with every flush, and the system fills the building with sewer gas — which is exactly what venting prevents.**

**The VENTILATION arrangements:**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **The SOIL STACK carried up and open ABOVE ROOF LEVEL** ← | **The main vent — it must terminate clear of windows, typically 900 mm above any opening within 3 m** ← (option c) |
| **ANTI-SIPHONAGE (vent) pipe** | **Connected just downstream of each trap, equalising the pressure so the seal cannot be drawn or blown out** ← |
| **A large-radius bend at the foot of the stack** | **Reduces the back-pressure surge** ← |
| **The stack sized so it never runs FULL** | **A full stack is a piston; a partly full one lets air pass** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE DESIGN PRINCIPLE UNDERLYING ALL OF IT: a soil stack is deliberately oversized so that the water runs down its WALLS as an annular film, leaving an air core in the middle.**

> **That air core is the vent. As long as it exists, air can move freely up and down the stack and no trap is disturbed.**

> **An undersized stack runs full, the air core closes, and the stack becomes a piston that draws every seal on the system — which is why the stack diameter is specified by the number of appliances rather than by the flow they produce, and why reducing it "because the flow is small" is a serious error.**

examTip.trick: **A water seal of 50 mm (waste) or 75 mm (soil and gully) blocks GAS while passing water.** Options (b) and (c) name the grease trap and the vent pipe — real parts of the same system.
examTip.trap: **Five ways the seal is lost: SELF-siphonage, INDUCED siphonage, BACK PRESSURE, EVAPORATION and CAPILLARY action.** The first three are pressure effects and all three are cured by VENTILATION.
examTip.mnemonic: **A soil stack is oversized on purpose so an AIR CORE survives in the middle** — that core is the vent. Undersize it, the stack runs full, and it becomes a piston that pulls every seal in the building.

questions.stem: In a GRIT CHAMBER at a sewage treatment works, the flow velocity is maintained at about 0.3 m/s in order that:
options: All suspended solids settle out completely
The sewage is aerated as it passes
Heavy INORGANIC GRIT settles while lighter ORGANIC matter stays in suspension and passes on
The detention time is at least 30 minutes
questions.solution:
**So that the heavy INORGANIC GRIT settles out while the lighter ORGANIC matter remains in suspension and passes on to the next unit.**

**The principle — a SELECTIVE separation:**

| Material | Specific gravity | Behaviour at 0.3 m/s |
|---|---|---|
| **GRIT — sand, gravel, cinders, egg shells, coffee grounds** | **About 2.65** ← | **SETTLES — it is dense and settles quickly** ← |
| **ORGANIC matter — faecal solids, food waste, paper** | **About 1.02 to 1.2** ← | **Stays in SUSPENSION and passes forward** ← |

> **THE VELOCITY IS THEREFORE A DELIBERATE COMPROMISE, and that is the whole design idea:**

| If the velocity were | Then |
|---|---|
| **TOO LOW (below about 0.15 m/s)** | **ORGANIC matter would settle too — and putrescible organic material in the grit makes it foul-smelling, difficult to handle and impossible to dispose of as inert fill** ← |
| **0.15 to 0.35 m/s, nominally 0.3** | **Grit settles, organics pass — the design condition** ← |
| **TOO HIGH (above about 0.4 m/s)** | **The GRIT is carried through as well, and the chamber achieves nothing** ← |

> **So the grit chamber is not trying to settle everything — it is trying to settle ONE class of material and NOT another, which is why the velocity must be controlled rather than merely kept low.**

> **Option (a) describes the PRIMARY SEDIMENTATION tank, which comes later and does have that objective.**

**Why removing grit matters:**

| Consequence of grit reaching the works | Note |
|---|---|
| **ABRASION of pumps, pipes and mechanical equipment** ← | **Grit is quartz sand — harder than the metal** ← |
| **Accumulation in DIGESTERS and sedimentation tanks** | **Occupying volume designed for sludge, and very difficult to remove** ← |
| **Blockage of pipes and channels** | ← |
| **Wear on sludge pumps and scrapers** | ← |

> **The DIGESTER accumulation in the second row is the most damaging: grit settles in the digester and cannot be removed without emptying and manually cleaning it — a major shutdown.**

> **A works without effective grit removal will lose a substantial share of its digester capacity within a few years, and the loss is largely irreversible in practice.**

**How the velocity is held CONSTANT despite a varying flow — the elegant part:**

> **The sewage flow varies through the day by a factor of two or three, so a simple channel would run at quite different velocities at different hours — defeating the whole selective principle.**

| Solution | How it works |
|---|---|
| **A PROPORTIONAL (Sutro) WEIR at the outlet** ← | **Its curved profile is shaped so the DISCHARGE is proportional to the DEPTH — which makes the velocity in the channel constant at all flows** ← |
| **A PARSHALL FLUME at the outlet** | **Achieves the same, and MEASURES the flow at the same time** ← |
| **Multiple parallel channels, brought into use as the flow rises** | A cruder alternative |
| **AERATED grit chamber** | **A spiral roll induced by diffused air; the velocity of the roll, not the through-flow, does the separating** ← |

> **THE SUTRO WEIR IS A GENUINELY CLEVER DEVICE and worth understanding: an ordinary rectangular weir has Q ∝ H^1.5, so as the flow rises the depth rises less than proportionally and the velocity increases.**

> **The Sutro weir's profile — wide at the bottom, narrowing according to a specific curve — makes Q ∝ H exactly.**

> **Since the channel's area is also proportional to H, and velocity is Q/A, the velocity becomes CONSTANT at every flow.**

> **A shaped plate therefore does the work that would otherwise need a control system, and it does it with no moving parts, no power and no maintenance — which is exactly the kind of solution that suits a works without skilled operators.**

> **The AERATED chamber in the last row is the modern alternative and it decouples the problem entirely: the air-induced spiral sets the scouring velocity regardless of the through-flow, so the chamber works over a wide flow range and can also provide some pre-aeration and grease flotation.**

**And the place of the grit chamber in the treatment train:**

> **SCREENING → GRIT REMOVAL → primary sedimentation → biological treatment → secondary sedimentation → disinfection**

| Unit | Removes |
|---|---|
| **SCREENS** | **Rags, plastics, timber and large debris — protecting everything downstream** ← |
| **GRIT chamber** | **Inorganic sand and grit** ← |
| **PRIMARY sedimentation** | **Settleable organic solids — 50-70 % of suspended solids, 30-35 % of BOD** ← |
