> **The order is not arbitrary and cannot be rearranged: screens protect the grit chamber's mechanical equipment from rags, the grit chamber protects the pumps and the primary tank from abrasion, and the primary tank protects the biological stage from a solids overload.**

> **Each unit exists partly to protect the one after it — which is the organising principle of every treatment train, in water supply as much as in sewage.**

examTip.trick: **0.3 m/s settles GRIT (SG 2.65) while ORGANICS (SG ~1.1) pass on.** Too slow and organics settle too, making the grit putrescible; too fast and the grit passes. Option (a) is the primary tank's job.
examTip.trap: **Grit reaching the DIGESTER accumulates and cannot practically be removed** — a works without effective grit removal loses digester capacity permanently within a few years.
examTip.mnemonic: **A SUTRO (proportional) weir makes Q ∝ H, so the velocity stays constant as the flow varies** — a shaped plate doing what would otherwise need a control system, with no power or moving parts.

questions.stem: In a bar SCREEN at the inlet to a sewage works, the velocity of flow through the screen openings should be kept between about 0.6 and 1.2 m/s because:
options: Higher velocities would aerate the sewage excessively
Below 0.6 m/s GRIT would DEPOSIT in the channel, and above 1.2 m/s the screenings would be FORCED THROUGH the bars
It is the velocity at which the screen self-cleans
It gives the required detention time
questions.solution:
**Below 0.6 m/s grit would DEPOSIT in the approach channel, and above about 1.2 m/s the screenings would be FORCED THROUGH the bars.**

**The two bounds, each with its own reason:**

| Bound | Reason |
|---|---|
| **MINIMUM 0.6 m/s** | **The self-cleansing velocity — below it, grit and solids settle in the approach channel and it silts up** ← |
| **MAXIMUM 1.2 m/s (some codes 0.9)** | **A high velocity DRIVES soft material — rags, plastic, paper — THROUGH the openings, and the screen stops working** ← |

> **So the screen's velocity is bounded exactly as the sewer's is, and for the same reason at the lower end — 0.6 m/s is the self-cleansing velocity throughout wastewater engineering.**

> **The upper bound is peculiar to the screen: a rag pressed hard enough against a 20 mm gap will extrude through it, and once through it is downstream of the only device meant to catch it.**

**The classes of screen:**

| Screen | Clear opening | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **COARSE (bar rack)** | **50 to 100 mm** ← | **Timber, large debris; protects pumps** |
| **MEDIUM** | **20 to 50 mm** ← | **The usual inlet screen at a works** |
| **FINE** | **Below 20 mm; micro-screens to 6 mm** ← | **Removes more solids; blinds easily and needs mechanical cleaning** ← |
| **Inclination to the horizontal** | **30 to 60° for hand-raked; 60 to 90° for mechanically raked** ← | **The rake must be able to travel up the face** |

> **The INCLINATION serves two purposes: it enlarges the effective screen AREA for a given channel width (so the velocity through it is lower than the channel velocity), and it lets a rake be drawn up the face.**

**Why the screen is FIRST in the train:**

| It protects | From |
|---|---|
| **PUMPS** | **Rags wrapping around impellers — the commonest cause of pump failure at a sewage works** ← |
| **The grit chamber's mechanical equipment** | Entanglement |
| **Pipes, valves and channels** | Blockage |
| **Every downstream process** | Debris |

> **THE RAG PROBLEM IN THE FIRST ROW HAS BECOME MARKEDLY WORSE IN RECENT YEARS, and it is worth naming: so-called "flushable" wet wipes do not disperse as paper does.**

> **They combine with fat and grease in the sewer to form solid masses — the phenomenon now widely reported as a "fatberg" — which block sewers, jam pumps and overwhelm screens.**

> **The engineering responses are better screening, more frequent cleaning and grease traps at commercial kitchens; the real solution is at the point of disposal, which is a public information problem rather than an engineering one.**

**HEAD LOSS through a screen, since it must be allowed for:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Clean screen loss** | **Small — typically 150 mm or less** ← |
| **As the screen BLINDS, the loss rises steeply** | **And the upstream level rises with it** ← |
| **A BYPASS channel with a coarse screen is provided** | **So that a blocked screen cannot flood the works or back sewage up the incoming sewer** ← |
| **Mechanical screens are triggered by the DIFFERENTIAL LEVEL across them** ← | **Which is a direct measure of how blinded they are** ← |

> **The DIFFERENTIAL-LEVEL trigger in the last row is a neat piece of control design: rather than raking on a timer, the machine rakes when the water level upstream rises above the level downstream by a set amount — that is, precisely when the screen actually needs it.**

> **It raked less in dry weather and more in a storm, automatically, with a float switch and no intelligence required.**

**And the disposal of SCREENINGS, which is the unglamorous end of the process:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Quantity** | **0.005 to 0.05 m³ per 1,000 m³ of sewage** ← |
| **Character** | **Offensive, wet, and rapidly putrescible** ← |
| **Handling** | **Washed and pressed (dewatered) to reduce volume and organic content** ← |
| **Disposal** | **Burial, incineration or landfill — NOT to be returned to the flow** ← |
| **COMMINUTION as an alternative** | **A cutting device shreds the solids and returns them to the flow, so there are no screenings to handle at all** ← |

> **The COMMINUTOR in the last row looks attractive because it removes a disagreeable task, and it has largely fallen out of favour — because shredding the rags does not destroy them, it merely makes them smaller.**

> **The fragments pass forward, re-combine in the sludge, and cause exactly the same problems in the digester and the pumps that the screen existed to prevent.**

> **That is a recurring lesson in treatment plant design: a process that makes a problem less VISIBLE has not necessarily removed it, and material taken out of the flow is dealt with once, while material left in it must be dealt with repeatedly.**

examTip.trick: **0.6 m/s minimum so grit does not deposit; 1.2 m/s maximum so soft screenings are not extruded through the bars.** The lower bound is the same self-cleansing velocity used throughout wastewater engineering.
examTip.trap: **Screens are inclined 30-60° partly to ENLARGE the flow area**, so the velocity through the openings is lower than the channel velocity — as well as to let a rake travel up the face.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mechanical screens are triggered by the DIFFERENTIAL LEVEL across them** — they rake when blinded, not on a timer. And a COMMINUTOR only makes rags smaller: the fragments recombine downstream, so removal beats shredding.

questions.stem: Among the common air pollutants, PM2.5 is regarded as the most hazardous to health because these particles:
options: Are small enough to penetrate DEEP into the lungs and enter the bloodstream
Are the most chemically reactive
Have the strongest odour
Reduce visibility more than other pollutants
questions.solution:
**They are small enough to penetrate DEEP into the lungs — into the alveoli — and to pass from there into the bloodstream.**

**Why particle SIZE governs the hazard:**

| Particle size | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| **Above 10 µm** | **Trapped in the nose and throat; largely harmless, and coughed or sneezed out** ← |
| **PM10 (below 10 µm) — "respirable"** | **Reaches the upper airways and the bronchi** ← |
| **PM2.5 (below 2.5 µm) — "fine"** | **Reaches the ALVEOLI, the gas-exchange surface, and crosses into the BLOODSTREAM** ← |
| **Ultrafine, below 0.1 µm** | **Can reach other organs, including the brain** ← |

> **The body's natural defences — nasal hairs, mucus, the cilia of the airways — are effective against LARGE particles and useless against fine ones, which is precisely why PM2.5 is the parameter of concern.**

> **Option (d) is true of fine particles (they do reduce visibility, and that is why polluted air looks hazy) but it is not why they are HAZARDOUS.**

**The health effects, which reach well beyond the lungs:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Respiratory: asthma, bronchitis, COPD, reduced lung function in children** | ← |
| **CARDIOVASCULAR: heart attack, stroke, hypertension** ← | **Because the particles enter the BLOOD and cause systemic inflammation** ← |
| **Lung cancer** | **PM is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen** ← |
| **Low birth weight and adverse pregnancy outcomes** | ← |
| **Premature mortality** | **Air pollution is among the leading global risk factors for death** ← |

> **THE CARDIOVASCULAR ROW SURPRISES MOST PEOPLE AND IS THE LARGEST PART OF THE BURDEN: more deaths attributed to particulate pollution are from heart disease and stroke than from lung disease.**

> **That follows directly from the mechanism in the answer — once the particles are in the blood rather than merely in the airways, the effects are systemic rather than respiratory.**

**The standards, and Kathmandu's position:**

| Parameter | WHO 2021 guideline (annual) | Typical national standard | Kathmandu winter reality |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PM2.5** | **5 µg/m³** ← | **40 µg/m³ (India NAAQS); Nepal similar** ← | **Frequently 80 to 150 and above** ← |
| **PM10** | **15 µg/m³** | **60 µg/m³** | Often several times that |
| **SO₂, NO₂, CO, O₃, Pb, NH₃, benzene** | — | Each specified | — |

> **The gap between the WHO guideline of 5 and the observed winter values in the Kathmandu valley is a factor of twenty or more, and it is one of the most severe urban air quality problems in the world.**

**Why Kathmandu is so badly affected — the factors combine:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **A BOWL-SHAPED valley enclosed by hills** ← | **Pollutants cannot disperse laterally** ← |
| **Winter TEMPERATURE INVERSION** | **A layer of warm air sits above cold valley air, capping it — so pollution accumulates for days** ← |
| **Vehicle emissions, many from old poorly maintained engines** | ← |
| **BRICK KILNS around the valley** | **Traditional kilns are a major seasonal source** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION and road dust** | **Directly a civil engineering contribution** ← |
| **Open waste burning** | ← |
| **Domestic biomass burning** | ← |

> **THE TEMPERATURE INVERSION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE MECHANISM THAT MAKES THE OTHERS SO DAMAGING, and it is worth understanding: normally air cools with height, so warm polluted air rises and disperses.**

> **In an inversion the air ALOFT is warmer, so the cold valley air cannot rise — the atmosphere is stable, vertical mixing stops, and the day's emissions simply accumulate on top of the previous day's.**

> **That is why the pollution builds through a still winter week and clears within hours of the first wind or rain, and why the same emissions cause far worse air quality in December than in July.**

**And the CONSTRUCTION contribution, since it is the one within a civil engineer's control:**

| Source | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| **Excavation, demolition and material handling** | **WATER SPRAYING — cheap and effective** ← |
| **Haul roads and site access** | **Damping down; wheel washing at the exit** ← |
| **Uncovered material stockpiles** | **Cover or spray; site them away from the boundary** ← |
| **Uncovered trucks carrying spoil, sand and aggregate** | **SHEETING — a legal requirement, widely ignored** ← |
| **Cutting, grinding and mixing** | Local extraction or wet cutting |
| **Plant and generator exhausts** | Maintenance; low-sulphur fuel |
| **Unpaved roads left after the works** | **Paving or surfacing, which pays back permanently** ← |

> **Every one of these is inexpensive, and together they can substantially reduce a site's dust emission — which makes construction dust the pollution source most readily improved by the profession itself.**

> **It is also the one that belongs in the CONTRACT rather than in a policy document: dust control measures written into the specification as measured, paid items get done, and those left as general obligations do not — the same conclusion reached under environmental management plans.**

examTip.trick: **PM2.5 reaches the ALVEOLI and crosses into the BLOODSTREAM** — the body's defences stop large particles and are useless against fine ones. Option (d) is true but is not why they are hazardous.
examTip.trap: **Most deaths from particulate pollution are CARDIOVASCULAR, not respiratory** — heart attack and stroke — which follows directly from the particles entering the blood.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kathmandu's winter INVERSION caps the valley so emissions accumulate for days** — the same sources cause far worse air in December than July. And CONSTRUCTION DUST is the source most within our own control: spray, sheet, wash wheels, and put it in the BOQ.

questions.stem: Under Nepal's environmental legislation, a PUBLIC HEARING in the affected area is a mandatory step in the preparation of:
options: A Brief Environmental Study only
An Initial Environmental Examination only
Neither, since public consultation is discretionary
An ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT
questions.solution:
**An ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT** — the public hearing is a mandatory step for an EIA.

**The tiered requirements:**

| Study | Public consultation requirement |
|---|---|
| **Brief Environmental Study (BES)** | **The lightest requirements** |
| **Initial Environmental Examination (IEE)** | **A public notice and the recommendation of the affected local body — but NO formal public hearing** ← |
| **ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT (EIA)** | **A public notice, a formal PUBLIC HEARING held IN THE AFFECTED AREA, and the recommendation of the local body** ← |

> **The graduated requirement matches the graduated depth of the studies themselves — the more significant the anticipated impact, the more the affected public are formally brought into the process.**

**The consultation steps for an EIA:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A PUBLIC NOTICE in a national daily newspaper** | **Inviting written comments, typically within 15 days** ← |
| **Notices posted at the affected wards, schools, health posts and offices** | ← |
| **Collection of written DEEDS of public opinion** | ← |
| **A PUBLIC HEARING held IN THE AFFECTED AREA** ← | **Not in a distant capital — the point is that affected people can attend** ← |
| **RECOMMENDATION of the concerned local body (ward or municipality)** | ← |
| **The comments and the hearing's minutes ANNEXED to the report** | **So the reviewing authority can see what was said** ← |
| **Review and approval by the Ministry of Forests and Environment** | ← |

> **THE LOCATION REQUIREMENT IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE THAT DETERMINES WHETHER THE PROCESS IS REAL, and it is worth stating plainly: a hearing held in Kathmandu about a project in a remote district is a formality.**

> **A hearing in the affected village, in a language the residents speak, at a time they can attend, is a consultation.**

> **The legal requirement specifies the affected area precisely because the distinction matters, and it is the requirement most often complied with in letter rather than in substance.**

**Why public consultation is worth having, beyond the legal obligation:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Local people know things the study team does not** ← | **Where the landslides occur, where the springs are, where the river floods, which paths and grazing land matter** ← |
| **It identifies impacts the technical team would miss** | **Loss of access to a water source, severance of a trail, disturbance to a cultural site** ← |
| **It builds consent, which reduces later obstruction** | **Projects halted by local opposition are far more costly than the consultation would have been** ← |
| **It is the affected people's only formal voice** | **They bear the costs and frequently receive none of the benefits** ← |
| **It improves the mitigation** | Local solutions are often better and cheaper |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ARGUMENT THAT CONVINCES ENGINEERS, and it should: a village that has lived beside a river for generations knows its flood levels and its landslide history in far more detail than a two-week survey will establish.**

> **That is genuine data, obtainable at no cost, and a study that dismisses it as anecdote discards the longest observational record available for the site.**

**The common failings of the process, stated honestly:**

| Failing | Note |
|---|---|
| **The hearing is held AFTER the design is fixed** | **So nothing said at it can change anything — consultation reduced to announcement** ← |
| **Notice is given in ways the affected people do not see** | A newspaper in a low-literacy area |
| **The proceedings are technical and in an unfamiliar language** | ← |
| **Attendance is dominated by those with the most influence** | Not those with the most at stake |
| **The comments are recorded and not acted upon** | ← |
| **The EMP's commitments are never funded** | **The point made earlier — write them into the bill of quantities** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL ONE AND IT MIRRORS THE INFLUENCE CURVE FROM PROJECT MANAGEMENT: the ability to change the outcome is greatest at the beginning and negligible once the design is complete.**

> **A consultation held at the point where the alternatives are still open can change the alignment, the site or the technology — which is where the large environmental gains are.**

> **A consultation held when the drawings are finished can adjust the compensation and little else.**

> **So the timing of the hearing determines its value, and holding it early is both better practice and, on the evidence of stalled projects, cheaper.**

**And the legislation itself, for reference:**

| Instrument | Note |
|---|---|
| **Environment Protection Act and the Environment Protection Rules** | **The governing framework, setting out which projects need BES, IEE or EIA** ← |
| **Schedules listing the project types and thresholds** | **By sector and by size — a road above a stated length, a hydropower plant above a stated capacity** ← |
| **Approving authority** | **The concerned ministry for BES and IEE; the Ministry of Forests and Environment for EIA** ← |
| **A project in a SENSITIVE AREA** | **Requires an EIA regardless of its size** ← |

> **The last row repeats the principle met earlier and worth restating: it is the RECEIVING ENVIRONMENT, not merely the project's size, that determines the level of assessment — a small intervention in a national park or beside a cultural heritage site is treated as a major one, because the consequence of getting it wrong is major.**

examTip.trick: **A formal PUBLIC HEARING in the affected area is mandatory for an EIA, not for an IEE** — the IEE needs a public notice and the local body's recommendation, but no hearing. The requirement is graduated with the depth of the study.
examTip.trap: **"In the affected area" is the operative phrase** — a hearing in Kathmandu about a remote district project is a formality, and it is the requirement most often met in letter rather than substance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Consultation held AFTER the design is fixed is announcement, not consultation** — the influence curve again. And local people hold the longest observational record of the site's floods and landslides; dismissing it discards free data.

questions.stem: In the Indian subcontinent, the KHARIF crop season is the one:
options: From about June to October, coinciding with the MONSOON
From about October to March, the winter or dry season
From about March to June, between the two main seasons
Extending over the whole year for perennial crops
questions.solution:
**KHARIF is the MONSOON season crop — roughly June to October.**

**The three crop seasons:**

| Season | Period | Character | Typical crops |
|---|---|---|---|
| **KHARIF (monsoon)** | **June to October** ← | **Sown with the onset of the monsoon, harvested after it** ← | **PADDY (rice), maize, millet, jute, cotton, sugarcane** ← |
| **RABI (winter)** | **October to March** ← | **Sown after the monsoon on residual moisture, grown through the dry winter** ← | **WHEAT, barley, gram, mustard, potato, peas** ← |
| **ZAID (hot weather)** | **March to June** | A short third season between the two | Melons, vegetables, fodder |

> **Options (b) and (c) name RABI and ZAID correctly — they are the right descriptions attached to the wrong name, which is exactly how this question is usually set.**

**Why the distinction MATTERS to the irrigation engineer, which is the real content:**

| Season | Irrigation demand |
|---|---|
| **KHARIF** | **LOW — the monsoon supplies most of the water, and irrigation only supplements it during breaks in the rain** ← |
| **RABI** | **HIGH — there is almost no rainfall, so essentially the whole crop water requirement must be supplied by irrigation** ← |

> **THAT IS THE PARADOX AT THE CENTRE OF IRRIGATION PLANNING IN THIS REGION: the season with the most water in the rivers is the season with the least need for it, and the season with the greatest need has the least river flow.**

> **A run-of-river canal taking its supply from a Himalayan river has abundant water in July and August, when the paddy hardly needs it, and very little in January and February, when the wheat needs it most.**

> **Everything that follows from that mismatch — STORAGE reservoirs, groundwater development, and the whole argument for multipurpose projects — exists to move water from the season of surplus into the season of scarcity.**

**The consequences for canal design:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal's CAPACITY is fixed by the peak demand, which usually falls in the RABI season or at the KOR watering** ← | **Not by the season of greatest river flow** ← |
| **The INTENSITY of irrigation is quoted SEPARATELY for kharif and rabi** ← | **A scheme might irrigate 40 % of its CCA in kharif and 30 % in rabi — a total intensity of 70 %** ← |
| **The design duty differs by season** | **Kharif crops such as paddy have a large delta; rabi crops a smaller one** ← |
| **INUNDATION canals can serve kharif only** | **They flow only when the river is in flood** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW EXPLAINS AN ARITHMETIC THAT OFTEN CONFUSES: an intensity of irrigation greater than 100 per cent is perfectly possible and not an error.**

> **It means that some land is cropped TWICE in the year — once in kharif and once in rabi — so the total irrigated area over the year exceeds the physical area of the command.**

> **A scheme with 60 % kharif and 60 % rabi intensity has a total annual intensity of 120 per cent, and that is a mark of intensive, well-watered agriculture rather than a mistake in the calculation.**

**And the DELTA figures, since they follow directly from the season:**

| Crop | Approximate delta |
|---|---|
| **PADDY (kharif)** | **1,000 to 1,250 mm — much the largest, because the field is kept ponded** ← |
| **Sugarcane (long duration)** | **About 800 to 900 mm** |
| **WHEAT (rabi)** | **About 375 to 400 mm** ← |
| **Gram, barley (rabi)** | **250 to 300 mm** |
| **Cotton** | **About 500 mm** |

> **The paddy figure is the striking one and it is not a measure of the plant's thirst: most of that depth is PERCOLATION and evaporation from the standing water in which the crop is grown, not transpiration by the plant.**

> **Which is why paddy on a permeable soil demands so much more water than paddy on a clay, and why puddling the field — deliberately destroying the soil structure to form an impermeable layer — is the traditional and highly effective response to it.**

examTip.trick: **KHARIF = monsoon, June-October, paddy and maize. RABI = winter, October-March, wheat and gram.** Options (b) and (c) give the right descriptions of rabi and zaid under the wrong name.
examTip.trap: **The demand is INVERSE to the supply** — kharif has abundant river flow and little need, rabi has great need and least flow. Everything about storage reservoirs follows from that mismatch.
examTip.mnemonic: **An intensity above 100 % is NOT an error** — it means land cropped twice, kharif and rabi. And paddy's 1,000+ mm delta is mostly PERCOLATION from the ponded field, not the plant's transpiration.

questions.stem: The duty of water at the HEAD of a canal is 800 hectares per cumec and the conveyance efficiency between the head and the field outlet is 80 per cent. The duty at the FIELD OUTLET is:
options: 640 hectares per cumec
800 hectares per cumec
960 hectares per cumec
1,000 hectares per cumec
questions.solution:
**1,000 hectares per cumec.**

**The reasoning, which is entirely about which discharge is in the denominator:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Duty D = area irrigated ÷ discharge** | **D = A / Q, in hectares per cumec** ← |
| **At the HEAD, D_head = A / Q_head = 800** | So A = 800 Q_head |
| **Conveyance efficiency 80 %** | **Q_field = 0.80 Q_head — one fifth of the water is LOST in transit** ← |
| **At the FIELD, D_field = A / Q_field** | **= A / (0.80 Q_head) = 800 Q_head / (0.80 Q_head)** |
| **D_field = 800 / 0.80** | **= 1,000 hectares per cumec** ← |

> **So the duty at the field is HIGHER than the duty at the head, by exactly the factor 1/η.**

**Why HIGHER is the right direction, since this is the whole point of the question:**

> **DUTY IS AN EFFICIENCY MEASURE DRESSED AS A RATIO: it is the area a unit discharge can irrigate, so a LARGER duty means water is being used BETTER.**

| Point in the system | Discharge needed for the same area | Duty |
|---|---|---|
| **At the FIELD** | **Small — only what the crop actually receives** ← | **HIGH** ← |
| **At the HEAD** | **Larger — it must also cover everything lost on the way** ← | **LOW** ← |

> **THE MEMORABLE FORM IS THIS: the further UPSTREAM you measure, the MORE water you must be passing to irrigate the same land, and therefore the LOWER the duty.**

> **Duty rises as you move down the system, and falls as you move up it.**

> **Option (a), 640, is the same arithmetic with the efficiency applied the WRONG WAY — multiplying by 0.8 instead of dividing — and it is the answer that will be marked wrong most often, because the calculation is right and only the direction is not.**

**A check by the DELTA, which is a useful independent route:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Δ = 8.64 B / D**, with Δ in metres, B the base period in days and D the duty in ha/cumec | ← |
| **At the head, for B = 120 days: Δ_head = 8.64 × 120 / 800 = 1.296 m** | The depth that must be RELEASED |
| **At the field: Δ_field = 8.64 × 120 / 1,000 = 1.037 m** | **The depth actually DELIVERED to the crop** ← |
| **Ratio 1.037 / 1.296 = 0.80** | **The conveyance efficiency, recovered — which confirms the direction** ← |

> **That the depth released exceeds the depth delivered is obviously right, and it settles the direction of the duty relation without having to remember it.**

**The EFFICIENCIES in an irrigation system, to place the 80 per cent:**

| Efficiency | Definition | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **CONVEYANCE, η_c** | **Water delivered to the field ÷ water released at the head** | **60 to 80 % unlined; 85 to 95 % LINED** ← |
| **APPLICATION (field), η_a** | **Water stored in the root zone ÷ water delivered to the field** | **50 to 70 % for surface irrigation; 90 % for drip** ← |
| **OVERALL, η_o = η_c × η_a** | **The product** ← | **Often only 30 to 45 % for a traditional surface scheme** ← |
| **Distribution efficiency** | Evenness of application across the field | — |

> **THE OVERALL FIGURE IN THE THIRD ROW IS SOBERING AND IT IS THE FIGURE THAT MATTERS: a scheme with 70 per cent conveyance and 60 per cent application delivers just 42 per cent of the water released to the crop's root zone.**

> **More than half of a very expensive supply is lost, and the cheapest additional water available to almost any existing scheme is therefore the water it is already losing.**

> **That is the argument for lining, for improved on-farm distribution, and for drip and sprinkler systems: raising efficiency from 42 to 60 per cent gives the same result as building a new headworks to increase the supply by 40 per cent, and it costs a fraction as much.**

> **It is also, characteristically, much harder to do — because it requires changing how thousands of farmers manage water on their own land, rather than building one structure that an engineer can design and supervise.**

examTip.trick: **D_field = D_head / η = 800 / 0.80 = 1,000 ha/cumec.** Duty is area per unit discharge, so the smaller field discharge gives the LARGER duty.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 640 is the efficiency applied the wrong way.** Duty RISES going downstream and FALLS going upstream — further upstream, more water passes for the same land.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check with Δ = 8.64 B / D**: the depth released (1.296 m) exceeds the depth delivered (1.037 m), and their ratio is exactly 0.80. Overall efficiency η_c × η_a is often only 30-45 %, so the cheapest new water is the water already being lost.

questions.stem: The bed material of a channel has a mean particle size of 0.325 mm. Lacey's SILT FACTOR for this material is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 1.00.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Lacey's silt factor** | **f = 1.76 √m, with m the mean particle size in MILLIMETRES** ← |
| **√0.325** | **= 0.570** |
| **f = 1.76 × 0.570** | **= 1.003** |
| **Answer** | **f ≈ 1.0** ← |

> **0.325 mm is the STANDARD SILT for which Lacey's factor is unity — which is not a coincidence but the definition on which the whole scale was calibrated, and it is worth memorising as the anchor point.**

> **Option (a) 0.57 omits the coefficient; option (c) 1.76 is the value for m = 1 mm; option (d) 3.09 divides instead of multiplying.**

**Typical silt factors, so the scale means something:**

| Material | m (mm) | f |
|---|---|---|
| Very fine silt | 0.05 | **0.4** |
| Fine silt | 0.12 | **0.6** |
| **STANDARD silt** | **0.325** | **1.0** ← |
| Medium sand | 0.5 | **1.25** |
| Coarse sand | 0.725 | **1.5** |
| **Boulders and shingle** | **Large** | **Up to 6 to 20** ← |

**Where f is used — the whole of Lacey's regime theory rests on it:**

| Relation | Form |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75 √Q** ← (independent of f — worth noting) |
| **Hydraulic mean depth** | **R = 0.47 (Q / f)^(1/3)** ← |
| **Velocity** | **V = (Q f² / 140)^(1/6)** |
| **Bed slope** | **S = f^(5/3) / (3340 Q^(1/6))** ← |
| **Regime scour depth** | **R = 0.47 (Q/f)^(1/3) for the whole discharge; or 1.35 (q²/f)^(1/3) for discharge per metre** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ONE THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS WORTH DWELLING ON: the wetted perimeter depends ONLY on the discharge, and not at all on the silt.**

> **Lacey's claim is that a channel in regime adopts a width set by how much water it carries, while the silt determines how DEEP and how STEEP it is.**

> **Coarse material gives a large f, hence a shallower section (R falls) and a steeper slope (S rises) — which matches observation: a boulder river is wide, shallow and steep, and a silt river is narrower for its depth and much flatter.**

**LACEY against KENNEDY, since the two theories are always compared:**

| Aspect | KENNEDY | LACEY |
|---|---|---|
| **Basis** | **Critical velocity for non-silting, non-scouring, from the Upper Bari Doab canal** ← | **The REGIME concept — a channel in equilibrium in all respects** ← |
| **Silt characterised by** | **The critical velocity ratio m (CVR)** ← | **The SILT FACTOR f, tied to particle size** ← |
| **Slope** | **NOT given by the theory — must be assumed and checked with Kutter's formula** ← | **GIVEN directly by the theory** ← |
| **Section shape** | **Assumed (trapezoidal, B/D ratio chosen by the designer)** ← | **Determined by the theory (semi-elliptical in principle)** ← |
| **Procedure** | **TRIAL AND ERROR** ← | **Direct** ← |
| **Considers side slopes' silt support** | No | Yes |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS LACEY'S DECISIVE ADVANTAGE AND THE REASON HIS METHOD DISPLACED KENNEDY'S: Kennedy's theory tells you what velocity to aim for but not what slope will produce it, so the designer must guess a slope, work out the section, check the velocity, and iterate.**

> **Lacey's equations deliver the perimeter, the depth, the velocity and the slope from the discharge and the silt factor alone, in one pass.**

> **Both are empirical, both were derived from canals in the Indus basin, and neither is a general truth — but a theory that closes the problem is worth a great deal more than one that leaves it open, and that is why Lacey is what gets used.**

examTip.trick: **f = 1.76 √m with m in mm: 1.76 × √0.325 = 1.76 × 0.570 = 1.00.** 0.325 mm is the STANDARD SILT defined to give f = 1 — memorise it as the anchor.
examTip.trap: **P = 4.75 √Q depends only on the DISCHARGE, not on the silt.** Lacey says the water sets the width and the silt sets the depth and slope — which is why boulder rivers are wide, shallow and steep.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kennedy gives no SLOPE, so it needs trial and error with Kutter; Lacey delivers perimeter, depth, velocity and slope in one pass.** A theory that closes the problem beats one that leaves it open.

questions.stem: In an unlined alluvial canal, the MAXIMUM permissible velocity is governed by the risk of ______ and the MINIMUM permissible velocity by the risk of ______.
options: Seepage; evaporation
Evaporation; seepage
SCOUR of the bed and banks; SILTING of the section
Silting of the section; scour of the bed and banks
questions.solution:
**Maximum velocity limited by SCOUR; minimum velocity limited by SILTING.**

**The two bounds:**

| Bound | Governed by | If violated |
|---|---|---|
| **MAXIMUM velocity** | **SCOUR — the flow erodes the bed and banks** ← | **The section deepens and widens, the banks fail, and the canal loses its shape and its command** ← |
| **MINIMUM velocity** | **SILTING — the flow can no longer carry its sediment load** ← | **The section fills, the capacity falls, and the canal must be desilted repeatedly** ← |

> **Option (d) reverses the two, which is the trap; options (a) and (b) name seepage and evaporation, which are real canal losses but have nothing to do with the velocity limits.**

> **A canal in ALLUVIUM is a channel cut in the very material it is carrying, so it is in continuous exchange with its bed — which is why both bounds exist at once and why the design velocity is squeezed between them.**

> **A LINED canal has no such lower problem from the section's own material, but it still needs a minimum velocity to keep the incoming silt moving, and its upper bound is set by the lining's durability rather than by scour.**

**Typical permissible velocities:**

| Material | Maximum velocity |
|---|---|
| **Fine sand / very light soil** | **0.3 to 0.5 m/s** ← |
| **Sandy loam** | **0.5 to 0.7 m/s** |
| **Loam / clay loam** | **0.7 to 1.0 m/s** |
| **Stiff CLAY** | **1.0 to 1.5 m/s** |
| **Gravel** | **1.2 to 1.8 m/s** |
| **LINED — cement concrete** | **2.0 to 2.5 m/s or more** ← |
| **Minimum (non-silting) for a normal canal** | **About 0.3 m/s at least; commonly designed at 0.6 to 1.0 m/s** ← |

> **THE JUMP AT THE LINING ROW IS THE POINT WORTH TAKING: lining does not merely stop seepage — by permitting a much higher velocity it permits a much SMALLER SECTION for the same discharge.**

> **A lined canal carrying a given flow at 2.0 m/s needs roughly a third of the cross-sectional area that an unlined canal in sandy loam needs at 0.6 m/s.**

> **So the lining pays for itself three times over: in the water saved from seepage, in the land not acquired for a wide section, and in the excavation not carried out.**

> **That third saving is the one usually omitted from the economic comparison, and it is often the largest — which is why lining frequently proves cheaper than it first appears when the whole cost, and not merely the lining itself, is put into the account.**

**KENNEDY'S CRITICAL VELOCITY, which is the classical statement of the same idea:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **V₀ = 0.55 m D^0.64** | **With D the depth in metres, m the critical velocity ratio, V₀ in m/s** ← |
| **The critical velocity is that at which the channel neither silts NOR scours** ← | **Which is the velocity the two bounds converge on** ← |
| **m, the CVR** | **Below 1 for finer silt than the standard; above 1 for coarser — typically 0.8 to 1.2** ← |
| **The velocity rises with DEPTH** | **A deeper channel can carry a faster flow without scouring, because the eddies that lift sediment are generated at the bed** ← |

> **THE DEPTH DEPENDENCE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE PHYSICAL INSIGHT UNDERNEATH KENNEDY'S EMPIRICISM: Kennedy observed that the silt-supporting power of a channel comes from the vertical eddies generated at the BED, and that a deeper column of water gives those eddies more room to lift sediment through.**

> **So depth, not velocity alone, determines whether the load stays in suspension — and a shallow, fast channel may scour while a deep, slower one stays stable.**

> **Lacey later argued that the eddies rise from the whole WETTED PERIMETER rather than the bed alone, which is why his relations use the hydraulic mean radius R in place of Kennedy's depth D, and it is the single conceptual step that separates the two theories.**

examTip.trick: **Too FAST scours, too SLOW silts.** Option (d) reverses them. Seepage and evaporation are canal losses but have nothing to do with the velocity bounds.
examTip.trap: **Lining's third saving is usually forgotten** — at 2.0 m/s instead of 0.6 m/s the section is roughly a third the area, so land and excavation are saved as well as water.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kennedy V₀ = 0.55 m D^0.64 — the velocity that neither silts nor scours, rising with DEPTH** because the silt-lifting eddies start at the bed. Lacey's step was to say they rise from the whole perimeter, hence R instead of D.

questions.stem: In Khosla's method of INDEPENDENT VARIABLES, the pressures obtained for each simple standard form must then be adjusted by corrections for:
options: Temperature, shrinkage and creep
Wind, seismic and impact effects
Silt load, afflux and freeboard
MUTUAL INTERFERENCE of piles, THICKNESS of the floor, and SLOPE of the floor
questions.solution:
**Mutual INTERFERENCE of the piles, the THICKNESS of the floor, and the SLOPE of the floor.**

**The method's logic:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A real weir floor is a complex profile with several sheet piles at different depths** ← | **For which no closed solution exists** |
| **Khosla BREAKS IT DOWN into simple standard forms** ← | **A straight floor with a pile at the upstream end, at the downstream end, or at an intermediate point; and a depressed floor** ← |
| **Each simple form has an exact solution** | **From conformal mapping — the pressures are read from Khosla's curves** ← |
| **The simple results are then CORRECTED for the three real effects** ← | **Which is where the three corrections come in** |

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) name corrections belonging to structural design, to loading, and to canal hydraulics — none of them to seepage analysis.**

**The three corrections in detail:**

| Correction | Cause | Sign |
|---|---|---|
| **MUTUAL INTERFERENCE of piles** | **A neighbouring pile alters the flow net, so the pressure at a pile is not what it would be if that pile stood alone** ← | **Can be either; computed from Khosla's interference formula, depending on which side the other pile lies** ← |
| **THICKNESS of the floor** | **Pressures are computed at the pile's junction with the floor TOP, but they act on the floor's BOTTOM — and the two differ** ← | **The correction moves the value toward the interior of the profile** ← |
| **SLOPE of the floor** | **A sloping floor changes the creep path and the pressure distribution along it** ← | **NEGATIVE for a DOWN slope in the direction of flow, positive for an up slope; applied only to the pile at the START of the slope** ← |

> **THE THICKNESS CORRECTION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD, and the reason for it is worth being clear about:**

> **The theory computes the pressure at a mathematical point where the pile meets the floor. But the floor is a real slab, perhaps 1.5 m thick, and the uplift acts on its UNDERSIDE, which is 1.5 m lower down the pile.**

> **Since the pressure varies along the pile, the value at the underside is different from the value at the top — so a linear interpolation between the pile's top and bottom pressures is applied.**

> **It is a geometric correction rather than a hydraulic one, and it always moves the pressure in the direction that the flow is heading down the profile.**

**Why Khosla's theory replaced BLIGH's, which is the examinable comparison:**

| Aspect | BLIGH's creep theory | KHOSLA's theory |
|---|---|---|
| **Basis** | **The creep length is the sum of ALL the paths, horizontal and vertical, weighted EQUALLY** ← | **Potential flow theory and the FLOW NET, solved by conformal mapping** ← |
| **Horizontal vs vertical creep** | **Treated as equally effective** ← | **VERTICAL creep is far MORE effective than horizontal — the central correction of Bligh** ← |
| **Failure criterion** | **Creep ratio C: L ≥ C H** | **EXIT GRADIENT at the downstream end** ← |
| **Intermediate piles** | Treated as fully effective | **Found to be largely INEFFECTIVE unless deeper than the end piles** ← |
| **Verdict** | **Simple, safe-sided in some cases and unsafe in others** ← | **Sound, and the basis of modern practice** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW WAS KHOSLA'S MOST PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT FINDING AND IT CAME FROM FAILURES: several weirs designed by Bligh's method failed, and investigation of them showed that intermediate sheet piles were contributing far less than the theory credited them with.**

> **The remedy that follows is a design rule still applied: put the sheet piles at the ENDS of the floor and make the DOWNSTREAM pile the deepest, since it is the one that controls the exit gradient — which is the quantity that actually governs failure by piping.**

> **The general lesson is one that recurs through hydraulic engineering: theories are corrected by failures more often than by experiments, and a design method's real test is the structures built to it rather than its internal elegance.**

examTip.trick: **Three corrections: mutual INTERFERENCE of piles, THICKNESS of floor, SLOPE of floor.** Break the profile into simple forms with exact solutions, read the curves, then correct.
examTip.trap: **The thickness correction is geometric** — pressure is computed where the pile meets the floor TOP but acts on its UNDERSIDE, so it is interpolated down the pile.
examTip.mnemonic: **Khosla's finding from actual failures: INTERMEDIATE piles are largely ineffective, and VERTICAL creep beats horizontal.** Hence piles at the ENDS, with the DOWNSTREAM one deepest — it controls the exit gradient that governs piping.

questions.stem: At a diversion headworks, the CANAL HEAD REGULATOR is the structure that:
options: Raises the river water level to the required command level
REGULATES the supply entering the off-taking canal, controls the entry of silt, and permits the discharge to be measured
Passes the flood discharge of the river safely downstream
Trains the river to approach the works centrally
questions.solution:
**It regulates the supply entering the off-taking canal, excludes silt, and allows the discharge to be measured.**

**Its three functions:**

| Function | How |
|---|---|
| **REGULATE the discharge admitted into the canal** ← | **Gates on the openings, adjusted to admit the required supply and to shut the canal off completely for maintenance or in a flood** ← |
| **Control the entry of SILT** ← | **A SILL raised above the under-sluice floor, so that the canal draws the cleaner upper water and the silt-laden bottom water passes on to the under-sluices** ← |
| **MEASURE the discharge** | **The gated openings act as submerged orifices with a known coefficient** ← |
| **(and) exclude river floods from the canal** | **By closing the gates** |

> **Options (a), (c) and (d) describe the WEIR or barrage, the SPILLWAY or waterway, and the GUIDE BANKS — the other three principal components of the same headworks, which is what makes them good distractors.**

**THE RAISED SILL IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE SILT-CONTROL PRINCIPLE OF THE WHOLE HEADWORKS, and it deserves stating properly:**

> **Sediment in a river is NOT uniformly distributed through the depth. Coarse sand and bed load travel along the BOTTOM; the water near the surface is far cleaner.**

> **So the single most effective silt-exclusion measure costs nothing at all: set the canal's sill HIGHER than the under-sluice floor — usually 1.2 to 1.5 m above it — and the canal skims the clean upper layer while the dirty bottom layer is drawn away through the under-sluices and returned to the river.**

> **Every other silt-control device at a headworks — the still pond, the silt excluder, the silt ejector — is a refinement of that one idea, and the raised sill does most of the work before any of them is called on.**

**The COMPONENTS of a diversion headworks, to place the regulator:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **WEIR or BARRAGE** | **Raises the water level to command the canal, and passes the flood** ← (option a and part of c) |
| **UNDER-SLUICES (scouring sluices)** | **A deeper bay adjacent to the head regulator, kept clear to scour silt away from the canal mouth** ← |
| **DIVIDE WALL** | **Separates the under-sluice pocket from the weir proper, and keeps cross-currents away from the regulator** ← |
| **CANAL HEAD REGULATOR** | **This question** ← |
| **FISH LADDER** | **Allows fish to migrate past the barrier** |
| **GUIDE BANKS and marginal bunds** | **Train the river to approach centrally and protect the flanks** ← (option d) |
| **SILT EXCLUDER / EJECTOR** | **Excluder in the river upstream of the regulator; ejector in the canal downstream of it** ← |
| **Approach and river training works, launching aprons** | Protection against scour |

> **The layout has an internal logic worth seeing as a whole: the divide wall creates a still POCKET in front of the canal mouth; within that pocket the water slows and drops its coarse sediment; the under-sluices then scour that deposit away downstream; and the raised sill ensures the canal never draws from the bottom of the pocket in the first place.**

> **Four structures, each simple in itself, combining to solve the one problem that determines whether the canal survives — because a canal that admits the river's bed load will silt up within a season or two, and desilting it every year costs more than the entire headworks.**

**The STILL POND versus OPEN FLOW operation, which is how the pocket is actually used:**

| Mode | Operation | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **STILL POND** | **The under-sluice gates are kept CLOSED while the canal draws, so the water in the pocket is nearly still** ← | **The sediment settles in the pocket; the gates are then opened periodically to flush it out** ← |
| **OPEN FLOW (semi-open)** | **The under-sluice gates are kept partly OPEN continuously** | **A current runs past the regulator carrying sediment on; simpler, but less effective** ← |

> **The still pond method gives better silt exclusion and is preferred where water can be spared for the periodic flushing, and the open flow method is used when it cannot — which is the same trade between water and sediment met at a hydropower settling basin, and resolved the same way.**

examTip.trick: **Regulate the supply, control silt entry, measure the discharge.** The other options describe the weir, the spillway and the guide banks — the other components of the same headworks.
examTip.trap: **The RAISED SILL, 1.2-1.5 m above the under-sluice floor, is the cheapest and most effective silt control there is** — the canal skims the clean upper water while the bed load passes to the under-sluices.
examTip.mnemonic: **Divide wall makes a pocket → sediment settles in it → under-sluices scour it away → raised sill keeps the canal off the bottom.** Four simple structures solving the one problem that decides whether the canal survives.

questions.stem: A river reach in which the bed level RISES over time, because the sediment supplied from upstream exceeds the reach's capacity to transport it, is described as:
options: AGGRADING
Degrading
In regime
Meandering
questions.solution:
**AGGRADING** — the bed builds up because more sediment arrives than leaves.

**The three states of a river reach:**

| State | Sediment balance | Bed level |
|---|---|---|
| **AGGRADING (building up)** | **Supply EXCEEDS transport capacity** ← | **RISES** ← |
| **DEGRADING (scouring down)** | **Transport capacity EXCEEDS supply** ← | **FALLS** ← |
| **IN REGIME (stable, poised)** | **Supply EQUALS transport capacity** ← | **Unchanged on average over the long term** ← |

> **Option (d), MEANDERING, describes the river's PLAN FORM rather than its vertical behaviour — a separate classification, and a river may be meandering while aggrading, degrading or stable.**

**What causes each, which is where the engineering enters:**

| Cause of AGGRADATION | Note |
|---|---|
| **Heavy sediment yield from the catchment** | **Deforestation, landslides, road cutting, agriculture on steep slopes** ← |
| **A reduction in slope** | **Where a steep hill river debouches onto a flat plain — the classic case** ← |
| **A reduction in the flood flows that flush the bed** | **Upstream storage that traps water as well as sediment** |
| **An obstruction raising the base level** | **A weir, a barrage, or a downstream tributary's fan** ← |

| Cause of DEGRADATION | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sediment TRAPPED behind an upstream dam** ← | **Clear water released downstream has spare capacity and takes its load from the bed — "hungry water"** ← |
| **Sand and gravel MINING from the bed** | **A very large cause in Nepal and across South Asia** ← |
| **Channelisation increasing the slope or velocity** | Cut-offs, straightening |
| **A drop in the downstream base level** | ← |

> **THE HUNGRY WATER EFFECT IN THE FIRST ROW OF THE SECOND TABLE IS ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES IN RIVER ENGINEERING, and it is worth understanding properly:**

> **A reservoir traps the incoming sediment, so the water released below the dam carries almost none. Its capacity to transport sediment is unchanged — but it now has nothing to transport.**

> **So it picks up material from the bed and banks of the reach below, and the river degrades, sometimes by several metres over decades.**

> **The consequences reach far beyond the river: bridge piers and abutments are undermined, intake sills are left above the water, bank protection is outflanked from below, and the water table in the adjoining land falls with the river.**

> **None of these appears in the dam's own accounts, and all of them are eventually paid for by somebody — which is a standard example in the literature on how project boundaries are drawn too narrowly.**

**The Nepali context, since both processes are conspicuous here:**

| Setting | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Rivers debouching from the hills onto the TERAI** | **Strongly AGGRADING — the slope drops abruptly, the sediment load is enormous, and alluvial fans build up** ← |
| **The Koshi, the Bagmati, the Rapti in their plains reaches** | **Beds rising, channels shifting, embankments needing continual raising** ← |
| **Reaches below sand and gravel extraction** | **DEGRADING, with bridge foundations exposed** ← |
| **Reaches below storage projects** | Degrading |

> **THE SECOND ROW CARRIES A SERIOUS AND UNDER-APPRECIATED HAZARD: when an aggrading river is confined between embankments, the bed continues to rise INSIDE the embankments while the surrounding land does not.**

> **Over decades the river bed can climb above the level of the country beside it — a "perched" river — held in only by its embankments.**
> **A breach then does not merely flood the land; it lets the river ABANDON its channel altogether and find a new course across the plain, which is what happened in the Koshi breach of 2008.**

> **The engineering conclusion is uncomfortable but has to be faced: embanking an aggrading river reduces flooding in the short term and increases the CONSEQUENCE of failure in the long term, so embankments on such rivers are a commitment to permanent, funded maintenance rather than a one-time work.**

examTip.trick: **Aggrading = supply exceeds capacity, bed RISES. Degrading = capacity exceeds supply, bed FALLS. In regime = balanced.** Meandering describes plan form, a separate classification entirely.
examTip.trap: **"HUNGRY WATER" below a dam** — clear released water has full transport capacity and nothing to carry, so it takes its load from the bed, undermining bridges and leaving intakes dry for decades afterwards.
examTip.mnemonic: **An embanked aggrading river becomes PERCHED — its bed climbs above the surrounding country.** A breach then lets the river change course entirely, as at Koshi in 2008. Embankments on such rivers are a permanent maintenance commitment.

questions.stem: In a SIPHON AQUEDUCT, as distinct from an ordinary aqueduct:
options: The canal passes beneath the drainage under pressure
Canal and drainage are carried at the same level in a common channel
The canal is carried OVER the drainage, and the DRAINAGE passes beneath it UNDER PRESSURE
The drainage is carried over the canal in a trough
questions.solution:
**The canal is carried OVER the drainage, and the drainage runs beneath it UNDER PRESSURE.**

**The four cross-drainage arrangements, which must be kept apart:**

| Work | Canal | Drainage | Condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **OVER** ← | **Under, in an open channel with free water surface** ← | **The drainage HFL is BELOW the canal trough's underside** ← |
| **SIPHON AQUEDUCT** | **OVER** ← | **Under, running FULL and UNDER PRESSURE** ← | **The drainage HFL is ABOVE the canal trough's underside, so it must be forced through** ← |
| **SUPER-PASSAGE** | **UNDER** ← | **Over, in a trough** ← (option d) | The canal's FSL is below the drainage trough |
| **CANAL SIPHON (siphon)** | **UNDER, running FULL and UNDER PRESSURE** ← (option a) | **Over, in a trough** | The canal's FSL is above the trough's underside |
| **LEVEL CROSSING** | **Both meet in a common pool and are separated again by regulators** ← (option b) | — | Used where both are large |
| **INLET AND OUTLET** | A small drain is admitted into the canal and let out further along | — | Only for very small drains |

> **THE NAMING RULE THAT SETTLES ALL OF THEM: the FIRST word of the name tells you what the CANAL does, and the word "siphon" tells you which channel runs under pressure.**

> **AQUEDUCT — the canal is carried over, like a Roman aqueduct carrying water across a valley. SUPER-PASSAGE — the drainage passes over the top, the canal beneath.**

> **Add "siphon" and the lower channel is drowned: in a SIPHON AQUEDUCT the canal is still on top but the drainage below is pressurised; in a CANAL SIPHON the canal itself is the one running full underneath.**

**Why a siphon aqueduct is needed at all:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The drainage's flood level is HIGH, and the canal cannot be raised further** ← | **Raising the canal means raising it for kilometres either side, which is prohibitive** ← |
| **So the drainage is contracted and forced through barrels beneath the canal trough** | **Running full, under a head** ← |
| **The head required drives the flow through** | **Created by the afflux upstream of the work** ← |

> **The design consequence is significant and often underestimated: forcing a flood through a restricted pressurised opening RAISES the water level upstream of the work, and that afflux floods land that was not previously flooded.**

> **So a siphon aqueduct's barrels must be sized not merely to pass the flood, but to pass it with an acceptable afflux — and the land affected by the remaining afflux must be accounted for in the project.**

**The design points common to cross-drainage works:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Site them where the two channels cross at RIGHT ANGLES if possible** | **A skew crossing lengthens and complicates the structure** ← |
| **Site where the drainage is well defined and stable** | Not on a shifting reach |
| **Provide adequate WATERWAY for the drainage's design flood** | **Usually by Lacey's regime perimeter, P = 4.75 √Q** ← |
| **Protect against SCOUR on both sides** | **Aprons, cut-off walls, pitching — the drainage is being contracted, so its velocity rises** ← |
| **Provide an inspection road or path across** | Often the works double as a crossing |
| **UPLIFT on the floor must be checked** | **Both from the drainage's own head and from the seepage from the canal above** ← |

> **THE UPLIFT CHECK IN THE LAST ROW IS THE CRITICAL STRUCTURAL DESIGN CASE for a siphon aqueduct's floor, and it has two independent sources acting at once.**

> **The drainage running under pressure exerts uplift from within the barrel; and the canal above, seeping down through and around the structure, raises the water table and exerts uplift from outside.**

> **The worst case is the one designers sometimes miss: the drainage barrel EMPTY while the canal above is running full — so there is no water inside to weigh the floor down, and the full seepage uplift acts beneath it.**

> **A floor designed only for the flood condition can float in dry weather, which is a failure mode that has actually occurred, and it is why relief holes with inverted filters are commonly provided through the barrel floor.**

examTip.trick: **The FIRST word says what the CANAL does; "siphon" says which channel runs under pressure.** Aqueduct = canal over, drainage free. Siphon aqueduct = canal over, drainage pressurised. Super-passage = canal under. Canal siphon = canal under, pressurised.
examTip.trap: **All three wrong options name real cross-drainage works** — canal siphon, level crossing and super-passage — so the distinction has to be exact, not approximate.
examTip.mnemonic: **Worst uplift case: barrel EMPTY, canal above running FULL** — no water inside to hold the floor down, full seepage uplift beneath it. Floors have floated in dry weather; hence relief holes with inverted filters.

questions.stem: A CANAL ESCAPE is provided principally to:
options: Admit water from a natural drain into the canal
Measure the discharge flowing in the canal
Lower the canal bed where the ground slope is steep
DISPOSE OF SURPLUS WATER from the canal safely into a natural drainage or depression
questions.solution:
**To dispose of SURPLUS water from the canal safely into a natural drainage channel, river or depression.**

**Why a canal ever has surplus water:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **A sudden CLOSURE of outlets downstream** | **Rain over the command, so cultivators stop drawing — and the water already in the canal has nowhere to go** ← |
| **Heavy RAINFALL adding runoff to the canal** | ← |
| **A BREACH or blockage downstream** | **The canal must be emptied above the damage** ← |
| **Mis-regulation at the head** | **More admitted than the demand** |
| **Emptying for MAINTENANCE or repair** | **A scouring escape near the tail or at low points** ← |

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) describe an INLET, a metering flume and a canal FALL — all genuine components of a canal system.**

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE COMMONEST AND MOST DANGEROUS CASE, and it is worth seeing why: when it rains over the command, every cultivator closes his outlet at once.**

> **The canal is still carrying its full supply, admitted at the head hours or days earlier and travelling down at a few kilometres an hour. That water cannot be recalled.**

> **With the outlets shut, the level rises, the canal overtops its banks, and a BREACH follows — which floods the very land the canal was built to serve and takes weeks to repair.**

> **The escape is the relief valve that prevents this, and it is the reason escapes are regarded as a safety requirement rather than a convenience.**

**The types of escape:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURPLUS WATER escape (weir escape)** | **A side weir set at the canal's FSL — it operates AUTOMATICALLY as soon as the level rises above FSL, with no gates and no operator** ← |
| **SCOURING escape** | **A gated opening at BED level, used to empty the canal completely for maintenance, and to flush accumulated silt** ← |
| **Tail escape** | **At the very end of the canal, keeping the tail reach at its full supply level** ← |

> **THE AUTOMATIC OPERATION OF THE WEIR ESCAPE IN THE FIRST ROW IS ITS WHOLE VALUE and deserves emphasis: the emergency it protects against arrives at night, in the rain, when nobody is at the structure.**

> **A gated escape that must be opened by an operator will not be opened in time, and the canal will breach while somebody is being sent for.**

> **A side weir at FSL needs no decision, no power and no attendance — it simply starts spilling the moment the level exceeds the design value, and stops when it falls back.**

> **That is the same reasoning that puts an automatic spillway on a dam rather than relying on gates, and the same reasoning behind the Sutro weir at a grit chamber: for a function that must never fail, a device with no moving parts and no operator beats a controlled one, even if the controlled one performs better on an average day.**

**Where an escape can be sited, which constrains the design:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **A natural drainage, river or depression must be available nearby, at a LOWER level** ← | **Which is the real siting constraint — an escape needs somewhere to escape TO** ← |
| **The escape channel must be able to carry the flow without scour** | **Lined or protected, with energy dissipation at the outfall** ← |
| **It must not flood the land it discharges over** | **Or the escape becomes a nuisance in its own right** ← |
| **Usually sited immediately UPSTREAM of a cross-drainage work or a long embanked reach** ← | **So that the vulnerable reach can be relieved before the water reaches it** ← |

> **The last row is the piece of practical judgement that distinguishes a well-planned canal: escapes are placed to protect the reaches where a breach would be most damaging or most difficult to repair.**

> **A breach in an ordinary cut section is a day's work with a bulldozer. A breach in a high embankment across a valley, or the loss of an aqueduct, is a season's supply lost and a major reconstruction.**

> **So the escape goes immediately above the expensive reach, and the canal is designed so that any surplus is shed before it can reach the structures that cannot afford to fail — which is the same principle as a fuse protecting the costly part of a circuit rather than the wire.**

examTip.trick: **An escape disposes of SURPLUS canal water into a natural drain.** The wrong options describe an inlet, a metering flume and a fall — all real canal components.
examTip.trap: **The commonest emergency is RAIN over the command** — every cultivator shuts his outlet at once while the canal is still running full, the level rises, and a breach floods the land the canal was built to serve.
examTip.mnemonic: **A side weir set at FSL operates automatically, at night, in the rain, with nobody there** — the same argument as an ungated spillway or the Sutro weir. And escapes are sited just UPSTREAM of the reach that would be costliest to breach: a fuse before the expensive part.

questions.stem: The standard amendment applied to reclaim an ALKALI (sodic) soil, in which exchangeable SODIUM has destroyed the soil structure, is:
options: Lime
GYPSUM, followed by leaching with good quality water and adequate drainage
Common salt
Ammonium sulphate alone, without drainage
questions.solution:
**GYPSUM (calcium sulphate), followed by LEACHING with good quality water, with DRAINAGE in place.**

**The chemistry, which explains why gypsum specifically:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **The problem: exchangeable SODIUM occupies the clay's exchange sites** ← | **Sodium ions DISPERSE the clay particles, destroying the crumb structure** ← |
| **The consequence** | **The soil becomes impermeable, hard when dry, sticky when wet, and almost impossible to cultivate** ← |
| **Gypsum supplies CALCIUM ions** ← | **Ca²⁺ REPLACES Na⁺ on the exchange complex — a divalent ion displacing a monovalent one** ← |
| **Calcium FLOCCULATES the clay** | **The crumb structure re-forms and the soil becomes permeable again** ← |
| **The displaced sodium is now in solution as sodium sulphate** | **And must be LEACHED away, or it simply returns to the exchange sites** ← |
| **The leachate must be REMOVED by drainage** | **Otherwise the salts stay in the profile and nothing has been achieved** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS ARE THE PART MOST OFTEN OMITTED, AND OMITTING THEM WASTES THE WHOLE OPERATION: gypsum alone does not reclaim anything, because it only moves the sodium from the clay into the soil water.**

> **Unless that water is flushed through and carried away, the sodium re-attaches as soon as the soil dries.**

> **So reclamation is a THREE-part operation — amendment, leaching, drainage — and drainage is the part that must be in place FIRST. Applying gypsum to land with no outfall achieves nothing but expense.**

> **Option (d) makes exactly that mistake explicit, and option (c), common salt, would add sodium and make matters worse.**

**SALINE against ALKALI soils, which must be distinguished because the remedies differ:**

| Property | SALINE (white alkali) | ALKALI / SODIC (black alkali) |
|---|---|---|
| **Problem** | **Excess soluble SALTS** ← | **Excess exchangeable SODIUM** ← |
| **pH** | **Below 8.5** | **Above 8.5, often 9 to 10** ← |
| **Electrical conductivity** | **HIGH, above 4 dS/m** ← | **Low** |
| **Exchangeable sodium percentage** | **Below 15** | **Above 15** ← |
| **Structure** | **PRESERVED — the salts actually flocculate the clay** ← | **DESTROYED — dispersed and impermeable** ← |
| **Appearance** | **WHITE crust of salt** ← | **DARK surface, from dispersed organic matter** ← |
| **Remedy** | **LEACHING alone is sufficient, with drainage** ← | **Gypsum FIRST, then leaching — this question** ← |

> **THE STRUCTURE ROW IS THE KEY TO THE WHOLE DISTINCTION AND EXPLAINS WHY THE REMEDIES DIFFER: a saline soil is still permeable, so water can be passed through it and the salts washed out directly.**

> **A sodic soil is impermeable — water will not pass through it at all — so leaching cannot even begin until the structure has been restored, and that is what the gypsum is for.**

> **There is also an unpleasant trap in the sequence: leaching a SALINE-SODIC soil with good water WITHOUT first applying gypsum removes the salts, which were holding the clay flocculated, and leaves the sodium behind — converting a manageable saline soil into an intractable sodic one.**

> **So the order of operations is not a matter of preference. Amendment before leaching, always, where sodium is present.**

**The wider prevention, since reclamation is far costlier than avoidance:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provide DRAINAGE from the start of an irrigation scheme** ← | **Salinity is the near-universal consequence of irrigation without drainage** ← |
| **Control canal SEEPAGE by lining** | **Rising water tables bring salts to the surface by capillary action** ← |
| **Apply water efficiently, avoiding over-irrigation** | ← |
| **Maintain a LEACHING FRACTION — a small planned excess to carry salts down** ← | **Deliberate, and quite different from careless over-watering** ← |
| **Conjunctive use of surface and groundwater** | **Pumping lowers the water table while supplying water — one action solving two problems** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW STATES THE LESSON THAT IRRIGATION ENGINEERING LEARNED AT ENORMOUS COST, and it should be stated plainly: irrigation projects built without drainage have gone saline and been abandoned across every major irrigated region in the world, from Mesopotamia onward.**

> **The drainage is invariably the item cut from the budget, because it produces no visible benefit in the first years while the canals produce an immediate and dramatic increase in yield.**

> **By the time the need is obvious the land is damaged and the cost of retrofitting is several times what it would have been to build it at the outset — which makes irrigation drainage a textbook case of a cost that is easy to defer and ruinous to have deferred.**

examTip.trick: **GYPSUM supplies Ca²⁺ which displaces Na⁺ from the clay and reflocculates it** — then the displaced sodium must be LEACHED out and the leachate DRAINED away. Three parts, not one.
examTip.trap: **SALINE = excess salts, pH < 8.5, structure PRESERVED, leaching alone suffices. SODIC = excess sodium, pH > 8.5, structure DESTROYED, needs gypsum first** — because an impermeable soil cannot be leached at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Leaching a saline-SODIC soil without gypsum first makes it WORSE** — it removes the salts holding the clay flocculated and leaves the sodium. Amendment before leaching, always. And drainage must exist before either.

questions.stem: Under Nepal's hydropower licensing practice, the MINIMUM ENVIRONMENTAL RELEASE that must be left flowing in the dewatered reach below a diversion weir is:
options: Ten per cent of the plant's design discharge
Twenty per cent of the mean annual flow of the river
No release is required, since the water is returned at the tailrace
Ten per cent of the MINIMUM MONTHLY AVERAGE discharge of the river, or the quantity required by downstream users, whichever is GREATER
questions.solution:
**Ten per cent of the MINIMUM MONTHLY AVERAGE discharge, or whatever downstream users and the aquatic environment require — whichever is GREATER.**

**Reading the requirement carefully, because each part of it matters:**

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ten per cent** | **A floor, not a target** ← |
| **Of the MINIMUM MONTHLY AVERAGE discharge** ← | **Of the DRIEST month — not of the mean annual flow, and not of the design discharge** ← |
| **Or the requirement of downstream users** | **Existing irrigation, water supply, mills, and the aquatic ecosystem** ← |
| **Whichever is GREATER** ← | **So the ten per cent can never be used to justify taking water that somebody downstream already depends on** ← |

> **Option (a) is the most tempting error and is wrong in a way worth understanding: the design discharge is a property of the PLANT, chosen by the developer, while the release must be a property of the RIVER.**

> **Tying the release to the design discharge would let a developer reduce the environmental flow simply by installing a smaller plant, which is precisely backwards.**

> **Option (b) uses the MEAN ANNUAL flow, which on a Himalayan river is dominated by the monsoon and may be five or ten times the dry-season flow — so ten per cent of it could exceed the entire flow available in February.**

**Why the DEWATERED REACH is the central environmental issue of run-of-river hydropower:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The reach between the WEIR and the TAILRACE loses almost all its flow** ← | **Often several kilometres long** ← |
| **In the dry season, the plant may divert essentially the whole river** | **Leaving the reach dry but for the mandated release** ← |
| **Consequences** | **Loss of aquatic habitat, fish passage blocked, water quality decline, loss of use for washing, watering stock and irrigation** ← |
| **Local people see the river taken away** | **And the electricity generally goes to the national grid, not to them** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHY THIS IS AS MUCH A SOCIAL QUESTION AS A TECHNICAL ONE, and it should be stated honestly: the costs of a run-of-river scheme fall on the households along the dewatered reach, and the benefits go to the grid.**

> **Unless something is deliberately done to return value locally — the local shareholding requirement, rural electrification obligations, royalty sharing with the district — the arrangement is straightforwardly extractive, and communities respond to it accordingly.**

> **Projects delayed or halted by local opposition are common enough in Nepal that benefit-sharing has become a practical engineering concern rather than a matter of goodwill: an unresolved local grievance stops construction just as effectively as a geological problem.**

**The wider licensing framework, for reference:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURVEY license, then GENERATION license** | **Issued by the Department of Electricity Development** ← |
| **License period** | **Typically 35 years for a generation license, after which the plant transfers to the government** ← |
| **Environmental study** | **IEE or EIA according to the installed capacity — an EIA above the stated threshold** ← |
| **Power purchase agreement with the utility** | **Which determines the project's actual bankability** ← |
| **Royalty** | **Payable on capacity and on energy, at rates that rise after the first 15 years** ← |
| **Local shareholding** | **A share of the equity offered to residents of the affected district** ← |

> **The 35-year transfer in the second row shapes the whole commercial design of these projects and is worth appreciating: the developer must recover the investment and its return within that period, after which the asset — a civil structure with a physical life of a century or more — passes to the state.**

> **So the tariff has to amortise the plant over 35 years rather than over its real life, which makes hydropower look more expensive than it is, and it puts a premium on getting the plant built quickly.**

> **It also creates a known incentive problem near the end of the term, when there is little reason to invest in maintenance whose benefit accrues after transfer — which is why handover conditions and maintenance obligations in the final years are written into the license rather than left to judgement.**

examTip.trick: **Ten per cent of the MINIMUM MONTHLY average flow, or the downstream requirement, whichever is GREATER.** Not of the design discharge, and not of the mean annual flow.
examTip.trap: **Tying it to the DESIGN discharge would let a developer cut the environmental flow by installing a smaller plant** — the release must be a property of the river, not of the plant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Costs fall on the DEWATERED REACH, benefits go to the grid** — which is why local shareholding and royalty sharing are engineering concerns: an unresolved grievance stops construction as surely as a geological one.

questions.stem: The principal advantage of developing a river basin as a CASCADE of hydropower plants, rather than as isolated schemes, is that:
options: The head of the river is used repeatedly along its length, and an upstream STORAGE plant can regulate the flow for every plant below it
Each plant needs a smaller powerhouse
The environmental release requirement is waived
Transmission lines become unnecessary
questions.solution:
**The available head is used REPEATEDLY down the length of the river, and an upstream STORAGE reservoir regulates the flow for every plant below it.**

**What a cascade is:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A series of plants along the same river, one after another** ← | **The tailrace of one discharging into, or near, the intake of the next** ← |
| **The whole fall of the river between two points is developed** | **Rather than one reach of it** ← |
| **Often one STORAGE plant at the head, with run-of-river plants below** ← | **The arrangement that gives the greatest benefit** ← |

**The advantages, which compound:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **The head is used AGAIN and AGAIN** ← | **Water passing through the top plant is still available, at a lower elevation, to every plant below** ← |
| **UPSTREAM REGULATION benefits every downstream plant** ← | **The reservoir stores monsoon water and releases it in the dry season, so the run-of-river plants below get a firmer flow all year** ← |
| **The downstream plants gain FIRM POWER without building a reservoir themselves** ← | **This is the largest single benefit, and it is free to them** ← |
| **Shared infrastructure** | **Access roads, transmission, camps, quarries, and one project office** ← |
| **Shared hydrological and geological investigation** | ← |
| **Sediment is trapped at the top** | **Which helps the plants below, though it hurts the reservoir itself** ← |
| **Staged construction matches demand growth** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE POINT THAT MAKES CASCADE PLANNING A POLICY QUESTION RATHER THAN AN ENGINEERING ONE, and it should be seen clearly:**

> **A run-of-river plant on its own generates almost nothing firm in the dry season, because the river is low. Put a storage reservoir upstream and its dry-season flow is transformed, so its firm power and its revenue rise sharply.**

> **But the reservoir was paid for by somebody else, and reservoirs are expensive, slow, and carry the resettlement and inundation costs that run-of-river plants avoid.**

> **So the benefits of storage accrue substantially to plants that did not pay for it — the classic case of an external benefit — and unless there is a mechanism to compensate the storage developer, nobody builds the storage and the whole basin remains run-of-river.**

> **That is a fair description of where Nepal's hydropower development has actually arrived, and it is why downstream benefit-sharing arrangements are a live and difficult subject rather than an academic one.**

**The complications of a cascade, stated fairly:**

| Complication | Note |
|---|---|
| **Operation must be COORDINATED** | **One operator's release is another's inflow; uncoordinated peaking upstream wrecks the plant below** ← |
| **A failure upstream propagates downstream** | **A dam break above puts every plant below at risk** ← |
| **Cumulative environmental impact** | **A dozen dewatered reaches on one river is not twelve small impacts but one large one** ← |
| **The whole river's fish migration is blocked** | **Fish passes on each barrier rarely add up to a working migration route** ← |
| **Sediment management interacts** | **Flushing at one plant loads the next** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ISSUE THAT ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT HANDLES WORST, because each project is assessed on its own: a scheme that dewaters four kilometres is judged acceptable, and so is the next, and the next.**

> **Assessed individually every one is minor; assessed together they may leave most of a river's length dewatered.**

> **CUMULATIVE IMPACT ASSESSMENT at basin level is the recognised answer, and it is administratively awkward because there is no single applicant to require it of — which is precisely why it must be done by the regulator, at the planning stage, rather than by the developers.**

> **Options (b), (c) and (d) are all false: powerhouse size is set by the discharge and head, the environmental release applies to every plant in the cascade, and the power still has to be transmitted.**

examTip.trick: **The same water is used again at each successive fall, and an upstream reservoir firms up the flow for every plant below.** The other options are simply false.
examTip.trap: **The storage plant's benefit accrues largely to the run-of-river plants BELOW it, which did not pay for it** — a textbook external benefit, and the reason storage does not get built without a sharing mechanism.
