examTip.mnemonic: **Each dewatered reach is minor; a dozen of them on one river is not.** Individual EIAs miss this entirely — hence CUMULATIVE impact assessment at basin level, which only the regulator can require.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant of 30 MW installed capacity operates at an annual PLANT CAPACITY FACTOR of 0.60. The energy it generates in a year is approximately:
options: 94.6 GWh
questions.solution:
**About 157.7 GWh.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Hours in a year** | **365 × 24 = 8,760 h** ← |
| **Energy if the plant ran at FULL capacity all year** | **30 MW × 8,760 h = 262,800 MWh = 262.8 GWh** ← (option d) |
| **Multiply by the plant capacity factor** | **262.8 × 0.60** |
| **Annual energy** | **= 157.68 ≈ 157.7 GWh** ← |

> **Option (d) is the answer with the capacity factor forgotten — the theoretical maximum, which no plant achieves.**

> **Option (b) is the arithmetic with a factor of 0.5, and option (a) with 0.36.**

**The definition, stated precisely because it is easily confused:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **PLANT (capacity) FACTOR** | **Energy actually generated ÷ energy that WOULD be generated at INSTALLED capacity for the whole period** ← |
| **LOAD FACTOR** | **Average load ÷ PEAK load over the period** ← |
| **UTILISATION factor** | **Maximum demand ÷ installed capacity** ← |
| **The relation** | **Plant factor = load factor × utilisation factor** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: the plant factor measures the plant against its OWN installed capacity, while the load factor measures the demand against its own peak.**

> **A plant may have a high load factor and a low plant factor at the same time — if it is generously oversized relative to the load it serves, it runs steadily but far below its rating.**

**Typical plant factors, so the 0.60 means something:**

| Plant | Typical factor |
|---|---|
| **Run-of-river in Nepal** | **0.45 to 0.60 — limited by the dry-season flow, not by demand** ← |
| **Storage plant** | **0.30 to 0.50 — deliberately low, because it is built to serve PEAKS** ← |
| **Base-load thermal** | **0.70 to 0.90** |
| **Solar photovoltaic** | **0.15 to 0.20** |
| **Wind** | **0.25 to 0.40** |

> **THE SECOND ROW SHOWS WHY A LOW PLANT FACTOR IS NOT A CRITICISM, and this is the insight the question is really testing:**

> **A peaking storage plant is designed to sit idle much of the day and to run hard for a few hours when the system peak arrives. Its capacity factor is low BY DESIGN, and it is valuable precisely because of that flexibility.**

> **Judging such a plant by its capacity factor is like judging a fire engine by its annual mileage.**

> **A run-of-river plant, by contrast, generates whatever the river offers whether the system wants it or not, so its low winter output is a genuine limitation rather than a design choice — and the two therefore command quite different prices for their energy.**

**And the ROR figure in the first row explains Nepal's winter deficit:**

| Month | Situation |
|---|---|
| **Monsoon, June to September** | **Rivers full; every ROR plant runs at full capacity; the country has a SURPLUS and exports** ← |
| **Winter, December to March** | **River flows fall to a fraction of the design discharge; the same plants generate perhaps a third of their rating** ← |
| **The consequence** | **A large seasonal deficit met by imports, in a country whose installed capacity on paper exceeds its peak demand** ← |

> **So installed capacity is a misleading headline for a run-of-river system, and the meaningful measures are the annual ENERGY and the DRY-SEASON firm capability.**

> **The engineering answers are storage, peaking run-of-river, and interconnection with a system whose seasonal pattern differs — which is the argument for regional power trade, and the reason it appears in every basin plan.**

examTip.trick: **E = 30 MW × 8,760 h × 0.60 = 157.7 GWh.** Option (d), 262.8, is the same sum with the capacity factor forgotten.
examTip.trap: **Plant factor = energy ÷ energy at INSTALLED capacity; load factor = average ÷ PEAK load.** Different denominators entirely, and plant factor = load factor × utilisation factor.
examTip.mnemonic: **A peaking storage plant's low capacity factor is a DESIGN CHOICE, not a fault** — judging it by capacity factor is like judging a fire engine by its mileage. For an ROR plant the same low figure is a real limitation.

questions.stem: The PLANT CAPACITY FACTOR of a power station becomes numerically EQUAL to its LOAD FACTOR when:
options: The plant runs continuously at full output
The MAXIMUM DEMAND on the plant equals its INSTALLED CAPACITY
The load is entirely a base load
The plant is shut down for part of the year
questions.solution:
**When the MAXIMUM DEMAND on the plant equals its INSTALLED CAPACITY** — that is, when the utilisation factor is unity.

**The algebra, which settles it immediately:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Plant capacity factor** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED CAPACITY** ← |
| **Load factor** | **Average load ÷ MAXIMUM DEMAND** ← |
| **They differ only in the DENOMINATOR** ← | **So they are equal precisely when maximum demand = installed capacity** ← |
| **Equivalently** | **Plant factor = load factor × utilisation factor, and utilisation factor = 1** ← |

> **Both factors have the SAME numerator — the average load, or equivalently the energy generated divided by the period.**

> **Everything therefore turns on what the average is compared against: the plant's rating, or the peak actually experienced.**

**Why they are normally DIFFERENT, which is the useful part:**

| Situation | Effect |
|---|---|
| **A RESERVE margin is provided — installed capacity deliberately exceeds the peak** ← | **Utilisation factor below 1, so the plant factor is LOWER than the load factor** ← |
| **Capacity installed ahead of demand growth** | **Same effect, and it is the normal condition of a growing system** ← |
| **Units held for maintenance outage cover** | Same |
| **The plant factor can therefore never EXCEED the load factor** ← | **Since maximum demand cannot exceed installed capacity in normal operation** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A USEFUL CHECK IN A NUMERICAL PROBLEM: if your computed plant factor comes out larger than your load factor, one of the two is wrong.**

> **Option (a) describes a plant factor and load factor both equal to 1 — a special case in which they happen to be equal, but not the general condition the question asks for, and one that no real plant sustains.**

**The family of factors, gathered for reference:**

| Factor | Definition | Range |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD factor** | Average load ÷ maximum demand | **Always ≤ 1** |
| **PLANT capacity factor** | Average load ÷ installed capacity | **Always ≤ 1** |
| **PLANT USE factor** | **Energy generated ÷ (installed capacity × hours the plant was actually IN SERVICE)** ← | ≤ 1 |
| **UTILISATION factor** | Maximum demand ÷ installed capacity | ≤ 1 |
| **DEMAND factor** | **Maximum demand ÷ total CONNECTED load** ← | **< 1, because not everything is switched on at once** ← |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | **Sum of individual maximum demands ÷ maximum demand of the system** ← | **Always ≥ 1** ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS CARRY THE MOST USEFUL IDEA IN THIS WHOLE SET OF DEFINITIONS, and it is worth spelling out because it is what makes electricity supply economic at all:**

> **Every consumer has a maximum demand, but they do not all reach it at the same moment. One household cooks at seven, another at eight; one factory starts at six, another at nine.**

> **So the system's peak is very much LESS than the sum of the individual peaks — that ratio is the DIVERSITY factor, and it is always greater than one.**

> **Because of it, a utility can serve a thousand consumers with far less than a thousand times one consumer's capacity, and the more diverse the load mix the less plant is needed per consumer.**

> **This is also why a utility actively wants a MIX of domestic, commercial, industrial and irrigation load rather than a uniform one: diversity between the classes is what keeps the required capacity down, and it is a real economic benefit created by nothing more than a difference in when people use power.**

> **It is the same reasoning, in a different currency, as the argument for interconnecting systems with different seasonal patterns — diversity in time is worth money.**

examTip.trick: **Same numerator (average load), different denominators — installed capacity against maximum demand.** They are equal exactly when the two denominators are equal, i.e. utilisation factor = 1.
examTip.trap: **The plant factor can never EXCEED the load factor** — a useful check on any numerical answer, since maximum demand cannot exceed installed capacity in normal operation.
examTip.mnemonic: **DIVERSITY factor is the only one of the family that is always ≥ 1** — consumers do not all peak at once, so the system peak is far below the sum of individual peaks. That single fact is what makes electricity supply affordable.

questions.stem: A GROUT CURTAIN formed by pressure grouting beneath the heel of a concrete gravity dam is provided principally to:
options: Increase the compressive strength of the dam concrete
Anchor the dam against overturning
REDUCE SEEPAGE through the foundation and lower the UPLIFT pressure beneath the dam
Provide access for inspection of the foundation
questions.solution:
**To reduce seepage through the foundation rock and, with it, the UPLIFT pressure acting on the base of the dam.**

**What it is and how it is formed:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A line — usually a row or several rows — of holes drilled into the foundation near the HEEL** ← | **The upstream edge of the base** |
| **Cement grout injected under pressure** | **Filling joints, fissures and voids in the rock** ← |
| **Depth** | **Commonly 0.3 to 0.7 times the head of water, sometimes more in poor rock** ← |
| **Drilled and grouted from the FOUNDATION GALLERY** ← | **Which is why that gallery exists at all, along with drainage** ← |
| **Forms a low-permeability barrier across the seepage path** | ← |

> **Option (d) names the gallery's OTHER function, and options (a) and (b) describe things a grout curtain does not do.**

**UPLIFT, which is what the curtain is really fighting:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water under the reservoir head penetrates the foundation and the dam–rock contact** ← | **And pushes UPWARD on the base** ← |
| **It acts over the WHOLE base area** | **Modern practice takes the full area, not a reduced fraction** ← |
| **It is a very large force** | **It directly reduces the effective weight, which is the only thing holding a gravity dam in place** ← |
| **It worsens EVERY stability check at once** | **Overturning, sliding and the no-tension condition at the heel** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY UPLIFT DOMINATES GRAVITY DAM DESIGN, and it deserves to be stated in the plainest terms:**

> **A gravity dam resists the water by its own WEIGHT. Uplift subtracts directly from that weight.**

> **So uplift attacks the single mechanism the whole structure depends on, and an underestimate of it is not a small error in one check but an overestimate of the dam's entire resistance.**

> **The history of gravity dam failures is largely a history of uplift being underestimated, and the shift from ignoring it, through allowing for it over part of the base, to taking it over the full base, tracks that history directly.**

**The TWO measures used together — and the second is the more important:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **GROUT CURTAIN near the heel** | **Reduces the QUANTITY of seepage and cuts the head at the upstream end** ← |
| **DRAINAGE HOLES just downstream of the curtain, discharging into the gallery** ← | **RELIEVE the pressure — they give the water a path to atmosphere, so the uplift diagram drops sharply at the drain line** ← |

> **THE PAIRING IS THE KEY IDEA AND THE ORDER IS DELIBERATE: the curtain restricts the flow, and the drains relieve whatever gets past it.**

> **The uplift diagram at the base is therefore not a straight line from full reservoir head at the heel to tailwater at the toe — it falls steeply at the DRAIN LINE, typically to about one third of the difference between the two, and then declines linearly to the toe.**

> **That reduction is worth a great deal of concrete, which is why drainage holes are provided in every gravity dam and why keeping them CLEAR is one of the most important items of dam maintenance.**

> **A dam whose drains have silted or calcified up over decades is carrying an uplift its designer never allowed for, and it will not show any outward sign of it — which is why drain flows are measured and recorded as routine surveillance data rather than merely checked when something looks wrong.**

**And a note on grouting types, since the terms recur:**

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **CURTAIN (deep) grouting** | **The seepage barrier described here — high pressure, deep holes near the heel** ← |
| **CONSOLIDATION (blanket) grouting** | **Shallow, over the whole foundation area, to stiffen and strengthen the near-surface rock** ← |
| **CONTACT grouting** | **Fills the gap between the concrete and the rock, or behind a tunnel lining** ← |

> **The three are done at different stages and for different reasons, and the common examination confusion is between the first two: curtain grouting is deep and narrow and fights WATER; consolidation grouting is shallow and wide and fights DEFORMATION.**

examTip.trick: **The curtain cuts the seepage; the DRAINAGE HOLES just downstream of it relieve the pressure.** The two work as a pair, and the drains do more for the uplift diagram than the curtain does.
examTip.trap: **Uplift subtracts directly from the WEIGHT, which is the only thing holding a gravity dam up** — so it worsens overturning, sliding and the no-tension check all at once. Modern practice takes it over the FULL base area.
examTip.mnemonic: **Curtain grouting is deep and narrow and fights WATER; consolidation grouting is shallow and wide and fights DEFORMATION.** And blocked drains load a dam with uplift its designer never allowed for, invisibly — hence recorded drain flows.

questions.stem: The portion of a reservoir's capacity that lies BELOW the lowest outlet level and is reserved for the accumulation of sediment over the project's life is called:
options: DEAD storage
Live (useful) storage
Surcharge storage
Valley storage
questions.solution:
**DEAD STORAGE.**

**The storage zones of a reservoir, from the bottom up:**

| Zone | Bounded by | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **DEAD storage** | **Below the lowest (minimum) draw-down level, or the sill of the lowest outlet** ← | **Sediment accumulation over the design life; it cannot be drawn on** ← |
| **LIVE (useful) storage** | **Between the minimum draw-down level and the FULL RESERVOIR LEVEL** ← | **The water actually available for power, irrigation or supply** ← |
| **SURCHARGE storage** | **Between FRL and the maximum water level reached during the design flood** ← | **Temporary, during flood routing only — it cannot be relied on for supply** ← |
| **VALLEY storage** | **The water the river valley held naturally before the dam** ← | Subtracted when assessing flood absorption |
| **BANK storage** | Water absorbed into the reservoir's banks and later released | Small, usually ignored |

> **The distinction between LIVE and SURCHARGE storage is the one most often blurred, and the reason matters: surcharge storage exists only while a flood is passing over the spillway, and the reservoir empties itself of it automatically.**

> **It cannot be counted as available water, because there is no way to keep it.**

**Why DEAD STORAGE is provided at all — the sedimentation problem:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Every river carries sediment; a reservoir slows the water and it deposits** ← | **The reservoir is, unavoidably, a very efficient settling basin** ← |
| **TRAP EFFICIENCY** | **The fraction retained — commonly 90 to 98 % for a large storage reservoir** ← |
| **The deposit accumulates from the bottom and from the head** | **A DELTA builds at the upstream end and advances toward the dam** ← |
| **Dead storage is sized so that the deposit does not encroach on the live storage within the design life** ← | **Usually 50 to 100 years** ← |

> **THE NEPALI SEDIMENT PROBLEM IS EXCEPTIONAL AND WORTH FACING SQUARELY: Himalayan rivers carry among the highest sediment loads in the world, from young, rapidly rising, heavily fractured mountains, with monsoon rainfall and widespread landsliding.**

> **Sediment yields of a few thousand tonnes per square kilometre per year are ordinary here, against a few hundred in most of the world.**

> **So a reservoir designed with dead storage sized on textbook figures may fill in a fraction of its intended life, and reservoir sedimentation is the principal technical threat to the economics of storage projects in Nepal — ahead of geology, ahead of seismicity.**

**What can actually be done about it:**

| Measure | Effectiveness |
|---|---|
| **CATCHMENT treatment — afforestation, check dams, terracing, gully control** ← | **The right answer in principle; slow, diffuse, hard to fund, and it cannot address natural landsliding** ← |
| **DRAWDOWN FLUSHING — emptying the reservoir at high flow to scour the deposit out** ← | **Effective in narrow reservoirs; wastes water and stored energy; devastates the downstream reach if done carelessly** ← |
| **SLUICING — passing the sediment-laden monsoon flow straight through** | **Requires low-level outlets of adequate size, decided at the DESIGN stage** ← |
| **DENSITY CURRENT venting** | **Releasing the sediment-laden underflow through a low outlet before it settles** ← |
| **Dredging** | **Almost always uneconomic at reservoir scale** ← |
| **Providing generous dead storage** | **Accepts the loss rather than preventing it** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CARRIES THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL LESSON HERE: sediment management is decided when the OUTLETS are designed, not when the reservoir starts to fill.**

> **A dam built without large low-level outlets can never be flushed or sluiced, however badly it needs to be — the capability has to be built in, at some cost, decades before it is used.**

> **Retrofitting low-level outlets into an existing dam is extraordinarily difficult and expensive, and has rarely been done.**

> **So the decision is irreversible in the strictest sense, and it is made early, by designers who will not be there to see the consequence — which is exactly the kind of decision that deserves more attention than it usually gets.**

examTip.trick: **Dead storage sits below the lowest outlet and is reserved for sediment; LIVE storage runs from minimum draw-down to FRL; SURCHARGE sits above FRL and exists only while a flood passes.**
examTip.trap: **Surcharge storage cannot be counted as available water** — the reservoir sheds it automatically over the spillway, so there is no way to keep it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Himalayan sediment yields are ten times the world norm, so textbook dead storage fills far too fast.** And flushing or sluicing is only possible if LARGE LOW-LEVEL OUTLETS were built in at the start — they cannot practically be retrofitted.

questions.stem: A TYROLEAN (bottom rack, or trench) INTAKE is particularly suited to:
options: Large lowland rivers carrying fine silt
Reservoirs with a deep, stable water level
Canal off-takes from a barrage
STEEP MOUNTAIN STREAMS carrying boulders and heavy bed load, where a conventional side intake would be blocked or damaged
questions.solution:
**Steep mountain streams carrying boulders and a heavy bed load** — the conditions in which a conventional side intake is repeatedly blocked, buried or damaged.

**How it works:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A trench is built ACROSS the stream bed, covered by an inclined RACK of parallel bars** ← | **The bars run in the direction of flow** ← |
| **Water falls THROUGH the rack into the trench below and is led away to the settling basin** ← | **Gravity does the diverting; there are no gates in the stream** |
| **Bed load, boulders and debris pass OVER the rack** ← | **And continue down the stream** ← |
| **Bar spacing** | **Typically 20 to 60 mm clear, set by the sediment to be excluded** ← |
| **Rack slope** | **About 1 in 5 to 1 in 10 down the direction of flow, to help debris slide off** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE WHOLE IDEA AND IT IS AN ELEGANT ONE: instead of trying to keep the boulders out of the intake, the intake is placed UNDERNEATH them and lets them roll past overhead.**

> **A side intake on a steep stream must resist the boulder load, and a boulder-laden flash flood will eventually damage or bury it.**

> **A Tyrolean intake is buried in the bed by design, and the flood passes across the top of it doing no harm.**

**Its advantages:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Excludes coarse bed load and boulders automatically** ← | **The dominant problem on a Himalayan stream** ← |
| **No gates in the river; nothing for a flood to destroy** | ← |
| **Requires no operator during a flood** | **It works the same whether anybody is present or not** ← |
| **Little or no afflux and no reservoir** | **So no submergence of land upstream** ← |
| **Simple, low cost, and buildable with local materials and labour** | **Which suits small and micro-hydro schemes** ← |
| **Small footprint** | ← |

**Its limitations, which are real:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The rack CLOGS with leaves, twigs and fine gravel** ← | **Requiring regular manual cleaning — the principal operating burden** ← |
| **It admits SAND and fine sediment freely** ← | **So a settling basin downstream remains essential** ← |
| **Limited capacity** | **Best for small to medium discharges; the rack becomes very long for a large one** ← |
| **Efficiency falls at low flows** | **Water may run past without falling through** |
| **The rack bars wear and are damaged by boulder impact** | **Robust bars and a replaceable design are needed** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MISCONCEPTION WORTH CORRECTING, because it is a common one: a Tyrolean intake excludes BOULDERS, not SAND.**

> **The bars are tens of millimetres apart, so everything finer passes straight through with the water.**

> **On a Himalayan stream the fine fraction is precisely the damaging one — quartz and feldspar sand at high velocity through a turbine erodes runner buckets and guide vanes rapidly — so the settling basin downstream is not optional, and the intake's success does not reduce its size at all.**

> **The two structures do quite different jobs: the intake keeps out what would BLOCK the system, and the settling basin keeps out what would WEAR it.**

**And the comparison with the alternatives, to place it:**

| Intake type | Best suited to |
|---|---|
| **TYROLEAN / bottom rack** | **Steep, boulder-laden mountain streams; small to medium discharge** ← |
| **SIDE intake with a diversion weir** | **The standard arrangement for medium rivers; drawing from the outer bank of a bend, where the secondary current sweeps bed load away from the mouth** ← |
| **FRONTAL intake** | **Simple, but draws bed load straight in — generally avoided** ← |
| **Reservoir (tower) intake** | Storage plants |

> **The SIDE INTAKE row records the other piece of natural physics that hydraulic engineers exploit here, and it is worth remembering alongside the Tyrolean idea: at a river bend the surface water moves outward and the bottom water inward, so the bed load migrates toward the INNER bank.**

> **Placing the intake on the OUTER bank of the bend therefore gets cleaner water for nothing, in the same spirit as the raised sill at a headworks.**

> **Both devices work by understanding where the sediment already is, and then simply not putting the intake there — which is almost always cheaper than removing sediment after admitting it.**

examTip.trick: **A trench across the bed under an inclined rack: water falls THROUGH, boulders roll OVER.** The intake is buried in the bed by design, so a boulder flood passes harmlessly across the top of it.
examTip.trap: **It excludes BOULDERS, not SAND** — bars are tens of mm apart, so the fine, turbine-eroding fraction passes straight through. The settling basin downstream is not reduced at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Intake keeps out what would BLOCK; settling basin keeps out what would WEAR.** And a side intake belongs on the OUTER bank of a bend, because the secondary current sweeps the bed load to the inner one.

questions.stem: A steel penstock of 1.2 m internal diameter carries water at a design internal pressure of 1.5 MPa. Taking the permissible hoop stress in the steel as 120 MPa and a joint efficiency of 100 per cent, the required shell THICKNESS (before adding any corrosion allowance) is:
options: 7.5 mm
15 mm
questions.solution:
**7.5 mm.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Thin cylinder HOOP stress** | **σ = p D / (2 t)** ← |
| **Rearranged for thickness** | **t = p D / (2 σ)** ← |
| **Substituting, with consistent units in N and mm** | **p = 1.5 MPa = 1.5 N/mm²; D = 1,200 mm; σ = 120 N/mm²** |
| **t = 1.5 × 1,200 / (2 × 120)** | **= 1,800 / 240** |
| **t** | **= 7.5 mm** ← |

> **Option (a) 3.75 mm is the LONGITUDINAL stress formula, t = pD/(4σ), which gives half the required thickness — and using it would be a genuine and dangerous error.**

> **Option (c) 15 mm omits the factor 2 altogether.**

**Why HOOP governs and not longitudinal, which is the concept the question is testing:**

| Stress | Expression | Relative size |
|---|---|---|
| **HOOP (circumferential)** | **σ_h = p D / (2 t)** ← | **The LARGER — it governs the design** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL (axial)** | **σ_l = p D / (4 t)** ← | **Exactly HALF the hoop stress** ← |

> **THE FACTOR OF TWO HAS A SIMPLE PHYSICAL EXPLANATION worth carrying, because it makes the two impossible to confuse:**

> **Split the pipe LENGTHWAYS and the pressure on the projected area D per unit length is resisted by TWO walls, each of thickness t — hence 2t in the denominator.**

> **Split it ACROSS and the pressure on the full circular area πD²/4 is resisted by the whole ring of material, area πDt — and πD²p/4 ÷ πDt gives pD/(4t).**

> **A cylinder under internal pressure therefore always bursts along a LONGITUDINAL seam, not a circumferential one, which is why longitudinal welds in a penstock are the ones subject to the strictest inspection and radiography.**

**What a real penstock design adds to this figure:**

| Addition | Note |
|---|---|
| **WATER HAMMER (surge) pressure rise** ← | **Added to the static head — commonly 20 to 50 % of it, and the governing case** ← |
| **JOINT (weld) EFFICIENCY** | **t = pD / (2 σ η); η typically 0.85 to 1.0 depending on the weld and its inspection** ← |
| **CORROSION allowance** | **1 to 2 mm** ← |
| **A MINIMUM thickness for handling and transport** | **Often t_min = (D + 500) / 400 mm, regardless of the stress** ← |
| **Buckling check for EXTERNAL pressure** | **On an emptied or vacuum condition — a thin pipe can collapse inward** ← |
| **Stiffener rings, expansion joints, anchor and support blocks** | ← |

> **THE MINIMUM THICKNESS RULE IN THE FOURTH ROW OFTEN GOVERNS A LARGE, LOW-HEAD PENSTOCK, and that is a genuinely useful thing to know:**

> **For a 3 m pipe the rule gives (3,000 + 500)/400 = 8.75 mm — which may be far more than the pressure requires at a low head.**

> **The pipe is then sized not by the water inside it but by the need to survive being rolled, transported, lifted and welded without deforming.**

> **THE BUCKLING CHECK IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN, and it has caused real failures: when a penstock is drained, or when a valve closes downstream while the pipe continues to drain, a partial vacuum can form inside.**

> **Atmospheric pressure outside then crushes the pipe — and a thin cylinder is enormously weaker against external pressure than against internal, because it fails by INSTABILITY rather than by yielding.**

> **The remedy is an AIR VALVE at the high point, admitting air as the pipe drains, and it is a small, cheap device whose failure destroys a very expensive one — which is why air valves are inspected as safety-critical items rather than as fittings.**

examTip.trick: **t = pD/(2σ) = 1.5 × 1200 / 240 = 7.5 mm.** Option (a) is the LONGITUDINAL formula pD/(4σ) — half the thickness needed, and a dangerous mistake.
examTip.trap: **Hoop stress is exactly TWICE the longitudinal** — split lengthways and two walls resist; split across and the whole ring resists. So a pressurised cylinder bursts along a LONGITUDINAL seam, which is why those welds get radiographed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Real design adds surge (20-50 %), joint efficiency, corrosion allowance, and a handling minimum (D+500)/400** — which governs large low-head pipes. And check EXTERNAL buckling: an air valve failing on a draining penstock crushes it flat.

questions.stem: The SPECIFIC SPEED of a turbine is defined as:
options: The speed at which the turbine develops maximum efficiency
The runaway speed of the runner with the load thrown off
The speed of a geometrically similar turbine developing UNIT POWER under UNIT HEAD, expressed as Nₛ = N √P / H^(5/4)
The synchronous speed of the coupled generator
questions.solution:
**The speed of a geometrically SIMILAR turbine that would develop UNIT POWER under UNIT HEAD — Nₛ = N √P / H^(5/4).**

**Reading the definition:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **N** | **The actual rotational speed, rpm** |
| **P** | **The power developed, in kW (or metric horsepower in older texts — the numerical values differ)** ← |
| **H** | **The net head, in metres** |
| **Nₛ** | **A pure characteristic of the RUNNER SHAPE, not of the individual machine** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE WHOLE VALUE OF THE CONCEPT: specific speed is a shape parameter.**

> **Every turbine of the same geometric family has the same specific speed, whatever its physical size or the head it works under — so a single number identifies the TYPE of runner required, before any detailed design begins.**

> **Option (b) names the RUNAWAY speed, which is a real and important quantity — the speed reached if the load is lost and the governor fails, typically 1.8 to 2.0 times normal — but a different one.**

**The ranges, which are the examinable part:**

| Turbine | Specific speed (kW, m units) | Head range | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PELTON, single jet** | **8 to 30** ← | **Above about 250 m, up to 1,800 m** ← | **IMPULSE** |
| **Pelton, multi-jet** | **30 to 70** | High | Impulse |
| **FRANCIS, slow to fast** | **60 to 400** ← | **About 25 to 350 m** ← | **REACTION, mixed flow** |
| **KAPLAN / propeller** | **300 to 1,000** ← | **Below about 60 m** ← | **REACTION, axial flow** |
| **Cross-flow (Banki)** | **20 to 90** | **Low to medium; favoured for micro-hydro because it is simple to fabricate locally** ← | Impulse |

> **THE PATTERN IS CONSISTENT AND WORTH FIXING IN MIND: specific speed rises as the head falls.**

> **A high head with a small discharge gives a LOW specific speed and demands an impulse machine; a low head with a large discharge gives a HIGH specific speed and demands an axial-flow one.**

> **The physical reason is visible in the formula: H^(5/4) is in the denominator, so a large head drives Nₛ down hard, while a large power (which at low head means a large discharge) drives it up.**

**How it is used in practice — the design sequence:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The HEAD and the DISCHARGE are given by the site** ← | **They are not the designer's to choose** |
| **The power follows: P = ρ g Q H η** | ← |
| **The SPEED N is nearly fixed by the generator** | **N = 120 f / p, so only a discrete set of speeds is available** ← |
| **Nₛ is then computed, and it tells you which runner type is required** ← | **The choice is essentially made for you** ← |
| **If Nₛ falls awkwardly between two types** | **Adjust N by changing the number of poles, or split the flow between more units or more jets** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE DESIGNER'S ONE REAL DEGREE OF FREEDOM, and it is exercised more often than one might expect.**

> **Splitting a plant into two units halves the power per unit, which reduces Nₛ by a factor of √2 and can move the design cleanly into a better runner family — as well as giving the operational advantages of two machines: part-load efficiency, and generation continuing during maintenance.**

> **Similarly, adding jets to a Pelton wheel raises the specific speed of the installation while keeping each jet's own specific speed low, which is how Pelton machines are used at heads lower than a single jet would suit.**

> **So the apparently rigid classification by head is in fact a set of overlapping ranges, and where they overlap the choice is settled by cost, by sediment (Pelton buckets are far easier to replace than a Francis runner), and by the part-load efficiency the operating pattern demands.**

examTip.trick: **Nₛ = N √P / H^(5/4)** — the speed of a similar machine at unit power and unit head. It is a SHAPE parameter, identical for every member of a geometric family whatever its size.
examTip.trap: **Option (b), runaway speed, is a real quantity (1.8-2.0 × normal with the load lost) but a different one.** And Nₛ values differ between kW and metric-horsepower conventions — check the units of any quoted range.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pelton 8-70, Francis 60-400, Kaplan 300-1,000 — specific speed RISES as head FALLS**, because H^(5/4) sits in the denominator. Splitting into two units divides Nₛ by √2, which is the designer's main lever.

questions.stem: CAVITATION in a reaction turbine is most effectively guarded against by:
options: Increasing the turbine's rotational speed
Using a larger diameter penstock
Widening the spiral casing
Limiting the SETTING of the runner above the tailwater level, so that the pressure at the runner outlet stays above the vapour pressure
questions.solution:
**By limiting the SETTING — the height of the runner above the tailwater level — so that the pressure at the runner outlet never falls to the vapour pressure of water.**

**What cavitation is:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Local pressure falls to the VAPOUR PRESSURE of water** ← | **On the low-pressure side of the runner blades, and at the draft tube inlet** ← |
| **Vapour BUBBLES form** | **The water boils, at ordinary temperature, because the pressure is low** ← |
| **The bubbles are carried into a region of higher pressure** | ← |
| **They COLLAPSE violently and almost instantaneously** ← | **Producing extremely high local pressures and micro-jets against the metal surface** ← |
| **The metal is progressively eroded** | **A characteristic spongy, pitted surface** ← |

> **The consequences are noise, vibration, a loss of efficiency, and severe PITTING of the runner and draft tube — which shortens the runner's life and eventually requires it to be repaired or replaced.**

**Why the SETTING is the controlling variable:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The pressure at the runner outlet is set by the atmospheric pressure, LESS the height of the runner above tailwater, LESS the velocity head recovered** ← | **So the higher the runner is set, the LOWER the pressure there** ← |
| **THOMA'S cavitation factor** | **σ = (H_a − H_v − H_s) / H, with H_a atmospheric head, H_v vapour pressure head, H_s the setting above tailwater, and H the net head** ← |
| **The design must satisfy σ ≥ σ_critical** ← | **σ_critical rises with the SPECIFIC SPEED — so high-specific-speed machines are far more cavitation-prone** ← |
| **If σ is too small, LOWER the runner** ← | **Sometimes below tailwater level entirely, which is why many Kaplan installations sit in a pit** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW LINKS THIS DIRECTLY TO TURBINE SELECTION AND IS THE PART WORTH REMEMBERING: a Kaplan turbine, with its high specific speed, needs a much larger σ than a slow Francis, and therefore must be set much lower relative to the tailwater.**

> **That is why low-head Kaplan plants are frequently built with the runner BELOW the tailwater surface — which costs a deep and expensive excavation, and is unavoidable.**

> **A designer who sets such a runner high to save on excavation buys the saving with a runner that erodes, and the repair will cost more than the concrete.**

**The ALTITUDE effect, which matters a great deal in Nepal:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **H_a is the ATMOSPHERIC pressure head — 10.3 m at sea level** ← | **But it FALLS with altitude** ← |
| **At 2,000 m it is about 8.1 m; at 3,000 m about 7.2 m** ← | **A loss of two to three metres from the numerator of Thoma's expression** ← |
| **So the permissible setting H_s is reduced by the same amount** ← | **A machine acceptable at sea level may cavitate at a Himalayan site** ← |

> **THIS IS A REAL AND OFTEN OVERLOOKED TRAP: turbine catalogues and standard settings are quoted for sea level, and a plant at 2,000 m has more than two metres less atmospheric head available.**

> **On a low-head machine, where H is small, losing two metres from the numerator can be a large proportional change in σ, and the setting must be lowered accordingly.**

> **The correction is trivial to apply and expensive to omit, and it belongs in the specification handed to the turbine supplier rather than being left for the supplier to assume.**

**And the other measures, since the setting is not the only one:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cavitation-resistant materials** | **Stainless steel runners and stainless overlay on the vulnerable areas** ← |
| **Avoid running far off the design point** | **Part-load operation of a Francis machine can cause a vortex rope in the draft tube, with severe pressure pulsation** ← |
| **Careful draft tube design** | **A smooth, gradual expansion recovering the velocity head without separation** ← |
| **AIR ADMISSION into the draft tube** | **A small admitted air flow cushions the collapse and greatly reduces the damage and noise** ← |
| **Smooth blade surfaces, well maintained** | **Roughness and previous pitting both promote further cavitation** ← |

> **The AIR ADMISSION entry is a nice piece of practical engineering: the bubbles cannot be prevented, so a small quantity of air is deliberately let in to make their collapse less violent.**

> **It costs a little efficiency and saves a great deal of metal, and it is a good illustration of a general habit in machinery design — when a damaging phenomenon cannot be eliminated economically, the next best thing is to make it gentler.**

examTip.trick: **σ = (H_a − H_v − H_s)/H must exceed σ_critical.** The SETTING H_s above tailwater is the variable in the designer's hands — lower the runner and the pressure at its outlet rises.
examTip.trap: **σ_critical RISES with specific speed**, so a Kaplan must sit much lower than a Francis — often below tailwater, in an expensive pit. Setting it high to save excavation buys an eroding runner.
examTip.mnemonic: **Atmospheric head falls with ALTITUDE: 10.3 m at sea level, ~8.1 m at 2,000 m** — so a catalogue setting quoted for sea level can cavitate at a Himalayan site. Put the altitude in the turbine specification.

questions.stem: In Nepal, the STRATEGIC ROAD NETWORK (SRN) differs from the LOCAL ROAD NETWORK (LRN) principally in that the SRN:
options: Consists only of roads with a bituminous surface
Comprises the national highways and feeder roads, and is planned, built and maintained by the DEPARTMENT OF ROADS
Comprises only roads inside metropolitan areas
Is restricted to roads built with foreign assistance
questions.solution:
**The SRN comprises the NATIONAL HIGHWAYS and FEEDER ROADS, and is the responsibility of the DEPARTMENT OF ROADS.**

**The two networks:**

| Network | Contents | Responsible agency |
|---|---|---|
| **STRATEGIC ROAD NETWORK (SRN)** | **National Highways (H) and Feeder Roads (F)** ← | **DEPARTMENT OF ROADS, under the federal ministry** ← |
| **LOCAL ROAD NETWORK (LRN)** | **District roads, urban (municipal) roads, village roads and agricultural roads** ← | **The local governments — rural and urban municipalities — with technical support from the department responsible for local infrastructure** ← |

> **The division is by FUNCTION and by the authority responsible, not by surface type, location or funding source — which disposes of options (a), (c) and (d).**

> **An SRN road may be earthen or gravelled in a remote district, and a municipal road may be well surfaced; the classification does not turn on the pavement.**

**The functional classes within them:**

| Class | Function |
|---|---|
| **NATIONAL HIGHWAY (H)** | **The main arterial routes running the length and breadth of the country, connecting the major regions** ← |
| **FEEDER ROAD (F)** | **Connects district headquarters, major economic centres and important places to the highways** ← |
| **DISTRICT ROAD** | **Roads of importance within a district, linking areas of production and markets to the SRN** ← |
| **URBAN (municipal) ROAD** | **Roads within a municipality serving local traffic** ← |
| **VILLAGE / agricultural ROAD** | **The lowest order — access to settlements and farmland** ← |

> **THE FUNCTIONAL HIERARCHY BEHIND THIS IS THE SAME ONE USED EVERYWHERE, and it is worth stating because it explains why the classification exists at all:**

> **A road serves two conflicting purposes — MOBILITY (moving traffic quickly over distance) and ACCESS (reaching individual properties).**

> **A highway maximises mobility and deliberately restricts access; a village road is nearly all access and offers little mobility.**

> **The classes in between grade from one to the other, and the reason for insisting on the hierarchy is that a road attempting BOTH does neither well — which is exactly what happens when frontage development is allowed to spread along a highway, and it is the single commonest way a good highway is spoiled.**

**Why the SRN/LRN split matters in practice, particularly since federalisation:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Design STANDARDS differ** | **The Nepal Road Standard governs the SRN; separate rural road standards apply to the LRN** ← |
| **Budget lines and funding sources differ** | **Federal budget and the Roads Board for the SRN; local budgets and grants for the LRN** ← |
| **Technical capacity differs sharply** | **The Department of Roads has engineers and equipment; a small rural municipality may have very few** ← |
| **MAINTENANCE responsibility follows the classification** | **And an unclear boundary means a road maintained by nobody** ← |
| **A road can be RECLASSIFIED** | **Usually upward, when its traffic and function grow** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES A REAL AND COMMON FAILURE, and it deserves to be named plainly: where responsibility for a road is disputed or simply unclear, neither authority maintains it, and it deteriorates while both wait for the other.**

> **This is not a technical problem and cannot be solved by engineering. It is solved by a definitive, published inventory of which authority owns which road — which is why road asset inventories are as much a part of road management as pavement design.**

> **The related and larger issue is that a great deal of the LRN in Nepal has been built by local initiative with bulldozers and no engineering design at all — no drainage, no slope stabilisation, excessive gradients — with the result that the roads trigger landslides, wash out in the first monsoon, and consume in repeated repairs far more than a designed road would have cost.**

> **The engineering lesson is uncomfortable and worth stating: on a hillside, an undesigned road is not a cheap road. It is an expensive road whose cost has been deferred and multiplied.**

examTip.trick: **SRN = National Highways + Feeder Roads, under the Department of Roads. LRN = district, urban, village and agricultural roads, under local government.** The split is by FUNCTION and AUTHORITY, never by surface type.
examTip.trap: **A road serves MOBILITY or ACCESS, and the hierarchy grades between them** — a road attempting both does neither well, which is what frontage development does to a highway.
examTip.mnemonic: **Where ownership of a road is unclear, nobody maintains it** — solved by an asset inventory, not by engineering. And on a hillside an UNDESIGNED road is not cheap: its cost is merely deferred and multiplied.

questions.stem: Among the four stages of engineering survey for a new highway, the stage at which the CENTRE LINE is finally pegged out on the ground and detailed levels and cross-sections are taken is the:
options: Map (desk) study
Reconnaissance survey
Preliminary survey
FINAL LOCATION and DETAILED SURVEY
questions.solution:
**The FINAL LOCATION and DETAILED SURVEY.**

**The four stages, in order:**

| Stage | What is done | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **1. MAP (desk) STUDY** | **Topographic maps, geological maps, aerial photographs and satellite imagery are examined in the office** ← | **A few broadly feasible corridors identified, without going to site** ← |
| **2. RECONNAISSANCE survey** | **A rapid inspection ON THE GROUND of each corridor, with hand instruments — abney level, compass, barometer** ← | **The impractical corridors eliminated; two or three retained** ← |
| **3. PRELIMINARY survey** | **A detailed instrument survey of the retained alignments — traverse, levels, soil and material surveys, drainage and traffic studies** ← | **Comparison of alternatives and SELECTION of the best alignment** ← |
| **4. FINAL LOCATION and DETAILED survey** | **The chosen centre line is TRANSFERRED TO THE GROUND and pegged; detailed levels, cross-sections, drainage and structure details are taken** ← | **The data for the working drawings, quantities and estimate** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION HAS A CONSISTENT LOGIC WORTH SEEING: each stage covers a SMALLER area in GREATER detail than the one before.**

> **The map study looks at a whole region cheaply; the final survey looks at a strip a few tens of metres wide, very precisely.**

> **Doing it the other way round — surveying in detail before the corridor has been settled — wastes most of the survey effort on alignments that are then abandoned, which is the commonest and most expensive procedural error in road location.**

**What is decided at each stage, since the question is really about that:**

| Stage | Decision |
|---|---|
| **Map study** | **Which corridors are worth looking at** |
| **Reconnaissance** | **Which corridors are not feasible — an ELIMINATION stage** ← |
| **Preliminary** | **WHICH alignment — the key decision of the whole process** ← |
| **Final location** | **Not which, but exactly WHERE on the ground and to what levels** ← |

> **THE PRELIMINARY SURVEY IS THEREFORE THE DECISIVE STAGE, and it is the one most often skimped when a project is in a hurry.**

> **Once the alignment is chosen, everything afterwards is elaboration; a poor alignment cannot be recovered by good detailed design, and it imposes its cost on every vehicle that uses the road for the next fifty years.**

> **This is the same influence curve that governs project management generally, applied to road location: the cheapest hour of the whole project to spend well is an hour spent choosing the alignment.**

**What the survey must collect for a hill road in particular:**

| Item | Why |
|---|---|
| **GEOLOGY and slope stability** | **The dominant control on a Himalayan alignment — an alignment through unstable ground will never be stable, whatever is spent on it** ← |
| **Existing and potential LANDSLIDES** | **To be avoided, not stabilised, wherever there is a choice** ← |
| **Cross-drainage points and catchment areas** | **Culvert and bridge locations and sizes** ← |
| **Availability of construction materials** | **Haulage dominates hill road cost** ← |
| **Sources of water, and spoil disposal sites** | **Spoil tipped down a slope causes more damage than the cutting** ← |
| **Settlements, cultivated land and land acquisition** | ← |
| **Traffic and economic data** | ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS CARRY THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL ADVICE FOR ROAD LOCATION IN NEPAL, and it can be put in one sentence: a road can be routed AROUND a landslide for a fraction of what it costs to route through one and then try to hold the slope.**

> **Geological input at the RECONNAISSANCE and PRELIMINARY stages is therefore worth many times its cost, and its absence is why so many hill roads spend their lives being repaired at the same three or four chainages.**

> **The SPOIL DISPOSAL entry deserves a closing word because it is so routinely neglected: material cast down the hillside from a cutting buries vegetation, blocks drainage, loads the slope below and starts the next slide — and it is usually a specification failure rather than a design one, remedied simply by identifying tipping sites in advance and paying for the haul.**

examTip.trick: **Map study → reconnaissance → preliminary → final location.** Each stage covers a SMALLER area in GREATER detail. The centre line is pegged only at the last stage.
examTip.trap: **The PRELIMINARY survey is where the alignment is actually CHOSEN** — the final location survey only fixes it on the ground. A poor alignment cannot be recovered by good detailed design.
examTip.mnemonic: **Route AROUND a landslide, not through it** — geological input at reconnaissance costs a fraction of holding an unstable slope for fifty years. And name the spoil tipping sites in the contract, or the cutting starts the next slide.

questions.stem: At a HAIRPIN BEND on a hill road, IRC practice requires that the bend be designed with:
options: A minimum design speed, a minimum radius, a compensated (flatter) GRADIENT through the bend, and full widening of the carriageway
The steepest gradient permitted anywhere on the road, to gain height quickly
No superelevation, since speeds are low
The normal camber maintained right through the bend
questions.solution:
**A minimum design speed, a minimum radius, a COMPENSATED (flatter) gradient through the bend, and full widening of the carriageway.**

**The IRC requirements for a hairpin bend:**

| Requirement | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum design speed** | **20 km/h** ← |
| **Minimum radius at the centre line** | **14 m for hill roads (the absolute minimum; 15 to 20 m preferred)** ← |
| **Minimum length of transition curve** | **15 m** ← |
| **GRADIENT through the bend** | **Not steeper than 1 in 40 (2.5 %), and not flatter than 1 in 200 for drainage** ← |
| **Superelevation** | **1 in 10 (10 %)** ← |
| **Widened carriageway** | **11.5 m for a two-lane road; 9 m for a single lane at the bend** ← |
| **Minimum distance BETWEEN successive hairpin bends** | **60 m** ← |

> **THE GRADIENT LIMIT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE MOST COUNTER-INTUITIVE ITEM, which is exactly what option (b) is designed to catch:**

> **A hairpin bend is where a hill road turns back on itself to gain height, so the instinct is to climb hard through it. IRC requires the opposite — the gradient through the bend must be FLATTENED to 2.5 % or less.**

> **The reason is that a vehicle on a sharp bend is already using much of the available tyre friction to turn. Add a steep gradient and a heavily loaded truck has too little traction left to climb, so it stalls, or slips, or must reverse — and reversing on a hairpin bend above a drop is how vehicles are lost.**

> **The height must therefore be gained on the STRAIGHTS between the bends, not on the bends themselves, and that is why the minimum spacing of 60 m between successive bends exists as well.**

**The other items, each with its reason:**

| Item | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Full WIDENING** | **A long vehicle needs mechanical widening on a sharp curve — its rear wheels track well inside the front, and on a 14 m radius the offtracking is severe** ← |
| **Superelevation of 1 in 10** | **The maximum permitted anywhere, since the radius is at its minimum — option (c) is wrong** ← |
| **The camber must be removed and reversed into the superelevation** | **Through the transition — so option (d) is wrong** ← |
| **A retaining structure is almost always needed on the outside** | **The bend projects from the hillside** ← |
| **Adequate SIGHT DISTANCE across the inside of the bend** | **Set-back distance; and the parapet or cut face must not obstruct it** ← |
| **Drainage carefully arranged** | **A hairpin collects water from above and concentrates it** ← |

> **THE DRAINAGE POINT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST FREQUENT CAUSE OF HAIRPIN BEND FAILURE IN THE HILLS, and it is worth being explicit about:**

> **A hairpin bend is a flat platform cut into a slope at a re-entrant, which is precisely where the hillside's own drainage naturally converges.**

> **So the bend receives the runoff from a large area above it, and unless that water is intercepted above the bend and carried across in a properly built cross-drain, it saturates the fill on the outside of the bend and takes it away.**

> **The outer half of hairpin bends is therefore the most commonly failed element of a Nepali hill road, and the cause is almost always drainage rather than the retaining wall's structural design.**

> **The practical rule that follows is one experienced hill road engineers repeat: build the drainage first, and the road will survive; build the road first and the drainage as an afterthought, and you will build the road twice.**

examTip.trick: **Design speed 20 km/h, minimum radius 14 m, gradient FLATTENED to 1 in 40, superelevation 1 in 10, full widening, and 60 m minimum between successive bends.**
examTip.trap: **The gradient through a hairpin must be FLATTER, not steeper** — a vehicle turning on a 14 m radius is already using most of its available friction, so height is gained on the straights between bends.
examTip.mnemonic: **A hairpin sits in a re-entrant, where the hillside's drainage converges** — the outer fill is the most commonly failed element of a hill road, and the cause is nearly always water, not the wall. Build the drainage first.

questions.stem: For a design speed of 80 km/h, with a superelevation of 0.07 and a coefficient of lateral friction of 0.15, the minimum RADIUS of the horizontal curve is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 229 m.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Equilibrium on a superelevated curve** | **e + f = V² / (127 R), with V in km/h and R in metres** ← |
| **Rearranged** | **R = V² / [127 (e + f)]** ← |
| **Substituting** | **R = 80² / [127 × (0.07 + 0.15)]** |
| **Numerator and denominator** | **= 6,400 / (127 × 0.22) = 6,400 / 27.94** |
| **R** | **= 229.1 ≈ 229 m** ← |

> **Option (a) 129 m comes from using the constant 225 in place of 127 — 225 belongs to the DESIGN superelevation formula e = V²/(225 R), which is deliberately three quarters of the equilibrium value, and it must not be used here.**

> **Option (d) 336 m ignores the superelevation and uses friction alone.**

**Where the constant 127 comes from, since knowing it prevents the commonest slip:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **In consistent units, e + f = v² / (g R) with v in m/s** | ← |
| **Converting V from km/h: v = V / 3.6** | **so v² = V² / 12.96** |
| **Dividing by g = 9.81** | **12.96 × 9.81 = 127.1** ← |
| **Hence e + f = V² / (127 R)** | **The 127 is simply 3.6² × 9.81** ← |

> **THE THREE CONSTANTS MUST BE KEPT APART, and confusing them is the single most common error in this topic:**

| Constant | Formula | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **127** | **e + f = V²/(127 R)** | **The true equilibrium relation — used to find the MINIMUM RADIUS, as here** ← |
| **225** | **e = V²/(225 R)** | **IRC's DESIGN superelevation — three quarters of the equilibrium value, assuming 75 % of the design speed** ← |
| **9.5** | **A different empirical relation used for some checks** | — |

> **The reason for the 225 is worth understanding rather than memorising: superelevation designed for the full design speed would be uncomfortable and, in slow-moving or stationary traffic, unsafe — a heavily laden bullock cart or a stationary truck on a steeply banked curve can slide or overturn inward.**

> **So IRC designs the superelevation for 75 per cent of the design speed and lets side friction take the remainder at full speed, then checks that the friction required does not exceed the permissible value.**

**The design procedure in full, since the numerical is only one step of it:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Compute e for 75 % of the design speed, ignoring friction** | **e = V²/(225 R)** ← |
| **2. If e ≤ e_max, adopt it** | **e_max = 0.07 in plain and rolling terrain; 0.10 in hills without snow** ← |
| **3. If e exceeds e_max, set e = e_max and CHECK the friction required at full speed** | **f = V²/(127 R) − e_max** ← |
| **4. If the required f ≤ 0.15, accept** | ← |
| **5. If it still exceeds 0.15, either RESTRICT the speed or INCREASE the radius** ← | **Increasing the radius is much the better answer where it is possible** ← |

> **STEP 5 IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS IN PRACTICE AND THE ONE MOST OFTEN FUDGED: the honest options are a bigger radius or a lower posted speed, and a speed restriction on a road that otherwise invites fast driving is not a design — it is a hope.**

> **Drivers select their speed from what the road LOOKS like it permits, not from the sign. A curve that feels like an 80 km/h road but is signed at 50 will be taken at 70 by a large fraction of drivers, and the design must survive that.**

> **This is the principle of SELF-EXPLAINING design, and it is why consistency of geometric standard along a route matters as much as the standard itself: the dangerous curve is not the sharpest one, but the sharp one that follows several miles of easy ones.**

examTip.trick: **R = V²/[127(e+f)] = 6400/(127 × 0.22) = 229 m.** The 127 is just 3.6² × 9.81 — the unit conversion built into the formula.
examTip.trap: **127 for equilibrium and minimum radius; 225 for IRC DESIGN superelevation** (which assumes 75 % of design speed, so slow traffic is not endangered by over-banking). Option (a) uses 225 by mistake.
examTip.mnemonic: **Drivers read the ROAD, not the sign** — a curve that looks like 80 km/h will be driven at 70 whatever it is posted at. The dangerous curve is the sharp one that follows several easy ones.

questions.stem: In the VISCOSITY GRADING system for paving bitumen, a grade designated VG-30 indicates that the binder has:
options: A penetration value of 30 at 25 °C
A minimum absolute VISCOSITY of 2,400 poise at 60 °C, the grade number denoting the viscosity class
A softening point of exactly 30 °C
A ductility of 30 cm at 27 °C
questions.solution:
**A viscosity grade — VG-30 denotes a minimum absolute viscosity of about 2,400 poise at 60 °C, the grade number identifying the class.**

**Why viscosity grading replaced penetration grading:**

| Aspect | PENETRATION grading (e.g. 60/70, 80/100) | VISCOSITY grading (VG-10, VG-20, VG-30, VG-40) |
|---|---|---|
| **Measured at** | **25 °C — near ambient temperature** ← | **60 °C, close to the maximum PAVEMENT temperature in service** ← |
| **Property measured** | **The depth a needle penetrates in 5 s under 100 g — an EMPIRICAL consistency test** ← | **Absolute VISCOSITY — a fundamental engineering property** ← |
| **Relevance to performance** | **Indirect** | **Direct: rutting resistance depends on stiffness at high temperature** ← |
| **Reproducibility between laboratories** | **Poorer** | **Better** ← |
| **Also specifies** | — | **KINEMATIC viscosity at 135 °C, which governs MIXING and COMPACTION temperatures** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE HEART OF THE CHANGE AND IT IS A SOUND PIECE OF ENGINEERING REASONING: a pavement ruts in the summer, when its surface may reach 60 °C, and a needle pushed into bitumen at 25 °C tells you rather little about how it will behave then.**

> **Two binders can have identical penetration at 25 °C and quite different stiffness at 60 °C, because their temperature susceptibility differs — so penetration grading could pass a binder that would rut badly.**

> **Grading at the temperature where the failure actually occurs is obviously better, and that is the whole argument.**

**The grades and their use:**

| Grade | Viscosity at 60 °C (min) | Roughly equivalent penetration | Where used |
|---|---|---|---|
| **VG-10** | **800 poise** | 80/100 | **Spraying work — surface dressing, paving in COLD climates and high altitude** ← |
| **VG-20** | **1,600 poise** | — | Cold climate paving |
| **VG-30** | **2,400 poise** | **60/70** ← | **The general-purpose paving grade for most of India and Nepal's plains and hills** ← |
| **VG-40** | **3,200 poise** | **30/40** ← | **HEAVILY trafficked roads and hot climates — junctions, toll plazas, climbing lanes** ← |

> **THE VG-40 ROW POINTS AT THE PRACTICAL SELECTION RULE, and it is a genuinely useful one: use a STIFFER binder where the loading is slow and heavy or the temperature high.**

> **Rutting is a viscous, time-dependent deformation, so it is worst where vehicles are slow or stationary — approaches to junctions, bus stops, toll plazas, and long climbing gradients where trucks crawl.**

> **Those are precisely the places to specify VG-40 rather than VG-30, and it is a change of specification over a few hundred metres that costs very little and prevents the deep ruts that otherwise appear at every junction approach within two or three summers.**

**The other bitumen tests, so the family is complete:**

| Test | Measures | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** | **Consistency at 25 °C, in tenths of a mm** ← | Still widely quoted |
| **SOFTENING POINT (ring and ball)** | **The temperature at which it flows under a standard ball** ← | **Higher is stiffer; typically 40 to 55 °C** |
| **DUCTILITY** | **The length in cm to which a briquette stretches before breaking at 27 °C** ← | **A measure of the binder's ability to strain without cracking; minimum 40 to 75 cm** ← |
| **FLASH and FIRE POINT** | **Safety in handling and heating** | ← |
| **Loss on heating / thin film oven test** | **AGEING during mixing** ← | **Predicts how much the binder will harden in the plant** ← |
| **Solubility in trichloroethylene** | **Purity — the proportion of true bitumen** | ← |

> **THE THIN FILM OVEN TEST IN THE FIFTH ROW MEASURES SOMETHING GENUINELY IMPORTANT that the others miss: bitumen hardens irreversibly when heated in the mixing plant, and hardens further, slowly, in service.**

> **An over-heated plant can age the binder more in two hours than the road will in five years, producing a mix that is brittle from the day it is laid and cracks early.**

> **So the mixing TEMPERATURE is not a matter of convenience — overheating destroys the binder that the whole specification was written to secure, and it is one of the few site errors that cannot be corrected afterwards.**

examTip.trick: **VG grades are absolute VISCOSITY at 60 °C: VG-10 = 800, VG-20 = 1600, VG-30 = 2400, VG-40 = 3200 poise.** VG-30 ≈ penetration 60/70.
examTip.trap: **Penetration is measured at 25 °C; viscosity grading at 60 °C — the temperature at which pavements actually rut.** Two binders with equal penetration can differ greatly at 60 °C.
examTip.mnemonic: **Specify VG-40 where traffic is SLOW and HEAVY** — junction approaches, bus stops, toll plazas, climbing lanes. And never overheat the binder in the plant: two hours of overheating ages it more than five years of service.

questions.stem: A bitumen EMULSION differs from a CUTBACK bitumen in that the emulsion:
options: Contains no bitumen at all
Is bitumen dissolved in a volatile petroleum solvent
Can only be used when heated above 150 °C
Is bitumen dispersed as fine droplets in WATER with an emulsifier, so it can be applied COLD and sets by the water breaking away
questions.solution:
**An emulsion is bitumen DISPERSED as fine droplets in WATER with an emulsifying agent** — so it can be applied cold, and it sets when the emulsion "breaks" and the water separates and evaporates.

**The three fluid forms of bitumen:**

| Form | How it is made fluid | How it sets | Applied |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HOT bitumen** | **By HEATING to 150-165 °C** ← | **By cooling** | Hot |
| **CUTBACK** | **DISSOLVED in a volatile petroleum SOLVENT — kerosene, diesel or naphtha** ← (option b) | **By EVAPORATION of the solvent — "curing"** ← | Warm or cold |
| **EMULSION** | **DISPERSED as droplets in WATER, held apart by an emulsifier** ← | **By BREAKING — the droplets coalesce and the water runs off and evaporates** ← | **COLD** ← |

> **The essential distinction is that in a cutback the bitumen is DISSOLVED in a hydrocarbon, while in an emulsion it is merely SUSPENDED in water and never dissolved at all.**

**Why emulsions have largely displaced cutbacks:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **NO flammable solvent** | **Cutbacks are a fire hazard in storage, transport and use** ← |
| **No hydrocarbon lost to the atmosphere** | **A cutback's solvent evaporates into the air — a pollutant, and a waste of a fuel** ← |
| **Can be used on DAMP aggregate and in damp weather** ← | **A very large practical advantage; hot bitumen and cutbacks need a dry surface** ← |
| **No heating on site** | **Saves fuel, equipment and risk** ← |
| **Safer to handle — no burns** | ← |
| **Suitable for small-scale and manual work** | **Pothole patching, hand-laid maintenance, remote sites** ← |

> **THE DAMP AGGREGATE ADVANTAGE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE DECISIVE ONE FOR NEPAL, and it deserves to be spelled out:**

> **Hot bitumen will not adhere to a wet stone — the water film keeps them apart, and the patch fails within weeks.**

> **A cationic emulsion is water-based to begin with, and its positively charged droplets are actively attracted to the negatively charged surface of most aggregates, displacing the water film.**

> **So emulsion patching can be done in the monsoon, when hot-mix work is impossible and when potholes are forming fastest.**

> **That is not a marginal convenience: it means maintenance can be carried out in the season when it is needed, rather than deferred to the dry months by which time the pothole has become a failed pavement.**

**The classes of emulsion, since the grade must match the job:**

| Class | Sets | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **RS — Rapid Setting** | **Breaks quickly on contact with aggregate** ← | **Surface dressing, tack coat — where the binder must set before traffic returns** ← |
| **MS — Medium Setting** | Intermediate | **Premix with coarse aggregate; patching** ← |
| **SS — Slow Setting** | **Breaks slowly, so it stays workable** ← | **Prime coat, soil stabilisation, fine-aggregate mixes — where it must penetrate or be mixed at length** ← |

> **CATIONIC emulsions (positively charged) are the standard choice, because most road aggregates — granite, quartzite, gneiss — carry a negative surface charge and therefore attract the droplets, giving good adhesion.**

> **ANIONIC emulsions suit limestone and other basic aggregates, which are positively charged.**

> **The matching of charge to aggregate is a real specification point rather than a chemical curiosity: an emulsion of the wrong charge on the wrong stone strips under traffic and water, and the failure looks exactly like a poorly compacted mix.**

> **This is also, incidentally, the same adhesion problem addressed by ANTI-STRIPPING agents in hot mix — the whole difficulty of bituminous work being that water and bitumen compete for the surface of the stone, and water usually wins unless something is done about it.**

examTip.trick: **Emulsion = bitumen droplets SUSPENDED in water, sets by BREAKING. Cutback = bitumen DISSOLVED in a petroleum solvent, sets by EVAPORATION.** Option (b) describes the cutback.
examTip.trap: **Emulsions work on DAMP aggregate** — cationic droplets are attracted to the negatively charged stone and displace the water film. So monsoon patching is possible, which hot mix cannot do.
examTip.mnemonic: **RS for surface dressing and tack coat, MS for premix and patching, SS for prime coat and stabilisation.** Match the CHARGE too: cationic for granite and quartzite, anionic for limestone.

questions.stem: In road safety work, a BLACK SPOT is best defined as:
options: A location at which the number or severity of accidents is significantly HIGHER than at comparable locations, identified from accident records over a period of years
Any location at which a fatal accident has occurred
A section of road with a dark or worn surface
A location where the road is not lit at night
questions.solution:
**A location at which accidents are significantly MORE frequent or MORE severe than at comparable locations, identified from records over a period of years.**

**What makes the definition work:**

| Element | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Identified from RECORDS, not from impression** ← | **Perceptions of where accidents happen are notoriously unreliable** ← |
| **Over SEVERAL YEARS, typically three to five** ← | **Accidents are rare, random events; one year's data is dominated by chance** ← |
| **Compared with SIMILAR locations** | **A busy junction naturally has more accidents than a quiet one — the comparison must be like for like** ← |
| **Significantly higher — a statistical test, not a ranking** ← | **Otherwise the top of any list is a black spot by definition** ← |

> **Option (b) is the trap, and understanding why is the point of the question.**

> **A single fatal accident does not make a black spot. Fatal accidents happen at ordinary locations for reasons that have nothing to do with the road — a drunk driver, a mechanical failure, a moment's inattention.**

> **Treating every fatality as evidence of a road defect spreads a limited safety budget across sites where engineering can achieve nothing, and away from the sites where the road really is contributing.**

**REGRESSION TO THE MEAN, which is the statistical trap that ruins naive black-spot work:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **A site records an unusually high number of accidents in one year** | **Partly because the site is genuinely bad, partly by chance** ← |
| **It is identified as a black spot and treated** | ← |
| **The following year the count falls** | **Partly because of the treatment, and partly because the chance element was not going to repeat** ← |
| **The whole fall is credited to the treatment** ← | **Overstating its benefit, sometimes by a factor of two** ← |

> **THIS IS A REAL AND WELL-DOCUMENTED EFFECT, AND IT IS WHY MULTI-YEAR DATA AND PROPER BEFORE-AND-AFTER STUDIES WITH CONTROL SITES ARE INSISTED ON.**

> **A site selected because it had a bad year will improve next year whether anything is done to it or not, and an engineer who does not allow for that will conclude that whatever was done worked — and will keep doing it.**

> **The practical safeguard is exactly the one in the definition: several years of data, and comparison against similar sites rather than against the location's own worst year.**

**The tools of accident investigation:**

| Tool | Shows |
|---|---|
| **COLLISION DIAGRAM** | **The MOVEMENTS of the vehicles involved, drawn with standard arrows — not to scale** ← |
| **CONDITION diagram** | **The physical layout to scale: geometry, signs, markings, sight lines, surface** ← |
| **Accident spot map** | **Pins on a network map, to find concentrations** ← |
| **Accident RATE** | **Per 100 million vehicle-km for a length; per million entering vehicles for a junction** ← |
| **Road safety AUDIT** | **A formal check of a DESIGN, before it is built — prevention rather than cure** ← |

> **THE ACCIDENT RATE ROW MATTERS BECAUSE IT NORMALISES FOR EXPOSURE: a road carrying ten times the traffic will have more accidents without being any more dangerous, and comparing raw counts between roads of different traffic volumes is meaningless.**

> **THE LAST ROW POINTS AT THE MORE IMPORTANT SHIFT IN PRACTICE, and it is worth ending on: black spot treatment is REACTIVE — it waits for a pattern of casualties to accumulate before acting, which means the information is bought with injuries.**

> **A road safety AUDIT examines the drawings before construction and finds the hazards that would have generated the accidents, at a cost of a few days of an independent engineer's time.**

> **The economics are overwhelming, and yet audits remain the exception while black-spot programmes are routine — largely because an accident that never happened is invisible, and nobody gets credit for it.**

examTip.trick: **Significantly more or more severe accidents than COMPARABLE locations, from three to five years of records.** One fatality does not make a black spot.
examTip.trap: **REGRESSION TO THE MEAN** — a site picked because it had a bad year improves the next year whether treated or not, so naive before-and-after studies overstate the benefit, sometimes twofold.
examTip.mnemonic: **COLLISION diagram = movements, not to scale. CONDITION diagram = physical layout, to scale.** And a road safety AUDIT is prevention: black-spot treatment buys its information with injuries.

questions.stem: In a cement concrete pavement, TIE BARS differ from DOWEL BARS in that tie bars are:
options: Plain round bars at transverse joints, permitting the slabs to slide
Placed only at the corners of every slab
DEFORMED bars across LONGITUDINAL joints, BONDED to the concrete, provided to HOLD the slabs TOGETHER rather than to transfer load
Provided in place of reinforcement in the body of the slab
questions.solution:
**Tie bars are DEFORMED bars across LONGITUDINAL joints, fully BONDED to the concrete, provided to HOLD the adjacent slabs together — not to transfer wheel load.**

**The two compared:**

| Feature | DOWEL BAR | TIE BAR |
|---|---|---|
| **Joint** | **TRANSVERSE (contraction and expansion joints)** ← | **LONGITUDINAL joints, between adjacent lanes** ← |
| **Type of bar** | **PLAIN ROUND, smooth** ← | **DEFORMED (ribbed)** ← |
| **Bond** | **DEBONDED on one side — greased, painted or capped, so it can SLIDE** ← | **Fully BONDED on both sides** ← |
| **Purpose** | **LOAD TRANSFER across the joint** ← | **To prevent the slabs SEPARATING or the joint opening; to keep the lanes tied** ← |
| **Does it carry wheel load?** | **YES — that is its whole function** ← | **NO — it is not a load transfer device** ← |
| **Typical size** | **25 to 38 mm diameter, 450 to 500 mm long, at 300 mm centres** ← | **8 to 16 mm diameter, 500 to 1,000 mm long, at 300 to 750 mm centres** ← |

> **Option (a) describes the DOWEL bar exactly, which is what makes it the effective distractor.**

> **THE ROW THAT SETTLES EVERYTHING IS THE BOND ROW, and the logic is worth following because it explains the bar type as well:**

> **A dowel MUST be free to slide, because the slab shortens and lengthens with temperature and the joint must be able to open and close. Restrain it and the slab cracks. So a dowel is smooth, and greased or capped on one side.**

> **A tie bar must NOT slide, because its whole purpose is to stop the joint from opening. So it is deformed, for maximum bond, and anchored in both slabs.**

> **Plain against deformed is therefore not an arbitrary detail — it follows directly from what each bar is for, and getting it backwards defeats both. A deformed "dowel" locks the joint and cracks the slab; a plain "tie bar" pulls out and the lanes drift apart.**

**Why longitudinal joints need tying at all:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Slabs tend to separate under traffic and thermal movement** | **Especially where the subgrade settles differentially** ← |
| **An open longitudinal joint admits WATER to the subgrade** ← | **Which is the beginning of pumping, faulting and failure** ← |
| **Load transfer across the longitudinal joint is by AGGREGATE INTERLOCK** ← | **Which only works while the joint stays tight — tie bars keep it tight** ← |
| **Untied lanes drift apart and the shoulder edge drops** | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE SUBTLE AND IMPORTANT ONE: although a tie bar does not itself transfer load, it PRESERVES the mechanism that does.**

> **The rough, interlocking faces of the crack below a sawn longitudinal joint carry shear between the slabs perfectly well — so long as the two faces stay pressed together.**

> **Let the joint open a few millimetres and the interlock is lost entirely, at which point the free edge of each slab must carry the wheel load unaided, and edge stresses in a rigid pavement are far higher than interior stresses.**

> **So the tie bar, a cheap 12 mm bar, protects the pavement from a change in its whole structural behaviour — which is a good illustration of how the small details of jointing govern the performance of rigid pavements far more than the concrete strength does.**

**The joints in a rigid pavement, for completeness:**

| Joint | Purpose | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTRACTION (transverse)** | **Controls shrinkage and thermal cracking by inducing the crack at a chosen line** ← | **Sawn to about ¼ of the depth; DOWELS** ← |
| **EXPANSION (transverse)** | **Allows thermal expansion; now used sparingly** ← | **A full-depth gap with compressible filler; DOWELS, capped one side** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL** | **Separates lanes; controls warping cracks** ← | **TIE BARS — this question** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION** | **Where a day's work ends** | Dowels or tie bars as appropriate |

> **The contraction joint's principle is one of the more satisfying ideas in pavement engineering: concrete WILL crack as it shrinks, and no amount of strength prevents it — so rather than fight it, a groove is sawn to weaken the slab along a straight line, and the crack obediently forms there, underneath a sealed joint where it does no harm.**

examTip.trick: **Dowel: PLAIN, transverse joint, DEBONDED one side, transfers LOAD. Tie bar: DEFORMED, longitudinal joint, BONDED both sides, holds slabs TOGETHER.** Option (a) describes the dowel.
examTip.trap: **Plain vs deformed follows from the function** — a dowel must slide so the joint can open; a tie bar must not. Swap them and a deformed dowel cracks the slab while a plain tie bar pulls out.
examTip.mnemonic: **A tie bar transfers no load but PRESERVES the aggregate interlock that does** — let the joint open a few mm and each slab's free edge carries the wheel alone, at far higher stress.

questions.stem: In Westergaard's analysis of stresses in a rigid pavement, the three critical positions of the wheel load are the interior, the edge and the corner. Of these, for a slab of given thickness, the position generally producing the GREATEST tensile stress in the slab is the:
options: Interior loading
CORNER loading
Edge loading, always by a wide margin
All three produce equal stress
questions.solution:
**CORNER loading** generally produces the greatest stress, with edge loading next and interior loading least.

**The three positions:**

| Position | Load located | Support available | Relative stress |
|---|---|---|---|
| **INTERIOR** | **Well away from any edge, in the body of the slab** ← | **Slab supported on ALL sides — the load spreads in every direction** ← | **LOWEST** ← |
| **EDGE** | **At the middle of a free edge** | **Support on one side only lost** ← | **Intermediate — typically 1.5 times the interior stress** ← |
| **CORNER** | **At the intersection of two free edges** ← | **Support lost on TWO sides — the corner is a cantilever in two directions** ← | **GENERALLY the HIGHEST** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION IS SIMPLY A MATTER OF HOW MUCH SLAB IS AVAILABLE TO SHARE THE LOAD, and that is the whole intuition:**
