> **A load in the interior can spread its effect radially in every direction, and a large area of slab participates in carrying it.**

> **At an edge, half of that area is missing. At a corner, three quarters of it is missing, and the load sits on a wedge of slab supported only by the subgrade beneath it.**

> **Option (c) overstates the edge case and ignores the corner; option (d) is simply false.**

**The distinguishing feature of each, which is examinable in its own right:**

| Position | Where the tension occurs | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Interior** | **At the BOTTOM of the slab, directly under the load** ← | Classic plate bending on an elastic foundation |
| **Edge** | **At the BOTTOM of the slab, at the edge under the load** ← | ← |
| **CORNER** | **At the TOP of the slab, at some distance back from the corner** ← | **The corner acts as a cantilever, so the tension is on the UPPER surface — the reverse of the other two** ← |

> **THE CORNER CASE'S REVERSED SIGN IS THE DETAIL MOST WORTH REMEMBERING, and it has a direct practical consequence: corner cracks in a concrete pavement start at the TOP surface and work downward, so they are visible early — unlike interior and edge cracks, which begin at the bottom and only appear at the surface when they have propagated right through.**

> **So a corner crack is a warning, and a mid-slab crack that has become visible is already a full-depth failure.**

**The other stresses acting, since wheel load is not the only source:**

| Stress | Cause | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **WHEEL LOAD stress** | **Traffic, at the three positions above** | ← |
| **WARPING (temperature) stress** | **A temperature DIFFERENCE between the top and bottom of the slab makes it curl; its own weight and the dowels restrain the curl** ← | **Can be comparable in magnitude to the wheel load stress** ← |
| **FRICTIONAL stress** | **Uniform temperature change causes the whole slab to expand or contract; the subgrade friction resists it** ← | **Governs the spacing of contraction joints and the design of tie bars** ← |

> **THE CRITICAL COMBINATIONS ARE THE POINT OF PUTTING THESE TOGETHER, and they are the standard examination question in this area:**

| Season and time | Combination |
|---|---|
| **SUMMER, mid-day** | **Top hotter than bottom, so the slab curls DOWN at the edges — warping tension at the BOTTOM adds to edge and interior load stress** ← |
| **WINTER, night** | **Top cooler, so the slab curls UP at the corners and edges — the corner loses its subgrade support entirely and the load stress rises** ← |

> **The winter night case is the one that most often governs the corner, and it is a genuinely nasty combination: the corner lifts clear of the subgrade, so a wheel arriving there is loading an unsupported cantilever.**

> **That is why corner breaks are the characteristic distress of rigid pavements, why the corner region is where dowels and adequate slab thickness matter most, and why a stable, non-erodible subbase — which keeps the support intact and prevents PUMPING of fines from beneath the corner — is worth as much as extra concrete.**

examTip.trick: **Interior < edge < corner** — because the load can spread in every direction at the interior, half as much at an edge, and hardly at all at a corner.
examTip.trap: **Corner tension is at the TOP of the slab; interior and edge tension is at the BOTTOM.** So corner cracks appear early at the surface, while a visible mid-slab crack is already full-depth.
examTip.mnemonic: **Winter NIGHT is the corner's worst case** — the slab curls UP, the corner loses its subgrade support, and a wheel loads an unsupported cantilever. Hence corner breaks, dowels, and a non-erodible subbase.

questions.stem: In road asset management, PERIODIC maintenance differs from ROUTINE maintenance in that periodic maintenance:
options: Is carried out only after the road has failed completely
Consists of day-to-day activities such as drain clearing and vegetation control
Is undertaken at intervals of several years to restore the pavement's condition — for example resealing or an overlay
Is the same as new construction
questions.solution:
**Periodic maintenance is undertaken at intervals of several years to RESTORE the pavement's condition — resealing, surface dressing, or a structural overlay.**

**The categories of road maintenance:**

| Category | Frequency | Typical work |
|---|---|---|
| **ROUTINE** | **Continuous or annual** ← | **Clearing side drains and culverts, cutting vegetation, patching potholes, repairing shoulders, cleaning and repairing signs, crack sealing** ← (option b) |
| **PERIODIC** | **Every 3 to 8 years** ← | **Surface dressing, resealing, thin or structural OVERLAY, regravelling an unsealed road** ← |
| **EMERGENCY / special** | **As required** | **Clearing landslides, restoring a washed-out section, repairing flood damage** ← |
| **REHABILITATION / reconstruction** | **At the end of the pavement's life** ← | **Not maintenance at all — a capital work** ← (option d) |

> **The distinction is by FREQUENCY and PURPOSE: routine maintenance PRESERVES the road's condition from day to day, and periodic maintenance RESTORES it after several years of gradual loss.**

**Why the distinction matters — the deterioration curve, which is the substance of the topic:**

| Phase | Condition | Cost to repair |
|---|---|---|
| **Years 0 to about 10** | **Slow, gradual deterioration** ← | **Low — periodic maintenance restores it cheaply** ← |
| **Beyond a threshold** | **Deterioration ACCELERATES sharply as water enters the structure** ← | **Rising steeply** ← |
| **Final phase** | **Structural failure of base and subgrade** | **RECONSTRUCTION, at several times the cost of the maintenance that would have prevented it** ← |

> **THE ACCELERATION AT THE THRESHOLD IS THE WHOLE ECONOMIC ARGUMENT FOR MAINTENANCE, and the figure usually quoted for it is striking: a rupee not spent on maintenance at the right time costs three to five rupees in rehabilitation later, and considerably more once the subgrade is affected.**

> **The mechanism is straightforward. A sealed surface keeps water out of the pavement structure. Once cracks open and the seal is lost, water enters, the base loses strength, the subgrade softens, and traffic then breaks up a structure that has lost its support.**

> **So resealing a sound pavement — which looks like spending money on a road that is not broken — is precisely the intervention with the highest return, and deferring it is one of the most expensive economies available to a road authority.**

**Why maintenance is nevertheless chronically underfunded, stated honestly:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **New construction is visible and politically rewarding; maintenance is not** ← | **Nobody opens a resealed road** ← |
| **The consequence of deferral appears years later** | **Usually under a different administration** ← |
| **Donor and development funds favour capital works** | **Maintenance is generally a domestic budget obligation** ← |
| **Maintenance budgets are the easiest line to cut in a bad year** | **With no immediate visible effect — which is exactly the trap** ← |

> **The recognised institutional remedy is a dedicated ROADS BOARD funded by a fuel levy and road user charges, held outside the annual budget negotiation, so that maintenance money cannot be diverted to construction — an arrangement Nepal has adopted, and one whose whole rationale is that maintenance loses every argument it is allowed to be part of.**

**And the drainage point, which for a hill road dominates everything else:**

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| **Clearing side drains, catch drains and culverts before the monsoon** ← | **The single highest-value maintenance activity on a Nepali hill road** ← |
| **A blocked culvert diverts a stream onto the road or into the fill** | **And a culvert costing a few thousand rupees to clear takes a road away** ← |
| **Cracks sealed before the monsoon** | **Keeps water out of the structure at the season it matters** ← |
| **Vegetation cut back from drains and sight lines** | ← |

> **THE TIMING IS THE ENGINEERING POINT AND IT IS OFTEN MISSED: this work must be completed BEFORE the monsoon, not during or after it.**

> **A drain cleared in April protects the road through the whole wet season; the same drain cleared in August is cleared after the damage has been done.**

> **So the maintenance calendar matters as much as the maintenance budget, and a road authority that spends its full allocation at the wrong time of year gets very little for it.**

examTip.trick: **ROUTINE = continuous, day-to-day (drains, vegetation, potholes). PERIODIC = every 3-8 years, restoring condition (reseal, overlay, regravel).** Option (b) is routine; option (d) is reconstruction.
examTip.trap: **Deterioration ACCELERATES once water gets into the structure** — a rupee deferred costs three to five later. Resealing a road that does not look broken is the highest-return work there is.
examTip.mnemonic: **Clear the drains BEFORE the monsoon, not during it** — April work protects the whole wet season; August work comes after the damage. The maintenance calendar matters as much as the budget.

questions.stem: In an engineering drawing, an edge that is HIDDEN behind the visible surfaces of the object is shown by:
options: A thin SHORT-DASHED line
A thick continuous line
A long chain line of alternating long dashes and dots
A thin continuous wavy line
questions.solution:
**A thin SHORT-DASHED line.**

**The standard line types and what each means:**

| Line | Appearance | Represents |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous THICK** | **A solid heavy line** ← | **VISIBLE outlines and edges** ← (option b) |
| **Continuous THIN** | A solid light line | **Dimension lines, extension lines, leaders, hatching, outlines of adjacent parts** ← |
| **Short DASHES, thin** | **- - - - -** ← | **HIDDEN edges and outlines** ← |
| **Long chain, thin (long dash-dot)** | **— · — · —** ← | **CENTRE lines, axes, pitch circles** ← (option c) |
| **Long chain, thin with THICK ends** | ← | **CUTTING PLANE for a section** ← |
| **Long chain, THICK** | ← | Surfaces requiring special treatment |
| **Continuous thin WAVY or zig-zag** | ← | **A short BREAK, or an irregular boundary** ← (option d) |
| **Long chain, thin double-dot** | **— ·· — ·· —** | **Outlines of adjacent parts, extreme positions of moveable parts, initial outlines before forming** ← |

> **THE THICKNESS IS AS MUCH PART OF THE CONVENTION AS THE DASH PATTERN, and it carries most of the information at a glance:**

> **THICK means "this is the object" — its visible outline. THIN means everything else: hidden detail, dimensions, centres, notes.**

> **A drawing in which every line is the same weight is far harder to read, even when the dash patterns are all correct, because the eye can no longer separate the object from the annotation.**

> **Two line thicknesses in the ratio of about 1 to 2 — commonly 0.35 and 0.7 mm — are all that is needed, and using them properly does more for a drawing's legibility than any other single habit.**

**The precedence rule, which resolves the common conflict:**

| Rank | Line |
|---|---|
| **1 (highest)** | **VISIBLE outline — a thick continuous line** ← |
| **2** | **HIDDEN line** ← |
| **3** | **Cutting plane line** |
| **4** | **Centre line** ← |
| **5** | Dimension and extension lines |

> **Where two lines coincide, the HIGHER-RANKED one is drawn and the other omitted at that point — so a visible edge that happens to fall on a centre line is shown as a visible edge, not as a centre line.**

**And when hidden lines should be omitted altogether, which is a matter of judgement rather than rule:**

| Situation | Practice |
|---|---|
| **In a SECTIONAL view** | **Hidden lines are normally OMITTED — the section was taken precisely to reveal the interior, and keeping them defeats the purpose** ← |
| **When they add nothing** | **A complicated object shown with every hidden edge becomes an unreadable mesh** ← |
| **When the detail is better shown by another view or an added section** | **Add the view rather than the hidden lines** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS A RULE WORTH APPLYING FIRMLY, because it is broken so often by drawing software defaults: a sectional view exists to make the interior VISIBLE, and once it is visible it is drawn with continuous lines.**

> **Leaving the hidden lines switched on in a section produces a drawing that shows the same features twice in two different conventions, which is exactly the sort of ambiguity the conventions exist to eliminate.**

> **The general principle behind all of this is worth stating, since it applies to every drawing: a drawing is a means of COMMUNICATION, not a complete record of the geometry. Anything that does not help the reader understand the object should be left off, and the test of a good drawing is whether a competent person can build from it without asking a question.**

examTip.trick: **Hidden = thin SHORT DASHES. Visible outline = THICK continuous. Centre = thin long chain (dash-dot). Break = thin wavy.** All four options name a real line type.
examTip.trap: **Precedence when lines coincide: visible > hidden > cutting plane > centre > dimension.** A visible edge falling on a centre line is drawn as a visible edge.
examTip.mnemonic: **THICK means "this is the object"; THIN means everything else.** Two weights in about 1:2 (0.35 and 0.7 mm) do more for legibility than anything else. And omit hidden lines in a SECTION — the section exists to make them visible.

questions.stem: In the ISO A series of drawing sheet sizes, an A1 sheet measures:
questions.solution:
**594 mm × 841 mm.**

**The A series:**

| Size | Dimensions (mm) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **A0** | **841 × 1189** ← | **Area exactly 1 square metre** ← (option c) |
| **A1** | **594 × 841** ← | **A0 halved across its long side** ← |
| **A2** | **420 × 594** ← (option b) | |
| **A3** | **297 × 420** ← (option a) | |
| **A4** | **210 × 297** ← | **The familiar letter size** |
| **A5** | 148 × 210 | |

> **Every wrong option is a genuine A-series size, so the sizes themselves have to be known rather than reasoned out from the shape.**

**The two rules that generate the whole series, which make it memorable:**

| Rule | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **A0 has an AREA of exactly 1 m²** ← | **Which fixes the absolute scale of the series** ← |
| **The ratio of the sides is √2 : 1 in every size** ← | **Which is what makes halving work** ← |

> **THE √2 RATIO IS THE ELEGANT PART AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT MUST BE √2:**

> **For a sheet to halve into two sheets of the SAME SHAPE, the long side must become the new short side, and the short side must become the new long side halved.**

> **So if the sides are L and S with L/S = r, then after halving the ratio is S / (L/2) = 2S/L = 2/r. For the shape to be unchanged, r = 2/r, hence r² = 2 and r = √2.**

> **Checking: 1189 / 841 = 1.4137, and √2 = 1.4142. Exact but for the rounding to whole millimetres.**

> **The practical consequence is the one everybody uses without thinking about it: any A-size document photocopies onto any other A size with NO change of shape and no wasted margin — an A3 drawing reduces exactly onto A4 at 71 per cent, which is 1/√2.**

**Practical points for drawing sheets:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A BORDER is left inside the trimmed edge** | **Typically 20 mm on the binding (left) edge and 10 mm on the others** ← |
| **A TITLE BLOCK in the bottom right corner** ← | **Title, drawing number, scale, projection symbol, date, revision, and the names of the drawer, checker and approver** ← |
| **A REVISION table** | **Every issued change recorded with its date and reason** ← |
| **The scale stated, and "NOT TO SCALE" marked where it does not apply** | ← |
| **The PROJECTION SYMBOL — the truncated cone** | **Declaring first or third angle, which otherwise must be guessed** ← |

> **THE TITLE BLOCK'S SIGNATURE ROW IS NOT A FORMALITY, and it is worth ending on because it connects the drawing to professional practice:**

> **The names of the person who prepared the drawing, the person who checked it and the person who approved it are a record of RESPONSIBILITY, and in a dispute or an investigation they are the first thing examined.**

> **An approved drawing carries the professional weight of whoever signed it, which is precisely why signing a drawing one has not actually checked is a serious matter rather than a clerical shortcut.**

> **The revision table serves the same function over time: it establishes what was issued, when, and to whom — so that a structure built to revision B cannot later be judged against revision D.**

examTip.trick: **A0 = 841 × 1189, then halve the long side each time: A1 = 594 × 841, A2 = 420 × 594, A3 = 297 × 420, A4 = 210 × 297.** Every distractor is a real A size.
examTip.trap: **A0 has an area of exactly 1 m², and every sheet has sides in the ratio √2 : 1** — the only ratio under which halving preserves the shape, since r = 2/r gives r = √2.
examTip.mnemonic: **A3 reduces onto A4 at 71 % = 1/√2, with no wasted margin.** And the title block's prepared/checked/approved names are a record of RESPONSIBILITY — the first thing examined in a dispute.

questions.stem: A piece of construction plant costs Rs 5,00,000, has an estimated salvage value of Rs 50,000 and a useful life of 10 years. By the STRAIGHT LINE method, the annual depreciation charge is:
questions.solution:
**Rs 45,000 per year.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Straight line depreciation** | **D = (First cost − Salvage value) ÷ Useful life** ← |
| **Substituting** | **D = (5,00,000 − 50,000) / 10** |
| **Numerator** | **= 4,50,000, the total amount to be written off** ← |
| **Annual charge** | **= Rs 45,000** ← |

> **Option (c) Rs 50,000 forgets to deduct the salvage value — the commonest error, and it writes off Rs 5,00,000 over the life, leaving the book value at zero when the machine is in fact worth Rs 50,000.**

> **Option (d) Rs 55,000 ADDS the salvage value instead of subtracting it.**

**The book value year by year, which shows what "straight line" means:**

| End of year | Book value |
|---|---|
| 0 | **Rs 5,00,000** |
| 1 | Rs 4,55,000 |
| 5 | **Rs 2,75,000** |
| 9 | Rs 95,000 |
| **10** | **Rs 50,000 — exactly the salvage value** ← |

> **The book value falls by the same amount every year, which is what gives the method its name and its single great virtue: it is simple, predictable and easy to check.**

**The methods compared, since the choice materially changes the early years:**

| Method | Formula | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT LINE** | **D = (P − S) / n** ← | **Equal charge every year — simple, and the usual default** ← |
| **DECLINING BALANCE** | **D_t = k × (book value at start of year t)** ← | **ACCELERATED — a large charge early, small later** ← |
| **SUM OF YEARS' DIGITS** | **D_t = (P − S) × (remaining life) / (sum of digits)** ← | **Also accelerated, but linearly declining** ← |
| **SINKING FUND** | **A fund earning interest accumulates to (P − S)** ← | **DECELERATED — small charge early, large later** ← |
| **PRODUCTION (service output) units** | **D per unit of output or per hour run** ← | **Charge follows USE rather than time — the most realistic for construction plant** ← |

> **THE ACCELERATED METHODS ARE PREFERRED BY OWNERS FOR A REASON WORTH UNDERSTANDING, and it is a tax reason rather than an accounting one:**

> **Depreciation is a deductible expense, so a large charge early means less tax paid early, and money not paid this year is worth more than money not paid in eight years' time.**

> **The total depreciation over the asset's life is identical under every method — only its TIMING differs — but because of the time value of money, the timing is worth real money.**

> **That is why tax authorities specify which methods and rates are allowable rather than leaving the choice open, and why the depreciation used for tax often differs from the depreciation used in the company's own accounts.**

> **THE PRODUCTION UNITS METHOD IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE MOST DEFENSIBLE FOR CONSTRUCTION PLANT, and it is under-used:**

> **An excavator does not wear out with the calendar; it wears out with hours worked. A machine idle for two years has lost very little except its market value, while one worked double shifts has lost a great deal.**

> **So charging depreciation per operating hour gives a truer cost of owning and operating the machine, which is exactly the figure needed when building up a rate for an item of work — and using a time-based charge instead systematically understates the cost of intensively used plant and overstates the cost of plant standing idle.**

examTip.trick: **D = (P − S)/n = (5,00,000 − 50,000)/10 = Rs 45,000.** Option (c) forgets the salvage deduction; option (d) adds it instead.
examTip.trap: **Total depreciation is the SAME under every method — only the TIMING differs.** Accelerated methods are preferred because tax deferred is money earned, not because the asset really loses value faster.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plant wears out by HOURS, not by the calendar** — the production-units method gives the truest owning-and-operating cost for building up a rate, and time-based charges understate intensively used plant.

questions.stem: In engineering economic analysis, a SUNK COST is:
options: The cost of foundations and other below-ground work
The lowest cost among the alternatives being compared
A cost already incurred that CANNOT be recovered, and which is therefore IRRELEVANT to a decision between future alternatives
The cost of an asset at the end of its useful life
questions.solution:
**A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered, and which is therefore IRRELEVANT to any decision about the future.**

**The principle:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The money is already spent and cannot be got back** ← | **Whatever is decided now** |
| **It will be the same under EVERY alternative** ← | **So it cannot distinguish between them** ← |
| **Only FUTURE cash flows differ between alternatives** ← | **And only differences are relevant to a choice** ← |
| **Therefore a sunk cost is excluded from the analysis entirely** | ← |

> **Option (a) plays on the word "sunk" in its civil engineering sense, which is exactly the trap the term invites; option (d) describes salvage value.**

**Why this is so hard to accept in practice — the SUNK COST FALLACY:**

| The reasoning that feels right | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| **"We have already spent Rs 4 crore on this design; we cannot abandon it now"** ← | **The Rs 4 crore is gone whether you continue or stop — it is not an argument for continuing** ← |
| **"Stopping would waste everything spent so far"** | **The waste already happened; continuing merely adds to it if the project is not worth completing** ← |
| **"We must finish what we started"** | **The only question is whether the REMAINING cost is justified by the REMAINING benefit** ← |

> **THE CORRECT QUESTION IS ALWAYS THE SAME AND IT IS WORTH FIXING IN MIND: given where we are NOW, is the money still to be spent worth the benefit still to be gained?**

> **The past does not enter into it. A project that would not be started today, on the basis of its remaining cost and remaining benefit, should not be continued today either — and the amount already spent is not a reason to differ.**

> **This is genuinely counter-intuitive and is resisted for reasons that are human rather than economic: abandoning a project means admitting that the earlier spending was a mistake, and continuing defers that admission. The fallacy is therefore about accountability as much as arithmetic, which is why it persists among people who understand the theory perfectly well.**

**The related concepts, which are the ones that ARE relevant:**

| Concept | Definition | Relevant? |
|---|---|---|
| **SUNK cost** | **Already incurred, unrecoverable** | **NO** ← |
| **OPPORTUNITY cost** | **The benefit forgone by not choosing the next best alternative** ← | **YES — and it is often omitted, which is the mirror-image error** ← |
| **INCREMENTAL (differential) cost** | **The difference in cost between alternatives** ← | **YES — the only thing that matters** ← |
| **MARGINAL cost** | **The cost of one more unit** | YES |
| **Salvage value** | **The recoverable value at the end of life** | **YES — it is a future cash flow** ← |

> **THE OPPORTUNITY COST ROW IS THE COMPLEMENT TO THE SUNK COST AND EQUALLY OFTEN MISHANDLED, in the opposite direction:**

> **A sunk cost is counted when it should not be; an opportunity cost is ignored when it should be counted.**

> **Land the organisation already owns is the standard example. It is treated as free because no cheque is written for it — but it could have been sold or used for something else, so its market value is a genuine cost of using it here.**

> **A project appraisal that charges nothing for land the client already holds systematically favours land-hungry solutions, and it is a common and consequential error in public sector appraisals.**

> **The two errors together produce a characteristic pattern: organisations persist with failing projects because of what they have spent, and choose wasteful options because they undervalue what they already own.**

examTip.trick: **Already incurred, unrecoverable, identical under every alternative — therefore irrelevant.** Only FUTURE cash flows that DIFFER between alternatives matter. Option (a) plays on the civil engineering sense of "sunk".
examTip.trap: **"We have spent too much to stop now" is the fallacy** — the correct question is whether the REMAINING cost is justified by the REMAINING benefit. The past does not enter into it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sunk cost is counted when it shouldn't be; OPPORTUNITY cost is ignored when it should be counted.** Land already owned is not free — charging nothing for it favours land-hungry designs.

questions.stem: In network analysis, the FREE FLOAT of an activity differs from its TOTAL FLOAT in that free float is the delay that can be absorbed:
options: Without delaying the EARLY START of any SUCCEEDING activity
Without delaying the project completion date
Only on the critical path
Without increasing the direct cost of the activity
questions.solution:
**Without delaying the EARLY START of any succeeding activity.**

**The float types compared:**

| Float | Definition | Delay affects |
|---|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | **LS − ES, or LF − EF** ← | **Delaying by more than this delays the PROJECT** ← (option b, which defines total float) |
| **FREE float** | **(Earliest start of the following activity) − EF of this activity** ← | **Delaying by more than this delays a SUCCESSOR's early start — but may still not delay the project** ← |
| **INDEPENDENT float** | **The float available if all predecessors finish as LATE as possible and all successors start as EARLY as possible** ← | **The float that belongs to the activity alone, borrowed from nobody** ← |
| **INTERFERING float** | **Total float − free float** | **The part of the float that, if used, pushes successors later** ← |

> **THE RELATIONSHIP THAT MATTERS: free float ≤ total float, always.**

> **Total float is shared along a chain of activities — if the first activity in a non-critical chain consumes all of it, none is left for the others.**

> **Free float belongs to the individual activity and can be used without affecting anybody else at all.**

> **So free float is the float a planner can spend freely, and total float is the float that must be spent with the whole chain in mind — which is exactly why both are computed and reported rather than only the larger one.**

**Why the distinction is practically important:**

| Situation | Which float to use |
|---|---|
| **Deciding whether an activity's delay threatens the completion date** | **TOTAL float** ← |
| **Deciding whether a delay will disturb the plans of the following trades** | **FREE float** ← |
| **Resource SMOOTHING — shifting activities to even out labour demand** | **Free float first, since it disturbs nothing; then total float, with care** ← |
| **Assessing a contractor's claim for an extension of time** | **TOTAL float — and WHO OWNS it is often the whole dispute** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW OPENS A GENUINELY CONTENTIOUS QUESTION IN CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS, and it is worth knowing that it is contentious:**

> **If an activity has ten days of total float and the employer causes a five-day delay to it, has the contractor suffered a compensable delay? The project completion is unaffected — but the contractor's cushion against its OWN future problems has been consumed.**

> **Different contract forms and jurisdictions answer this differently: some hold that float belongs to the PROJECT and is available to whoever needs it first; others that it belongs to the CONTRACTOR, who planned it.**

> **Modern practice increasingly writes the answer explicitly into the contract, precisely because leaving it to be argued afterwards is expensive — which is a good illustration of the general rule that the questions worth settling in advance are the ones on which reasonable people disagree.**

**A worked illustration, since the definitions are abstract:**

| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Successor's ES | Total float | Free float |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **B** | **5** | **10** | **8** | **13** | **12** | **LS − ES = 3** ← | **12 − 10 = 2** ← |

> **So activity B may be delayed by 3 days without affecting the project, but only by 2 days without pushing its successor's earliest start.**

> **The third day of total float is INTERFERING float: using it delays the successor, though the successor's own float absorbs the delay and the project still finishes on time.**

> **That is the whole distinction in one line, and it explains why a site manager who shifts an activity "within its float" can still find the following trade complaining — the float used was total, and the free float was less.**

examTip.trick: **Total float = LS − ES: delay beyond it delays the PROJECT. Free float = successor's ES − this activity's EF: delay beyond it disturbs the SUCCESSOR.** Free float ≤ total float, always.
examTip.trap: **Total float is SHARED along a chain; free float belongs to the activity alone.** If the first activity in a non-critical chain uses all the total float, none is left for the rest.
examTip.mnemonic: **Who OWNS the float is a live contractual dispute** — the project's, or the contractor's who planned it? Modern contracts say so explicitly, because arguing it afterwards is expensive.

questions.stem: The essential difference between PERT and CPM is that:
options: PERT uses activity-on-node networks and CPM uses activity-on-arrow
CPM can only be used for construction and PERT only for manufacturing
PERT requires a computer and CPM does not
PERT is PROBABILISTIC, using three time estimates per activity, while CPM is DETERMINISTIC, using a single time estimate and allowing time-cost trade-off
questions.solution:
**PERT is PROBABILISTIC — three time estimates per activity — while CPM is DETERMINISTIC, with one time estimate, and adds the time-cost trade-off.**

**The comparison:**

| Aspect | PERT | CPM |
|---|---|---|
| **Time estimate** | **THREE: optimistic (t_o), most likely (t_m), pessimistic (t_p)** ← | **ONE, deterministic** ← |
| **Expected duration** | **t_e = (t_o + 4 t_m + t_p) / 6** ← | The single estimate |
| **Variance** | **σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²** ← | **Not applicable** |
| **Orientation** | **EVENT-oriented** ← | **ACTIVITY-oriented** ← |
| **Developed for** | **R&D and one-off projects, where durations are UNCERTAIN — originally the Polaris programme** ← | **Repetitive construction and maintenance work, where durations are KNOWN — originally by DuPont** ← |
| **Cost** | **Not originally part of it** | **Explicit TIME-COST TRADE-OFF — crashing** ← |
| **Answers** | **"What is the PROBABILITY of finishing by a given date?"** ← | **"What does it cost to finish by a given date?"** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW CAPTURES THE PRACTICAL DIFFERENCE BETTER THAN ANY OTHER, and it is the answer to give if asked to distinguish them in one sentence.**

> **Options (a) and (c) are false — either network form can be used with either technique, and both were done by hand long before computers.**

**What PERT's probability calculation actually gives:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Compute t_e for every activity** | **The weighted average, giving the most likely time four times the weight of the extremes** ← |
| **Find the critical path using the t_e values** | ← |
| **Sum the VARIANCES of the critical activities only** ← | **Variances add; standard deviations do not** ← |
| **σ_project = √(sum of critical variances)** ← | ← |
| **Z = (target date − expected date) / σ_project** ← | **And read the probability from the standard normal table** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG IN EXAMINATIONS: you add the VARIANCES of the critical activities and then take the square root — you never add the standard deviations.**

**The limitations of PERT, which are real and worth knowing:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Only the critical path's variance is counted** ← | **A near-critical path with high variance can easily become critical, and PERT's calculation ignores it — so PERT is OPTIMISTIC about the completion date** ← |
| **The three estimates are themselves guesses** | **And people are systematically poor at estimating the pessimistic case** ← |
| **The beta distribution assumption is a convenience** | **Not derived from evidence** |
| **The normal approximation needs enough activities on the path** | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT CRITICISM AND IT IS A STRUCTURAL ONE, not a matter of poor practice:**

> **A project may have one critical path of 100 days with low variance, and three other paths of 95 days each with high variance. PERT reports the probability of finishing in 100 days using only the first path — but the project finishes when the LAST path finishes, and with three other paths that could easily overrun, the true probability is considerably lower.**

> **This is called the MERGE EVENT BIAS, and its effect is that PERT consistently understates the expected completion time.**

> **The honest remedy is MONTE CARLO simulation, which samples every activity's duration repeatedly and lets whichever path happens to be longest govern each run — giving a distribution of completion dates that accounts for all the paths.**

> **That is now the standard approach in serious risk analysis, and PERT survives mainly as a teaching device and as a simple approximation — which is a fair description of its status, and worth saying rather than presenting it as current best practice.**

examTip.trick: **PERT: three estimates, probabilistic, EVENT-oriented, for uncertain one-off work. CPM: one estimate, deterministic, ACTIVITY-oriented, with time-cost trade-off.** Options (a) and (c) are simply false.
examTip.trap: **Add the VARIANCES of the critical activities, then take the square root** — never add standard deviations. σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]².
examTip.mnemonic: **MERGE EVENT BIAS: PERT counts only the critical path's variance, so near-critical paths that could overrun are ignored** — it therefore understates the completion time systematically. Monte Carlo is the honest fix.

questions.stem: In a construction contract, a PERFORMANCE SECURITY (performance bond) differs from the BID SECURITY (earnest money) in that the performance security is:
options: Submitted by all bidders with their tenders
Furnished by the SUCCESSFUL bidder on award, as a guarantee that the works will be completed according to the contract, and is typically a larger percentage of the contract price
Deducted from each running bill as the work proceeds
Paid by the employer to the contractor before work starts
questions.solution:
**It is furnished by the SUCCESSFUL bidder on award of the contract, guaranteeing performance of the works, and is a substantially larger percentage than the bid security.**

**The securities in a construction contract:**

| Security | When furnished | Typical amount | Guards against |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BID SECURITY (earnest money)** | **With the TENDER, by every bidder** ← (option a) | **1 to 3 per cent of the estimated cost** ← | **A bidder withdrawing during validity, or refusing to sign the contract if awarded** ← |
| **PERFORMANCE SECURITY** | **On AWARD, by the successful bidder only** ← | **5 to 10 per cent of the contract price** ← | **Failure to complete the works to the contract's requirements** ← |
| **RETENTION money** | **DEDUCTED from each running bill** ← (option c) | **5 to 10 per cent of each bill, capped** ← | **Defects appearing after completion** ← |
| **ADVANCE payment guarantee** | **When a mobilisation advance is paid** ← | **Equal to the advance** ← | **The advance not being repaid or earned** ← |
| **Defect liability / warranty security** | **Retention released against it at completion** | Half the retention | Defects in the liability period |

> **The four are for four different risks at four different stages, and none substitutes for another — which is why a contract has all of them rather than one large one.**

> **Option (d) describes the mobilisation ADVANCE, which flows the other way, and is precisely what the advance payment guarantee secures.**

**Why the amounts differ so much, which is the logic behind the whole arrangement:**

| Security | Size of the risk it covers |
|---|---|
| **Bid security at 1-3 %** | **The loss if a bidder withdraws is the cost of re-tendering and the difference against the next lowest bid — real, but limited** ← |
| **Performance security at 5-10 %** | **The loss if a contractor abandons the works part-built is very much greater: re-tendering, remobilisation, a higher price from a contractor taking over a part-finished job, and the delay** ← |

> **The proportions are not arbitrary; they track the size of the loss the employer would actually suffer, which is the correct basis for sizing any security.**

> **THE TAKING-OVER PROBLEM IN THE SECOND ROW IS WORTH DWELLING ON because it explains why 10 per cent is often not enough:**

> **A contractor who abandons a half-built structure leaves an employer in a weak position. The new contractor must accept responsibility for work it did not do and cannot fully inspect, so it prices the risk high, and the remaining work commonly costs far more than the original balance.**

> **A performance security of 10 per cent may therefore cover only part of the real loss, which is why prequalification — satisfying yourself of the contractor's capability and financial standing BEFORE the tender — is worth more than any security.**

> **The security is a remedy after failure; prequalification is an attempt to prevent it, and the second is nearly always the better investment.**

**The forms a security may take:**

| Form | Note |
|---|---|
| **UNCONDITIONAL (on-demand) BANK GUARANTEE** ← | **The bank pays on the employer's written demand, without proof of default — strong for the employer, harsh for the contractor** ← |
| **Conditional bond (surety bond)** | **Payable only on proof of default — commoner in some jurisdictions** ← |
| **Cash deposit** | Ties up the contractor's working capital |
| **Government bonds or securities** | Sometimes accepted |

> **THE FIRST ROW CONTAINS A REAL HAZARD FOR CONTRACTORS AND IS WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: an unconditional guarantee can be called even where the contractor disputes that any default has occurred.**

> **The bank must pay, and the contractor is left to recover the money afterwards through arbitration or litigation — having lost both the cash and the negotiating position.**

> **That is why the validity period, the wording, and the conditions for release of a performance guarantee are negotiated carefully rather than accepted as boilerplate, and why an expired guarantee left uncancelled on a bank's books is a live liability rather than a piece of old paperwork.**

examTip.trick: **Bid security: with the tender, from everyone, 1-3 %. Performance security: on award, from the winner, 5-10 %.** Option (c) is retention money, option (d) the mobilisation advance.
examTip.trap: **The percentages track the SIZE of the loss** — a withdrawn bid costs a re-tender; an abandoned half-built works costs remobilisation, a risk premium from the replacement contractor, and the delay.
examTip.mnemonic: **PREQUALIFICATION beats any security** — the bond is a remedy after failure, prequalification an attempt to prevent it. And an UNCONDITIONAL guarantee pays on demand, without proof of default.

questions.stem: A VARIATION ORDER issued under a construction contract is:
options: A notice terminating the contract
A revision of the contractor's programme requested by the contractor
A written INSTRUCTION from the employer or engineer altering the scope, quantity, quality or sequence of the works, valued under the contract's rules
A penalty imposed for late completion
questions.solution:
**A written INSTRUCTION from the employer or the engineer that alters the scope, quantity, quality, timing or sequence of the works, and which is valued according to the rules the contract lays down.**

**What may be varied:**

| Variation | Example |
|---|---|
| **A change in QUANTITY of an item** | **More or less excavation than the bill provided for** ← |
| **A change in QUALITY or specification** | **A higher grade of concrete; a different finish** ← |
| **A change in LEVELS, lines, position or dimensions** | ← |
| **OMISSION of work** | **A variation too — and one the contractor may resist, since it removes earned overheads** ← |
| **ADDITIONAL work necessary for completion** | ← |
| **A change in the SEQUENCE or timing of construction** | **Which may cost a great deal without changing a single quantity** ← |

> **Option (d) describes LIQUIDATED DAMAGES and option (a) termination — both real contractual mechanisms, neither a variation.**

**How a variation is VALUED, which is the part that generates disputes:**

| Situation | Basis of valuation |
|---|---|
| **Work of the SAME character and conditions as a billed item** | **The BILL RATE applies directly** ← |
| **Similar work, but under different conditions or quantity** | **The bill rate used as the BASIS, suitably adjusted — a "pro-rata" or "star" rate** ← |
| **Work of a wholly different character** | **A NEW rate agreed between the parties, built up from first principles** ← |
| **Where no rate can be agreed** | **DAYWORK — actual labour, plant and materials, plus a percentage** ← |
| **A large change in QUANTITY of an existing item** | **May justify re-rating, because the contractor's fixed costs are spread differently** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A POINT CONTRACTORS RAISE OFTEN AND EMPLOYERS RESIST, and both have a case worth understanding:**

> **A rate quoted for 1,000 m³ of excavation includes a share of mobilising the plant. If the quantity falls to 100 m³, the same mobilisation is spread over a tenth of the work, and the original rate no longer covers it.**

> **Conversely if the quantity rises tenfold, the contractor recovers the fixed element ten times over.**

> **Most standard contracts therefore allow re-rating when a quantity changes beyond a stated threshold, and the argument is then about the threshold and the adjustment rather than about the principle.**

**Why variations must be in WRITING and instructed before the work is done:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **An oral instruction is disputed later, and memories differ** ← | **The contractor says it was instructed; the engineer says it was suggested** ← |
| **The contract requires it, and payment may be refused without it** ← | **A contractor who does extra work on a verbal instruction may find it unpayable** ← |
| **It records WHO authorised the change and on what authority** | **The engineer's authority to vary is limited by the contract, and beyond that limit the employer's approval is needed** ← |
| **It fixes the time and cost consequences while they can still be assessed** | **Rather than months later, from records that no longer exist** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A TRAP THAT CATCHES CONTRACTORS REPEATEDLY, and the safeguard is standard practice worth knowing: where an oral instruction is given and the contractor is unwilling to delay, the contractor confirms it IN WRITING to the engineer within a stated period, and it becomes a valid instruction unless the engineer contradicts it.**

> **That mechanism exists in most standard forms precisely because site work cannot always wait for paperwork, and it protects both parties — the contractor's payment, and the engineer's record of what was actually authorised.**

> **The wider lesson is one that applies to the whole of contract administration: the contemporaneous WRITTEN record is what determines the outcome of a dispute, not what actually happened. An engineer who instructs well but records badly will lose arguments they should win, and site diaries, instruction books and photographs are professional tools rather than clerical burdens.**

examTip.trick: **A written instruction altering scope, quantity, quality, timing or sequence — valued by the contract's rules.** OMISSION of work is a variation too. Options (a) and (d) are termination and liquidated damages.
examTip.trap: **Valuation ladder: bill rate → adjusted (star) rate → newly built-up rate → daywork.** A large change in quantity can justify re-rating, because fixed costs are spread differently.
examTip.mnemonic: **Confirm an oral instruction IN WRITING within the stated period, or it may be unpayable.** The contemporaneous written record decides disputes, not what actually happened — site diaries are professional tools.

questions.stem: A civil engineer with no experience of geotechnical design is asked by a long-standing client to design the foundations for a high-rise building on soft soil. Under the codes of professional conduct, the engineer should:
options: DECLINE, or accept only in association with a qualified geotechnical specialist, since an engineer must practise only within their area of COMPETENCE
Accept, since a registered engineer is legally entitled to sign any civil engineering design
Accept and follow a textbook example closely
Accept, and disclaim liability for the foundation design in the contract
questions.solution:
**Decline, or accept only in association with a qualified geotechnical specialist** — an engineer must practise only within their area of COMPETENCE.

**The rule and its basis:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Every code of ethics contains a COMPETENCE clause** ← | **"Engineers shall perform services only in areas of their competence"** ← |
| **Competence means education, training AND experience** ← | **A degree is a foundation, not a qualification in every specialism** ← |
| **The remedy is not to refuse all unfamiliar work** | **It is to ASSOCIATE with, or be supervised by, someone competent — and to say so openly** ← |
| **Registration permits practice; it does not certify competence in every field** ← | **Which disposes of option (b)** ← |

> **OPTION (B) STATES A GENUINE MISCONCEPTION AND IT IS WORTH ADDRESSING DIRECTLY: a license to practise is a minimum threshold, not a warrant of universal expertise.**

> **A doctor is licensed to practise medicine and would not perform neurosurgery on that basis. The engineering position is exactly the same, and the fact that the law may not stop you is not the question the code is asking.**

> **Option (d) is worse than useless: a disclaimer does not remove a professional's duty of care to those affected by the work, and it certainly does not protect the occupants of the building.**

> **Option (c) is the most dangerous of all, because it feels responsible — but following a textbook example requires the judgement to know when the example applies, and that judgement IS the competence being tested. Soft soil under a high-rise is precisely the case where the standard example does not transfer.**

**Why competence matters most in exactly this case:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **Soft soil foundation design is among the most JUDGEMENT-DEPENDENT areas of civil engineering** ← | **Site investigation interpretation, settlement prediction, negative skin friction, construction effects on neighbours** ← |
| **The consequence of error is CATASTROPHIC and often not immediately visible** | **Differential settlement appears over years** ← |
| **It cannot be inspected or corrected afterwards** | **The foundation is buried under the building it supports** ← |
| **Seismic performance depends on it heavily** | **Liquefaction, soil-structure interaction, site amplification — highly relevant in Nepal** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ARGUMENT THAT SHOULD SETTLE ANY HESITATION: most engineering errors can be found and put right. A foundation error cannot.**

> **The work is covered by the structure within weeks, and the defect declares itself years later as cracking and tilting, by which time remediation may cost more than the building.**

> **Irreversibility raises the standard of care required, and that is a general principle worth carrying beyond this question: the less correctable a decision is, the more competence it demands before it is made.**

**How the engineer should actually handle it, since "decline" is rarely the whole answer:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Tell the client honestly what one can and cannot do** ← | **Clients generally respect this; the relationship survives it far better than a failure would** ← |
| **Propose ASSOCIATION with a geotechnical specialist** | **The engineer may still lead the project and coordinate the design** ← |
| **Ensure the specialist's scope, responsibility and fee are properly defined** | **Vague sub-consultant scopes cause the gaps that failures fall into** ← |
| **Take responsibility for the parts one IS competent in** | ← |
| **Treat it as a reason to acquire the competence** | **Through supervised experience, not by practising on a live project unsupervised** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WORTH EMPHASISING BECAUSE THE FEAR OF LOSING THE CLIENT IS WHAT DRIVES MOST BREACHES OF THIS RULE, and the fear is largely misplaced.**

> **A client told plainly "this needs a specialist, and I will bring one in and coordinate them" receives a professional service and generally values it.**

> **A client whose building settles receives a lawsuit, and the engineer's career does not recover from it. The commercial calculation and the ethical one point the same way, which is true more often in professional practice than cynicism suggests.**

examTip.trick: **Practise only within your COMPETENCE — education, training AND experience.** The remedy is association with a specialist, not blanket refusal. Registration permits practice; it does not certify expertise in every field.
examTip.trap: **A DISCLAIMER does not remove a professional's duty of care**, and following a textbook example requires the very judgement being tested — soft soil under a high-rise is exactly where the standard case fails to transfer.
examTip.mnemonic: **A foundation error cannot be inspected or corrected — it is buried under the building.** The less correctable a decision, the more competence it demands. And the commercial and ethical calculations point the same way.

questions.stem: Under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, a FOREIGN NATIONAL engineer engaged on a specific project in Nepal may practise:
options: Freely, without any registration, provided the employer is a foreign firm
Only after obtaining full permanent registration on the same terms as a Nepali citizen
Not at all, under any circumstances
Under a TEMPORARY registration granted for the period and the specific work concerned
questions.solution:
**Under a TEMPORARY registration, granted for the specific project and limited to its duration.**

**The categories of registration maintained by the Council:**

| Category | Who | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **REGISTERED ENGINEER (general)** | **A Nepali citizen holding a recognised engineering degree** ← | **The ordinary category, entitling the holder to practise** ← |
| **PROFESSIONAL ENGINEER** | **A registered engineer with the prescribed further experience and qualification** ← | **A higher grade, recognising established practice** ← |
| **TEMPORARY registration** | **A FOREIGN national engaged on a particular project** ← | **Valid for that work and that period only; it lapses with the project** ← |

> **Option (a) is a common and mistaken assumption — the employer's nationality is irrelevant, since it is PRACTISING in Nepal that requires registration, not being employed by a Nepali firm.**

> **Option (b) is wrong because permanent registration is tied to citizenship and to recognised qualifications, and requiring it would make ordinary international project work impossible.**

> **Option (c) overstates the restriction: a country importing large infrastructure projects necessarily imports engineers with them, and the framework accommodates that.**

**Why a temporary category exists at all — the balance it strikes:**

| Objective | How temporary registration serves it |
|---|---|
| **Bring in expertise Nepal needs** ← | **Specialist tunnelling, large dam design, long-span bridges — capabilities not always available domestically** ← |
| **Keep foreign practitioners within the Council's DISCIPLINARY reach** ← | **A registered person is accountable to the Council; an unregistered one is not** ← |
| **Protect the domestic profession from open-ended competition** | **The registration is tied to a specific project and lapses with it** ← |
| **Maintain a record of who is practising in the country** | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE POINT MOST OFTEN MISSED AND IT IS THE STRONGEST JUSTIFICATION FOR THE REQUIREMENT: registration is not primarily a barrier to entry, it is the mechanism of ACCOUNTABILITY.**

> **An engineer on the register can be investigated, reprimanded, suspended or struck off. An engineer practising outside the register cannot be reached by any of that — the Council has no jurisdiction over a person it has not registered.**

> **So requiring temporary registration is what brings a visiting specialist within the same professional discipline as everyone else practising in the country, and that protects the public rather than the profession.**

**The Council's functions, to place this one:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGISTER engineers and maintain the register** ← | **Including the categories above** |
| **RECOGNISE academic qualifications and accredit institutions** ← | **Determining which degrees qualify for registration** ← |
| **Prescribe and enforce the CODE OF ETHICS** ← | **And take disciplinary action for its breach** ← |
| **Grant the LICENSE to practise, and to renew it** ← | ← |
| **Advise government on engineering education and practice** | ← |
| **It does NOT execute works, employ engineers or fix fees** ← | **A regulator, not a professional association or an employer** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE DISTINCTION MOST OFTEN CONFUSED IN EXAMINATIONS, and it is a real one: a regulatory COUNCIL exists to protect the PUBLIC, and a professional ASSOCIATION or society exists to serve its MEMBERS.**

> **The Nepal Engineering Council is the former — a statutory regulator. A body such as the Nepal Engineers' Association is the latter — a voluntary membership organisation.**

> **The two do quite different things, and the distinction matters when the interests diverge: a regulator that acted to protect its registrants' livelihoods rather than the public would have abandoned its purpose, and the separation of the two roles into two bodies exists precisely so that neither has to serve both masters.**

> **Which is a fitting note to end a paper on, because it states in institutional form the principle that runs through the whole of professional practice: the engineer's paramount duty is to the safety and welfare of the public, and every other obligation — to the client, the employer and the profession — is subordinate to it.**

examTip.trick: **Three categories: Registered Engineer (Nepali citizen, recognised degree), Professional Engineer (further experience), and TEMPORARY registration for a foreign national on a specific project.**
examTip.trap: **The employer's nationality is irrelevant** — it is PRACTISING in Nepal that triggers the requirement, not who pays the salary.
examTip.mnemonic: **Registration is an ACCOUNTABILITY mechanism, not a barrier** — the Council has no jurisdiction over someone it has not registered. And a COUNCIL protects the public; an ASSOCIATION serves its members.
